en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
*Saddanīti-pakaraṇa*: The Garland of Grammatical Roots.
15. The Chapter on Consonants (Saravagga), Section Five: The Element of Pure Sound (Suddhassaradhātu).

From here onwards, however, [the elements] will be treated according to their consonantal order, beginning with the letter *ka*, as well as the various elements derived from the primary elements (*dhātu*) and the material phenomena (*rūpa*) produced by those elements.
Having examined the method according to my ability within the Piṭaka together with its commentaries and the word of the Victor, I shall speak in brief.

Regarding the sense of "going" (*gati*): for those verbal roots whose meaning is "going," their meaning is also "understanding" (*buddhi*), and also "reaching a state of occurrence" (*pavatti-pāpuṇana*). Therein—
Going is twofold: bodily going and cognitive going. Among these, bodily going refers to movement by way of the postures (*iriyāpatha*), while cognitive going refers to the arising of knowledge.

Therefore, according to the specific application, the word "goes" (*gacchati*) can also have the meaning "knows," it can have the meaning "occurs," and it can have the meaning "reaches," depending on whether it refers to movement by way of the postures...
The meaning "goes" also occurs; the meaning "goes by means of the movement of knowledge" also occurs.

For instance, in such expressions as "he goes quickly," the term "going" refers to the movement of the bodily posture (*iriyāpatha*). In the phrase "gone to the beautiful Nibbāna," it refers to the movement of the body;

however, in "one who possesses going" (*gatimā*), etc., it refers to the movement of knowledge. Thus, the meaning of all verbal roots (*dhātu*) having the sense of "going" should be understood according to their respective application.
For this [root], these forms occur: *iti*, *eti*, *udeti*. In the causative, the form *udāyati* occurs;
the meaning is "he causes to arise," with the letter *d* being an augment (*āgama*). [Other forms include:
*upati*, *samupati*, *veti*, *apeti*, *aveti*, *anveti*, *sameti*, *abhisameti*, *samaya*, *abhisamaya*, *īdi*, *udi*, *ekodi*, *paṇḍita*, *ito*, *udito*, *upeto*, *samupeto*, *anvito*.
*Apeta*, *sameta*, *etabba*, *paccetabba*, *paṭiyamāna*, *paṭicca*, *enta*, *adhippeto*, *adhippāyo*, *paccayo*;
other [forms] should also be applied accordingly. By means of "itā," "ita," and so forth, they should be applied as appropriate according to the feminine and neuter genders.
*Paccetuṃ*, *upetuṃ*, *samupetuṃ*, *anvetuṃ*, *sametuṃ*, *abhisametuṃ*, *icca*, *paṭicca*, *samecca*.
*Abhisamecca*, *apecca*, *upecca*, *paṭimukhaṃ itvā*, *itvāna*, *upetvā*, *upetvāna*, *upetuna*—
these and other [forms] should also be applied according to the terminology of the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*). Thus,
the verbal particle *iti* is not seen in the Suttantas.
This should not be said here; it was spoken by me for the sake of clarification alone.
For the Pāli text is seen as follows:
"He has come in the form of anger," spoken by the Sage in the Aṅguttara Nikāya.
For this was said by the Blessed One in the Aṅguttara Nikāya while censuring anger:
“Come now, this one in the form of anger, The lord of death, dwelling in the cave—
Cut him off completely with self-control, With wisdom, energy, and right view.”

In this context, the word *ita* means "they go" (*ayanti*), which is the analysis [of the term]. And the word *iti* means "it goes" or "it proceeds. Now, here is the meaning of the words in the sutta:
that fault which is called "anger" (*kodha*) by the common people of the world should not, in its actual sense, be called "anger.
How, then, should it be called? For it is the King of Death himself, residing in the cave known as the body, who acts through the influence of anger.
One should say that it proceeds along the continuum of beings while causing intoxication.
One who desires welfare should sever with self-control, wisdom, energy, and right view that anger—which brings harm to many people and should be called the "King of Death.
Furthermore, regarding the word *eti*, its meaning is "it comes. For in this case, the prefix *ā-* is concealed by the requirements of euphonic combination (*sandhikicca*).
It is not manifest, like the full moon shrouded by clouds. For here, there is a grammatical analysis (*sandhiviggaha*) such that *ā* means "it comes" (*eti*);
and the vowel *ā* undergoes substitution with *e* only when followed by the vowel *i*. Therefore, in expressions such as “*ayaṃ so sārathī eti.
Etu vessantaro rājā*” (“This charioteer comes. Let King Vessantara come”), the meaning must be explained as “he comes,” “let him come,” and so forth.
For even in the science of grammar (*byākaraṇasattha*), the grammatical analysis (*sandhiviggaha*) "ā eti" is seen; therefore, this rule too should be carefully borne in mind.
Alternatively, the word *iti* is stated with a short vowel (*rassa*) to signify going, while *eti* is stated with a long vowel (*vuddhi*) to signify coming and so forth according to usage.
Indeed, words possess distinct meanings even by virtue of their prosodic measure (*mattā*).
How so? One who has gone forth in the Teaching, one who has gone forth from the kingdom. Also by way of confinement and non-confinement:
how so? A person goes out from a village; a person goes to fame. Therefore, this rule too should be carefully attended to. On this point it is said:
When the root *gati* is stated as having reached growth (*vuddhim*), [the form] is explained.
Then, for the purpose of arrival, there is the verbal [suffix] *pāya* by way of its function (*vasā*).
For the purpose of posture (*iriyāpatha*), there is *he-sā*, which is always verbal in its arrival;
"This charioteer comes" is the illustration here.
The wise one should understand it as follows:
in the sense of a non-active posture, in proceeding, in going, and in coming.
In such passages as "it proceeds to the fruit dependent [on causes]," it occurs in the sense of proceeding.
This root called *ikā* functions when it has reached its full development (as *eti*).
However, in such cases as “When the sun has set, the beasts...,” it may signify "gone";
and in such cases as “it goes, thus it is *iti*,” it may signify "coming."
For it is thus: *īti* means that which comes (*eti*) for the sake of harm; it is a calamity. Here, the sense of "coming" (*āgamana*) should be understood.
And it is said in the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*: “It comes, thus it is *īti*; this is a designation for those adventitious causes of misfortune that partake of unwholesomeness.”
Now, the extraction of the meanings of the words beginning with *iti*, which are included among particles (*nipāta*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), and nouns (*nāmika*), will be stated as appropriate.
In this context, the word *iti* has many distinct meanings, such as cause, completion, reversal of the meaning of a word, manner, determination, illustration, and so forth.
For instance, in such passages as, "It is deformed, monks, therefore it is called 'form' (*rūpa*)," it is seen in the sense of a cause.
In such passages as, “Therefore, monks, be my heirs to the Dhamma, not my heirs to material things; I have compassion for you, thinking:
‘How may my disciples be heirs to the Dhamma, not heirs to material things?’”—it has the sense of conclusion.
In such passages as, “Thus, or in this manner, he abstains from visiting displays of various kinds”—it has the sense of beginning. [And] “Māgaṇḍiya” refers to that brahmin.

In such passages as "concept (saṅkhā), designation (samaññā), description (paññatti), common usage (vohāra), name (nāma), naming (nāmakamma), denomination (nāmadheyya), linguistic expression (nirutti), phrasing (byañjana), and utterance (abhilāpo)," it refers to the variation of word-meanings.
In such passages as "Thus, monks, the fool is full of peril, while the wise man is free from peril; the fool is beset with calamity, while the wise man is free from calamity;
the fool is accompanied by misfortune, while the wise man is free from misfortune," it refers to a manner or way. "There exists... [and so forth].
In such passages as, "When asked, 'Is it because of this specific condition that there is aging and death? one should answer, 'It exists.
And if he should ask, 'By what condition is there aging and death? one should answer him, 'Aging and death are conditioned by birth,'" the term is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
Also in such passages as, "'It exists,' Kaccāna, is one extreme; 'it does not exist,' Kaccāna, is the second extreme."
In the sense of illustration (*nidassana*). Those applications should be understood by way of particles (*nipāta*) alone.
However, in the phrase “*itāyaṃ kodharūpenā*” (she has come in the form of anger), the word *iti* is seen by way of a verb (*ākhyāta*) in the sense of going. This very meaning is intended here;
the meaning of a particle, however, is not desired [here]. It is stated merely as a summary of meanings for the sake of instilling skill in the discerning in grasping meanings.
It should be understood that [the word] "āgato" (come) is used.
However, the other [usage], namely "anvito," occurs as follows: "The word 'ito' functions in the sense of motion (gatyattha) and in the sense of the word 'cit';
thus, in the sense of motion, it would be in the nominative case."
In the sense of the word *imasadda*, the ablative case occurs in Pāli passages such as, “From here [is] that southern direction,” and so forth.
Here, the sense of motion (*gatyattha*) is intended; the other senses are not intended.
This [explanation] was stated for the purpose of extracting the meaning for the benefit of the wise.

However, here we shall not state the extraction of the meaning of the word *samaya* along with its etymology, but will discuss it further below only in relation to the verbal root *i*, because the word *samaya* consists of three elements by way of that verbal root *i*. In this context, the word *iti* refers to a word ending immediately after the vowel *i*.

Furthermore, the chains of words for such expressions as "eti" (comes) and "udeti" (arises), which end in the vowel *e*, as well as other similar chains of words, should generally be constructed by excluding one's own [specific] words as appropriate. For in such instances, the construction of chains of verbs is difficult;
however, in this treatise, both the easy and the difficult chains of words ending in *ty* must be understood.
Therefore, regarding the ninety-six forms prescribed for the eight classes of roots beginning with *bhū*,
we shall explain the method of the word-series (*padamālā*), both general and specific:
"The wise one [should know] the rows of words ending in the vowel *a*."
One should join [the words] such as *rundhati* and others everywhere and in every way.
Thus, regarding these lines of words,
the wise should join those preceded by a pure vowel according to what is appropriate.
There are also lines of words ending in vowels other than *ā*,
such as "yāti," "suṇāti," and "asnāti," according to their respective contexts.
There are also Pāli passages of words ending in vowels other than *i*.
One should appropriately join [the suffix] after verbs such as *rundhati* and *rundhīti*,
as well as after the word *suti*— which ends in the vowel *u*— and after the word *mālaṃ*,
which functions in the sense of "spreading," according to what is appropriate.
Also for words ending in *e* or *o*, as appropriate—
such as "jeti," "rundheti," "kāreti," and "kārāpeti"—
and for words ending in *o* that follow the sequence of syllables; [these are to be treated in the same manner].
“‘It does,’ ‘it becomes,’ ‘it is’”—teach this through logical reasoning.
Thus, the method of the string of words has been explained by me in seven ways;
apart from this, there is no other method whatsoever for a verb.
“‘He takes up and performs [the action] after death’—through such demonstrations of method and by means of appropriate reasoning, the statement has been spoken here.
Now, the sequence for a word ending in the letter *i* immediately following [another vowel] is stated: *iti*, *inti*; *isi*, *itha*; *imi*, *ima*. [The form] is incomplete.
The present mode (*vattamānānaya*): *itu*, *intu*; *ihi*, *itha*; *imi*, *ima*. The fifth mode (*pañcamīnaya*) is incomplete.
Here, moreover, these are the supporting words for the conformity of these two [modes] to the Teaching (*sāsana*): "veti," "apeti," and "anvetī. In that context, *vi* is "veti";
the meaning is "it departs" (*vigacchati*). Here, the word *iti* signifies "going. Likewise, *apa* is "apeti."
The meaning is "it departs. *Anu* means "it follows. The meaning is "it goes after. The teachers, however, say that *anu eti* means "it follows.
This refers to the verse: "Just as the female elephant follows the forest tusker, the tusked one who roams through mountain fastnesses, on level ground and on uneven terrain..."
"I shall follow him thus, taking my children behind me.
This does not accord with the canonical text because of the expressions "he follows the victor" (*jessantaṃ anveti*) and "I follow" (*anugacchāmi*).
For where the word *eti* denotes a posture (*iriyāpatha*), it indicates only coming, not going.
Therefore, because the sense of "coming" (āgamana) is inappropriate and the sense of "going" (gamana) is appropriate, the elision by *vi* and so forth should be understood.

And the very Pāḷi text establishes both the existence and the logical consistency of these words—which have undergone elision by means of the word *iti*—in the passage: "She has come (*itā*) in the form of anger.
For that very reason, according to the method found in the elision of words such as "he follows" (*anveti*), one should analyze [the term] as "anu iti," "anu inti," "anu isī," and so forth.
The method of the present fifth case (vattamānā-pañcamī) of the aforementioned type has been shown by way of the *parassapada* (active voice).
The forms of the seventh case (*sattamī*) and so forth are entirely unestablished. These, however, are the future forms: *sittā*, *te*, *lahumessati*; *issati*, *issanti*;
*issasi*, *issatha*; *issaṃ*, *issāma*; *issate*, *issante*; *issase*, *issavhe*; *issaṃ*, *issāmhe*. Even when not belonging to the *asabba* verbal roots...
Because the sound *dhātu* is pure (*suddha*), the augment *ikāra* is not obtained. The method will be complete.
Now, the forms for the past tense (*kālātipatti*) are: *issa*, *issasu*. *isse*, *issatha*. *issaṃ*, *issamhā*. *issatha*, *issisu*.
*issase*, *issavhe*. *issaṃ*, *issāmhase*. And because it is in the state of past tense and lacks the *asabbadhātuka* designation...
And even though there are pure vowels, the augment *a* (akāra) is not obtained because it is not a productive agent (*akarī-kārāgama*);

or rather, the augment *a* does not occur because it is non-conclusive (*anekantikatta*) and because its occurrence is untenable (*anupapattattā*). Here, the concurrence of two pure vowels in immediate succession (*anantarika*) from one side is untenable.
The method for the lapse of time (*kālātipatti*) is complete.

In this context, however, for the purpose of generating supreme skill in the meanings of the words among listeners of the Buddha’s word—the Tipiṭaka together with its commentaries—one should take the method from the Pāḷi text, beginning with:
“Have you not heard, O Brahmin, that while the discourse is being recited, the gods do not even envy human prowess?
Thus, there are phrases identical in form to those containing future tense endings, yet which possess entirely different meanings.
We shall now set forth the forms of the present tense and those of the future and past tenses, which are slightly similar to one another.
First, according to the present tense, all should be construed as follows: *issati, issanti; issasi, issatha*.
However, the meaning should be stated as "he performs envy" (*issaṃ karoti*), and so forth. In that same sense, according to the future tense:
“*Ississati*, *ississanti*. *Ississasi*, *ississathā*”—thus it should be completed.
But the meaning should be stated as “he will act with envy,” and so forth. However, by way of the past tense (*kālātipatti*), “*Ississā*, *ississaṃsu*.
*Ississe*, *ississathā*”—thus it should be completed; but the meaning should be stated as “he would have acted with envy,” and so forth.
This is the method of connecting [the forms] by way of different verbal roots (*dhātu*).
Now, the sequence for the word ending in *-ant* following the vowel *e* is stated:
*eti*, *enti*; *esi*, *etha*; *emi*, *ema*.
"Come, come! Come here, come!
I am coming, we are coming!"—yet a wise person would not place their trust until they have reached the end of suffering, even after building dwellings for the illustrious King of Videha.
When I shall send for you, then you should come, O Kṣatriya.
[Optative forms: *eyya*, *eyyuṃ*; *eyyāsi*, *eyyātha*; *eyyāmi*, *eyyāma*. [Imperative forms: *etha*, *eraṃ*; *etho*, *eyyāvho*; *eyyaṃ*, *eyyāmhe*.

That man should come (*eyya*), they should come (*eyyuṃ*). You should come (*eyyāsi*), you all should come (*eyyātha*). I should come (*eyyāmi*), we should come (*eyyāma*). That man comes (*etha*), they come (*eraṃ*). You come (*etho*), you all come (*eyyāvho*). I come (*eyyaṃ*), we come (*eyyāmhe*).
The forms of the remote past (*parokkha*), the future (*hyyyatta*), and the present (*ajjatani*) are entirely unestablished [in this context].
*Essati*, *essanti*; *essasi*, *essatha*; *essāmi*, *essāma*; *essate*, *essante*; *essase*, *essavhe*; *essaṃ*, *essāmhe*.
They go along in mutual delight, like birds taking up their nets.
When they quarrel, then they will come under my power.
From the observation of such expressions as "He has arrived at midnight; come now," other forms of the future tense should also be understood.
Ehiti, ehinti. Ehisi, ehitha. Ehimi, ehima. Ehite, ehinte. Ehise, ehivhe. Ehissaṃ, ehissāmhe.
*Essā*, *essāṃsu*. *Esse*, *essatha*. *Essaṃ*, *essāmha*. *Essatha*, *essisu*. *Essase*, *essavhe*. *Essiṃ*, *essāmhasē*.
Now, there is also another sequence for words ending in the vowel *e*:
*udeti*, *udenti*; *udesi*, *udetha*; *udemi*, *udema*.
Udetu, udentu. Udehi, udetha. Udemi, udema, udāmase. Udeyya, udeyyuṃ.
The rest is to be understood accordingly. Udissati, udissanti. The rest is to be understood accordingly. Udissā, udissaṃsu. The rest is to be understood accordingly.
These are the forms of the pure *assara* root.
The verbal root beginning with *ka* (*kakārantadhātu*) is *ku* in the sense of sound (*sadde*). Thus, *koti*, *kavati*, and *kāyati* are agentive forms (*kattupadāni*).
*Kuyyati* and *kiyyati* are objective forms (*kammapadāni*). *Kānanaṃ*, *kabbaṃ*, and *jātakaṃ* are nominal forms (*nāmikapadāni*). [Examples of gerunds: *kutvā*, *kutvāna*, *kavitvā*.
*Kavitvā*, *kāvitvā*, *kavitvāna*, *kāyituṃ*—these are indeclinable words (*abyayapada*).
In that context, *kānanaṃ* means a forest (*vanaṃ*); it is called *kānanaṃ* because at the time when midday has arrived, it "cries out" (*kavati*), making a sound.
For instance: "When midday has arrived, and the birds have settled down..."
"It rustles as it were in the vast forest; that delight appears to me," so it is said.
Alternatively, *kānana* is that wherein cuckoos, peacocks, and others cry out, sound, and warble. Because it captivates the mind, it is certainly praised (*kuyyati*) by the wise;
thus it is *kabba*. [Synonyms: *kāviya*, *kāveyya*. But elsewhere, it is "this of the poets" (*kavīnaṃ idaṃ*).
The meaning should be understood through the addition of a secondary suffix (*taddhita*). Some, however, maintain that *kābya* is the actual word form;

that is not authoritative for the sacred texts (*pāvacana*), because it belongs to the Pāli language. Indeed, even from the perspective of the Sanskrit language, the teachers adopt the grammatical method.
That which was born, come into being, or past—the conduct of the Blessed One—is called a *jātaka* because by means of it (*etena*) it is praised (*kīyati*) or told (*kathīyati*). Thus, *Jātakapāḷi*.
For here [in this context], they are called "Jātakas. But elsewhere, it should be understood that only what was born (jāta) is a "Jātaka.
Thus, the word *jātaka* applies to the teaching as well, in such passages as "the Itivuttaka, the Jātaka, and the Adbhutadharma";
and it also applies to birth (*jāti*), in such passages as "he compiled the Jātaka."
"Pakkā" means in a low state of existence (*nīcagati*). "Going low" (*nīcagamana*) refers to a base course of action or a base mode of conduct.
For the word *nīca* here signifies "base," as in the expression "reborn in a low family. In this context, the form *pakkā* appears as a verb (*kriyāpada*), not a noun (*nāmikapada*).
Wherever a noun is not seen, there one must examine and supply the appropriate noun.
Indeed, it is the verbal noun (kriyāpada) that is difficult to perceive; however, one must not say that when a verbal noun exists, a nominal noun (nāmikapada) does not exist.

Therefore, it should be understood that even such nominal nouns denoting abstract states as "cooking" (*pakkana*) and "churning" (*takanā*), and so forth, are obtainable from all roots as appropriate.
*Taka* means to laugh; *hasanaṃ* is laughter. *Taki* means to live in hardship;
"hardship" (*kiccha*) refers to a difficult life. *Taṅkati*, *ātaṅkati*, and *ātaṅko*. *Ātaṅka* is a disease that makes life difficult;
for thus the masters of the commentaries [explain] in this context: "little affliction, little illness" (*appābādhaṃ appātaṅkaṃ*).
In certain places in the Pāli, they have explained the meaning as follows:

“‘Affliction’ (ābādha) refers to a discordant sensation that, having arisen in one part, seizes the entire body as if binding it with an iron band. ‘Malady’ (ātaṅka) is a disease that makes life difficult.
Alternatively, a disease that can be sustained is a malady, while the other is an affliction. Or, a minor disease is a malady, whereas a powerful one is an affliction.”
“Affliction. However, some say: “That which originates internally is affliction (ābādha); that which originates externally is illness (ātaṅka).
Illness (ātaṅka), malady (āmaya), disease (roga), affliction (byādhi), affliction (ābādha), plague (gada), and pain (rujā) [are synonyms].
*Akallañceva gelaññaṃ*: "Sickness" is a designation for disease.

*Suka* [is derived from] the root *gati* (to go). One who sorrows (*sokati*) is a *suka*, a *sukī*. In this context, *suka* means a bird. It is called a *suka* because it goes by means of a pleasant flight; its female mate is a *sukī*.

*Bukka* means barking. Here, "barking" (*bhassana*) refers specifically to the barking of a dog—as in the expression "having barked like a dog"—and not in the sense found in such passages as "the dwelling, the range, and the bark" (*āvāso gocaraṃ bhassaṃ*).
It is the act of barking consisting of speech; it barks (*bukati*). *Dhaka* means to strike back and to go. "Striking back" (*paṭighāta*) means repelling.

It strikes back (*dhakati*). *Caka* means to satisfy and to strike back. "Satisfying" (*titti*) means satiation; "striking back" (*paṭighāta*) is synonymous with repelling. It strikes back (*cakati*).

*Ak* is in the sense of crooked movement; it means "to go. Those learned in the science of grammar (*saddasatthavidū*) say that these roots beginning with *ku* and ending with *ak* denote the speech of another.
In their opinion, these [roots] fall only within the scope of [suffixes such as] *ti*, *anti*, *tu*, *antu*, and so forth. However, there is no such restriction in the Canon (*pāḷi*);
therefore, that [opinion] is not authoritative here.
Regarding *ajjhāyana*: *ajjhāyana* means recitation or learning. [From the roots] *ayati*, *adhīyati*, *ajjhayati*, *adhīte*, *ajjhenaṃ*, and *ajjhāyako*.
"You practice divine illusion" (*dibbaṃ adhīyase māyaṃ*). "O Great King, here the wise practice divine illusion" (*adhīyanti mahārāja, dibbamāyidha paṇḍitā*).
"The noble lords of men practiced the earth" (*ajjhenamariyā pathaviṃ janindā*). In this context, *ajjhāyako* means one who practices (*ajjhayati*), that is to say, one who repeats the mantras.

Regarding the root *u* (to protect): *avati*, *avanti*, *avasī*. Here, the canonical passage, “*yo ātumānaṃ sayameva pāvā*,” should be understood as an application of the verbal root *udhātu* preceded by the prefix *pa*. It is also appropriate to state that it is an application of the elision of the letter *da* from the verbal root *vadadhātu* preceded by the prefix *pa*.
Regarding the root *vaṅka* (crookedness): *vaṅkati*. *Vaṅkaṃ*. Indeed, the word *vaṅka* has the same meaning as the word *vakkha*, and the word *vakkha* has the same meaning as the word *vaṅka*.
For instance: “Whatever tree upon which creatures depend, this very [tree] releases fire;”
"O Vakkaṅgas, resort to the directions; there is danger born from taking refuge [in them].
Thus the Pāḷi is seen. However, this word *vakkasa* becomes one containing the conjunct syllable *kka-ra* when it reaches the Sanskrit language;
its verbal root (*dhātu*) has not been stated by the ancients, and therefore no verbal form (*kriyāpada*) is seen for it. Of this—
Furthermore, the verbal root nature of the word *vaṅka* is stated as “*vaṅka* [means] to be crooked,” and the verb form “*vaṅkatī*” is also mentioned;
however, the verb form “*vaṅkatī*” is not seen in the Pāḷi text, nor is the noun *vaṅka* used as an abstract quality (*bhāva*).

Nevertheless, the word *vaṅka* is seen in various places with its gender varying according to the object it qualifies. Therefore, even though the verb form “*vaṅkatī*” does not exist in the Pāḷi, it must certainly be accepted.
The word *nāthati* functions like a verb. However, the existence and non-existence of the noun-form *vaṅka* (crooked) must be repeatedly examined in the Pāli canon and other texts.

Here, some might object: "If the noun *vaṅka* does not exist, how is the compound ‘aṭṭhavaṅkaṃ maṇiratanaṃ uḷāraṃ’ (the excellent eight-curved jewel-treasure) formed? In this case, however, [it refers to] the eight places...

"Vaṅka" means crooked (*aṭṭhavaṅka*); it refers to that which has no crookedness. It should be understood that the word *vaṅka* denotes the substance (*dabbavācaka*), not the abstract state (*bhāvavācaka*).
Crooked (*vaṅka*), curved (*vakka*), bent (*kuṭila*), slanted (*jimha*), and uneven (*rimha*, *amanuja*);
these words beginning with *vaṅka* agree in gender with their referent and possess all three genders.

Alternatively, this word *vaṅka* occurs in the masculine in such contexts as “*vaṅkaghaṭṭā*” and so forth, referring to a fishhook (*baḷisa*) and a mountain peak (*giribheda*). For this word occurs in reference to a fishhook in such passages as:
“These people, like those with crooked hands, lie down; just as a fish [seizes] a hook covered with meat, or like a lotus-root-eater with a crooked hand.”

Here it might be argued: "But surely, sir, in the passage 'Just as a fishhook is covered with meat on its hook' (*vaṅkaṃ maṃsena chāditaṃ*), the word *vaṅka* is a quality-denoting adjective serving as a qualifier;
since the fishhook is qualified by it, the meaning understood is that the fishhook is 'crooked' (*kuṭila*)?
That is not so, for even if the word *vaṅka* were not uttered, the meaning of "crookedness" is already present because the very nature of a fishhook is crooked.

The term *pākaṭo* (manifest) has no need for a qualifying word. However, this expression “the hook is crooked” (*baḷisaṃ vaṅkaṃ*) is a synonymous expression—just like the expressions “elephant, nāga,” “lotus, saroruha,” or “elephant, kuñjara, nāga.
Therefore, the meaning of the word *vaṅkaṃ* should not be taken as “crooked” (*kuṭilaṃ*). Alternatively, just as [in the phrase] “as the forest-dweller... [the context determines the specific sense].

In the passage, "The female elephant follows the male elephant" (*nāgaṃ, dantiṃ anveti hatthinī*), although the words *nāga* and *dantī* are synonyms for one another, the commentary explains the meaning of *dantī* as "possessing beautiful tusks.
Likewise, although the words *baḷisa* (hook) and *vaṅka* (crooked) are also synonyms for each other, the meaning of *vaṅka* should be stated as "curved. For it is thus...
When there is a purpose, it becomes fully blossomed like a king of *sāla* trees, and the teaching reaches its full elegance. However,
a grammatical coreferential relationship (*samānādhikaraṇabhāva*) based on the quality-possessor relation (*guṇaguṇīvasena*) between words such as "crooked" and "fishhook" need not be intended,
just as in the case of the coreferential relationship between "the Buddha" and "the Blessed One" in expressions such as "The Buddha, the Blessed One, dwells at Verañjā."
Because it is not intended [as such]. For in such instances, the ancient masters do not accept a state of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇabhāva*).
As it is said: "Where there is such a Teacher, without rival in the world, the Tathāgata who has attained power, the Fully Awakened One who has attained final Nibbāna."
In such passages as “Buddhaṃ buddhaṃ nikhilavisayaṃ suddhiyā yāva suddhin” and so forth, however, it is permitted [to use the accusative].

For here, the terms “of such a kind,” “one without a superior,” “Tathāgata,” “one who has attained power,” “the Fully Awakened One,” and “one who has attained final Nibbāna” stand in grammatical apposition with the word “Teacher. Likewise, “Buddhaṃ... [is used].
In the phrase "Buddha," the latter word stands in grammatical apposition with the former.
Thus, in the expression, "Just as a fishhook is concealed by meat, though it is crooked," the word *vaṅka* follows immediately after the word for the hook (*baḷisa*) and does not denote a quality.
In this way, the word *vaṅka* refers to the hook. [It is used] in such passages as, "We go to Mount Kaṅka; Mount Vaṅkata is far away."

However, it applies to a specific mountain. And here, although one should say "Vaṅkapabbata" (Crooked Mountain), for the sake of ease of pronunciation, the letter *t* is inserted in the middle without a vowel marker according to the rules of etymology (*niruttinaya*), and thus it is called "Vaṅkatapabbata.
Alternatively, "vaṅkatā" is simply "vaṅka" itself, just as "deva" is "devatā," and as "disā" is "disatā"; likewise, by means of the suffix *-tā*, it is "vaṅkatā."
It is called "Vaṅkatapabbata" (Crooked Mountain) because it is a mountain that is crooked; this should be understood by way of the short vowel in the middle [of the compound].

Alternatively, the suffix *ta* is used in the sense of possession (*mantuattha*), as in "that which has a crooked shape is crooked (*vaṅka*)," just as "that which has ridges (*pabba*) is a mountain (*pabbata*).
Thus, it is "Vaṅkatapabbata" because it is both crooked and a mountain. It is simply "Vaṅkapabbata."
Or it is a designation (*paṇṇatti*); however, for the sake of completing the syllables of the verse, it should be understood that it is stated as "the mountain bent from afar.
Regarding *loka-dassana*: it looks (*lokati*), thus it is *loka*. *Āloka*—other forms should also be understood here.

But having reached the *cur-ādi* class [of verbs], its forms become such as "he looks" (*loketi*), "he surveys" (*lokayati*), "he gazes at" (*oloketi*), "he gazes upon" (*olokayatī*), and so forth. Thus, *loka*.

There are three worlds: the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*), the world of beings (*sattaloka*), and the world of space (*okāsaloka*). Among these, that which is stated as, “The world is one: all beings subsist on nutriment,” is the world of formations;
it is simply formations that are the world of formations. Beings themselves are the world; it is the world of beings.

The space comprised by the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) is the world of space; this is also called the “receptacle world. Among these, it is called “world” (*loka*) because formations disintegrate (*lujjati*).
For this was said by the Blessed One: “It breaks up, it falls apart, bhikkhu; therefore it is called the world (loka).
A being is a world because merit and demerit, as well as their result, disintegrate therein. Space, reckoned as the world-system (cakkavāḷa), is a world because it is seen in its various forms.
Furthermore, since the word *loka* is also seen to refer to a collection, [the world] disintegrates by way of its constituent aggregates.
"Loka" is so called because it is manifested (*paññāpiyati*); the meaning "aggregation" (*samūha*) should also be understood here. Alternatively, "loka" refers to the three worlds:

the world of defilements (*kilesaloka*), the world of existence (*bhavaloka*), and the world of faculties (*indriyaloka*). We shall explain their specific characteristics and manifold diversity in the section on the *curādigaṇa* [of verbal roots].
As for external usage, however, poets have stated only this much: "The world (*loka*) is the universe and the people."
*Siloka* means a collection (*saṅghāta*). A collection is a grouping (*piṇḍana*). One praises (*silokati*), thus it is *siloka*; "I shall proclaim the *siloka*.
A *siloka* is a verbal composition regulated by syllables and words. It is called *pajja* (verse); for thus the poets say:

"The illustrious *siloka* is a *pajja*. *Deka* and *dheka* mean to sound and to exert. Sound (*sadda*) is noise; exertion (*ussāha*) is effort (*vāyāma*). One sounds (*dekati*); one exerts (*dhekati*).
*Reka* means to suspect. *Rekati*. It means to doubt; "my mind doubts in that regard. *Saṅkā* (doubt).
*Aki* is used in the sense of marking. *Aṅkati*, *aṅko*, *sasaṅko* (marked, having a mark).
*Maki* is used in the sense of adorning. Adornment is decoration; *maṅkati*.

*Kata* means *loliya*. *Loliya* is the state of being fickle (*lolabhāva*), just as *dakkhiya* [is derived from *dakṣa*]. *Kakati*, *kāko*, *kākī*. Here, these are synonyms for a crow: *kāko*, *dhaṅko*, *vāyaso*, *bali*, *bhoji*, *ariṭṭho*.
*Kuka* and *vaka* mean "to take. *Kukati*, *vakati*, *koko*, *vako*. Here, *koko* refers to a wild dog. *Vako* refers to a small leopard;
some also call it a tiger (*byaggho*). *Vaka* means "splendor" and "resistance. Splendor (*ditti*) is beauty; [thus] it shines (*vakati*).
The roots *kaṅk*, *vaṅk*, *sakk*, *tik*, *ṭik*, *sek*, and *gatyatthā* (those meaning "to go") are as follows: *kaṅkati*, *vaṅkati*, *sakkati*, *nisakkati*, *parisakkati*, *osakkati*.

There is also the phrase "striving for slaughter" (*vadhāya parisakkanaṃ*), and even "the mere crawling of a cat" (*biḷāranisakkamattampi*). Then there are *tekati*, *ṭekati*, *ṭīkā*, and *sekati*. Here, regarding *ṭīkā*:

it is called *ṭīkā* because by means of it the meaning is made known (*ṭikiyati*) or understood (*jāniyati*) through a commentary (*saṃvaṇṇanā*). These [roots] beginning with *idha* and ending with *seka* [are now concluded].
Grammarians (saddasatthavidū) state that the *dhātus* [beginning with] "attanobhāsā" are [verbs]. In their opinion, these [roots] have as their domain only forms such as "te ante" and "taṃ antaṃ";
however, in the Pāvacana, there is no such restriction.
[The root] *hikka* means "in an indistinct sound. An indistinct sound (*abyattasaddo*) is a sound whose meaning is not clearly manifested, and it is a meaningless sound. [One] hikkati.
It is *hikkate*. They call this "shining on both sides" (*ubhayatobhāsā*).

However, this accords with the authoritative tradition (*pāvacana*), for in the Teaching, the forms of roots that shine in both the third person and the first person are generally seen in pairs, such as *bhavati*, *bhavate*; *bādhate*, *bādhati*, and so forth.
These are the forms of roots ending in the letter *k*.
The verbal root *khā* ending in *kha*:
*khā* is used in the sense of "explaining" (*pakathana*), as well as *khyā*. "Explaining" means declaring or teaching. From the root *khā*, we have *saṅkhāti*.

When preceded by the prefix *ā-*, the letter *kha* becomes doubled due to its dissimilarity [with the following consonant], and because the vowel *ā* is preceded by a conjunct consonant, it becomes short; thus, *akkhāti*.
The Supreme Person has declared it. O Noble Lady, I shall declare that which is to be declared to you. "Dhamma" is so called because it is reckoned (*saṅkhāyati*) and it is declared (*akkhāyati*).
Here, however, there is the elision of the letter *ka*. Well-expounded by the Blessed One is the Dhamma; it is reckoned, it is declared. The Tathāgatas are the declarers;

the Venerable One is the reckoner of all phenomena. *Saṅkhā* means reflection (*paṭisaṅkhā*). It is called "declared" (*ākhyāta*) because it declares or tells of an action (*kriyaṃ ākyāti katheti*). Some...

However, they accept the forms *svākhāto*, *svākkhyāto*, and *svākhyāto*. Among these, the latter two are stated by adopting the method from the Sanskrit language, while the former is according to the derivation of the form as it stands; therefore, the words as they have been shown are more excellent.

In this regard, the extraction of the meaning of the word *saṅkhā* is set forth: the word *saṅkhā* [is used] in the senses of knowledge (*ñāṇa*), portion (*koṭṭhāsa*), designation (*paññatti*), and counting (*gaṇanā*).

It is seen [in various senses]. For in such passages as “Having reckoned, he partakes of one,” it is seen in the sense of knowledge (*ñāṇa*). In such passages as “The conceptual proliferations of perception and formations (*papañca-saññā-saṅkhā*) are active,” it is seen in the sense of a constituent part (*koṭṭhāsa*).
In such passages as “The reckoning (*saṅkhā*), the designation (*samaññā*), of those respective phenomena,” it is seen in the sense of a description or concept (*paññatti*).
In such passages as “It is not easy to reckon (*saṅkhātuṃ*),” it is seen in the sense of counting (*gaṇanā*). Herein, this is said:
“The word *saṅkhā* appears in the sections on the enumeration of the designations for knowledge;
it should be illustrated as such in the teaching that is the island of the Dhamma.

*Khi* means exhaustion. That which has the nature of being exhausted is called *khīyati*. According to the rules of the Sāsana, the vowel *i* undergoes the substitution of *iyya*, thus becoming *khiyyati*.

“*Khayo*, *khaṃ*” — thus are forms to be known. In this context, *khayo* means the act of wasting away (*khiyanaṃ*), hence decay. Alternatively, it is called *khayo* because defilements waste away (*khiyanti*) therein;
thus, it refers to the Path and Nibbāna. Because the Fruit is reached by means of the Path—which is characterized as decay—it too is called *khayo*.
*Khaṃ* is empty, void, secluded, and barren; or, *khaṃ* is space.
*Nivāse*: *khīyati* or *khiyyati*. According to the rules of the Sāsana, the substitution of *ikāra* with *īya* or *iyya* should be understood here.

This [root] should also be included in the *divādigaṇa*. *Khaṃ* means destruction (*khaya*). "The delightful destruction of the kingdom" (*abhiramaṇīyaṃ rājakkhayaṃ*). Therein, "it is destroyed" (*khīyati*) means it dwells.
*Khanti* refers to the faculties such as the eye, in the sense of being the dwelling place for visual consciousness and so forth. *Khayaṃ* means a residence (*nivesanaṃ*).
"The destruction of the king" refers to the king's residence. Here is the canonical text:
"If today you bear the prince of lovely appearance, the khattiya born of Kusa, adorned with a girdle of gems of the same hue as himself;"
"Honored by your circle of kinsmen, you do not go to the destruction of Yama.
In this context, "the destruction of Yama" (yamakkhaya) refers to the abode of Yama.
Regarding the word *khu*: *khu* means it perishes (*khavati*).

*Khe* [is used] in the sense of eating. *Khāyati*: "The mice are seen. *Vikkhāyitakaṃ* (the gnawed), *gokhāyitakaṃ* (the cow-gnawed). "He appears like a corpse. "Even the directions do not appear to me. Here, at the beginning, it is called *khādati* because it manifests (*kāyati*).

Alternatively, it means it stands forth or is made known. Regarding *sukha* and *dukkha*, there is the action of that (*takriyā*). "Action of that" means the activity of the feelings of pleasure and pain;
what is meant is "pleasing and paining. These roots are intransitive (*akammakā*). *Sukhati*, *dukkhati*. *Sukhaṃ*, *dukkhaṃ*. *Sukhito*, *dukkhito*.
Pleasure is gratification; pain is affliction, misfortune, and defilement. In this context, "pleasure" (*sukha*) means it pleases (*sukhayati*);
the meaning is that whatever arises in one makes that person happy. "Pain" (*dukkha*) means it pains (*dukkhayati*);
the meaning is that whatever arises in one makes that person miserable. These etymological explanations are stated according to the function [of the terms].

This should be understood from the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), for the teachers, while explaining the meaning of the words *sukha* and *dukkha*, have provided an exposition by taking the sense of the object (*kamma*) of the verbal roots *sukhayati* and *dukkhayati*.
For instance, these are their forms as causative verbs (*kāritapada*): "it makes happy" (*sukheti*, *sukhayati*), "it causes to be made happy" (*sukhāpeti*, *sukhāpayati*);
"it makes painful" (*dukkheti*, *dukkhayati*), "it causes to be made painful" (*dukkhāpeti*, *dukkhāpayati*). [The root] *attānaṃ*...
"It gladdens" and "it refreshes," thus it is called *sukha*; "it causes suffering," thus it is called *dukkha*.
And: "If at any time, death should come before me..."
This is because we see such examples in the Pāli canon as:
"May Mahosadha cause my sons and grandsons to sleep happily.
Furthermore, in the *Saddasattha* and the *Dhātupāṭhasaṅkhepa*, these roots belong exclusively to the *curādigaṇa*.
[They] have been stated. Furthermore, [they] desire that "sukhayati" and "dukkhayati" be pure agent-terms (*suddhakattupada*) without expressed action.
However, we do not accept those word-forms as pure agent-terms in their own right because they contradict the Pāḷi and other authorities;
for that very reason, they are stated here in this *bhūvādigaṇa*. For our preference regarding the domain of the pure agent is: "sukhati."
"One who is happy is called 'suffering' when he suffers.
But, sir, are not the verbal forms "is happy" (*sukhati*) and "suffers" (*dukkhati*) seen in the Buddha’s word? True;
even so, they are indeed seen because they must be understood according to the method of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). For it is not in every respect...
The forms of all the elements are found either in the Teaching or in the world;
some are found, while others are not. Even so, they are indeed found by way of method (*naya*).
For when it is said, "Be mindful in what you fashion," even such expressions as "Go about, eat" and so forth, when seen [in that context], are indeed considered seen by way of method.

In this regard, the method is as follows. For in the *Visuddhimagga* and other works, the verb "dukkhati" (he suffers) is seen as belonging to the *bhū* class, being intransitive (*akammaka*) and expressing a pure agent (*suddhakattu*), in such passages as: "Even for one who has traveled a distance of only one or two leagues, the wind becomes disturbed and the limbs suffer.
In that same sense, there are also [forms] such as "sukhati," "sukhanti"; "sukhasi," "sukhatha"; "sukhāmi," etc.

And such forms as *sukhāmā* and so forth, as well as *dukkhati*, *dukkhanti*, *dukkhasi*, and *dukkhathā* and so forth, are called "seen" because a similar faultless method (*naya*) not yet seen must be grasped from what has been seen;

therefore, only the *bhū-ādi* method should be adopted here—namely, that one who experiences pleasure is "happy" (*sukhito*) and one who experiences pain is "unhappy" (*dukkhito*)—and not the *cur-ādi* method. Furthermore, in this regard:
Regarding the etymology: one for whom happiness has arisen is "sukhito"; the meaning is "one who has experienced happiness. This same method applies here to the term "dukkhito" as well.
Alternatively, one who proceeds by means of happiness is "sukhito. This same method applies here to the term "dukkhito" as well.
This principle is difficult to obtain; therefore, it should be carefully attended to in the mind.
*Mokkha* means releasing. This root is intransitive (*akammaka*). [Examples: *mokkhati*, *mokkho*, *pātimokkho*.

In the causative (*kārita*), there are forms such as *mokkheti*, *mokkhayati*, *mokkhāpeti*, and *mokkhāpayati*. However, some read this as *mokkha mocane* and include it in the *curādigaṇa* (the tenth class).
According to their view, *mokkheti* and *mokkhayati* become forms with a pure agent (*suddhakattupada*).
These [explanations] conflict with both the Canon (Pāḷi) and the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). For they conflict with the Canon in such passages as:
“They shall be released from Māra’s bonds”; “O ascetic, you shall not release me”; and “We shall perform a great sacrifice; thus we shall be freed from evil.

And they conflict with the Commentary, which states: “The Pātimokkha is that which protects and guards; it ‘releases’—that is, it liberates—one from the sufferings of the states of misery and so forth.”

And since they do not conflict, the Pāḷi does not say "mokkhesi, mokkhemā" (you will release, we will release), but rather says "mokkhasi, mokkhāmā," which expresses the pure agent (*suddhakattū*), and that too by taking it as having the ablative (*apādāna*) as its object.

In the Aṭṭhakathā, however, it is said "mokkheti, moceti," which expresses the causal agent (*hetukattu*), and that too by taking it as having the ablative as its object. Thus, regarding this verbal root...

It is known that [the root *muc*] is intransitive when its agent is a simple (pure) agent, whereas it is known to be transitive with a single object when its agent is a causal agent, as in the case of roots such as *pacati*, *chindati*, and so forth.
If it is argued that the element *mokkha* belongs to the second class (*dvigaṇika*), this is not so;

for it should be understood that in numerous passages of the Canon and its commentaries, forms of the simple agent—such as "he releases" (*mokkhati*) or "he causes to release" (*mokkhayati*)—are never observed.
*Kakkha* is used in the sense of laughing. *Kakkhati*.
*Okha*, *rākha*, *lākha*, *dākha*, and *dhākha* are used in the sense of drying (*sosana*) and killing (*ālamartha*). *Okhati*, *rākhati*, *lākhati*, *dākhati*, *dhākhati*.
*Sākha* is used in the sense of spreading (*byāpana*). *Sākhati*. *Sākhā*.

The roots *ukha*, *nakha*, *makha*, *rakha*, *lakha*, *raṅkha*, *laṅkha*, *iṅkha*, and *riṅkha* have the sense of motion. *Ukhati*. *Nakhati*. *Makhati*. *Rakhati*. *Lakhati*. *Raṅkhati*. *Laṅkhati*. *Iṅkhati*. *Riṅkhati*. *Rakkha* (in the sense of protection): *rakkhati*.

*Rakkhā*, *rakkhaṇaṃ*, "Devadatta has protected his virtue" (*sīlaṃ rakkhito devadatto*), "virtue was protected by Devadatta" (*sīlaṃ rakkhitaṃ devadattena*), "Devadatta is a protector of virtue" (*sīlaṃ rakkhako devadatto*).
*Akkha* (in the sense of being clever or skilled): *akkhati*, *akkhi*, *akkhaṃ*.
*Nikkha* means kissing. *Nikkhati*, *nikkham*. *Nakkha* means going.

*Nakkhati*. *Nakkhattaṃ*. Herein, *nakkhattaṃ* is so called because it protects (*tāyati*) its own course of movement (*gamanam*) by not wandering from this side to that side in an irregular path, but rather by proceeding along its own proper track;
thus it is a "protector" (*rakṣati*). Therefore it is called a "constellation" (*nakkhattaṃ*).
The Ancients, however, explained: "They do not perish, they do not disappear, thus they are *nakkhattāni*.
*Nakkhatta*, *joti*, *nirikkha*, and *bhaṃ* are synonyms.
[The root] *vekṣ* means to look at; it looks at (*vekṣati*).
*Makkha* is reckoned as smearing;
it smears. *Takkha* is burning; burning is a covering; it covers.
*Sukkha* is disregard; it disregards.
At times it is called *kakha*, at times *vakha*, at times *makha*, and at times *kaṅkhā*. One is doubtful regarding the Teacher; one wavers, one hesitates.

"Doubt, doubting, the state of having doubted, perplexity, uncertainty, double-mindedness, the path of two ways, suspense, the grasping of what is not one-sided, sliding back and forth, lack of penetration, rigidity of mind, mental scarifying"—these are synonyms for doubt. Now, among these:
In worldly parlance, these terms—“kaṅkhā,” “vimati,” “saṃsayo,” and “vicikicchā”—are used almost exclusively as synonyms.
This word *kaṅkhati* means to desire wealth, to long for it, or—as in the phrase “I do not long for death”—to yearn for something. [An example is] “wealth longed for.”
*Dakhi* and *dhakhi* mean "to bite" or "to sting," as in *kaṅkhāyañca* (and in biting). *Daṅkhati*. *Dhaṅkhati*.
*Ukkha* means "to sprinkle"; *ukkhati*.
*Kakha* means "to laugh"; *kakhati*.
And in *jakkha-bhakkhaṇe*. The letter *ca* is for the purpose of including *hasanānukaḍḍhana*. [From the root] *jakṣ*: *jakṣati*.
[From the root] *likh* in the sense of writing: *likhati*, *sallekhati*. "This ascetic is exceedingly austere" (*atisallekhatevāyaṃ samaṇo*).
*Lekhā*, *lekhanam*, *lekhako*, *likhitam*, *sallekhapaṭipatti*—those learned in grammar state that these words, beginning with *dakhi* and ending with *likha*, are "foreign words" (*parassabhāsā*).

In the sense of suffering, reproaching, and the afflictions of existence: *dhukkhati* (he suffers), *dhikkhati* (he reproaches). Those learned in the science of grammar (*saddasattha*), however, state that *dhukkhate* and *dhikkhate* are forms of the middle voice (*attanobhāsa*).
The same applies to the forms following this. *Rukkha* and *vakkha* mean "to obstruct. Obstruction means "hindering" (*saṃvaraṇa*). *Rukkhati*, *vakkhati*. A tree is called *rukkha* or *vakkha*.
And here, *vakkha* is indeed the same as *rukkha*; for instance, there is the reading in the *Jātaka*: "There are sweet and delightful trees born in the forest."
It is seen. These, moreover, are the names for a tree:
“Rukkho, mahīruho, vakkho, pādapo, jagatīruho;
ago, nago, kujo, sākhī, sālo, viṭapī, taru.”
“A *duma* is one that bears fruit; a *gaccha*, however, is a small tree.
Regarding this, some might say: “Is it not the case that by the word *sāla*, only the *sāla* tree is meant and nothing else, as seen in such usages as ‘*sālā*, *phandanā*, *māluvā*’?
Then for what purpose is any tree whatsoever expressed by the word *sāla*? It is not only the *sāla* tree [that is meant].

It is expressed by the word "sāla," yet other trees are also mentioned because the designation "sāla" is seen to be applied not only to the *sāla* tree, but also to the forest-lord (*vanappati*)—the king of trees—and indeed to any tree whatsoever. For even the *sāla* tree itself is called "sāla.
As it is said: "Just as, monks, near a village or a town, there is a great..."
There was a *sāla* grove, which was covered with *elaṇḍa* shrubs, between a pair of *sāla* trees. It is also the oldest tree among forest-dwellers. As it is said:
"In your very kingdom, O King, in your very pleasure grove, stand great *sāla* trees with straight trunks, blue-green in luster, and delightful."
Any tree whatsoever. As it is said: “Then, monks, that *māluva* seed might fall at the foot of a certain *sāla* tree. Regarding this, it is said:
“In a *sāla* tree, the eldest of trees, or in whatever tree it may be;”
"Sāla" is the sound;
it may be [the name] of one standing in a council hall.

"Sikkhā" refers to the acquisition of knowledge and skill. One trains (*sikkhati*). Training (*sikkhā*), the act of training (*sikkhanaṃ*), the craft learned (*sikkhitaṃ sippaṃ*), the student (*sikkhako*), and the one who has trained (*sikkhito*).
The terms are *sekkho* (the learner) and *asekkho* (the one beyond training). When the letter *k* is elided, the forms become *sekho* and *asekho*.

In this context, *sikkhito* means "one who has acquired training," or alternatively, *asikkhī* means "trained. For the usage of the agent (*kattūppayoga*) is seen there, as in: "I am indeed well-trained and skilled in my own ancestral craft of pottery."
*Bhikkha* means begging. One begs (*bhikkhati*). Thus: *bhikkhu*, *bhikkhā*, *bhikkhanaṃ*, *bhikkhaka*, and food obtained by begging (*bhikkhitaṃ bhojanaṃ*).
In this context, however, these are synonymous terms: *bhikkhu*, *yati*, *samaṇa*, *muni*, *pabbajita*, *anagāra*, *tapassī*, and *tapodhana*.
Among these, in the Teaching (*sāsana*), one who has received full ordination (*upasampanna*) is called a *bhikkhu*. Sometimes, however, [the term] "a hundred bhikkhus" (*bhikkhusataṃ*)...
In such expressions as "he fed," "he fed a thousand bhikkhus," the designation "bhikkhu" is applied even to novices (sāmaṇera).
Furthermore, ascetics (tāpasa) are also spoken of by terms such as "samaṇa," as in the example: "In the past, there was an ascetic who illuminated patience.
The root *dakkha* signifies growth and swiftness. [From it come] *dakkhati*, *dakkhiṇā*, and *dakkho*. Beings grow and increase.
It is called *dakkhiṇā* because by means of these aforementioned attainments, it becomes successful, increased, and brought to excellence; it is the object to be given.
It is called *dakkha*, meaning clever or skillful—also referred to as "expert"—because it proceeds swiftly due to its lack of sluggishness regarding wholesome action and other duties and non-duties.
The root *dikkh* occurs in the senses of shaving the head (*muṇḍī*), bringing near (*upanayana*), observance (*niyama*), vow (*vata*), and designation (*ādēsa*). [Thus: *dikkhati*.
One who has shaved his head is *dikkhita*. Here it might be asked: "But surely, Master, in this passage from the *Sarabhaṅga-jātaka*:
'The fragrance of the seers who have long been initiated (*ciradikkhita*) departs from the body and goes with the wind'—was this not stated by the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā?"...

It is stated: “‘Those who have long been ordained’ means those who have long gone forth. For it was not stated there that they were “those who have long had their heads shaved. This being so, why is it said here:
“The element of shaving (dikkhadhātu) is mentioned in the sense of ‘shaving’ (muṇḍiye)” [in the *Dhātupāṭha*]? True;

however, because the word *dikkhita* is used in the sense of one who has gone forth (*pabbajita*) in that [text], it was stated as “those who have long been gone forth,” and not for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of the verbal root.

This, however, was stated by Muṇḍī for the purpose of clarifying the meaning of the term *dhātu*. For ascetics (*tāpasa*) are appropriately described by the word *dikkhita*, which expresses the sense of being shaven-headed (*muṇḍiya*).

Thus, in the commentary on the meaning of the *Cakkavatti-sutta*, the Aṭṭhakathā masters, in explaining the meaning of this passage—“having shaved off hair and beard and donned saffron robes”—state: “the renunciation of an ascetic (*tāpasapabbajjā*”).
For those going forth first shave off their hair and beard; from that point on, they open [the door] after tying back their grown hair.
Thus it is said: "having shaved off hair and beard"—in this way the meaning is explained. *Ikkha* means seeing or a mark.

One sees (*ikkhati*), looks with equanimity (*upekkhati*), or regards (*apekkhati*). From *upekkhā*, *apekkhā*, and *paccavekkhaṇā*, when the letter *k* is elided, the forms become *upekhā*, *apekhā*, and *upasampadāpekho*.
*Duḥkha* means in the sense of suffering and harming.
*Dakkhati*. *Dakkhaka*. *Cikkha* and *cakkha* mean distinctness in speech. *Cikkhati*, *ācikkhati*, *abbhācikkhati*. *Ācikkhaka*. *Cakkhati*, *cakkhu*.
Here, *cakkhu* means "it sees" (*cakkhati*), thus it is called *cakkhu*; it refers to one who speaks clearly regarding what is even and uneven.

The meaning is "it appears as if. Alternatively, since the word *cakkhu* (eye) also carries the sense of "relishing" in expressions such as "he relishes the soup" (*sūpaṃ cakkhati*) or "he relishes the honey" (*madhuṃ cakkhati*), one should therefore also take the sense of relishing here:
"The eye, presided over by consciousness, appears as if it were relishing form. As it is said: "The eye, Māgaṇḍiya, delights in forms, rejoices in forms, and exults in forms."

For it has been said: "Even though the ear and other [senses] possess the quality of delighting in sounds and so forth, the word *cakkhu* (eye) occurs only with reference to the organ of sight, just as words such as *paṅkaja* (mud-born) occur specifically for the lotus and similar things.
*Cakkhu*, *akkhi*, *nayana*, *locana*, *diṭṭhi*, and *dassana* [are synonyms]."
The eye, the pupil, and the eyelashes are called "pakhuma.
Grammarians of the science of language state that these, beginning with trees and ending with the eye, are "self-luminous" (attanobhāsa).
These are the forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *kha*.
The verbal root beginning with *ga*: *gu* in the sense of evacuation. Evacuation (*karīsussagga*) means the act of voiding excrement. *Gavati*. *Ge* in the sense of sound.
*Gāyati*. *Gītaṃ*. *Vagga* in the sense of moving. *Vaggati*. *Vaggo*, *vaggitaṃ*. Here, by way of a collective sense, it refers to moving or proceeding.
*Vagga*. *Vaggitam* means going. For thus, in the commentary on the *Nāgapeta-vatthu*, while explaining the meaning of this passage:

“He who was our middle son, traveling in the midst [on] a chariot yoked with four mules, moving with beautiful gait (*suvaggitena*), shining as a generous lord of giving, free from stinginess,” they say:
“*Suvaggitena* means with a beautiful gait. Furthermore, there is also a verbal form...
And it is seen [in the texts]: “They shake, they leap, they move about in the sky.
[The roots] *ra-gi*, *la-gi*, *a-gi*, *va-gi*, *ma-gi*, *i-gi*, *ri-gi*, *li-gi*, *ta-gi*, *sa-gi* mean “to go. The letter *ca* is for the purpose of including the sense of motion.
*Raṅgati*. *Raṅgo*. *Laṅgati*. *Laṅgo*, *laṅgī*. *Aṅgati*, *aṅgeti*. *Aṅgo*, *samaṅgī*, *samaṅgitā*, *aṅgaṃ*, *aṅgaṇaṃ*.
Vaṅgati, vaṅgo; maṅgati, maṅgo, upaṅgo, maṅgalaṃ; iṅgati, iṅgitaṃ; riṅgati, riṅganaṃ;
liṅgati, liṅganaṃ, ulliṅgati, ulliṅganaṃ; taṅgati, taṅganaṃ; saṅgati, saṅganaṃ.
Therein, *aṅga* refers to a limb or part of any given thing; it is also used for the body and for a cause. *Aṅgaṇaṃ*...

In some instances, the defilements (*kilesa*) are called "stains" (*aṅgaṇa*), as in the passage beginning, "Lust is a stain. For lust and the other defilements are called "stains" because by means of them, persons possessing them fall into a state of degradation.

In other instances, "stain" refers to impurity or mud, as in the passage beginning, "He strives for the abandoning of that very dust or stain. For a stain (*aṅgaṇa*) is so called because it anoints (*añjati*) or smears.
“Stain,” etc. In some instances, such an open space is referred to as a “shrine courtyard” (*cetiyaṅgaṇa*) or a “Bodhi-tree courtyard” (*bodhiyaṅgaṇa*), and so forth.
For it is called an *aṅgaṇa* because it manifests (*añjati*) that which stands upon it due to its extreme beauty; it is an open area of ground. Thus, in this way:
In the defilements such as lust, in the mire, and in the bodily stain;
And when a portion of ground is uncovered, the term "courtyard" (*aṅgaṇa*) is applied.
[The roots] *yugi* and *jugi* mean to avoid; thus: *yuṅgati*, *juṅgati*.
*Ragi* means to suspect; thus: *raṅgati*.

*Laga* means to cling (*saṅge*). The particle *ca* refers to what was stated immediately prior. It clings (*lagati*). Clinging (*lagana*) does not arise from *ca*. One is caught by a snare (*baḷise laggo*).
*Thaga* is in the sense of restraining; it restrains (*thagati*).
*Agga* is in the sense of moving crookedly (*kuṭilagatiyaṃ*). It moves crookedly, thus it is fire (*aggi*); the meaning is that it goes in a curved manner.
Fire has smoke for its crest, it is light, Jātavedas, the crested, the consumer;
Agginī, Bhānumant, Tejas, Pāvaka, Tivaka, Anala;
Hutāsana, Dhūmaketu, Vessānara, and Accimā.

The letter *ga*—as in *ghaṭāsana*, *vāyusakha*, *dahana*, and *kaṇhavattani*—along with these beginning with *gu* and ending with *agga*, those learned in the science of grammar call "foreign sounds" (*parassabhāsā*).
*Gā* is in the sense of going; thus, *gāti*.
*Gu* means sound (*sadda*).

*Gavati*: *uggame*. *Uggama* means rising or becoming manifest (*pākaṭatā*). *Gavati*. However, those learned in the science of grammar (*saddasatthavidū*) state that these [roots] belong to the *attanopada* (middle voice) as "gāte" and "gavate.
These are the forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *ga*.
The verbal root *gha* with the letter *kāra* as its suffix:

*ghā* in the sense of grasping a scent. *Ghāti*. *Ghānaṃ*. Having smelled a scent (*gandhaṃ ghatvā*). Herein, this is the canonical text (*pāḷi*): "Having smelled a scent, mindfulness is lost. But when this [root] has entered the *divādi* class, the forms become *ghāyati* and *ghāyitvā*.
The root *ghu*: in the sense of approaching. Approaching is the same as reaching (*adhigamana*). *Ghoti*.

*Jaggha* means laughing. One laughs (*jagghati*), one laughs heartily (*sañjagghati*). "He laughed with me" (*sañjagghittho mayā saha*). Even to laugh [now] does not seem fitting. Having laughed (*jagghitvā*). *Taggha* means protecting.

One protects (*tagghati*). *Sighi* means smelling. Smelling is the perception of odors by the nose. One smells (*siṅghati*), one smells closely (*upasiṅghati*). Having smelled closely (*upasiṅghitvā*). "I smell the water-born [lotus] from afar" (*ārā siṅghāmi vārijaṃ*). Those learned in the science of grammar call these "words belonging to another dialect."
*Ghu*: in the sense of sound. *Ghoti*, *ghavati*. *Raghi* and *laghi*:

in the sense of leaping in motion. Leaping in motion (*gatyakkhepo*) means the leaping (*akkhepo*) of movement (*gati*). *Raṅghati*, *laṅghati*, *ullaṅghati*. *Laṅghitā*, *ullaṅghikāpi*, and *laṅghitvā*. *Maghi*: and in the sense of desire.
The word *ca* (and) refers back to the preceding [meaning]. *Maṅghati*.
*Rāgha* and *lāgha* are used in the sense of capability (*sāmatthiya*). One *rāghati*; one *lāghati*.
*Dāgha* is used in the sense of exertion (*āyāsa*) and fatigue (*kilamana*). The particle *ca* refers back to the sense of capability.

One *dāghati*. *Nidāgho* (heat). *Silāgha* is used in the sense of praising (*katthana*). Praise is commendation (*pasaṃsana*). One *silāghati*. *Silāghā* (praise). "He praises the Buddha. Having praised. Those learned in the science of grammar (*saddasatthavidū*) say that these belong to the *attano-bhāsā* (the middle voice).
The forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *gha*.
Thus, the forms of verbal roots ending in the *ka*-group in the *bhūvādi* class are completed.
Roots Ending in *c*:
Now the forms of roots ending in the *c*-group are stated—*suc* in the sense of grieving.
*Socati*. Grief (*soko*), grieving (*socanā*), [the present participle] *socaṃ*, *socanto*, *socantī*, the family that is grieving (*socantaṃ kulaṃ*), having grieved (*socitvā*).
*Kuca* means to cry out (*tāra*). *Tāra-saddo* is a very loud sound. *Kocati*: the meaning is that one makes a loud noise.
*Kuñca* is used in the senses of crookedness and contraction. *Kuñcati*. *Kuñcikā*, *kuñcitakeso* (curly hair).
*Kuñcitvā* (having contracted). *Luñca* is used in the sense of pulling away. *Luñcati*. *Luñcako*, *luñcitum*, *luñcitvā*.

*Añcu* is used in the sense of going and worshipping. It goes along the path; it approaches the Buddha. Having gone upwards, it moves horizontally, thus it is *tiracchāna*. *Kaṭukañcukatā* (harshness). *Vañcu*, *cañcu*, *tañcu* are in the sense of going.

It deceives (*vañcati*), it moves crookedly (*cañcati*), it stretches out (*tañcati*), it honors (*mañcati*). There are feet that do not deceive (*avañcanā*). "Not deceiving" means incapable of going by way of deception.
*Gucu* and *gaṇecu* are in the sense of committing theft. Theft (*theyya*) is stealing, pilfering. The act of that is "committing theft. It steals (*gocati*), it pilfers (*gaṇecati*).
*Acca* is used in the sense of honoring; it means "he honors," as in *brahmāsurasuraccito*.
It is also used in the sense of harming; it means "it torments.
*Cacca* is used in the senses of birth, reviling, and censuring; it means "he censures" or "he reviles. *Jacca* is used in the sense of birth; it means "he is born."
In the context of contraction, shrinking back, withdrawal, and cleansing: *kuc* means to contract; it shrinks. Contraction (*saṅkoca*).
*Tac* means to cover; covering is protection. It covers; thus, skin (*taco*).
*Dic* is in the sense of praise; it praises (*dicati*).
*Kuc* means contraction. It contracts; it shrinks.
Contraction (*saṅkoca*). *Byāc* means making a pretext. Making a pretext is the act of prevarication.
It prevaricates (*byācati*). *Vac* means distinctness of speech. This belongs to one who is distinct; it is distinctness. In that distinctness, in speech, in clarity.
The intended meaning is that they speak. For speech is called "articulate" (viyatta) by way of the person who speaks articulately.

However, while sounds such as "kucchi," "tiracchānagata," and so forth are called "inarticulate sounds" (abyattasadda), the sound consisting of speech is not called an "inarticulate sound" because its meaning is understood. [Examples include: *vatti*, *vacati*, *vacanti*, *vacasi*, and so on.
The words *vāceti* and *vācenti*, etc., are examples of agentive (hetu-kattṛ) forms with the suffix -aya.
The words *atthābhisamayā dhīro paṇḍitoti pavuccati*, *vuccanti*, and *santo sappurisā loke devadhammāti vuccare*, etc., are examples of objective (kamma) forms.
However, the teachers (garū), by means of the substitution of *u* for the letter *va*, accept such forms as *uttaṃ*, *uccate*, *uccante*, and so forth.
These [terms] are not well-established in the Dispensation (Sāsana), as they conform to the Pāli language.

For in the Dispensation, regarding the insertion of the letter *ra*, the substitution of *u* for the vowel of the word preceded by *ni-* is established in the case of *nirutti*, *niruttaṃ*, and *nerutta*.
The following are nominal words: *vacanaṃ*, *vācā*, *vaco*, *vacī*, *vuttaṃ*, *pavuttaṃ*, *vuccamānaṃ*, *adhivacanaṃ*, *vattabbaṃ*, and *vacanīyaṃ*.

Grammarians learned in the science of language (*saddasattha*) declare that these forms beginning with *tumanta*—namely, *vattuṃ*, *vattave*, *vatvā*, and *vatvāna*—are "words for others" (*parassabhāsā*).
Among them, *vattī* means "he speaks"; this is indeed a verb-form (*ākhyātapada*). Commentators on the meaning (*atthasaṃvaṇṇaka*) have also cited the etymological derivation:
"Speech (*vācā*) is so called because one speaks (*vatti*) by means of it. And such a verb-form is seen in the science of grammar. Here, however, some say:

‘The forms *vacati* and *vacantī* and so forth, being verbal forms, should be discarded because they do not appear in the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*), in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), in the sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*), or in the treatises (*sattha*).
That is not so; for in the Dispensation (*sāsana*) both pure agent-words such as *avaca* and *avaciṃsu*, and causal agent-words such as *vāceti* and *vācentī*, are seen.
Therefore, even though they do not appear in the Buddha’s word and other such texts, [they are valid].
The forms such as *vacaṭi* and *vacaṇtī* are to be understood. [Optative: *vaceyya*, *vuccatu*, *vucceyya*.
All the rest is to be taken in detail everywhere.
We shall state the forms for the remote past (*parokkhā*): *vaca*, *vacu*. *Vace*, *vacittha*. *Vacaṃ*, *vacimha*. *Vacittha*, *vacire*. *Vacittho*, *vacivho*. *Vaciṃ*, *vacimhe*.
We state the forms for the past tense (*hiyyattanī*): *avaca*, *avacū*; *avaco*, *avacuttha*; *avocaṃ*, *avacumha*; *avacuttha*, *avacutthuṃ*;

*avacase*, *avacuvhaṃ*; *avaciṃ*, *avacamhase*. We state the forms for the present day (*ajjatanī*): *avaci*, *avocuṃ*, *avaciṃsu*; *avoco*, *avocuttha*; *avociṃ*, *avocumha*; *avocā*, *avocu*; *avacase*, *avocivaṃ*; *avocaṃ*, *avocimhe*.

We shall state the forms for the future tense (*bhavissanti*): *vakkhati*, *vakkhanti*; *vakkhasi*, *vakkhatha*; *vakkhāmi*, *vakkhāma*; *vakkhate*, *vakkhante*; *vakkhase*, *vakkhavhe*; *vakkhassam*, *vakkhamhe*.
However, the meaning of these words should be expressed as "he will tell" (*kathessati*), "they will tell" (*kathessantī*), and so forth.
Having stated *vakkhati*, *vakkhanti*, *vakkhasi*, etc., for the root *ruś* (to speak), at the end, in the place of the third person singular, [the form is]...
“*Vakkhemi*” (I shall speak) is what should be said. However, the meaning of these [forms] should be expressed as “*rosati*, *rosanti*,” and so forth.
This is the method for correlating the forms of the roots *vac* and *vakkha* according to the future and present tenses.
There are also other future forms associated with the root *vac*: *vakkhissati*, *vakkhissanti*; *vakkhissasi*, *vakkhissatha*.
I will speak, we will speak. He will speak, they will speak. You will speak, you (plural) will speak. I will speak, we will speak.
Here is the canonical text:
“Having traversed the cycle of existence through many aeons free from fear;”
“In this kappa, I shall proclaim the conduct [I have] practiced; listen to me.

Also, in the *Gadrabha-pañha*, the reading of the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) is seen as follows: “The king, having exchanged greetings with you, will say to the householder, ‘Recognizing a suitable seat, please sit down,’ and so forth; therefore, it is of such a nature.”

The *padamālā* (string of forms) has been composed. Regarding the root *vakkha*, the future tense forms (*bhavissantī*) including those with the suffix *-sa* are *vakkhissati*, *vakkhissantī*, and so forth.
However, their meaning should be expressed as *rosissati*, *rosissantī*, and so on.
This is the method for correlating the forms of the roots *vac* and *vakkha* specifically by way of the future tense.

*Avacissā*, *vacissā*, *avacissaṃsu*, *vacissaṃsu*. The rest is all to be understood (*neyya*). However, although the extraction of the meanings for the word *vutta* as used here ought to be stated, we shall explain it further on, because there is much more that must be said regarding it.

*Cu* (cu) in the sense of falling away. *Cavati*. In the causative, the form is *cāveti*. "Fallen from the host of devas" (*devakāyā cuto*). "A fallen lotus" (*cutaṃ padumaṃ*). Infinitive: *cavituṃ*; gerund: *cavitvā*.
*Loca* in the sense of seeing. *Locati*. *Locanaṃ*.
Seca in the sense of drying: it dries (secati).
Saca in the sense of speaking clearly: it speaks (sacati).
Kaca in the sense of binding: it binds (kacati).
*Maca*, *muci*, *kakkana*. *Kakkana* means rubbing on the body. *Macati*; *muñcati*. *Maci* [is used] in the senses of holding (*dhāraṇa*), cleansing (*ucchāya*), and honoring (*pūjana*).
These are the three meanings: holding, cleansing, and honoring. Among these, cleansing is the removal of dirt. *Mañcati*. *Mañco*, *mañcana*.
Because it holds a person, it is called a *mañca* (bed).
*Paca* means to cook. *Pacati*. *Pāko*, *paripāko*, *vipāko*, *pakkaṃ phalaṃ* (cooking, ripening, maturation, the cooked fruit).
*Thuca* means to brighten. *Thocati*.
*Vaca* and *vaci* mean to shine. *Vacati*. *Vaṅcati*.

*Ruca* is used in the sense of light (*ditti*) and shining (*rocana*). Light is radiance (*sobhā*); shining is *ruci*. It shines; thus, *verocana* (the sun). Truth pleases the ascetic (*samaṇassa rocate saccaṃ*).

For you, who desire heaven, solitude (*ekatta*) has become pleasing (*uparocitaṃ*). This root, taken in the sense of "liking" (*ruciattha*) within the *divādigaṇa*, produces the form "it is pleasing" (*ruccatī*).
By this, the canonical passage "going is pleasing to me" (*gamanaṃ mayha ruccatī*) is seen. [In] the *curādigaṇa*...

However, taking it in the sense of "to please," it generates verbal forms such as *roceti* (he pleases) and *rocayati* (he causes to please). Therefore, Pāli passages such as "Why do you not please birth?
(*kiṃ nu jātiṃ na rocesi*) are seen. This root belongs to the *gaṇa* [of roots].
*Paca* means "to cook" (*saṃpāke*). [Examples: *pacati*, *pacanti*. Those learned in the science of grammar (*saddasatthavidū*), however, state that this is in the *attano-bhāsā* (middle voice).
And in the sense of going away (*byayagati*). *Byayagati* means the state of destruction (*vināsagati*). It goes (*añcati*). And in the sense of begging (*yācanāyaṃ*):
"The brahmin begs the nāga for the jewel. "The nāga was begged for the jewel by the brahmin. "They begged that from him.
"He begged that chariot from him. "He begs Devadatta. Thus are the forms in the case of the simple agent (*suddhakattari*).
[They] exist. A brahmin asks, causes [another] to ask, causes [a third] to be asked, or causes [a fourth] to be caused to ask a nāga for a jewel by means of another brahmin.

Thus [it is used] with the causal agent (*hetukattari*). The king is asked, caused to be asked, caused to be caused to be asked, or caused to be caused to be caused to ask for wealth by means of a brahmin.
Thus [it is used] with the object (*kammani*). [The forms are: *yācaṃ*, *yācanto*, *yācantī*, *yācantaṃ* [referring to] a family; *yācamāno*, *yācamānā*, *yācamānaṃ*.

*Kulaṃ*. [The following are] nouns and forms ending in the *tumun* suffix and others: *yācako* (one who begs), *yācanā* (begging), *yācitabbaṃ* (that which is to be begged), *yācituṃ* (to beg), *yācitvāna* (having begged), *yācituna* (not having begged), *yāciya*, *yāciyāna*.

Regarding the root *pac* (to cook): *odanaṃ pacati* (he cooks rice). Grammarians learned in the science of language (*saddasattha*) say that it is "luminous on both sides" (*ubhayatobhāsā*). However, as in the Teaching (*sāsana*), [it is explained as follows]:
Regarding the statement “he is called wise” (*paṇḍito ti pavuccati*), the verbal form is established as the passive (*kamma*) of the root *vac*; it is not so for the root *pac*.
Nevertheless, the teachers state that its passive form occurs in the sense of the object (*kamma*) in such an expression as “rice is cooked by you” (*tayā paccate odano*).

However, in the Dispensation (*Sāsana*), the verb belonging to the *divādigaṇa*, whether stated without distinction as “is cooked” (*paccate*) or “cooks” (*paccati*), is exclusively intransitive (*akammaka*).
The construction [of the verb] must be understood as intended, because of such examples as: “Devadatta is being cooked in hell; until his evil is cooked. Here, some might say:
“This is a construction where the agent is the object (kammakattuppayoga), belonging to the *bhū* class (the first conjugation), just like [the expression] ‘the water drinks itself.
Therefore, by supplying the word ‘himself’ (*sayameva*), the meaning is: ‘Devadatta himself is being cooked,’ and so forth.”
It should not be said [that it acts by itself]. For in the case of the statement, "The drinking water drinks itself," it is people who drink the water;

the water does not drink the water. It is drunk by people alone, not by itself. Thus, although it is the object of the action (kamma), because the act of drinking is easily accomplished for another, it appears as if it were being accomplished by itself through the ease with which that act of drinking is performed.
Regarding the phrase "it becomes," the usage is made by way of common convention (*rūḷhi*), as in "the water is drunk by itself.
In the case of "the mat is being made by itself" as well, it is people who make the mat; the mat does not make the mat. It is by means of people that the mat is made, not by itself.
Thus, with reference to the action of making performed by another, even though it has become the object (*kamma*), it is easily made.

Because it is easy by virtue of the action itself, it is as if it were being accomplished by oneself; thus, the usage “the mat is made by itself” (*sayameva kaṭo kariyate*) is employed according to conventional idiom (*rūḷhi*).

Here, just as in the expression “water is drunk by water itself, not by us,” and “the mat is made by the mat itself, not by us,” because these usages pertain to the domain of transitive verbs (*sakammaka*), they convey a specific meaning consisting in the negation of another agent for the action.
It does not express a specific meaning in that way [as a reflexive pronoun] in instances such as "Devadatta is cooked in hell;
rather, karma is cooked," because the word *sayaṃ* (itself), which you have supplied, is absent from these usages due to their being intransitive in scope.

Likewise, in the case of "is cooked" (*paccati*), because the nominative form "Devadatta" and so forth expresses an agent who is intransitive—and because it expresses a pure agent devoid of an object—[the reflexive sense does not apply].

This should be understood as the form belonging to the *div-ādigaṇa*. If it is argued that the verbal root *pac* is not mentioned in the *div-ādigaṇa* in the science of grammar (*saddasattha*), [we reply:
whether it is not there or whether it is there, what does the science of grammar matter here? The Canon (*pāḷi*) alone is the authority.
Therefore, following the method of the Canon of the Blessed One—who is skilled in worldly convention—we include this verbal root *pac* within the *div-ādigaṇa* as well.
We shall insert [this]. For indeed, the application of the *div-ādi* group [of roots] as formulated by the teachers Dhammapāla, Anuruddha, and others, is seen [as follows]:
"Having assigned the excellent *ñāṇayutta* [suffixes] there, together with the threefold causal condition (*tihetuka*) for the junction;
subsequently, two [roots] are cooked among the cooked roots in the eightfold occurrence."
"Without volitional effort it ripens, and with volitional effort it ripens," and so forth.
However, in this context, this [interpretation] does not accord with the Pāḷi.

For even though the root *bhū*—which occurs in the *cur-ādigaṇa* as transitive and in the *bhūvādigaṇa* as intransitive—is itself transitive when occurring in the *bhūvādigaṇa*, [the text treats it otherwise].
Having reached the *div-ādi* group [of roots], they maintain that the root *pac*, which is intransitive, becomes transitive.

But how could such a thing be found in the Buddha’s word as preserved in the Tipiṭaka together with its commentaries? Therefore, in order to eradicate the doubts of those who hear the Blessed One’s teaching, we shall here establish this principle:
Even without a prefix, roots such as *pac* (to cook) and others become transitive or intransitive through connection with various modes of enumeration.

A man cooks rice (*odanaṃ pacati*). He cooked the cooking-vessel (*bhūtapacaniṃ paci*). Rice is being cooked (*odano paccati*). The object is being cooked (*kammaṃ paccati*). The grain-head (*vīhisīsaṃ*).
It cooks. Fruits of trees ripen. An elephant breaks down a wall. The embankment of a pond breaks. That which is subject to breaking breaks.
And here, having supplied the word *sayaṃ* (self), even when it is stated as “the rice itself cooks,” and so forth, [this applies] to such usages as:
“The man himself kills a living being,” or “The Blessed One himself awakened to the dhamma that is to be known.”

Because it is stated by way of prohibiting the action of another— just as one prohibits the act of killing arising from another’s command, or the act of awakening arising from another’s instruction— the conceptualization of the self as both agent and object (*kammakatta*) based on the word *sayaṃ* (self) is not authoritative.
For the word *sayaṃ* is seen even in the sense of a pure agent (*suddhakattū*), not only in the phrase "it is drunk by itself."
