In such cases as "pānīyaṃ" (water for drinking), the meaning is strictly that of the object; therefore, those who know the method should grasp the meaning in accordance with the teaching.
Even without a prefix and even without another verbal root, the roots beginning with *div* (to play) function as both transitive and intransitive in terms of their meaning.
One is intoxicated by the strands of sensual pleasure; one is intoxicated by enemies. Other [examples] should also be applied accordingly.
Furthermore, there are prefixes that function across groups of words even without a difference in meaning;
and there are those such as *gama* (village) and others, which may be used with or without an object depending on their application.
A person goes along a path. Knowledge goes into even profound matters. One practices the Dhamma. One moves here and there.
Even without [an object], there are three kinds [of verbs]: from the distinction of form, such as direction and so forth, and from the diversity of application, such as groups and obstacles.
One sees the palace, one beholds the palace, the palace is seen. Other [roots] should also be applied in this manner.
By their very nature, roots such as *rud* (to weep) and *dhā* (to place) are considered transitive (*sakamma*);
by their very nature, roots such as *nand* (to rejoice) and *dhā* (to hold) are considered intransitive (*akamma*).
Or they weep for the dead, mother; here one rejoices, and after death one rejoices.
Through the influence of prefixes, some [roots] become both transitive and intransitive;
likewise, some others become intransitive even when they are transitive.
Some [examples] with prefixes, some with objects, and some without objects—this meaning is illustrated here:
"A man goes out from the village," "He acquires wealth," "The man overcomes the living being," "The great rivers originate from the Himavat. Other applications should also be formulated accordingly.

In this regard, if there were a grammatical function (*kamma*) for the passive voice (*pacadhātu*) in the Teaching, then just as there is the usage "the action is performed by the man" (*purisena kammaṃ kariyati*), one would expect the usage "rice is cooked by the man" (*purisena odano pacciyati*).

As for those teachers who accept such forms as "by you the rice is cooked" (*tayā paccate odano*), they likely speak on the basis of the principles of grammar (*saddasatthanaya*). Even so, having investigated it:

If they are appropriate, they should be accepted. In the case of the causative (*kārita*), the following forms arise: "A man causes a man to cook rice" (*puriso purisena purisaṃ vā odanaṃ pāceti*, *pācayati*, *pācāpeti*, *pācāpayati*);
and "By means of a man, a man is caused to cook rice" (*purisena puriso odanaṃ pāciyati*, *pācayiyati*, *pācāpiyati*, *pācāpayiyati*).
In such instances as "Just as a cowherd with a staff causes the cows to go to the pasture," another meaning should also be understood.
*Pacaṃ*, *pacanto*, *pacantī*, *pacamāno*, *pacamānā*. *Pātabbaṃ*, *pacitaṃ*, *pacitabbaṃ*, *pacanīyaṃ*, *pacituṃ*, *pacitvā*.
And here, the usage “*imassa maṃsañca pātabbaṃ*” (and the meat of this [animal] is to be eaten) is an example.
The sequence of words beginning with “*pacati*, *pacanti*, *pacasī*” is easy to understand.
*Sica* in the sense of sprinkling. It sprinkles; *seka*. They say it is "bilingual" (*ubhatobhāsā*).
These are the forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *c*. [Now] the verbal root ending in the letter *ch*.
From this point on, I shall not explain the status of *parassa-bhāsa* (the speech of others) and so forth for all the grammatical roots (*dhātu*), for such has not been proclaimed in the Sāsana.
*Chu* means "to cut. It is *cho*. Having cut the *moḷi* (topknot) scented with excellent perfumes, [he said]: "Alas! O tree, you have become a source of grief."
*Milecha*: this is a word [derived from] *aviyatta* (uncultivated). One desires (*miletī*), thus a *milakkhu*. He is born among the borderlands, among the *milakkhus*, those who do not understand.
*Vachi* is in the sense of desire; one desires (*vañchati*). Desired wealth is *vañchitaṃ dhanaṃ*.
*Achi* is in the sense of stretching; one stretches (*añcati*). Or, while stretching long, he understands: "I am stretching long."
*Huccha* means crookedness. *Hucchati*.
*Muccha* refers to delusion and fainting. *Mucchati*. "He fainted from the force of the poison; he became unconscious. *Mucchā*, having fainted.
*Phucha* means dispersal. *Phochati*.
Yuccha means negligence; one is negligent. Uchi means scavenging;
*uñcha* is the act of seeking alms. One scavenges (*uñchati*). Strive for the practice of scavenging (*uñchācariyā*).
Ucha means thirst; one thirsts (*uchati*).
One asks questions; one who has asked, an asker, one who is asked, one who has been questioned, questioning. A bhikkhu asks a question of one who holds the Vinaya.

He asked; he asked for the sake of asking; having asked. And herein, questioning is fivefold: questioning to illuminate what is not seen, questioning to verify what is seen, questioning to resolve doubt, questioning for assent, and questioning out of a desire to speak.
The distinctions between these [words] should be understood from the *Aṭṭhasālinī* and other sources.
The root *viccha* is used in the sense of moving; thus, one moves (*vicchati*), and hence a centipede (*vicchikā*).

The root *vacchu* is used in the sense of cutting; thus, one is cut down (*vucchati*), and hence "cut," "one who has cut," or "one whose head is cut" (*vuttā*, *vuttavā*, *vuttasiro*). This is the substitution of *utta* for the vowel *a* following the letter *va*.
The word *vutta* is seen even in the sense of "shorn," as in such passages as: "The young brahmin student was shorn-headed (*vuttasiro*).
And here, by the word *sira* (head), the hair of the head is meant—just as the word *mañca* (bed) refers to the bedstead, and the word *cakkhu* (eye) refers to the consciousness dependent on the eye.
It is also used in the sense of "sown," as in: "Just as autumn seed, sown in a field, grows (*virūhati*)," and so forth. It is also used in the sense of "spoken."
In such passages as, “This was said by the Blessed One, this was said by the Arahant,” the following is stated:
The word *vutta* occurs by the influence of the verbal roots *vac*, *vap*, and *vas*;
it refers respectively to hair being shaved, seeds being sown, and something being spoken.
Another method: the word *vutta* is seen in the sense of "equalizing" (*vāpa-samīkaraṇa*) in such passages as “no ca kho paṭivuttaṃ.

In the sense of "mode of livelihood" (*jīvitavutti*) it occurs in such passages as “pannalomo paradattavutto. In the sense of "departure" (*apagama*) it occurs in such passages as “paṇḍupalāso bandhanā pavutto.

In the sense of "produced according to the tradition of the teaching" (*pāvacanavasena pavattita*) it occurs in such passages as “gītaṃ pavuttaṃ samīhitam. But in common usage (*loke*), as in “vutto pārāyano,” it is used in the sense of "spoken."
It is seen in the sense of study; here it is said:
"In leveling the soil, and also in the maintenance of life;
in the removal [of faults], and as it occurs by way of the sacred word (pāvacana)."
"The word *vutta* appears in these very [meanings] regarding study.

Another method: the word *vutta*, both with and without prefixes, occurs in such senses as sowing, leveling, shaving the hair, the means of livelihood, the state of being released, and in the sense of "speaking" with respect to study as it is practiced according to the tradition of the scriptures.
It is seen thus:
"Cattle are born for him, what is sown in his field flourishes,
and he eats the fruit of what has been sown— he who does not deceive his friends."
In such contexts as these, it occurs in the sense of sowing. In passages such as “but it has not yet sprouted,” it refers to the leveling of the ground with eight-toothed harrows and the like.

In passages such as “the young brahmin student Kāpaṭika, with shorn hair,” it refers to the removal of hair. In passages such as “with hair on his body, living on what is given by others, dwelling with a mind become like that of a deer,” it refers to the means of livelihood.
In the passage “just as a withered leaf fallen from its stalk,” it refers to being detached from its bond.
In such passages as "incapable of remaining green," it refers to the state of being released from bondage.

In such passages as "For whom this ancient mantra-word has been sung, uttered, and intended," it refers to that which has proceeded by way of the sacred word (*pāvacana*). But in common usage, in such phrases as "the group has been recited" or "the *Pārāyana* has been recited," it refers to the act of study (*ajjhena*).
Furthermore, in the passage "This was indeed spoken by the Blessed One: 'Heirs to the Dhamma... [it refers to what has been spoken].
“Be heirs to the Dhamma, monks, not heirs to material things”—in such sayings as these. Regarding this, it is said:
The verbal roots *vapa*, *vatu*, and *vacchuva* are considered [the source] for the word *vasa*;
whether accompanied by a prefix (*sopasagga*) or without a prefix (*nopasagga*), the word *vutta* is used accordingly.
One should understand [the term *vasati*] in the sense of shaving (*vapane*), making level (*vāpasamīkaraṇe*), and being shaven-headed (*muṇḍatāya*);
in the sense of being released from the livelihood of a householder (*jīvavuttyā pamuttatthe*) with respect to the sacred word (*pāvacanassa*);
and in the sense of having been set in motion (*pavattite*), studied (*ajjhene*), and explained (*kathane*).
*Taccha* in the sense of carving. *Tacchati*. A wood-carver [carves] wood.
These are the forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *c*. Now, the verbal roots ending in the letter *j*.
He conquered. He conquers. He conquers, he causes [others] to be defeated. Practicing the Dhamma, he defeats his master. Practicing the Dhamma, he is defeated.
They caused the king to conquer. Having caused him to conquer. Here, "they caused him to conquer" means they uttered words of benediction, saying, "May your majesty be victorious.
Victory, the conquered, victory, the vanquished, the Conqueror, the victor, the one to be conquered; Māra was conquered. Māra.
*jita*, *jitavā*, *jitāvī*, *vijitāvī*, *māraji*, *lokaji*, *oghijino*, *anodhijino*, *jito*. *Vijito*, *jetuṃ*, *vijetuṃ*, *jitvā*, *vijitvā*.
Furthermore, when this verbal root has reached the *kiyādigaṇa* (the class of roots beginning with *kri*), its forms become such as *jināti*, *jinitvā*, and so forth.
The root *ji* means "to overcome. Thus, one who conquers is a *jina*. Regarding the phrase "forms as they were before," here the Pāli passage—"Ānanda, this has been conquered by you, the true men;
future generations will look down upon rice with fish and meat"—establishes the sense of overcoming.
For in this context, "conquered" (*vijitam*) means "overcome" (*adhibhūtam*).

*Ju* in the sense of going. Here, "swift motion" is intended. It goes quickly; hence *javana*, *java*, *javaṃ*, *javanto*, *javanacittaṃ*, *javanapañño*, *javanahaṃso*. It goes with the speed of thought wherever it desires. *Jekhaye*. It is worn out. The vowel *e* is substituted for the vowel *a*.

According to the tradition of the scriptures, the Pāḷi text is seen as: "What would you wear me out with wealth? (*kiṃ maṃ dhanena jīyethā*). However, those learned in the science of grammar state that the form is "it is born" (*jāyatī*).
*Sajja* in the sense of going. It sets out (*sajjati*).
*Kuju* and *khuju* mean to deceive. One deceives (*kojati*), one seeks (*khojati*).

*Vaja* means going. *Dhaja* and *dhaji* are also used. One goes (*vajati*), one goes forth (*abbajati*); one attains human status (*manussattaṃ ca abbaje*). *Vaja*, *vajanaṃ*, *pavajanaṃ*, *pabbajjā*, *pabbajito*, *pabbājito*.
He was expelled (*pabbājito*) from his own kingdom and went to another country.
One should make a large storehouse for the storing of insults.
*Dhajati*, *dhajo*, *dhañjati*, *dhañjanaṃ*. Here, *dhaja* means a banner (*ketu*). *Dhañjana* means going. [The root] *aja* is used in the sense of driving away.
The letter *ca* here is dependent on the preceding verb *gati* (to go). *Ajati*, *ajo*. Here, *aja* means a goat (*eḷaka*). These, moreover, are its—
These are synonymous terms for "goat": *eḷaka*, *urabbha*, *avi*, and *meṇḍa*. In this context, *urabbha* refers to a goat, which is also called *aja*.
*Avi* is a red-haired goat. *Meṇḍa* is a goat with curved horns. For it is thus stated separately in the Janaka Jātaka: "the goat-chariot and the ram-chariot.
Furthermore, from the separate mention of "goats and sheep" (*ajeḷaka*) as goats and sheep respectively, [it is clear].
By the word *eḷaka*, even a ram (*meṇḍa*) may be understood, for in the commentary on the Mahosadha Jātaka it is stated that there is no distinction between rams and goats.
*Ajja* and *sajja* [mean] "rubbing. Rubbing is the act of rubbing. [The roots are: *ajjati*, *sajjati*.
*Kajja* [means] "distressing. Distressing is injury. [The root is: *kajjati*.
*Khajja*, *majjana*, and [the particle] *ca*. *Majjana* means purification. The particle *ca* implies affliction (*byathanā*).
*Khajjati*: "khajjūra" (date palm). *Khaja* means to churn; *mantha* means stirring. *Khajati*: "khaji" means deficiency in movement.
"Venerable sir, why does the noble one limp? "Both of them limp. Limping (*khañjanaṃ*), to limp (*khañjituṃ*), having limped (*khañjitvā*).
*Khaja* means to shake. *Ejā*: it moves; it shakes. Here, "it moves" (*ejāti*) means it moves and shakes in dependence upon gain and so forth; this is a name for powerful craving (*taṇhā*).
*Buja* is used in the sense of the sound of a thunderbolt. Some scholars say it refers to the roar of a thunderbolt. *Bojati*.
*Khija*, *kuji*, and *guji* are used in the sense of indistinct sounds. *Khijati*. *Kuñjati*. *Guñjati*.
*Laja*, *lāja*, and *tajja* [are used] in the sense of speaking. One speaks (*lajati*), one causes to speak (*lājati*), one urges on (*tajjati*).

*Laji* is also used in the sense of radiance. The letter *ca* is intended to include the sense of speaking. Thus, *lañjati*. The third is *naya-lañjaka*. One who indicates (*lañjeti*)—that is, makes known—the meaning of the Sutta is a "guide" (*lañjaka*).
*Jaja* and *jaji* are used in the sense of fighting. Fighting (*yujjhana*) is battle (*yuddha*). One fights (*jajati*), one causes to fight (*jañjati*).
*Tuja* means to strike. *Tojati*. *Tuji* means to strike;
"striking" (*balana*) refers to the act of striking. The particle *ca* (and) is used in reference to "striking. *Tuñjati*.
*Gaja*, *kuji*, *muji*, and *gajja* have the meaning of sound. *Gajati*. *Kuñjati*. *Muñjati*. An elephant roars; a cloud thunders.
Where a slave born of a slave woman stands, he roars loudly. The jewel roars. The roaring of knowledge roars.
One capable of roaring. A roarer. Having roared. In this context, "gaja" means an elephant. For an elephant has many names:
*hatthī*, *nāgo*, *gajo*, *dantī*, *kuñjaro*, *vāraṇo*, *karī*.
Mātaṅga, dvirada, saṭṭhi-hāyana, aneaka, ibha, thambha, ramma, and dvipa are terms for an elephant;
while hatthinī and kareṇukā refer to a female elephant;
hatthipota and hatthicchāpa refer to a young elephant; and bhiṅka and kalabha refer to a calf elephant.
*Ca* means to abandon. To abandon; to relinquish. Abandonment; relinquishment. The act of abandoning. One who abandons; one who is abandoning. One who is in the process of abandoning.
*Sañj* means to cling. Clinging; attachment. He clings. One who is attached. The act of clinging, attachment. Intense attachment. To cling. Having clung. *Īj* means motion. He moves.
*Bhaji* means to fry. *Bhajjanaṃ* is the act of heating. "He fries sesame seeds" (*tilāni bhajjati*). "Sesame seeds being fried by a man" (*purisena bhajjamānāni tilāni*).
*Eja*, *bheja*, and *bhāja* mean splendor. Splendor is radiance. [The roots] *ejati*, *bhejati*, and *bhājati* [express this]. *Tija* means sharpening and patience.
Sharpening is the making of something sharp. Patience is forbearance. [The roots] *tejati* and *titikkhati* [express these].
*Tejano*. *Tejo*. In this context, *tejana* means an arrow, a shaft, or a bolt; *tejo* means the sun.
Alternatively, *tejo* refers to piercing, heat, warmth, or burning. Or, *tejo* refers to power or majesty.
*Sañj* means to abandon; *parissagga* means embracing. It is so called because it clings (*sañjati*).
*Khaji* in the sense of eating and in the sense of going: *khañjati*, *khañjanaṃ*.

*Rāja* in the sense of radiance and in the sense of sharing: *rājati*, *bhājati*. [Derivatives: *rājā*, *rājinī*, *vanarāji*, *rājitvā*, *virājitvā*. Here, in order to produce skill in explaining the meaning for the wise, we shall compose a verse:
"O Great King! O Great King! It is indeed I who am the Great King!"
Having said "Not his," two people engaged in a quarrel.
And here, in the second word of the first line, the division is "me ahi mahī," as in "puttā me atthi puttā matthī";
and the division is "mahi arāja mahārājā," as in "yopi ayaṃ yopāyaṃ. Here, the word *arāja*—

In the phrase “*atikaramakarācariyā*,” the word *akara* should be understood as having the sense of an agent (*akarī*), like the noun *akara*, and is here used with the aorist verbal suffix (*parokkhāvibhatti*).
The meaning is: “The snake shone without a king. This, however, is the summarized meaning of the verse: “‘O Great King, my snake has no king;
my snake alone has no king, not his,’ having said this, the two snake-charmers engaged in a quarrel.”
*Rañja* means to color. A monk dyes his robe (*cīvara*). A sentient being (*satta*) is colored by forms and so forth. [The derivatives are:
coloring, a dyer, passion (*rāga*), dispassion (*virāga*), turmeric dye, a king (*rājā*), and a queen (*rājinī*).

And for this root, which has entered the *div-ādi* class, the forms *rajjeti* and *virajjeti* occur. Therein, "coloring" (*rajanam*) refers to the substance used for dyeing. "Dyer" (*rajako*) refers to one who performs dyeing, a washerman of clothes.
Beings become impassioned by means of it, or it itself is impassioned, or it is merely the act of impassioning—thus it is *rāga*, which is craving (*taṇhā*).
These, moreover, are its synonyms:
*Rāgo lobho tasiṇā ca, taṇhā ejā visattikā;* *Esanā pariyeṭṭhi ca, āsā vā icchā ca jappanā.* Craving, greed, thirst, craving, impulse, attachment, seeking, quest, hope, desire, and longing.
Power, attachment, and infatuation, as well as the state of being greedy and greed itself;
sensual desire, longing, and wish, as well as craving and yearning;
the forest and the thicket of the forest, as well as regard and the conduit to existence.
Entreaty and lust, attachment and the mire, the seamstress;
delight-lust, compliance, greed, and likewise the progenitress;
as well as the mother and aspiration—craving is thus manifold.
"Dispassion" (*virāga*) refers to both the Path and Nibbāna. "King" (*rāja*) refers to the lord of the earth.
Here, the etymologies are derived by way of two elements (*dhātu*). He is a king because he reigns, delights, and shines through various excellences.
Furthermore, he is a king because he causes the great multitude to rejoice in himself through these four bases of sympathy: generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality.
*Rājinī* is the wife of a king. Their designations are stated along with other synonymous terms:
Rājā, bhūpati, deva, manujinda, disampati, patthiva, jagatipāla, bhūbhuja, pathavissara.
The lord of the realm, the protector of the earth, the ruler of men, the sovereign of people;
the lord of men, the kshatriya, the master of the field, and the progenitor.
He is called the "anointed king" (muddhābhisitta-rāja), while the other is described as follows:
One who is called a *rājañño* or a *khattiyo* is one born of the kṣatriya caste.
One consecrated on the head is called an *anurājā* or an *uparājā*.
A king of the four continents is called a *rājarājā* or a *cakkavattī*.
*Rājinī*, *uparī*, *devī*, *mahesī*, and *bhūbhujaṅganā* are synonyms for a queen.
*Khattiyā*, *rājapadumī*, *khattiyānī*, and *khattiyī* refer to a woman of the warrior caste.
*Itthāgāra*, *orodha*, and *uparī* are also used to denote the women's quarters.
*Bhaja* means to serve. [The forms] *bhajati*, *bhajanā*, *sambhajanā*, *bhatti*, *sambhatti*, and *bhattā* [are derived from this root].

*Yaja* is used in the senses of worshipping deities (*devapūjā*), bringing together (*saṅgatakaraṇa*), giving (*dāna*), and dhamma. By the inclusion of "worshipping deities," the worship of the Buddha and others is also included.
"Bringing together" means to assemble or to bring into union. For instance, in the case of the Elder Adhimutta: "Whatever assembly there may be... [and so on, up to] "...existence."
In the verse, “...or wherever it may be found,” the word *saṅgata* is stated as a synonym (*samodhāna*). *Dāna* means relinquishment. *Dhamma* refers to meditation, virtue, and so forth.
The verbal root *yaj* (to sacrifice) functions with these meanings. One sacrifices to the Buddha with flowers; one sacrifices to a deity.
The Blessed One is sacrificed to by gods and humans; he is successful (*ijjati*). [The past participle is] *yiṭṭha*; [the nouns are] *yañña*, *yāga*, and *dhammayāga*.
The sacrificer (*yajamāna*) in his own city. *Yiṭṭhuṃ* means to sacrifice. Having sacrificed various offerings. Desiring to perform a great sacrifice consisting of sixteen requisites.
*Majja* is for cleansing. He cleanses. He wipes the exterior. He sweeps the ground. *Majjanaṃ*. *Sammajjanī*. *Niñji* is for cleansing. He cleanses. He washes away.

To cleanse. To wash away. Having cleansed. Having washed away. This passage, however, is: "Then you, Moggallāna, having risen from your seat and washed your eyes with water, should look around in the directions."
*Niji* means inaudible sound. *Niñjati*. *Bhaja* means to roast.
"The sesame seeds are being roasted. "And the sesame seeds being roasted. *Uju* means uprightness.
"Uprightness" is the state of being upright. *Ojati*. "Upright."

*Saj* occurs in the senses of clinging (*vissagga*), being attached (*parissajjana*), and scattering (*abbhukkiraṇa*). It is *sajati*. "The worldly water clings [to the shore]. *Ruj* means breaking (*bhaṅge*). It is *rujati*. *Rujā*. *Rogo*.

Here, *rujā* refers to disease in the sense of breaking. *Rogo*: it breaks and shatters the limbs and members; thus it is a disease, which is precisely what is called "affliction" (*ātaṅka*) or "sickness" (*ābādha*).

*Bhuj* means to bend (*koṭille*). Preceded by *ā-*, it is used in other senses as well. The serpent (*uraga*) bends (*bhujati*). He folds his legs (*ābhujati*). A monk [assumes] the cross-legged posture (*pallaṅka*).
"Ābhujati" means he folds [his legs], that is, he assumes the cross-legged posture (*ūrubaddhāsana*). "The great ocean *ābhujati*" means it whirls. Some, however, state the meaning is "it recedes.
"*Ābhujati* 'gift of color'" means he attends to it, that is, he brings it to mind.
"One who splits the roots" (*mūlavibhujo*) refers to a chariot; here, "splits" (*vibhujati*) means cuts. "Bhoga" (enjoyment/wealth). "Bhogī" (possessor of enjoyment/wealth).
*Ābhoga*. *Ābhujitvā*. Here, *bhoga* means that which makes one bend or become crooked; thus, *bhoga* is the body of a snake (*ahi*). A *bhogī* is a serpent. *Raj* means to smear.

A *nāga* smears the earth with its tusks; it stains (*ārañjati*). In this context, the passage from the *Nettipakaraṇa*, "‘Stained by the Tathāgata’ (*tathāgatarañjita*) as well," serves as the illustration.
Its meaning is: "This holy life of the Dispensation (*sāsanabrahmacariya*), comprised within the three trainings..."

“It is called ‘the place of coloring’ (ārañjanaṭṭhāna) because it is colored and stained by the tusks of the Tathāgata’s scent-elephant—the tusks of the great diamond-like knowledge of omniscience—or rather, it is the place where the phenomena of the three planes are colored.
For the word *ruñjita* means that which is colored or pierced therein; it is a place of coloring (*rañjanaṭṭhāna*), just as in the expression “this is their *padakkanta*” and so forth.
Success (*siddhi*) is to be understood from the occurrence of the meaning of the verbal root.
The root *vij* is used in the senses of fear and movement. This is a verbal root ending in the vowel *ī*; therefore, it has no forms with nasalized (*niggahīta*) vowels or inserted vowels (*āgama*).

Examples include: *vejati* (he trembles), *vego* (speed/impulse), *dhammasaṃvego* (spiritual urgency), *saṃvigo vegena palāyi* (the terrified one fled with speed), *nadīvego* (the current of a river), *ūmivego* (the force of waves), and *vātavego* (the force of the wind).
Here, "spiritual urgency" (*dhammasaṃvega*) is knowledge accompanied by moral dread (*sahottappa*). The terms *vega*, *java*, and *raya* are synonymous.
However, for the root belonging to the *div-ādi* group, the forms *vijjati*, *saṃvijjati*, and *ubbijjati* occur because it belongs to two groups. *Lajj* [means] in the sense of modesty.
It takes the forms *lajjati*, *lajjā*, and *lajjā*. *Lajjā* is moral shame (*hirī*), which is also called "the state of being ashamed" (*viruḷhanā*).
*Vaḷaji* means to use for enjoyment;
it is used (*vaḷañjati*). *Kujja* means to turn downward; one turns down (*kujjati*), turns down completely (*nikujjati*), turns up (*ukkujjati*), or turns back toward (*paṭikujjati*).
Or, one might turn up what has been turned down. One turns back toward another bowl. "I lay down face down. In this context, *kujjati* and *nikujjati* mean [to turn downward].
These terms, “carati” and “vicarati,” have the same meaning, for their sense is “to turn face downwards.
“Ukkujjati” means to turn face upwards. “Paṭikujjati” means to place face against face.
The root *mujj* is used in the sense of sinking. [From it derive: *mujjati*, *nimujjati*, *nimuggo*, *ummuggo*.
*Opuñjati* means to smear or plaster. One smears the ground with cow dung.
These are forms of verbal roots beginning with the letter *ja*. [Next are] the verbal roots beginning with the letter *jha*.

One reflects (*cintāyaṃ*). One meditates (*jhāyati*), contemplates (*nijjhāyati*), closely contemplates (*upanijjhāyati*), laments (*ujjhāyati*), and recites (*sajjhāyati*). Meditation (*jhānaṃ*), contemplation (*nijjhānaṃ*), close contemplation (*upanijjhānaṃ*), lamenting (*ujjhāyanaṃ*), and recitation (*sajjhāyanaṃ*). Contemplated state (*nijjhatti*). Preceptor (*upajjhā*, *upajjhāyo*). Meditator (*jhāyī*), reciter (*ajjhāyako*).

In this context, "meditating" is a twofold meditation: the beautiful and the unbeautiful. Of these, the beautiful is to be seen in such passages as, "The brahmin who meditates shines," and "I meditate, free from fear on all sides.
The unbeautiful, however, is [to be seen] in such passages as, "Meditating here and there..."
It should be understood from such passages as: “He sat down,” and “He sat down brooding with his face cast downwards. *Jhāyī*:

One who is in the habit of meditating (*jhāyanasīlo*), one whose nature is to contemplate, either by means of contemplation upon an object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) or by means of contemplation upon characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*). The meaning is: one who meditates, a meditator. *Ajjhāyako*:
This refers to those who say, “They do not meditate now, they do not meditate now,” Vāseṭṭha; thus they are called *ajjhāyakas*, that is, reciters.
"The third syllable has arisen"—thus did a word of reproach arise against those brahmins who were devoid of meditation (jhāna) during the time of the first eon.
But now, they recite that [Veda], hence they are called *ajjhāyakas*; by the sense of "one who turns over the mantras," people employ this as a term of praise.
Furthermore, this meaning is based on the rule: "The root *i* preceded by *adhi* [is used] in the sense of studying (*ajjhāyane*)."
It should be understood by way of its root-meaning (*dhātu*). Thus, through the prefix *adhi* and the root *idh*, there occurs a shift in the meaning of this root.
It is with reference to this that it is said: "a reciter, a bearer of the mantras.
The root *jhi* means to shine. A lamp shines; pieces of wood burn. Here, "it shines" (*jhāyati*) means it burns. For the words "shining" and "burning" are synonymous.
*Jajjha* is used in the senses of reviling and threatening. *Jajjhati*.
The root *ujjha* means to abandon (*ussagga*). Abandoning is casting away (*chaḍḍana*). *Ujjhati*. *Ujjhitaṃ*.
These are the forms of the verbal roots ending in the letter *jh*.

The verbal root beginning with *ñ* is *ñā*, meaning "to understand. Forms such as *ñāti*, *ñanti*, *ñāsi*; *ñātu*, *ñantu*; *ñeyya*, *ñeyyu*, etc., should be understood according to the grammatical rules (*yathāpāvacana*). [Derived nouns include:
*ñāti* (kinsman), *ñātaka* (relative), *añña* (other), *ñattaṃ* (understanding), *ñatti* (motion), *paññatti* (proclamation), *viññatti* (intimation), *saññatti* (persuasion), *saññā* (perception).
Recognition, wisdom, discernment, knowledge, and consciousness.

In this context, "one who knows" (*ñātī*) means one who understands. Again, "one who knows" (*ñātī*) refers to a kinsman; for he is called a "kinsman" (*ñātī*) in the sense that he is to be known as "this is ours.
Thus, he is a relative (*ñātaka*). "Another" (*añña*) means one who does not know or understand matters pertaining to the present life and so forth; thus, he is another, being ignorant and foolish.
*Attha*: meaning. *Ñatta*: the state of knowing. The canonical text provides the illustration: “As long as it leads only to harm, knowledge arises in the fool. *Saññāṇa*: a sign or mark.
In its causative form, such words as “ñāpeti,” “saññāpeti,” and “viññāpeti” occur.
Furthermore, because “aññāti” means to penetrate, one will know for oneself or for another; thus there is the faculty of “I shall come to know the unknown” (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*).

The textual passages “ekacce nabbhaññaṃsu” and “ekacce abbhaññaṃsu” are seen; therefore, words such as “ñāti” and others are indeed seen as verbal roots (ākhyātika-pada) by way of grammatical method (naya).
For instance, in the word “aññāti,” the prefix “ā-” is indicated, which has been shortened due to the desire for the pronunciation of a conjunct consonant following the subsequent syllable.
Thus, “ñāti” is seen in the Teaching (Sāsana) as a verbal root.
Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever in forming a series of words (padamālā) such as "ñāti, ñanti, ñāsī," and so forth.

The root *ñā* [is used] in the senses of killing (*māraṇa*), pleasing (*tosana*), and sharpening (*nisāna*). Killing is the act of cutting off the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). Pleasing is satisfaction. Sharpening is keenness. *Ñatti*: agreeable; designation.
Here, *ñatti* means "he kills," or "he pleases," or "he sharpens. And this word *ñatti* occurs in [the phrase]: "vatti..."
In the phrase “*etāyāti vācā*,” it should be understood that *eti* is a verbal form (*ākhyātika-pada*), just like the word *vatti*.

Likewise, in the word *ādatta*, there is the conjunct nature of the syllable *ti*—which is a case ending—just as there is in the syllable *te*; furthermore, there is the shortening of the vowel following the final consonant of the root.
*Manuñña*: it is called *manuñña* because it thoroughly (*ābhūsa*) knows (*ñā*) the mind (*mana*), that is, it satisfies it. This is the meaning.
It should be understood by way of the root *ñā* (to know) preceded by *ā*, with *manas* as its prefix.
"Instruction" (*paññatti*) means the making known (*ñatti*), that is, the killing (*māraṇa*), of unwholesome states by preventing their occurrence in various ways.

Alternatively, it is the production of manifold kinds of mental joy in those listening to the Dhamma through the teaching of the Dhamma. For those of extremely sharp intelligence, [it is] in manifold ways...
Furthermore, "paññatti" means making knowledge sharp; likewise, it should be understood as "making known" (paññāpana) through the gladdening and the fixing of the minds of listeners.
Thus end the forms of verbal roots ending in the *c*-group in the *bhūvādi* class.
The section on the *ṭa*-group roots.
Now, the forms of roots ending in the *ṭa*-group consonants are being stated.
Soṭu: in the sense of swallowing. To swallow is *dabbana*. He swallows (*soṭati*). Yoṭu:
in the sense of connection. He connects (*yoṭati*). Meṭu and mileṭu:
in the sense of madness. He goes mad (*meṭati*); he goes completely mad (*mileṭati*).
*Kaṭa* [is used] in the sense of covering. *Kaṭati*.
*Saṭa* [is used] in the sense of reviling. *Saṭati*.
*Laṭa* [is used] in the sense of childhood as well; the word "as well" (*ca*) refers back to the preceding [root]. *Laṭati*. *Lāṭo*.

*Saṭ* [is used] in the senses of breaking, spreading, going, and ending. *Rujā* means affliction (*pīḷā*). *Visaraṇaṃ* means spreading (*vippharaṇaṃ*). *Gatyāvasānaṃ* is the end of going; it is the conclusion (*osānaṃ*), the bringing to non-existence, which is what is meant by "sitting down" (*nisīdanaṃ*).

It breaks: *saṭati*. A *sāṭa* is called a garment (*sāṭaka*). *Vaṭ* [is used] in the sense of piercing (*vedhana*). It pierces: *vaṭati*. A *vaṭa* (tree). A *vāṭa* (fence). *Khiṭ* [is used] in the sense of frightening (*uttāsana*). It frightens: *kheṭati*. A hunter (*ākheṭaka*). Spittle (*kheṭa*). Frightened (*ukkheṭita*). Completely frightened (*samukkheṭita*).

*Siṭa* is used in the sense of disrespect; it forms *seṭati*. *Jaṭa* and *ghaṭa* are used in the sense of entanglement; they form *jaṭati*. [The nouns] *jaṭā*, *jaṭila*, and *jaṭī* [arise]. Examples include: "Internal entanglement, external entanglement; by entanglement, people are entangled" (*Antojaṭā bahijaṭā, jaṭāya jaṭitā pajā*). In the causative, there is the usage: "He shall unravel this entanglement" (*So imaṃ vijaṭaye jaṭaṃ*). At the moment of the path of Arahantship, one indeed unravels it.
*Bhaṭa* is used in the sense of service; it forms *bhaṭati*. [The noun] *bhaṭo* [is formed], as in: "Wages, a hired servant" (*Vetanaṃ bhaṭako yathā*).
*Taṭ*: to rise up. *Ussaya* means ascent, elevation, or height. It rises; thus, *taṭa*, mountain slope, riverbank, *taṭī* (eminence), *taṭaṃ* (slope).
*Khaṭ*: to sound (like a bell). It sounds; thus, *khaṭo*. *Naṭ*: in dancing. It dances;
thus, *naṭo* (actor) and *nāṭakaṃ* (drama).

The root *piṭ* occurs in the sense of a basket or a collection. It means "to contain" (*peṭati*). Thus, there is *peṭaka* and *piṭaka*. The word *piṭaka* is seen in the sense of the scriptures (the Tipiṭaka) in such passages as, "Not by the acquisition of the Piṭakas...
In such passages as, "Then a man might come along carrying a spade and a basket (*kudālapiṭaka*)," it refers to any kind of vessel.
The root *haṭ* occurs in the sense of radiance or beauty. It means "to shine" (*haṭati*). Thus, there is *hāṭaka* and *haṭaka*. That which is called *jātarūpa* (gold) is termed *haṭaka*.
*Saṭ* means "in a limb. It *saṭati*.
*Luṭ* means "to roll about"; it *loṭati*. *Ciṭ* means "to send";
it *ceṭati*. A *ceṭaka* is a servant.

The root *viṭ* means "to weave. From it come *veṭati* (he weaves) and *veṭaka* (a woven cloth). The roots *aṭ*, *paṭ*, *iṭ*, *kiṭ*, and *kaṭ* signify motion. From them come *aṭati*, *paṭati*, *eṭati*, *keṭati*, and *kaṭati*.
The nominal form *paṭo* is thus seen. It is called *paṭo* because it moves toward a state of decay (*jiṇṇabhāva*). *Paṭo* is a garment; for a garment has many names.
*Paṭa*, *coḷa*, and *sāṭaka* are cloth; *vāsa*, *vasana*, and *aṃsuka* are garments;
*dussa*, *acchādana*, *vattha*, *cela*, *vasani*, and *ambara* are clothing.
*Muṭ* means to crush; it crushes (*moṭati*).
*Cuṭa* means in the sense of becoming diminished. *Coṭati*.
*Vaṭi* means in the sense of dividing; *vaṭati*. *Vaṇṭo*.
*Ruṭi* and *luṭi* mean in the sense of stealing; *ruṇṭati*, *luṇṭati*. *Ruṇṭako*, *luṇṭako*.
*phuṭa* in the sense of dispersing: *phoṭati*, *phoṭo*.
*ceṭa* in the sense of service: *ceṭati*, *ceṭako*.
*ghuṭa* in the sense of turning over: *ghoṭati*.
*Ruṭa* and *luṭa* mean to strike back. One *roṭati*; one *loṭati*.
*Ghaṭa* means to exert oneself. One *ghaṭati*. *Ghaṭo*: a jar is called *ghaṭo*. These are its synonyms:
*ghaṭo*, *kumbho*, *ghaṭī*, *kumbhī*, *tuṇḍikīro*, and also *ukkhalī*.
*Mahantabhājanaṃ* means a large vessel; *atikhuddaṃ* means a very small bowl.
*Caṭa*, *bhaṭa*, and *deṭa* are used in the sense of speaking or reproaching. *Caṭati*. *Bhaṭati*. *Deṭati*.
*Kuṭa* is used in the sense of crookedness. *Kuṭati*. *Paṭikuṭati*.
*Puṭ* means to defile; it defiles (*puṭati*).
*Cuṭ*, *chuṭ*, and *kuṭ* mean to cut; they cut (*cuṭati*, *chuṭati*, *kuṭati*).
*Phuṭ* means to blossom; it blossoms (*phuṭati*).
*Muṭa* is used in the senses of throwing into fire, sound, and crushing;
it means *muṭati*. *Tuṭa* is used in the sense of quarreling; it means *tuṭati*.
*Ghuṭa* is used in the sense of striking back; it means *ghuṭati*. [The derivative] *ghoṭaka* [is formed from this].
Forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *ṭ*.
The verbal root *ṭhā* ending in *ṭh* is used in the sense of stopping movement. Stopping movement is the cessation of the motion arising for one who is walking. [Examples: *ṭhāti*, *ṭhanti*.
He stands. He is established. He resolves. He determines. He composes himself. He composes himself. He resolves. He attends. Let him stand.
Let him stand. May he stand. He stood, he stood. He stood, they stood, he stood, they stood.
As long as his body shall remain, it will stand. You will stand eavesdropping. He will stand, they will have stood.
*Atiṭṭhissā*, *atiṭṭhissaṃsu*. To stand; to attend upon; to serve; to resolve; to determine. Having stood;
having determined. Having attended upon; having determined. Standing, stability, firm standing, steadfastness.
Configuration, foundation. Attendant, one who stands. "Standing on a mountain," "standing on the ground. "Attending upon," and so forth.
In this context, the word *ṭhāna* is seen in the senses of sovereignty (*issariya*), stability (*ṭhiti*), opportunity (*khaṇa*), and cause (*kāraṇa*).

For instance, in such passages as, "But what deed did the Venerable Lord of Devas perform to attain this position (*ṭhāna*)?", it is used in the sense of sovereignty. In such passages as, "He is skilled in the positions (*ṭhānakusala*) and a marksmen who hits the unerring spot," it is used in the sense of stability.

In such passages as, "It occurs to the Tathāgata that this is the right occasion (*ṭhānasovetaṃ*)," it is used in the sense of opportunity. And in the passage, "Having known the possible as possible (*ṭhānañca ṭhānaso ñatvā*)... [it is used in the sense of cause].

In such passages as "the non-occasion and from the standpoint of non-occasion," it refers to a cause. For a cause is called a *ṭhāna* (a standing-point) because the fruit stands therein, owing to its state of being dependent upon that [cause] for its existence.
It also refers to sovereignty, to stability, and to a moment.
The word *ṭhāna* occurs in these four senses: in the sense of *ṭha*, which is synonymous with *sadda* (sound);
in the sense of *ṭhīyati* (it stands); in the sense of *ṭhe*, which means *veṭhana* (binding or wrapping); and in the sense of *ṭhāyati* (it remains).
*Paṭha*: in the sense of distinctness of speech; he recites the Dhamma. *Pāṭha*: a reciter, a reciter of the constellations (*nakkhatta-pāṭhaka*);
he asked the reciter of the horoscope: "He will become a master of all recitations. [The forms: *paṭhitum*, *paṭhitave*, *paṭhitvā*, *paṭhitvāna*, *paṭhituna*, *paṭhiya*, *paṭhiyāna*.
Although I wish to explain such a classification of the suffixes beginning with *-tuṃ* in every instance as appropriate, I refrain out of fear of excessive prolixity in the text.
We do not say so. Even when unelaborated, such a classification should be applied everywhere as far as possible according to the method (naya).
However, where a specific demonstration of the Pāḷi text and so forth is desired, we shall show it right there.
*Vaṭha*, *thūliya*. *Vaṭhati*. *Vaṭhara*. *Vaṭhara* is a term used for one who has a stout and thick body.
For it is said in the Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā: "Vaṭhara means 'stout'; and what is meant is that this bhikkhu is stout and has a solid body. [The root] *maṭh* means "to dwell.
He dwells (*maṭhati*). A dwelling (*maṭha*).
*Kaṭha* means a difficult life. *Kaṭhati*. One who performs this is a *kaṭha*.
*Raṭha* means to revile. *Raṭhati*. *Sāṭha* means by force.
"By force" (*balakkāra*) means the overcoming of one who is weak according to one's own desire by means of one's own strength. *Sāṭhati*. A *sāṭha* (is one who acts thus).
The roots *uṭh*, *ruṭh*, and *luṭh* mean to strike or injure: *oṭhati*, *roṭhati*, *loṭhati*.
The root *piṭh* means to harm or to defile: *peṭhati*; a *piṭhara* (pot). The root *saṭh* means deceit;
the word *ca* (and) refers back to the preceding meanings. *Saṭhati*; one who is *saṭha* is called a *kerāṭika* (a rogue or deceiver).
*Suṭhi* is used in the sense of obstructing movement. Obstructing movement is *gatipaṭighāta*. It means "it obstructs.

*Kuṭhi* and *luṭhi* are used in the sense of laziness. The letter *ca* (and) implies the previous sense as well. It means "it is sluggish" (*kuṇṭhati*) and "sluggish" (*kuṇṭho*). It means "it rolls" (*luṇṭhati*) and "rolling" (*luṇṭho*).
*Suṭhi* is used in the sense of drying. It means "it dries" (*suṇṭhati*).
*Ruṭhi*, *luṭhi*, and *aṭhi* are used in the sense of movement: *ruṇṭhati*, *luṇṭhati*, *aṇṭhati*.
*Veṭha* means binding: *veṭhati*, *nibbeṭhati*; [the nouns] *veṭhanaṃ*, *nibbeṭhanaṃ*.
*Vaṭhi* means solitary wandering: *vaṇṭhati*.
The roots *maṭh* and *kuṭh* mean to grieve; they signify to suffer or to be distressed.
*Eṭh*, *heṭh*, and *viheṭh* mean to afflict; they signify to trouble, to harass, or to cause injury. *Luṭh* means to strike back;
it signifies to repel or to resist. *Loṭhati*.
*Paṭh* means to recite; *paṭhati*. *Luṭh* means to roll;
*loṭhati*. These are the forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *ṭh*.
The verbal root beginning with *ḍa*:

*ḍi* in the sense of moving through the air and mere movement. *Ḍeti*, *ḍayati*; *ḍemāno*. "A bird flying high" (*ucce sakuṇo ḍemāno*). "Those who formerly flew up toward me" (*ye maṃ pure paccuḍḍenti*).
*Ḍi* in the senses of throwing and flying upward. *Ḍeti*, *uḍḍeti*.
"Outside of this [teaching], those heretics take pleasure in their own views;
I do not approve of their doctrine, for they are not skilled in the Dhamma.

And here, 'heretics' (pāsaṇḍā) means those who cast snares (pāsaṃ ḍentīti); the meaning is that they hurl the snare of views into the minds of beings. Alternatively, they are called 'heretics' because they cast and scatter the snare of craving and the snare of views."
Muḍi means to shave. He shaves. They shaved the prince. Shaven.
Cuḍḍa means to cause to shave. He causes to shave.
Aḍḍa means to attack. He attacks.
*Gaḍi* means "in one part of the face"; *gaṇḍati*, hence *gaṇḍa* (a swelling).
*Huḍi* and *piḍi* mean "to heap together"; *huṇḍati*, *piṇḍati*, hence *piṇḍa* (a mass).
*Hiḍi* means "in moving"; *hiṇḍati*, *āhiṇḍati*.
Kuḍi means to burn; kuṇḍati; kuṇḍo.
Vaḍi and maḍi mean to surround; vaṇḍati; maṇḍati; maṇḍalaṃ.
Bhaḍi means to revile; bhaṇḍati; bhaṇḍanaṃ; bhaṇḍo.
*Maḍi* means to adorn; *maṇḍati*, *maṇḍanaṃ*.
*Tuḍi* means to strike; *tuṇḍati*, *tuṇḍo*. One might go taking [something] with the *tuṇḍa*.
*Bhuḍi* means to support; *bhuṇḍati*.
*Caḍi* means anger. *Caṇḍati*. *Caṇḍo*. *Caṇḍālo*, *caṇḍikkaṃ*.
*Saḍi* means affliction. *Saṇḍati*. *Saṇḍo*.
*Taḍi* means striking. *Taṇḍati*. *Vitaṇḍā*.
In the sense of understanding (*paḍi*). It understands (*paṇḍati*). Wisdom (*paṇḍā*), a wise person (*paṇḍita*). Here, "wisdom" (*paṇḍā*) means discernment (*paññā*).
For that [discernment] understands—that is, it goes into—even subtle matters; it knows the modes such as the oppression of suffering and so forth, and thus it is called "wisdom" (*paṇḍā*).
A "wise person" (*paṇḍita*) is one who has gone by means of this wisdom, or who proceeds [by it]; or else, one in whom wisdom has arisen is a "wise person. It understands (*paṇḍati*).
One who goes by way of knowledge is also called "wise" (*paṇḍita*). For thus it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "They are wise because they are wise (*paṇḍanti*);
the meaning is that they proceed by way of knowledge regarding matters pertaining to the present life and the future life. The root *gaḍi* means to be intoxicated; [from it comes] *gaṇḍati*.
*Khaḍi* means to churn. *Khaṇḍati*. [Past participle: *khaṇḍita*, [noun: *khaṇḍa*.
*Laḍi* means to lick the tongue. *Laṇḍati*. [Noun: *laṇḍa*. These are the forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *ḍa*.
The verbal root beginning with *ḍa*:
*vaḍḍha* in the sense of increasing. *Vaḍḍhati*. [Derivatives: *Sirivaḍḍhaka*, *dhanavaḍḍhaka*, *vaḍḍhita*, *vuḍḍha*. And here, there is the substitution of *ba* for *va*, and *cu* for *a*.
*Kaḍḍha* in the sense of dragging. *Kaḍḍhati*, *ākaḍḍhati*, *nikaḍḍhati*. "Reluctantly they are dragged away, like crows by an owl."
These are the verbal forms of roots ending in the letter *ḍh*.
Roots ending in the letter *ṇ*:
*Aṇ*, *raṇ*, *vaṇ*, *bhaṇ*, *maṇ*, *kaṇ*—meaning "sound. *Aṇati* (he sounds). *Aṇako brāhmaṇo* (a Brahmin who makes a sound). *Raṇati* (he sounds). *Raṇaṃ* (noise). *Vaṇati* (he sounds).
Vāṇaka. He speaks: bhāṇaka. He thinks: maṇati, maṇika. He sounds: kaṇati, kāṇa. In this context, a *brāhmaṇa* is so called because he "breathes" (*aṇati*) the *brahma*;
the meaning is that he recites the sacred hymns (*manta*). However, etymologists say that a *brāhmaṇa* is "the offspring of Brahmā.
But the Noble Ones [call him] a *brāhmaṇa* because he has banished evil (*bāhitapāpa*).
*Brāhmaṇa*, *sottiya*, *vippa*, *bhovādī*, *brahmabandhu*;
*brahmasūnu*, *dvija*, *brahmā*, and *kamalāsanasūnu*.

The term *raṇa-sadda* (the word "conflict") occurs in reference to the defilements (*kilesa*) in such passages as "states with conflict" (*saraṇā dhammā*) and "states without conflict" (*araṇā dhammā*). For it is said that they are called "conflicts" (*raṇa*) because by means of them one "quarrels" (*raṇanti*) or "laments" (*kandati*).
“The incomparable archer, the mighty prince, having waged war against all his enemies, entered into self-restraint. Here, *raṇa* is used in the sense of battle.
For the phrase “having waged war” (*raṇaṃ katvā*) means “having fought” (*yuddhaṃ katvā*). “Grass and wood...”
In the passage, “Making a *raṇa*, they ran in all eight directions,” the word *raṇa* functions in the sense of being crushed to pieces.

For “making a *raṇa*” means “making [them] crushed to pieces. Thus, even this explanation of the meaning should be understood as having been made by taking the meaning designated by the word (*sadda*) itself and treating it as internal [to the root], rather than by way of a different meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*). Now...

Or rather, there may be a connection with the excellence of the meaning of the verbal roots (*dhātu*); therefore, it should also be understood that this explanation of the meaning has been made in that way.

*Bhaṇa* means "to speak. One speaks a *paritta*; one speaks words. A long reciter (*dīghabhāṇaka*), one who speaks pleasantly (*piyabhāṇī*), a section of recitation (*bhāṇavāra*). Herein, as for "a section of recitation" (*bhāṇavāra*):
"Eight syllables are a single word; a single verse (*gāthā*) consists of four words."
A single verse is considered a "bond" (gantha), and a bond consists of thirty-two syllables.
Fifty bonds make one hundred and twenty syllables, which is reckoned as one recitation-section (bhāṇavāra); it contains exactly one thousand eight hundred syllables.
Thus, the recitation is said to consist of eight thousand syllables.
*Oṇ* means "to remove"; it forms *oṇati*.
*Soṇ* is used in the sense of "color" and "motion"; it forms *soṇati* and *soṇo*.
*Soṇa*, *siloṇa*, and *saṅghāta*: [the roots] *soṇati* and *siloṇati*. *Ghiṇi*, *ghuṇi*, and *ghaṇi*:
[the roots] for grasping (*gahaṇe*): *ghiṇṇati*, *ghuṇṇati*, and *ghaṇṇati*.
*Ghuṇa* and *ghuṇṇa*: [the roots] for going (*gamane*): *ghoṇati* and *ghuṇṇati*.

*Paṇ* is used in the sense of trade and praise. *Paṇati*: a merchant; the meaning is that he carries out business. *Saddho buddhaṃ paṇati*: the faithful one praises the Buddha; the meaning is that he extols him. *Āpaṇa*, *sāpaṇo gāmo*.
*Gaṇ* and *raṇ* are in the sense of going. *Gaṇati*. *Raṇati*.
*Caṇ* and *saṇ* are in the sense of giving. *Caṇati*. *Saṇati*.
*Phaṇa* in the sense of movement: *phaṇati*, *phaṇaṃ*.
*Veṇu* in the sense of knowing, thinking, and attending: *veṇati*. *Pīṇa* in the sense of swelling:
*pīṇanaṃ* is fullness; *pīṇati*. *Pīṇo* means one who does not eat during the day; *pīṇorakkhaṃsabāhu* (one whose shoulders and arms are well-filled).
*Miṇ* means to injure; *miṇati*. *Duṇ* means to go;
the letter *c* is added for the sake of expressing injury. *Duṇati*. *Saṇ* means an indistinct sound;
*saṇati*. "The Brahmā forest resounds" (*saṇateva brahmāraññaṃ*). "Resounds" (*saṇateva*) means as if it were crying out.
*Tuṇa* means to bend. *Toṇati*. *Puṇa* means cleverness.

*Puṇati*, *nipuṇati*. One who possesses the quality of being clever (*nipuṇadhamma*). And here it should be understood that the words *nipuṇa*, *saṇha*, and *sukhuma* are synonyms, just as the words *kusala*, *cheka*, and *dakkha* are.
*Muṇa* means to acknowledge. *Muṇati*.
The root *kuṇ* means to sound or to prepare; it forms *koṇati*.
The root *cuṇ* means to cut; it forms *coṇati*.
The root *maṇ* means to abandon; that which abandons enmity (*vera*) is called *veramaṇi*.
*Phuṇ* is used in the senses of scattering and shaking. *Phuṇati*. "Others scatter charcoal into the pit.
These are the forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *ṇ*.
Thus end the forms of verbal roots ending in the *ṭa*-group in the *bhū-vādi* class.
The section on roots ending in *t*.
Now, the forms of roots ending in the *tavagga* (the *t*-group) are stated:

In the sense of protecting (*pālana*). Protection (*pālana*) means guarding (*rakkhaṇa*). It protects (*tāyati*); thus it is *tāṇa*, *gotta*, and *nakkhatta*. [It is so called] because of being a protector (*tātā*) from suffering (*agha*).

Wealth acquired through hardship—[the Buddha said], "I have dispelled that [suffering] by means of that [wealth]. In this context, *gotta* means: it protects speech (*gaṃ*) and intellect (*buddhi*), thus it is *gotta*.
For speech and intellect occurring as "Gotama," "Kassapa," and so forth, protect [the person] by guarding them through their exclusive referentiality.
Lineage (*gotta*). Just as cognition cannot exist without an object that serves as its referent, so too expression cannot exist without that which is expressed;
therefore, that meaning designated as "lineage" is said to "protect" or preserve those [names]. But what is it?
It is a common generic form shared by all members belonging to that clan, originating with the first ancestor of that family and not shared with other lineages.

"Constellation" (*nakkhatta*): it is called a "constellation" because it protects (*tāyati*) or guards (*rakkhati*) its movement by traveling along its own path rather than traveling on an irregular course.
That [constellation] is of twenty-seven kinds, according to the divisions beginning with Assayuja.
For instance: Assayuja, Bharaṇī, Kattikā, Rohiṇī, Migasira, Addā, Punabbasu, Phussa, Assalissa, Māgha, and Pubbaphagguṇī.
Uttaraphagguṇī, Hattha, Citta, Svāti, Visākhā, Anurādhā, Jeṭṭhā, Mūla, Pubbāsaḷha, Uttarāsaḷha, Sāvaṇa,
Dhanassiṭṭhā, Satabhisatta, Pubbabhaddapada, Uttarabhaddapada, and Revatī—
these are the twenty-seven lunar mansions (nakkhattas). They do not deviate even slightly from their own respective positions.
Without traveling by an uneven course— sometimes fast, sometimes slow, sometimes fast at one moment and slow at another, or here and there—
but rather proceeding along their own paths with a perfectly measured motion as if joined in sequence upon the wheels of a machine,
they revolve around Sineru in a circular form. Thus, these protect and guard against the wandering of the constellations (*nakkhatta*).
They are called *nakkhattāni*. However, the ancients, by way of their hard nature (*kharadhātu*), said:
"They do not decay (*na kharanti*), they do not perish (*na nassanti*), thus they are *nakkhattāni*. "Nakkhatta," "joti," and "rikka"—these are names for the constellations and stars.
"Uḷu," "tārā," and "tārakā"—these, however, are common names for all stars. "Osadhī," on the other hand, is the name for a specific kind of star.

*Citī* [is used] in the sense of marking (*saññāṇe*). Marking (*saññāṇaṃ*) means a sign (*cihanaṃ*), that is, making a characteristic mark (*lakkhaṇakaraṇaṃ*). It marks; the meaning is "it makes a sign.

Because it is stated with a long vowel ending in *-ī*, there is no insertion of the nasal *m* (niggahīta) from this root—as there would be from a root like *saki*—due to the rule regarding roots ending in *-ī*.
This same principle applies to other similar instances as well.

In the sense of going: *patati* (he falls). *Papatati*, *papātaṃ*, *papateyyahaṃ*. It should be construed with the word *ahaṃ*: the meaning is "I have fallen into the terrible hell" (*pāpattaṃ nirayaṃ bhusaṃ*).
It should be construed as "the tender youth has fallen into the terrible hell" (*pāpattha nirayaṃ bhusaṃ sokumāro*), the meaning being "he has fallen.
For these two are words in the past tense (*parokkhāpadaṃ*), just like in the examples "pāvadaṃ pāvadā" and so forth.
There is the lengthening of the prefix (*upasagga*), followed by the substitution of *tta* for the sound *a*, and the substitution of *ttha* for the sound *as*.
For the method of the Pāḷi is indeed inconceivable.

[The root] *ata* means "continuous movement" (*sātaccagamana*). Continuous movement is uninterrupted movement. It moves (*atati*). Furthermore, because the verbal root *ata* expresses the sense of continuous movement, [the form *attano* arises].

Therefore, since one who runs from existence to existence constantly wanders toward, reaches, and encounters the manifold suffering of saṃsāra—divided into birth, aging, sickness, death, and so forth—the etymology *attā* should also be accepted as "one who goes. Furthermore, according to another sense, it is said:

"It is called *attā* because the conceit 'I' (*ahaṃmāna*) is placed (*āhita*) therein; thus it is the *attabhāva* (the personal entity)," and also: "It is called *attā* because it consumes (*adati*) and experiences pleasure and pain."
The meaning of "attā" and "attamano" should be understood as "a mind seized by joy and gladness.
Wherever and in whatever way a meaning is applicable, there it should be grasped accordingly.
[The root] *cut* is used in the senses of sprinkling and harshness. It [the verb] *cotati*.
*Ati* means binding. *Antati* (it binds). *Antaṃ*. It is called *antaṃ* because it is bound by the intestinal coil (*antaguṇa*).

Here, the extraction of the meaning of the word *anta* is stated: in the phrase "the *anta*, the intestinal coil, the stomach," the *anta* refers to the putrid matter included within the thirty-two bodily constituents.
In the phrases "it decays inside the waistband" or "green *anta*," it refers to the ultimate limit or boundary (*antima-mariyāda-anta*).
“End” (anta) means: In the phrase, “Bhikkhus, this is the end of livelihoods,” it refers to the inferior end. In the phrase, “Personal existence is one end,” it refers to a portion or division.
In the phrase, “This indeed is the end of suffering, through the destruction of its cause,” it refers to the limit. Thus:
The end of a corpse, the final [existence], a boundary, and the inferior.
*Koṭṭhāsa* means a portion; it is expressed by the word *anta*.
The root *kit* [is used] in the senses of dwelling and removing disease. One dwells (*ketati*). *Sāketa* is a town; *niketa*, he entered his dwelling (*niketa*).

He goes joyfully to his dwelling (*sanniketa*). He treats (*tikicchati*), he heals (*cikicchati*), healing (*cikicchā*), a healer (*cikicchaka*). In that context, *Sāketa*— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "In that context, Sāketa," which appears to be the beginning of a commentary on the term.]
It is called *Sāketa* because it was the place where [the Buddha] took up residence in the evening;

there is an elision of the word *yam*. From *yata*, [comes] *patiyatana*. *Patiyatana* means the performance of effort (*vāyāmakaraṇa*). [Derivatives include: *yatati*, *yati*, *yatavā*, *payatana*, *āyatana*, and *lokāyata*.

Here, *āyatana* means "from extending" (*āyatanato*), thus *āyatana*; these are the eye, visible forms, and so forth. For these [faculties and objects] are the doors and the objects for consciousness and mental factors.
They are called "bases" (*āyatanāni*) because phenomena (*dhammā*) come toward (*āyanti*), arise, strive, and exert themselves within them for the purpose of experiencing and so forth.
Furthermore, the meaning of the word "base" may also be explained here by way of the root *i* (to go); this will be clarified further below.
The word *āyatana* (base) is used in the senses of a dwelling place, a mine, a meeting place, a place of birth, and a cause.

Thus, in such expressions as “the abode of the Lord in the world” (*loke issarāyatana*) and “the abode of Vāsudeva,” the word *āyatana* occurs in the sense of a dwelling place. In such expressions as “a mine of gold” (*suvaṇṇāyatana*) and “a mine of silver” (*rajatāyatana*), it occurs in the sense of a mine.
In the Dispensation (*sāsana*), however, in such passages as “In delightful abodes, birds frequent them,” it occurs [in the sense of a place of birth].

It should be understood that this term functions in the sense of a "gathering place," as in "The southern region is the abode of cattle"; in the sense of a "place of birth," as in "The southern region is the abode of cattle" and so forth;
and in the sense of a "cause," as in "In each respective case, he attains the capacity for realization whenever there is a suitable occasion (āyatana).
Furthermore, it should be grasped according to its various modes of occurrence.
The term *āyatana* is used in the sense of dwelling, shape, birth-place, cause, and meeting place.
As for what is called *lokāyata*: "Everything is impure; everything is pure. A crow is white; a crane is black. By this [it is defined].

And for this reason as well—referring to the teaching of the heretics (tīrthikas) associated with such useless arguments, which is called in the world "the science of caviling" (vitaṇḍa-śāstra), and concerning which the Bodhisatta, the peerless and wise Vidhura, said:
"One should not study Lokāyata; this does not increase wisdom"—by means of that, the world does not strive for its future welfare.
It is called *lokāyata* because it does not strive (*na īhati*). What is it? It is the science of caviling (*vitaṇḍasattha*).

For, relying on that treatise, beings do not even arouse the thought of performing meritorious deeds. Indeed, it is stated elsewhere: "The craft of *lokāyata* is that which proceeds according to such methods as 'the crow is white because its bones are white;
the crane is red because its blood is red,' [and so forth], regarding the next world and Nibbāna..."
"Vitaṇḍa-sattha-sippaṃ" means the craft of the treatise of cavil.
The roots *yuta* and *juta* mean "to speak. Speaking is uttering. [From these roots we have: *yotati*, *jotati*; *jutadittiyaṃ*;
*jotati*, *vijjotati*; *juti*, *joti*. In the causative form: "he illuminates" (*joteti*), and "having illuminated the True Dhamma" (*jotayitvāna saddhammaṃ*).
...the applications. And here, "light" (*juti*) means illumination or glory (*siri*). "Radiance" (*joti*) means brilliance. Alternatively, "lights" (*joti*) refers to the moon and so forth.
As it is said in the *Sīrimā-vimāna-vatthu-aṭṭhakathā*: "‘Light’ (*joti*) is a common name for the moon, the sun, the constellations, and the stars.
Or else, according to the expression "one who is light and whose destiny is light," it refers to anyone who shines because of being born into such families as those of the Khattiyas.
And because it is endowed with beauty of form, it is called "light" (*joti*).

It is white in color. The term "white element" (*sita-dhātu*) applies to the white color. Although a general similarity of color is mentioned here, nevertheless, among blue, yellow, and so forth, only the white color is to be understood here by way of observing its practical application. It is white; it is a white cloth.
However, because it follows the gender of the word it qualifies (*vāccaliṅgatta*), the word *seta* (white) should be understood as being of three genders.
"White, pale, pure, bright, radiant, and also brilliant;
non-black, fair, and clear—these are indeed the names for white."
*Vat* in the sense of turning: it turns, proceeds, evolves, follows along, revolves.

*Pavattaṃ* (the process). *Kil* in the sense of becoming wet: "becoming wet" means the state of being moistened. It means "it becomes wet," "it becomes thoroughly wet," or "it moistens. In the causative form, *pakiloteti* or *pakilotayati*. Having made it thoroughly wet in hot water; the meaning is "having moistened it.
*Vat* in the sense of requesting: *vatati*.
Kita: to know. Ketati. Ketanaṃ, ketako, saṅketo.
Kati: to produce thread. He weaves the thread (suttaṃ kantati).
Kati: to cut. He cuts meat; he carves it; an iron-cutter; a hero who cuts away the arrows. May the king’s cooks not carve [us] today in the kitchen.
*Catī* [is used] in the sense of harming or odors. Because it ends in the vowel *ī*, there is no insertion of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) after this root.
It means "it harms. These are the forms of the verbal root ending in *t*. [Now follows] the verbal root ending in *th*.

Regarding *thā* in the sense of the cessation of going (*gatinivatti*): *thā* means a state (*avatthā*), a defining characteristic (*vavatthāna*), that which is defined (*vavatthita*), and a thicket (*vanatha*).
For instance, in the verse, “Having cut down the forest and the thicket,” large trees are called the “forest,” while the smaller ones situated within that forest are called the “thicket.”
Praise. One praises, one extols. Praise, extolling, eulogy, laudation.
For if it were material, my wisdom would not equal the earth;
this is the fruit of the praise of knowledge for the Blessed One Anomadassi.
He is praised and extolled by them, by whom this knowledge has been extolled and the Best of Buddhas lauded. In this context, "extolling" (thavana) means praising (pasaṃsanā).
For there are many synonyms for praise: extolling, praise, acclaim, description, eulogy, celebration, laudation, praise, proclamation, and the recital of virtues.
In the case of *saddasaṅghātesu*: it is stuck (*thīyati*), it sticks fast (*patitthīyati*). Thus, "thī. Here are these scriptural passages:
"He becomes angry, he is provoked, he becomes malevolent, he sticks fast, and he manifests anger, hatred, and resentment"; and "Women reviled him.
In that context, the forms "thīyati" and "patitthīyati" have arisen through the substitution of the short vowel *i* (*ekārassa-iyādesa*). It sticks fast to the combination (*saṅghātaṃ*).
"She who has a womb (gabbha) goes" is *thī*. However, the teachers (*ācariya*) state that this etymological derivation applies only to the word *itthī*, not to the word *thī*.
"It is our preference that *thī* means 'she whose womb is fixed' (*thīyati etissā*);
the teachers [prefer] that *itthī* means 'she whose womb is fixed' (*thīyati etissā*)."
Regarding their most difficult instruction, the occurrence of the word "itthī" (woman):
this determination has been reached; O sirs, listen to my conclusion.
Since the word *itthī* has the same meaning as the word *thī*, therefore—
Having applied the meaning found in the word *thī* to the word *itthī*, the understanding of the plural for things that are few is appropriate when [the plural marker] is taken;
for there is the illustration: "two, duve; craving, *taṇhā*; thirst, *tasiṇā*."
Alternatively, one should demonstrate that the term "woman" (*itthī*) is established through etymological definition (*niruttilakkhaṇa*) as well,
by means of the addition of phonemes (*vaṇṇāgama*) and so forth:
she is a "woman" because she desires a man, or because she causes [others] to desire.
This etymology should also be understood by one who seeks etymologies.
Herein, these are the designations for women:
*itthī*, *thī*, *vanitā*, *nārī*, *abalā*, *bhīru*, *sundarī*.
*Kantā*, *sīmaninī*, *mātugāma*, *piyā*, and *kāminī*;
*ramaṇī*, *pamadā*, *dayitā*, *lalanā*, *mahilā*, and *aṅganā*—
these are also names for those very same women, distinguished by their particular states.
A *gorī* is a girl (*dārikā*), a maiden (*kaññā*), a young woman (*kumārī*), or a little girl (*kumārikā*);
a *yuvatī* is a young woman (*taruṇī*) or a maiden (*māṇavikā*); an elder (*therī*) is an old woman (*mahallikā*).
Thus, an eight-year-old is called both a *gorī* and a *dārikā*. A ten-year-old is called a *kaññā*. One who has not yet reached puberty...
Or, a young woman is called a "maiden" (*kaññā*). A twelve-year-old girl is called both a "virgin" (*kumārī*) and a "young girl" (*kumārikā*).

Furthermore, one who has not reached old age is called a "youthful woman" (*yuvatī*), a "tender woman" (*taruṇī*), or a "young lady" (*māṇavikā*). But when she has reached old age, she is called an "elderly woman" (*therī*) or an "old woman" (*mahallikā*).
This same method should be understood as applicable to men as well, according to their respective circumstances.
Although such a restriction has been stated here, nevertheless, in some instances, conventional usage proceeds even by way of non-restriction.
For instance, according to these two scriptural passages— “The king, taking the prince, and the princess, the girl”— and “The bear, the black antelope skin, the maiden”—
a woman who may be designated by the word *dārikā* (girl) may also be designated by the word *kaññā* (maiden).
She is to be called "born" (*jātā*). Furthermore, she who is to be called by the word *kaññā* is also to be called by the word *dārikā*.

Likewise, according to such Pāli passages as "the king, taking the prince, and the princess, the girl," and "to Kumāriyā Upasenī, who was always adorned with a necklet," that woman who is to be called by the word *dārikā* may also be called by the word *kumārikā*.
She is to be called "born. Furthermore, she who is to be called by the term *kumārī* (maiden) is also to be called by the term *dārikā* (girl).

Moreover, here from the sight of these two canonical passages—"a princess named Rucā" and "then they bathed her with the Maddi, the maidens having assembled"—it follows that whether she is one whose virginity has not been broken or one whose virginity has been broken, as long as she [remains so] until old age...
As long as she does not reach [that stage], it should be understood that she is still called simply a "maiden" (kaññā).

Here, some might say: "Regarding what you stated—that one who is eight years old and fair-skinned is called both a 'girl' (dārikā) and a 'maiden'—in this statement, [the term] 'eight-year-old' is used because of the expression: 'When I was a boy, eight years from birth.'"

[If it is argued: "Let him be a boy; for how could the Great King Vessantara—who, according to the text, 'saw the prince there sporting in his own city'—be appropriately called a 'prince' (kumāra) when he had been raised with wife and children and was over twelve years of age? [The answer is:
It is indeed appropriate, by virtue of the Blessed One’s intention. For the Blessed One, being the Lord of Dhamma and skilled in conventional usage, [speaks] whatever...
Whatever teaching he wishes to deliver that is suitable for those to be trained, that very teaching he delivers;
therefore, with reference to his parents' existence and the fact that he had been raised with the care accorded to a prince, the Blessed One gave this instruction.
For instance, because the Venerable Kumārakassapa had been raised with the care accorded to a prince, even though he was grown, he was still known simply as "Kumārakassapa" (the Prince Kassapa).

It is so designated. However, in the passage, “‘This boy did not know his measure,’” it should be understood that even though white hairs had grown on his head, the Venerable Mahākassapa—possessing excessive confidence in that elder—addressed the Venerable Ānanda as “boy” (*kumāra*) while instructing him using the term for a youth.
In the *Udāna-aṭṭhakathā*, however, [it says]: “Beings, from the day they are born...”

"From birth until the age of fifteen, they are called children and fools; beyond that, for twenty years, they are youths"—so it is said. *Mantha* and *mattha* mean to churn or stir. He stirs (*manthati*).

Taking both the churned mixture (*mantha*) and the honey-cake (*madhupiṇḍika*). He grinds down (*abhimatthati*) the dull-witted one with a diamond-hard thunderbolt-jewel. Having made Sineru the object of his churning (*mattha*).

*Kuthi*, *puthi*, and *luthi* mean to injure or defile. He injures (*kunthati*). "The kuntha, the kuntha-ant. Having seen his own fallen son, soiled with dust (*paṃsukunthita*). He gathers together (*punthati*). He rubs away (*lunthati*).
*Nātha* [is used] in the sense of requesting (*yācana*), distressing (*upatāpa*), sovereignty (*issariya*), and wishing (*āsīsā*). The root *nātha* occurs in these four meanings:
requesting, distressing, sovereignty, and wishing. Therefore, the ancients said: “He is called a *nātha* because he *nāthati*;

he wishes for and aspires to the welfare and happiness of those to be trained (*veneyya*), or he distresses the afflictions and calamities residing in the mental continuum of others. ‘It is good, monks, that a monk...’”
The meaning is that [the Blessed One] requests various beneficial practices by saying, “From time to time, one should reflect upon one’s own perfection,” and so forth.
Alternatively, he is called the “Protector” (nātha) because he possesses supreme mastery over the mind, or because he rules over and surpasses all beings with his virtues;
thus, he is the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord (paramissara). As for those learned in the science of grammar (saddasatthavidū), they say: “He protects, therefore he is the Protector.”
Regarding those four meanings, they recite two verbal roots: *nātha* and *nādha*.
However, because it belongs to the *attanopada* (middle voice) conjugation, its forms are *nāthate* and *nādhate*.
Here one might object: "If *nātha* means 'one who begs' (*yācanatthena nāthati*), then in that case, anyone who is a beggar or poor would be a *nātha*."
“Would he alone be a protector (*nātha*)? But one who is successful without begging does not protect nor does he beg; thus, would he be ‘without a protector’ (*anātha*)? No.
For the word *nātha*, while occurring in the sense of begging and so forth, is conventionally established among superior persons by way of worldly designation.
And the Blessed One is preeminently the most superior among the superior; therefore, because he begs for this or that practice conducive to welfare, such is the meaning of the word *nātha*.

It has been said. Furthermore, the word *anātha* is conventionally established among ordinary people as meaning "one who has no protector" (*na nātho ti anātho*), or "one for whom there is no protector" (*natthi nātho etassāti anātho*).

This is by way of negating the presence of a protector (*dabbapaṭisedhavasena*), and not by way of negating the root-meaning as "one who does not seek refuge or does not entreat" (*na nāthati na yācatīti anātho*).
For one who serves as a refuge, a resort, and a foundation for another—
A protector (*nātha*) is one who is not a refuge, a resort, or a support for another, nor does he have another as his own refuge, resort, or support;
such a person is called "without a protector" (*anātha*) by way of conventional designation (*saṅketa*). For it has been said:
"Conventional speech is true, being the cause of worldly consensus. To clarify this meaning, at this point [the text says]: "The Lord of the World (*lokanātha*)."
“You alone are the refuge for all living beings,” and “Be a protector for those who are without a protector”—
having reflected thus, I gave away hundreds of millions of wealth to both those with protectors and those without, and then departed for the Himalayas.

The Pāḷi passages serve as illustrations. For in both the Dispensation and the world, one who begs is not called a "protector" (nātha), whereas one who does not beg is called "without a protector" (anātha).
In the world, however, that which is a refuge is called a "protector. One for whom no refuge exists is called "without a protector";
likewise, one who has attained success is called a "protector," while one who has not attained success is called "without a protector. Therefore:
The wise person, in all instances, should grasp the meaning according to its fitness, without overstepping worldly convention by relying merely on the etymological sense of the elements (*dhātu*).
This principle should be carefully kept in mind. [The root] *vi-thu* means "to beg.
[The root] *vi-tha* means "to surround."

*Satha* means crookedness (*seṭṭhilla*). One is "crooked" (*sathati*). For wandering with a crooked mind scatters even more dust [of defilement]. The reading *siṭhila* is also seen; in that case, the suffix *-ṭhi-* should be understood as a variant form of *-ṭhika*.
*Kathi* means crookedness (*koṭilla*). One "twists" (*kanthati*). *Kattha* means praise (*silāghā*).
One "boasts" (*katthati*) or "prattles on" (*vikatthati*). There are the terms *katthanā* and *vikatthanā*. In this context, *katthati* means...
He praises. "Boasts" (*vikatthati*) means he boasts in an improper manner, because he illuminates (proclaims) matters that are non-existent. In this context, there are such applications as:
"Though he may boast much, having gone to another country," and "In this case, someone is a boaster, a great boaster;
he boasts: 'I am endowed with virtue,' or 'I am endowed with proper conduct'—thus he boasts. Etc.

Regarding "byatha" in the sense of being shaken by fear and suffering: *byathati*. Those whose minds are wavering and shaken are called "byathita. Then, the princes, having heard the hunter's speech, were no longer shaken (*abyathitā*).
Thus, this pair consists of both "calan" (wavering) and "byathan" (being shaken). *Sutha*, *kutha*, and *katha* pertain to injury: *sothati*, *kothati*, *kathati*.
*Patha* pertains to going: *pathati*. "Patha" means a way; it is a path (*magga*). That is twofold: that which is to be traversed on foot by the common people...
The natural path (*pakatimagga*) and the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), which is designated as the "way of practice" (*paṭipadā*) to be followed by wise people seeking Nibbāna.
In this context, the natural path is called a "path" (*patha*) because it is traveled (*pathiyati*) or gone upon by people who have both duties to perform and duties yet to be performed;
however, the way of practice is traveled by sons of good family who, desiring to go to the great city of the Deathless, take up the provisions of faith (*saddhāpātheyya*).

"Path" (*patha*) means that which is to be practiced (*paṭipajjiyatīti*). Alternatively, it is "path" because it causes the person who acts (*pātheti kārakaṃ puggalaṃ*) to go, or brings them to the attainment of Nibbāna;

thus it is simply the way of practice (*paṭipadā*). We shall discuss the designation "path" (*magga*) in the section concerning the verbal root *magg* within the *curādigaṇa*. [The root] *katha* is used in the sense of accomplishment.
It is conjugated as *kathati*.
*Matha* means to roll about. *Mathati*.

*Potha* means in the sense of going around. *Pothati*. *Pothaka*. This root *potheti* also occurs in the *curādigaṇa*; therefore, the usage "they should go all around, striking [them] on the four sides" (*samantā anupariyeyyuṃ, nippothentā catuddisā*) is seen.
*Gottha* means in a bamboo pole. *Gotthati*. *Gotthula*, *gotthu*.
Puthu means "in detail" or "extensively. Pothati means "to strike. Puthavī means "the earth.
These are forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *th*. [Now follows] the verbal root ending in the letter *d*.
*Dā* means giving. Preceded by *ā*, it means taking up. A person of faith gives a gift, he bestows it; he takes up virtue, he adopts it.
These are pure agent-words (*suddhakattupada*), because they indicate that [action] itself. A person of faith causes one who lacks faith to give a gift, to take up virtue, to adopt it.

"The virtuous cause others to take up the Dhamma itself"—these are words of causation (*kāritapada*) and are also called words of causal agency (*hetukattupada*), because they indicate that [action]. By means of faith, the gift...
It is given (*dīyati*), virtue is taken up (*ādīyati*), it is formally undertaken (*samādīyati*); these are verbal forms because they illuminate that [meaning].

Furthermore, this root *dā*, meaning "to give" (*dāna*), having entered the *divādi* class according to the tradition of the scriptures, produces pure agent-nouns with the same stem-forms—such as "he sleeps" (*dāyati*), "he slumbers" (*niddāyati*), and "sleep" (*niddā*)—while expressing the action of sleeping.
When it expresses giving and breaking apart, it is said: "it is given" (*diyati*).
When expressing "giving," it generates the verbal roots *dā* and *da*, which are pure agentive forms.
When expressing "purifying," it generates the verbal roots *dāya*, *vedāya*, and *vodāna*, which are pure agentive forms.

However, in this *bhūvādigaṇa*, when expressing "giving" with the prefix *ā*, and when expressing "taking," it produces [the following forms]: *dadāti*, *deti*, *ādadāti*, *ādeti*, *dānaṃ*, and *ādānaṃ*.

It generates synonymous terms that are pure agent-words (*suddhakattupada*). Likewise, when speaking of "going in a censurable way" (*kucchitagamana*), it generates synonymous terms such as "one who cuts" (*dāti*), "one who cleanses" (*sudda*), "a *sudda*," and "a *suddī*," which are pure agent-words; this distinction is to be observed.
And just as here, so too elsewhere, those who know the method (*naya*) should examine the distinctions according to what is possible.
Now we shall explain its nominal forms beginning with those ending in *-tu*.
One should apply such forms as: *dānaṃ*, *deyyaṃ*, *dātabbaṃ*, *brahmadeyyaṃ*, *dinnaṃ*, *dāyako*, *dāyikā*, *dakkhiṇā*;
and likewise: *dātuṃ*, *padātuṃ*, *dātave*, *padātave*, *datvā*, *datvāna*, *dadātuna*, *daditvā*, *daditvāna*, *dadiya*, *dajjā*, *dadiyāna*, *ādātuṃ*, *ādāya*, *ādiya*, and so forth.
In this context, "giving" (*dāna*) means that which is to be given, or that by which one gives; thus, both the object to be given and the volition of giving are so called.
Why, then, is only the word *dinna* (given) used there, and not the word *datta*? There is a reason for not using it.
For in expressions such as "giving has been given," the word *datta* is not seen in place of the word *dinna*; therefore, it is not used.
The word *dattha* (given) is not seen as a derivative of the root *dā* (to give) in the utterances of the Victor (*jinabhāsita*),
such as the phrase "a gift was given by me with the mind" (*manasā dānaṃ mayā dinnaṃ*),
where the form *dinna* occurs; nor is it found in expressions such as "Devadatta," "Yaññadatta," or simply "Datta."
It is seen in the statement of conventional designation (*paṇṇatti*), both through compound and analysis.
