"yodhetha māraṃ paññāvudhena" (fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom); yuddhaṃ; caraṇāyudho or caraṇāvudho (one whose weapon is his feet); āvudhaṃ (weapon). However, for this root belonging to the *divādigaṇa*, the form is "yujjhati."
*Dīdhi* occurs in the sense of splendor (*dittivedhana*). *Dīdhati*. *Dīdhitī*. And here, *dīdhitī* means a ray (*rasmi*). For there are many names for a ray:
*rasmi*, *ābhā*, *pabhā*, *raṃsi*, *ditti*, *bhā*, *ruci*, *dīdhitī*;
*marīci*, *juti*, *bhānu*, *asu*, *mayūkha*, *kiraṇa*, *kara*.
*Nāgadhāma* and *āloka*—these are words denoting rays. These are forms ending in the letter *ca*.
[Now follows] the verbal root ending in the letter *na*.
To lead; not so; leads; leads away. Having removed distress from the heart. Brings; brings along. Leader. Trainer. Guide.
One to be led. One to be trained. One who trains. A person who is disciplined. While being led by a demon, father, what indeed does he look at? Being led. The means of leading. The guide.
The bond of existence has been uprooted. One who possesses the guide. For those who dig channels lead the water. The channel.
When one has gone straight and upright: *nettaṃ*, *nayanaṃ*, *vinayaṃ*, *āyatanaṃ*, *netuṃ*, *vinetuṃ*, *netvā*, *vinetvā*, and so forth.
In this context, *nettaṃ* means that which leads the personal existence (*attabhāva*) toward what is even or uneven; thus it is the eye (*cakkhu*). *Nettī* means that by which beings are led;
thus it is a rope (*rajjū*). *Bhavanetti* means the rope of existence; this is a name for craving (*taṇhā*), for by it beings—
Like oxen bound by the neck, they are led to this or that state of existence; therefore, it is called "the guide to existence" (*bhavanetti*).

"Guiders" (*nettikā*) refers to farmers. A "guide" (*netta*) is the leader of a herd, the bull. "Leading" (*naya*) means the act of leading, going, or guiding; it is the course of the text. Alternatively, "leading" (*naya*) means that which is to be led here and there;
it is the mode of being led through similarity. It is "led" (*nīyati*), thus it is a "leading" (*naya*); such as the "Leading of Suchness" (*tathattanaya*) and so forth.
"Leading by means of this" is *naya* (method), such as the method of avoiding the two extremes and so forth.

For thus there are six kinds of methods: the method of suchness (*tathattā-naya*), the method of attainment (*paṭipatti-naya*), the method of teaching (*desanā-naya*), the method of avoiding the two extremes (*antadvayavivajjana-naya*), the method of the inconceivable (*acinteyya-naya*), and the method of intention (*adhippāya-naya*).
Among these, the method of suchness is led by the method of avoiding the two extremes.
The method of the attainment (*patti-naya*) is led by way of the inconceivable method; the method of the teaching (*desanā-naya*) is led by way of the intentional method.

Herein, the first threefold method is called "method" (*naya*) because it is led by means of the objective case (*kamma-sādhana*); however, the latter threefold method is called "method" because it is led by means of the instrumental case (*karaṇa-sādhana*), as in the expression "by this [it is] the triad of methods such as suchness. When this meaning is elaborated upon...
The expansion of the text might be extensive; therefore, it has not been shown here in detail. There is yet another fourfold method:
the method of identity (*ekattanaya*), the method of difference (*nānattanaya*), the method of non-agency (*abyāpāranaya*), and the method of suchness (*evaṃdhammatānaya*).
It is called *vinaya* because beings are disciplined (*vineti*) therein, or by means of it; it is also *vinaya* because it disciplines body and speech. It is called an *āyatana*.
The suffering of saṃsāra, which has proceeded through a beginningless past and is exceedingly long, continues and indeed proceeds as long as it does not cease;
thus it is called an *āyatana*.

This, however, is the extraction of the meaning here: "In the phrase 'Kamboja is the *āyatana* of horses, the Southern Road is the *āyatana* of cattle,' *āyatana* means a place of birth (*sañjātiṭṭhāna*). [And]: 'In delightful *āyatanas*, birds frequent them.'"
In the passage, “Those seeking shade go to the shade; those seeking fruit go to the fruit-eating [tree],” it refers to the place of convergence (*samosaraṇaṭṭhāna*).

In the passage, “Monks, there are these five bases of liberation (*vimuttāyatana*),” it refers to the cause (*kāraṇa*). Furthermore, other applications are explained in the sense of “that from which one proceeds.
The root *nī* means “to lead away. It forms *neti*, *nayati*, and *nayanaṃ*.
Now for *thu*: *noti*, *navati*, *nuto*.
Now, however, for the roots *than* and *dhan* in the sense of sound: *thanati*, *panati*, *dhanati*.
For *kan* in the sense of beauty and luster: *kanati*, *kaññā*, *kanakaṃ*.
And herein, she is called *kaññā* because she shines (*kanati*), gleams, and radiates due to the charm of her form while remaining in the state of youth;
or alternatively, she is called *kaññā* because she is desired (*kaniyati*) and longed for by men—thus, a young woman.
As for *kanaka*, it is so called because it shines (*kanati*) or because it is desired (*kanīyati*); thus, it is gold. For gold indeed has many names.
Suvaṇṇa, kanaka, hema, kañcana, and also haṭaka;
jātarūpa, tapanīya, vaṇṇa— and furthermore,
its varieties are said to be jambunada, siṅgika, and cāmikara.
Regarding *vana-saṇa-sambhattiyaṃ*: it seeks (*vanati*), thus it is a "forest" (*vana*). It gathers (*sanati*);

therein they seek (*vananti*) and those beings such as peacocks and cuckoos share (*sambhajanti*) it, thus it is a "forest," meaning the wilderness (*arañña*). It seeks and shares with a person of defilement (*saṃkilesapuggala*), thus it is a "forest," meaning craving (*taṇhā*).
Regarding *mana-abbhāse*: it cognizes (*manati*), thus it is "mind" (*mano*).
*Māna* (pride) is for the purpose of *vīmaṃsā* (investigation);
it investigates. *Vīmaṃsā*. [The roots] *jana* and *suna* are for sound. It produces (*janati*) and it hears (*sunati*).

And here, the canonical text provides the illustration: “Why does one of your arms produce [sound], while the other arm of yours does not produce [sound]? In that context, “it produces” (*janati*) means it makes a sound by hearing.
*Khanu* means to dig in the sense of breaking open. *Sukhaṃ*, *dukkhaṃ*. A pit has been dug (*khato*).
Therein, *sukhaṃ* means it digs well; thus it is *sukhaṃ*. It digs badly, [causing] bodily and mental suffering;
thus it is *dukkhaṃ*. For these phenomena are mutual opposites. Alternatively, it is *dukkhaṃ* because it digs the mind in two ways. According to the *cur-ādi* class [of roots].
However, the etymologies should be understood as: "it brings happiness, thus it is happiness (sukhaṃ)"; "it brings suffering, thus it is suffering (dukkhaṃ).
Furthermore, there are also etymologies according to the analysis of compounds: "it is easily endured, thus it is happiness"; "it is difficult to endure, thus it is suffering.
For indeed, the derivation, the occurrence, and the cause of words are manifold.
*Dāna* is in the sense of breaking. *Dānati*. *Apadānaṃ*.
*Sāna* is in the sense of sharpening. *Tejanaṃ* means whetting; [the root] *sānati*.
*Hana* is in the sense of harming and going. Here, however, by the word "harming," both the oppression through harsh speech and the striking with sticks and so forth are intended.
It is included; therefore, the meaning of *hana* should be understood as "killing," "injuring," or "taking away. For instance, it is said: "Kings, having seized a thief, might kill him or bind him.

When those commenting on the meaning of this passage state, "‘Might kill’ means they might beat him and cut him," here "cutting" refers to the cutting off of hands, feet, and so forth, or by way of decapitation.
Or it means killing. For *han*, there is a substitution of *vadh* and a substitution of *ghāt*; thus: *hanti*, *hanati*, *hananti*; *hanasi*, *hanatha*.
All the rest is to be understood accordingly.
Four meanings, beginning with injury (*hiṃsā*), are obtained. However, in the phrase "he strikes with hands and feet," *hanti* means "he strikes" (*paharati*).
The meaning is: "For one who is angry kills his father; crying out with fierce [anger], he kills each of them in turn.
Here, *hanti* means "he kills" (*māreti*). There are also such forms as *vadhati*, *vadheti*, and *ghāteti*. In that regard, in passages such as:
"He strikes [but] does not weep—this is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Having struck himself again and again, he weeps," etc., [the term is used].
*Vadha* means striking. To strike a living being (*pāṇa*) is *pāṇavadha*. In such passages as “This is the killing (*vadha*) of Khaṇḍahāla;
he causes beings to be slain,” *vadha* means slaughter.
In the phrase “the sandal, the bride (*vadhū*),” the meaning of the words *hana* and *vadha* is going. [In the phrases] “he strikes a man” and “cold, heat...”
"Paṭihanati" and so forth are agentive words (*kattupada*). "Devadatto yaññadattena haññati" (Devadatta is struck by Yaññadatta).
"Tato vātātape ghore, sañjāte paṭihaññati" (Then, when a fierce wind and heat have arisen, he is struck back). The singular form of the nominative case (*paccattavacana*) is as in "vanappagumbe.

The word "vihārena" is to be connected [with these]; "iccādīni" (and so forth) are objective words (*kammapada*). Hantā (the slayer). Hato (the slain). Vadhako (the killer). Vadhū (the wife). Āghāto (hostility).
*Upaghāta*, *ghātaka*, *paṭigha*, *saṅgha*, *byaggha*, *sakuṇagghi*; *hantuṃ*, *hanituṃ*, *hantvā*, *hanitvā*;
*vajjhetvā*, *vadhitvā*—these and others are words ending in the infinitive suffix (*tumu*) and so forth that share the same root.
In this context, *upāhana* means that which goes toward (*upahanti*) and approaches (*upagacchanti*) various places, and from there strikes back (*āhananti*) and returns (*āgacchanti*).
"By this" means by a sandal. "A woman" (*vadhū*) refers to one who has the habit of approaching [a man] due to the influence of the defilements;
this term is common to all women. Alternatively, "woman" (*vadhū*) means a daughter-in-law. For instance, in the passage:
"Therefore, daughter-in-law, when you have reached your season and your flower has appeared, then you should inform me," here the word "daughter-in-law" (*vadhū*) is used. She...
Furthermore, she is called a *vadhū* because she is to be approached and recognized by her mother-in-law and father-in-law with the thought, "This is the wife of our son.
This meaning is indeed obtainable because, in some instances, verbal roots meaning "to go" (*gati*) are explained as having the sense of "to understand" (*buddhi*).

*Suṇhā*, *suṇisā*, and *vadhū* are synonyms. *Saṅgha* refers to the community of monks (*bhikkhusamūha*). It is so called because it approaches (*samupagacchati*) a united (*samagga*) formal act (*kamma*).
The Saṅgha is so called because it thoroughly destroys the defilements, or because it slays them by means of the various weapons of the Path;

these terms are stated according to the distinction between ordinary persons (puthujjana) and noble ones (ariya). It violently strikes and causes various beings to be slain, thus it is a "tiger" (byaggha);
that same word is also called "viyaggha" and "vaggha. Furthermore, "puṇḍarīka" is another name for it. It kills weak birds, thus it is a "bird-hunter" (sakuṇagghi).
The root *sen* (to strike), however, belongs to the *divādi* class and generates an intransitive agentive form in the sense of "it strikes back" (*paṭihaññati*).
Indeed, such scriptural passages as "the discourse of the Blessed Buddha strikes against the worldly ear" (*lokiye sote paṭihaññati*) are seen.

*Ana*: in the sense of breathing. Breathing (*pāṇana*) is the act of inhaling (*sasana*). It breathes (*anati*). Thus: *āna* (inhalation) and *pāna* (exhalation). In this context, *āna* is inhalation (*assāsa*), and *pāna* is exhalation (*passāsa*).
Regarding these, it is stated in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*: "In-breathing (*assāsa*) is the wind exiting outward; out-breathing (*passāsa*) is the wind entering inward.
However, in the *Suttanta-aṭṭhakathās*, this appears in reverse order.
In that context, because for all those dwelling in the womb, at the time of emerging from the mother's womb, first the internal wind exits outward, and afterwards the external wind [enters].
Taking up subtle dust, it enters within and is extinguished upon striking the palate; therefore, it is stated in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*:
"In-breathing (*assāsa*) is the wind going out, and out-breathing (*passāsa*) is the wind entering in.

Regarding these two methods, according to the method of the Vinaya, in-breathing is the breath arising within, and out-breathing is the breath arising without. According to the method of the Suttas...
However, even though it arises externally, it is an inhalation (*assāsa*) from within the body; even though it arises internally, it is an exhalation (*passāsa*) from outside the body.

And this same principle applies to the passage: "For one who follows with mindfulness the beginning, middle, and end of the inhalation, both the body and the mind become agitated, disturbed, and trembling due to the mind being distracted internally," and likewise for the beginning, middle, and end of the exhalation.

It should be understood that this accords with the following canonical passage: “For one who pursues [the object] with mindfulness, because the mind has become distracted externally, both the body and the mind become agitated, perturbed, and trembling.
[The term *dhana* means wealth. Wealth is the acquisition of prosperity; the meaning is the attainment of glory, merit, and wisdom. For it is the sense of the word *dhātu*.
It is generally explained according to the sense of "being" (bhāva), with the exception of specific categories such as the bark of the *vakka* tree and so forth.
Just as the word *thenanaṃ* becomes *theyyaṃ* by changing the letter *n* to *yy* in conjunction with the suffix *ya* when it expresses the sense of "being," so too here,
by changing the letter *n* to *ññ* in conjunction with the suffix *ya*, the word *dhananaṃ* becomes *dhaññaṃ*.

It is so called. Alternatively, *dhañña* is the state (*bhāva*) of one who possesses wealth (*dhana*); [it refers] to that *dhañña*. It destroys (*dhanti*), it moves (*dhanati*). [The past participle is] *dhanitaṃ*; [the noun is] *dhaññaṃ*.

However, since the attainment of glory, merit, and wisdom is included by the word *dhañña*, therefore in such passages as "she gave birth to a son endowed with the characteristics of *dhañña* and merit" (*dhaññapuññalakkhaṇasampannaṃ puttaṃ vijāyī*), only glory and wisdom are to be understood by the word *dhañña*, because merit (*puñña*) is mentioned separately.
“O bull among men, those who behold your face as you roar amidst the assembly, striking the chords of the musical instruments,
are truly fortunate. Your fingers are long, your nails are copper-colored, your hands are beautiful, and your heels are broad.”
“Those who shall bow at his feet are also fortunate, O bearer of virtues.
Those who shall hear his words— which are sweet, joyful, faultless, and beneficial— they too are the most excellent of men.”

In such passages as these, however, by the word *dhañña* (grain/wealth), the accomplishment of merit (*puññasampadā*) is to be understood; or rather, along with the accomplishment of merit, the accomplishment of glory and wisdom (*siripaṇṇāsampadā*) is also to be understood.
This is the etymological derivation here: "They possess glory, merit, and the accomplishment of wisdom, thus they are *dhaññā*.
But in the phrase "Grain is considered auspicious," it means that this [grain] is to be cherished and trusted as "this is the supreme treasure" (*uttamaratana*).
The meaning "endowed with prosperity," "endowed with glory," and "endowed with merit" is also appropriate.
Furthermore, in passages such as "grain, wealth, silver, and gold," because of the statement "there is no wealth equal to grain," *dhañña* means that which is to be valued as wealth; what is that?
It is the primary crop (*pubbaṇṇa*). Moreover, a specific medicinal herb is also called *dhañña*. [This is] regarding the word *dhana*.
Furthermore, by way of compound, a person who is destitute is called "adhana" or "niddhana," meaning one for whom there is no wealth (*natthi dhanaṃ etassa*).
However, in the phrase "he goes to destruction" (*nidhanaṃ yāti*), "destruction" (*nidhana*) is said to mean perishing, based on the verbal root *dhū*,
which expresses the sense of shaking or moving.

In the sense of "knowing" (muna gatiyaṃ): *munati*. In the sense of "conceiving" (cine maññanāyaṃ): this root is without elision (*alutta*), just as in *gile* and *mile*. *Cināyati*, *ocināyati*. Here, the canonical example (*pāḷi*) is: “Sabbo taṃ jano ocināyatū” (“Let all that people conceive [or disregard] it”). *Ocināyati* means “let him conceive [or disregard]” (*avamaññatu*).
Thus end the forms of roots ending in the *tavagga* (dental stop) class in the *bhūvādigaṇa*.
The End of the Section on *Pakāra*.
Now, the forms of the verbal roots ending in *vagganta* are being stated:
*Pā* means "to drink. *Pānaṃ* means "the act of drinking. Forms such as *pāti*, *pānti*, *pātu*, and *pāntu* should be applied accordingly.
"Quickly stretch out your neck; I will not give you life!
For this arrow, discharged by me, shall drink your blood."
For here, "pāssati" means "he will drink. According to the method beginning with "pāssati, pāssanti; pāssasi, pāssatha;
pāssāmi, pāssāma," and according to the method beginning with "apassā, apassasuṃ," all the remaining forms should be applied by those who know the grammatical method.
For who is capable of extracting all the various scattered jewels of verbal forms from the ocean of the Buddha’s word?
In order to demonstrate this, therefore, only the mere method for grasping all the verbal roots (dhātus) in brief has been shown.
*Pivati*, *pivanti*; *pivaṃ*, *pivanto*, *pivamāno*; he drinks the water of the Bhāgīrathī. In the causative (*kārita*), "he causes the prince to drink milk.
For a moment, you were made to drink milk by me, which allays thirst. In the passive (*kamma*), *pīyati*, *pītaṃ*. In the infinitive and other forms (*tum-ādi*), "to drink" (*pātuṃ*).

Forms such as *pivituṃ*, *pitvā*, *pivitvā*, and *pāyetvā* should be applied accordingly. In other instances as well, verbal forms should be constructed in this very manner, in accordance with the method of the Pāḷi.
[The root] *pā* means "to protect. *Pāti*. *Nipāti*. *Pitā*, *gopo*.
The root *pā* means "to fill. From it come *pāti* (protector) and *vippāti*.

*Vippo*—that is, a brahmin—is so called because he "fills" (*vippeti*). For he fills the world’s expectations through his own brahminical duties, such as the recitation of the Vedas with distinction, and he fills his own heart with the Vedas;
thus he is called a *vippo*. As it is said: "I was born into a family of *vippas*."
For here, a brahmin is called a *vippa*. His family is a *vippakula*. [The root] *pū* means to purify (*pavana*). It purifies (*pavati*).

[From this come] *putta* (son) and *puñña* (merit). Here, a son is called *putta* because he purifies (*pavati*) and cleanses his own family. However, having reached the *kiy-ādi* group [of roots], it should be stated as "he purifies" (*punāti*).
A son is also called *atrāja*, *suta*, and *sūnu*.
A son is called *tanuja* or *tanaya*;
furthermore, sons, grandsons,
and so forth are designated as *apacca*.
When the feminine gender is to be expressed, "puttī" (daughter) and "atrājāti" (born of the mother) should be used;
in the remaining places, one should utter [the appropriate forms] as is fitting.
For in the Pāḷi, the feminine "atrājāti" is spoken of as "puttī."
And here: “Then,
after two weeks had passed, the beloved daughter of the King of Videha,
the princess named Rucā, spoke to her nurse and mother.”
This Pāḷi passage is an illustration. "Puttī, dhītā, duhitā, attajā"—these are synonyms.

Thus, because the feminine gender is seen for words denoting a woman, such as *atrajā*, the method for determining the feminine gender should also be examined in the case of words like *suta* (son) and others, according to whether the feminine form is found or not.
For instance, in common usage, terms such as *vessa*, *sudda*, *nara*, and *kiṃpurisa* appear in pairs.
Feminine gender markers denoting women are seen in such terms as *vessī*, *suddī*, *nārī*, and *kiṃpurisī*.
However, because terms such as *puriso* and *pumā* exist in pairs [with their feminine counterparts], feminine gender markers denoting women are not seen here.

As for the word *puññaṃ*, it is called *puññaṃ* because it purifies (*pavati*) and cleanses (*sodheti*) its own agent; alternatively, having reached the *kiyādi* group of roots, it should be stated that it is *puññaṃ* because it purifies (*punāti*).
Another meaning may also be stated, based on the characteristics of etymology;
therefore, the derivation should be understood here as "that which produces the worship of people" and so forth.

It is called *puñña* because it generates further states of being worthy of worship (*pujja*). Or, it is called *puñña* because it causes one to always be worshipped (*pūjita*). It is called *puñña* because it purifies (*punāti*) people from their own misconduct. It is called *puñña* because it purifies (*punāti*) all demerit (*apuñña*) without exception.
One should designate *kalyāṇa*, *kusala*, *puñña*, and *subha* as synonyms for wholesome merit.
The term *adhi* is used skillfully in the expression of wholesome action (*kamma*).
... [In the sense of] going: *peti*, *penti*; *pesi*, *petha*. Here, monks, a certain wild colt, when told "go! (*pehi*), [acts accordingly].
Being pierced and urged by the charioteer, he retreats backward; he turns the chariot back from behind.
He takes to a wrong path; he makes the chariot go in reverse.
... [omission] ... He exerts himself toward decline. "Prosperity" (pāya) and "decline" (apāya). Here, "decline" (apāya) means there is no prosperity or growth there; thus it is called decline.

The meaning may also be derived by way of the *ayadhatu* (the root *i*, "to go"): it is an *apāya* because it is gone away from (*apeta*), or because it has departed from increase (*vuddhi*) or happiness (*sukha*). [These are] the hells, the animal womb, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the host of asuras.

... [The root] *suś* means to dry up. It causes to flow (*pāyati*) or flows (*payati*). *Nipaka*: here, *nipaka* is so called because one lies down (*nipayati*) and dries up the adversary, or because one lies down and protects (*nipāti*) oneself;
thus it means being fully aware (*sampajāna*). The root *gup* means to protect. One protects (*gopati*). A protector (*gopaka*).
Just as a frontier city is guarded both within and without, so should you guard yourself;
let not the opportune moment pass you by. "Guard" means one should guard, one should protect.
Vapa means to sow; it is used as *vapati*.
Sapa means to join together; it is used as *sapati*.
Cupa means slow movement; it is used as *copati*.
*Tup* means to injure. *Topati*, *tuppati*.
*Gup* means to hide and to loathe. *Gopati*, *jigucchati*. *Jigucchaṃ*, *jigucchamāno*, *jegucchī*, *jigucchitvā*, and so forth.
*Kapu* means to injure, to calculate, and to perfume. *Kappati*. *Kappūra*.
*Kapa* means to be capable. This is allowable for us; this is not allowable among us.
*Kapa* is in the sense of compassion. It means to pity. A *kapaṇa* (miserable person), the state of being miserable (*kāpañña*). In that context, *kapatī* means to feel compassion;

*kāpañña* means the condition of being miserable. *Sapa* is used in the sense of reviling. *Sapati*. A curse (*sapatha*), a sworn curse (*abhisapatha*), one who has been cursed (*abhisapita*), one who curses (*sapanaka*).
*Vap*: sowing seed. He sows seed. A sower. Seed that has been sown. Grain sown by a man. Seed is being sown.
An auspicious ceremony for sowing (*vappamaṅgala*). *Sup*: sleeping. He sleeps. The sages sleep happily, who are not bound to women. A sleeping man; sleep; the state of being asleep (*sutta*).
*Khip*: throwing. Throwing is pulverizing, grinding. He throws. A thrower.
*Khipe* means to utter an unskilled sound. *Khipati*. *Khipita-saddo*. And when teaching the Dhamma, the Leader of the World uttered [the word].
*Khipe* means to cast away. *Khipati*, *ukkhipati*, *vikkhipati*, *avakhipati*, *saṃkhipati*. Examples include *khittaṃ*, *ukkhittaṃ*, *pakkhitthaṃ*, *vikkhittaṃ*, and so forth.
*Ope* means to spit. Spitting is the casting out of saliva. *Opati*. Having prepared the medicine, he spits saliva into his mouth.
*Lipi* means to smear or anoint. *Lepati*. That which is smeared (*littaṃ*) with supreme brilliance.
*Khipi* means in motion; *khimpati*.
*Ḍipa* means to throw; *ḍepati*.

"Nibbapinga" means nibbapinga. "Nibbapinga" refers to taking hold of rice heads or millet heads on crops such as grain or trees, or bending small branches, and then—without cutting them off or breaking them—grasping them with the hand exactly where they stand, pulling them toward oneself, and taking only the seed or only the leaf.
For example: "A man nibbapings the rice head; he nibbapings the tree leaf."
*Nidampako*, *nidampitaṃ*, *nidampituṃ*, *nidampitvā*. The root *tapa* means "splendor.
Splendor is radiance. The sun shines by day. *Tapa* also means "agitation. Agitation is terror or timidity.
He is agitated; he is intensely agitated. *Ottappaṃ* and *ottappiyaṃ* refer to wealth [that inspires fear].

*Tapa* (to heat), *dhūpa* (to fumigate), *santāpa* (to torment). It heats (*tapati*). *Tapodhanaṃ* (wealth of austerity), *ātāpo* (ardor), *ātāpī* (ardent), *ātapaṃ* (heat). It fumigates (*dhūpati*), it is a fumigator (*sandhūpano*); in the passive sense, it is heated (*tāpiyati*). It is fumigated (*dhūpiyati*). In the abstract sense: heating (*tāpanaṃ*), heat (*tāpo*), burning (*paritāpo*), tormenting (*santāpo*).
Fumigation (*dhūpanaṃ*). These are the forms of roots ending in the letter *pa*. Now, the roots ending in the letter *pha*: *Phakārantadhātu* (Roots ending in the letter *pha*)
*Puppha* [is used] in the sense of blossoming. This [verb] is both intransitive and transitive. [Examples: *pupphati*, *pupphaṃ*, *pupphanaṃ*, *pupphito*, *pupphituṃ*, *pupphitvā*.
"The flowering trees (*pupphino dumā*) are blooming. "All flowers, whether born on land or born in water, bloom at that time.
The tree named *mañjūsaka* blooms with as many flowers as there are, whether in water or on land.
*Tupha* means violence; *tophati*.
*Dapha*, *daphi*, *vappha* mean going; *daphati*, *damphati*, *vapphati*.
*Dipha* means speaking, fighting, censuring, violence, and giving; *dephati*. *Depha*.
*Tapha* means to satisfy; *titti* is satisfaction, [as in] he satisfies (*tappati*).
*Dupha* means to defile; defilement (*upakkileso*) is the act of defiling; it defiles (*dophati*). *Gupha* means to knot;
a knot (*gantho*) is the act of making a knot; it knots (*gophati*).
Root-forms ending in the letter *pha*.
Root ending in the letter *ba*:
*Bhabba* in the sense of harming. It harms (*bhabbati*). It is capable of harming (*bhabbo*).

*Pabba*, *vabba*, *mabba*, *kabba*, *khabba*, *gabba*, *sabba*, *cabba* [are used] in the sense of going (*gati*). Thus: *pabbati*, *vabbati*, *mabbati*, *kabbati*, *khabbati*, *gabbati*, *sabbati*, *cabbati*. *Abba* and *sabba* are used in the sense of harming (*hiṃsā*) as well.
The letter *ca* is included because of its reference to "going" (*gati*). Thus: *abbati*, *sabbati*.
*Kubi* is used in the sense of covering (*acchādane*). Thus: *kubbati*.
*Lub* means to press down; *tub* means to press down. *Lumbinīvanaṃ* (the Lumbinī grove). *Udakatumbo* (a water-jar). Also, *dve ca tumbāni* (two jars).
*Cub* occurs in connection with the mouth; for example, "he kisses the son on the head" (*puttaṃ muddhani cumbati*) or "he kisses [him] on the face" (*mukhe cumbati*). Here it might be asked:

"If the root *cub* functions in connection with the mouth, how is it that in the expression ‘the peak kissed by drops from a cloud’ (*ambudharabinducumbitakūṭo*), it occurs where there is no mouth and no consciousness, namely, on the mountain peak?"
"Is it said that there is a kissing of raindrops? "It is true; however, that was said by taking into account the occurrence of a phenomenon similar in form to kissing.

Just as, even though trees do not see, it is said, 'Seeing children weeping, the lofty, massive trees [shed tears],' because they have arisen in a manner similar to seeing, so too for trees that lack eyes."
Just as "seeing" was mentioned [in the previous case], so too here, because they have arisen in a manner similar to the mode of kissing, the "kissing" of raindrops from clouds is also mentioned.
However, by their very nature, those lacking consciousness possess neither seeing nor kissing and the like; these belong only to those possessing consciousness.
This same principle should be applied to the phrases "moving," "stepping," and so forth.
*Ubbi*, *tubbi*, *thubbi*, *dubbī*, *dhubbi*—these have the sense of harming (*hiṃsatthā*). [Examples: *ubbati*, *tubbati*, *thubbati*, *dubbati*, *dubbā*, *dhubbati*.
Here, *dubbā* refers to *dabba* grass, which appears in the Canon as “the grass species called *tiriyā*.
In this context, it should be understood that *dubbā* is feminine gender (*itthiliṅga*) and *dabba* is neuter gender (*napuṃsakaliṅga*).
*Mubbi* is used in the sense of binding; *mubbati*.
*Kubbi* is used in the sense of arising; *kubbati*.
*Pubba*, *pabba*, and *sabba* are used in the sense of filling; *pubbati*, *pabbati*, *sabbati*. Here one might ask: "But, sir, are not the words *pubba* and *sabba*..."
"Why are these included in the investigation of roots (dhātucintā), even though they are all nouns? It is said in reply:

In the case of all nouns, as well as in particles and prefixes that are devoid of the *tumant* suffix and so forth, there is no such thing as an "investigation of roots. However, these [words] are not actually nouns;

they merely appear as if they were nouns due to their commonality in being heard [as such]. Therefore, because they are free from that status [of being nouns], they are included in the investigation of roots.
The term “pubba” (ancient) is used here to indicate that these forms were adopted by the ancient teachers (*pubbācariya*), as shown by the usage “[these are] all ancient.
If this is so, why do these forms not exist in the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*)? They do not exist because they have not been transmitted [in that specific way], not because they are non-existent.
Although these forms do not appear in the Buddha’s word, nevertheless, being approved by the ancients, they should be understood as belonging to the ancient language (*purāṇabhāsā*).

Just as in the expression “he protects, thus he is a protector” (*nāthatīti nātho*), the form *nāthati*—though not found in the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*)—must nevertheless be accepted, so it is with these forms as well.

Therefore, for the sake of the proficiency of the wise in common usage, even those worldly applications that do not exist within the Dispensation (*sāsana*) but are consistent with it must be accepted;
thus, the forms *pubbati* and *sabbati* have been included. This same principle should be understood to apply to other instances as well.
*Cam* in the sense of taking: *cammati*.
*Kabba*, *khabba*, *gabba*, *dabbe*. *Dabbo* is the ego (*ahaṅkāra*). *Kabbati*. *Khabbati*. *Gabbati*.
*Abi*, *dabi* in the sense of sound. *Ambati*. *Ambā*, *ambu*. *Dambati*.
*Labi* means hanging down. Hanging down is *avalambana*. It hangs, it hangs down, it hangs out. "The sun hangs low. It clings (*ālambati*).
*Ālambana*, *tadālambana*, *tadālambaṇa*, or *tadālamba*. Also, *lābu* or *alābu*;
for the letter *a-* is used in the sense of that very state.
Forms of the verbal root ending in *bh*.
The verbal root *bhā* ending in *bh*:
in the sense of shining. "The moon shines," "a question occurs to me," "the night shines forth. *Bhāṇu* (the sun), *paṭibhānaṃ* (inspiration). "The night has dawned."

*Bhī* means fear. One fears (*bhāyati*). [Derivatives include: *bhayaṃ* (fear), *bhayānaka* (terrible), *bhīma* (formidable), *bhīmasena* (the army of the formidable one), *bhīru* (timid), *bhīruka* (timid), *bhīrukajātiko* (of a timid nature). In the causative, there are forms such as *bhāyeti*, *bhāyayati*, *bhāyāpeti*, and *bhāyāpayati*.
*Sabhū* and *sambhū* mean to injure; [one] injures (*sabhati*), [one] injures thoroughly (*sambhati*).
*Sumbha* means to speak; the word *ca* (and) refers back to "injury. [One] speaks (*sumbhati*). [Derivatives include: *sumbha* (speech), *kusumbha* (safflower).

In this context, *sumbha* means a pit. “Dig a *sumbha*” is the illustration here. *Kusumbha* means a small pit; “filling the *kusumbhas*, which are filled with mountain clefts, ravines, and branches,” is the illustration here.
[The roots] *abbha*, *vabbha*, and *mabbha* mean to go. One goes (*abbhati*), thus it is *abbha*. One goes thoroughly (*vabbhati*), thus it is *vabbha*.
One goes completely (*mabbhati*), thus it is *mabbha*. Here, *abbha* means a cloud. For it is called “*abbha*” because it goes (*abbhati*) as many as hundreds of layers.
It is said: “Vijjumālī satakkaku. And *satakkaku* means that which has many hundreds of layers. Furthermore, in this context, the word *abbha* (cloud) should be understood as having three genders.
For instance, it is masculine in the passage: “He goes forth as soon as he has risen; once gone, he does not turn back. It is feminine in the passage:
“Clouds (*abbhā*), mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu. And it is neuter in the passage: “The clouds [obscure] the lunar disk (*abbhāni candamaṇḍalaṃ*).”
In the phrase "chādentī" (covering), it is used in the neuter gender.
These, moreover, are the names for a cloud:
Megha, Valāhaka, Laṅghi, Jīmūta, Ambuda, and Ghana.
Dhārādhara, ambudhara, pajjunna, and himagabbhaka [are names for clouds].

Regarding *yabha* in the context of sexual intercourse (*methuna*): this action of a pair, of a couple, is *methuna*; in that *methuna*, the verbal root *yabha* operates. [Examples: *yabhati*, *yābhaṃsaṃ*.
And here, the term "sexual intercourse" (*methuna*) is a word used in common parlance, because it is a form of speech that should not be uttered by persons endowed with a sense of shame.

For instance, this language occurs in the context of beautiful speech in such passages as, "The practice of sexual intercourse must not be indulged in," and, "The king is not my friend, nor is there sexual intercourse with the king.
However, language such as "yabhati" and so forth is indecent speech, like language beginning with "sikharaṇī";
for even a worldly person endowed with shame and moral dread would not utter such words.

Even so, the Blessed One, though possessed of the highest degree of moral shame and dread of blame, spoke in the midst of the assembly out of a heart impelled by great compassion and for the sake of sympathy for the world: "Oh, how great is the compassion of the Tathāgata!
These, moreover, are the names for the act of sexual intercourse:
Lying down together, embracing, sexual intercourse, being fond of it, delighting in it;
trembling, the village custom, the state of being intoxicated, delusion, and pleasure;
the practice contrary to the true Dhamma, the practice of the outcaste, and even filthiness—these are sensual pleasures.
The pair-by-pair union; a couple, a village, reaching to the water's edge.
*Sibh* and *vibh* mean to speak. *Sibhati*. *Vibhati*.
*Debha*, *abhi*, and *dabhi* mean sound. *Debhati*. *Ambhati*. *Ambho*. *Dambhati*.
And here, "ambho" refers to water. For even though it is devoid of life, it is called "ambho" because it "ambhati"—that is, it makes a sound—when it flows during floods and at other such times.
These are its names:
*pānīya*, *udaka*, *toya*, *jala*, *pāta*, and *ambu*.
Daka, kaṃ, salila, vāri, āpo, ambho, papam,
and ca; nīra, kepuka, pāni, amata, and elam—
these are the names for water, gathered from here and there.
And here, applications such as “*vālaggesu ca kepuke. Pivitañca tesaṃ bhusaṃ hoti pānī*” (and on the tips of hair-tufts...

their drink becomes very much drunk) should be shown. *Thabhi*, *khabhi*: to be bound; *thambhati*, *vitthambhati*. *Khambhati*, *vikkhambhati*. *Thambho*. *Thaddho*, *upatthambho*. *Upatthambhinī*. *Vikkhambho*.
*Vikkhambhitakileso*. *Jabha*, *jabhi*: to bend a limb; *jabhati*. *Jambhati*, *vijambhati*. *Vijambhanaṃ*, *vijambhitā*. *Vijambhanto*, *vijambhamāno*, *vijambhito*.
*Sabbha* means "in speaking. *Sabbhati*.
*Vabbha* means "in eating. *Vabbhati*.
*Gabbha* means "in conceiving. *Gabbhati*. *Gabbha*.
In this context, "womb" (*gabbha*) refers both to the mother’s belly and to the child residing within the belly.
For instance, in the passage, “The night in which the youth first dwelt in the womb,” it is the mother’s belly that is called the “womb.

However, in the passage, “O King, a womb has been established for me; but the womb has fallen to the ground,” it refers to the child residing in the belly. Furthermore, “womb” can also denote a particular type of dwelling.
In such passages as “entered the womb” (*gabbhaṃ paviṭṭho*), the word *ovaraka* (inner chamber) is called “womb” (*gabbho*).

The root *rabh* is used in the sense of impetuosity (*rābhasse*). With the prefix *ā-*, *rabh* is used in the senses of harming, doing, and exertion. Impetuosity (*rābhassaṃ*) is the state of being impetuous (*rābhasabhāvo*). However, in the Canon (*pāḷi*), that which possesses this quality is recorded as “fierce, obstructive, and impetuous” (*caṇḍā ruddhā rabhasā*).
In that context, “impetuous” (*rabhasā*) refers to the instrument (*karaṇa*). [The forms] *rabhati*, *ārabhati*, *samārabhati*, and *ārambhati* [are derived from it]. [The noun] *rabhaso*.

Initiation (*ārambho*). Undertaking (*samārambho*), one who initiates (*ārabhanto*), one who undertakes (*samārabhanto*). "My energy has been initiated" (*āraddhaṃ me vīriyaṃ*). With exertion (*sārambhaṃ*). Without exertion (*anārambhaṃ*).

"No exertion is found in you" (*sārambho te na vijjati*). Exertion for a specific purpose (*pakāraṇārambho*). Exertion of energy (*vīriyārambho*). In order to initiate (*ārabhituṃ*). Having initiated (*ārabhitvā*). Having undertaken (*ārabbha*).

Here, "exertion of energy" (*vīriyārambho*) refers to initiation (*ārambho*) characterized as energy. The word *ārambha* occurs in many senses: in the sense of an action (*kamma*), an offense (*āpatti*), an activity (*kriyā*), energy (*vīriya*), and violence (*hiṃsā*), as well as agitation (*vikopana*).
“Whatever suffering has arisen, all arises from undertaking;
through the cessation of undertakings, there is no arising of suffering.
Here, “undertaking” (*ārambha*) is understood as kamma. In the phrase “he undertakes and feels remorse,” it refers to an offense (*āpatti*).
In the phrase, “Great sacrifices, great undertakings, yet they do not bear great fruit,” it refers to activities such as the raising of a sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

In the phrase, “Exert yourselves, strive, apply yourselves to the teaching of the Buddha,” it refers to energy (*vīriya*). In the phrase, “They slaughter living beings for the sake of the ascetic Gotama,” it refers to violence (*hiṃsā*).
In the phrase, “He abstains from the destruction of seeds and the destruction of living plants,” it refers to...
"Vikopana" refers to the act of disturbing, such as cutting, breaking, and so forth.
Thus, it should be defined that the word "ārambha" (undertaking/initiation) occurs in the context of: an action, an offense, exertion, acts of violence, and disturbance.
*Labh* (to obtain): *labhe*. [Present tense: *labhati*, *labbhati*. [Nouns/Participles: *lābho*, *laddhaṃ*, *alattha*, *alatthuṃ*.
*Subh* (beauty): [Meaning: beauty. [Verb: *sobhati*. [Nouns/Participles: *sobhā*, *sobhanaṃ*, *sobhito*. *Khubh* (to shake): [Verbs:
*khubhati*, *saṅkhobhati*. [Examples: "The city was shaken by the elephant-king, Padinna; it was then agitated. [Nouns: *khubhā*, *saṅkhobho*.
*Nabha* means to strike; *nabhati*, *tubhati*.
*Sambha* means to trust; *sambhati*, *sambhatti*, *sambhatto*.
*Lubha* means to delude; *lobhati*, *palobhati*. The deluding of a grown-up maiden (*thullakumārīpalobhanaṃ*). In the causative, however, it is "lobheti."
"Palobheti, having enticed"—thus the forms *rūpāni* occur. However, upon reaching the *div-ādi* class, in the sense of greed (*giddhi*), the form *lubbhati* occurs.
*Dabh* in the sense of deceiving: *dambhati*, *dambhanaṃ*.
*Rubh* in the sense of obstructing: *rumbhati*, *sannirumbhati*; *sannirumbho*, *sannirumbhitvā*.

*Ubha*, *ubbha*, and *umbha* mean "to fill. [Examples of] *ubhati*, *ubbhati*, *umbhati*; *ubhanā*, *ubbhanā*, *umbhanā*. *Obho*. *Keṭubhaṃ*. *Ubbhaṃ*. *Kumbho*. *Kumbhī*. In the causative (*kārita*), the forms *obheti*, *ubbheti*, *umbheti* occur.
In this context, *keṭubhaṃ* refers to a treatise that provides various options for grammatical construction and serves as an aid for poets. Here is the etymological derivation (*nibbacana*):

it is called *keṭubhaṃ* because it "drives" (*kiṭeti*) or "leads" (*gameti") the classification of actions and so forth, or because it "drives away" (*keṭento*) or "removes" (*gamento") them by exhausting them without remainder; thus it "causes to fill" (*obheti").
It is called *keṭutaṃ* by way of the verbal root *kiṭubha*. It is *ubbhaṃ* because it is raised up (*ubbhati*), elevated (*ubbheti*), or filled (*pūreti*);
the meaning is "filling. Such a grammatical derivation is also seen in the *Cariyāpiṭaka*, as for example: "He bestowed a great gift, exceedingly sublime (*accubbhaṃ*) like the ocean.
And there, "exceedingly sublime" means filling the aspirations of supplicants to the highest degree.
"Akkhubbhanti" is also a reading. "Kumbho" means water (*kaṃ*); that which is to be filled with it is a "kumbho," and that same word, by virtue of its feminine gender, is "kumbhī.
In this context, there is the usage: "She washes the *kumbhī* while bent over.
The word "kumbha" refers to a jar, the frontal globe of an elephant, and a cluster of ten lotuses.
"It proceeds" is to be understood by the wise one who perceives the method.
[These are] the forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *bh*; [now follow] the verbal roots ending in the letter *m*.

*Mā* in the sense of pride (*māna*) and sound (*sadda*). *Māti*: mother (*mātā*). Here, "mother" refers to either the biological mother, the stepmother (*cūḷamātā*), or the foster mother (*mahāmātā*).
*Mū* in the sense of binding (*bandhana*): *mavati*. However, for this root belonging to the *kiyādi* class, the form is *munāti*.
*Me* in the sense of giving back and taking: *meti*, *mayati*. Wisdom (*medhā*).
"Medhā" here means wisdom (*paññā*). For it is called "medhā" because it quickly (*khippam*) "measures" (*meti*) and "bears" (*dhāreti*) even subtle meanings and phenomena.
In this context, however, "measures" (*meti*) means "grasps. Thus, it is said in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*:
"It is 'medhā' because it measures—that is, it destroys—defilements like a thunderbolt striking a mountain; or else, it is 'medhā' in the sense of quick grasping and bearing."

However, by way of the verbal root *medha*, which signifies meeting (*saṅgama*), the meaning should be understood as follows: "one meets" (*medhati*) with the true Dhamma—such as virtue, concentration, and so forth—and with glory;
thus, it is called *medhā*. On this point, it is said: "By means of two elements, one element, and also by means of two meanings and three [meanings];"
"One should know the derivation of the word *medhā* in the teaching of the Sugata.
*Oma* [is used] in the sense of capability (*sāmatthiya*). Capability is the state of being capable. This verbal root is without elision (*alutta*); thus it is *oma* and *omanti*.

Here is the canonical passage (*pāḷi*) for this: "Yes, venerable sir, the Blessed One is able (*omāti*) to approach the Brahma-world by means of psychic power with a mind-made body. In that context, *omāti* means he is able, he is capable.
*Timu* means to become wet. *Addabhāvo* is the state of being wet. It means to moisten; one who has moistened is *tinto*, [and] *temiyo*. Those desiring to moisten moistened (*temiṃsu*).

Here, *temiyo* refers to the Bodhisatta, the son of the King of Kāsi. For he was called "Temiya" because he was born moistening the hearts of both the king and the great multitude, bringing about a state of wetness and generating a state of coolness.
*Nitami* means to be weary. One is weary (*nitammāmi*); the heart burns, it is weary.
*Camu*, *chamu*, *japu*, *jhamu*, *umu*, *jimu*: to eat. *Camati*. *Camū*. *Camūti* means an army (*senā*). *Chamati*. *Jamati*. *Jhamati*. *Umati*. *Jemati*. *Kamu*: to step; to move by foot.
Moving by foot (*padavikkhepa*) is walking on foot. This term, however, is merely a conventional heading;
therefore, in such passages as "fire, poison, or a weapon does not affect his body," it also carries the sense of "not stepping" (i.e., not affecting).
It should be grasped. It moves. It walks back and forth; it passes over. It approaches; it retreats. It departs; it exerts itself.
It strides; it goes out; it traverses. Traversing; the act of traversing; the state of traversing.
Moving; walking back and forth. Passing over; approaching; retreating; departing; striding; going out. A person who has passed over. The night has passed.
It goes out; it goes forth. In the causative sense, it causes to go out.

Other [meanings] should also be applied accordingly. However, since this root, having entered the *cur-ādigaṇa* (the class beginning with *cur*), functions in the senses of desire and longing, we shall not state here the extraction of the meaning of the word *abhikkanta*—even though it ought to be stated by applying those meanings as qualified by prefixes—but shall explain it later within the *cur-ādigaṇa* itself.

*Yamu* means to cease (*uparame*). Cessation (*uparamo*) is abstention (*viramaṇaṃ*). *Yamabhi* means to restrain; thus, *yamo*. "Others do not know that we here restrain ourselves"—this is the illustration here. In this context, "we restrain ourselves" (*yamāmase*) means we cease, we perish, or we die.
*Nama* means sound in the sense of multiplicity. A sound in the sense of multiplicity is a loud sound. *Namati*.
*Ama*, *dama*, *hamma*, *mima*, *chama* mean going (*gatimhi*). *Amati*. *Damati*. *Hammati*. *Mimati*. *Chamati*. *Chamā*.
*Chamā* means earth. The word *chamā* should be understood as feminine in gender, because we see its usage in such passages as:

“The training is to be undertaken thus: ‘I shall not teach the Dhamma to one who is seated on a seat while I am sitting on the ground, unless I am ill,’” and “I roll on the ground like a fish in the heat.
And that [word] occurs in seven or eight case-endings and in two numbers.
It should be applied as follows: *chamā* means "that wherein they go" (*chamanti gacchanti ettha*).
The root *dham-* occurs in the senses of sound and conjunction with fire. The verbal root *dham-* pertains both to sound and to the conjunction of fire with the breath of the mouth.
In that regard, for the first sense (sound): "he blows the conch" (*saṅkhaṃ dhamati*), "conch-blower" (*saṅkhadhamako*); "he beats the drum" (*bheriṃ dhamati*), "drum-beater" (*bheridhamako*).

The usage is: *dhame dhame nātidhame* (“blow, blow, but do not blow too much”). In the second sense, it means “to fan”; the usage is: *aggiṃ dhamati samuṭṭhāpeti attānaṃ aṇuṃ aggiṃ va sandhamam* (“he fans the fire, kindling himself like a tiny spark”).
*Bhāma* means anger; [the verb] *bhāmati*.
Namu, namane; namati; namo; nataṃ, namanaṃ; nati; namaṃ; namamāno; namanto;
namito; nāmaṃ; nāmitaṃ; namituṃ; natvā, natvāna; namitvā, namitvāna, namituna.
In the causative, the forms “nāmeti, nāmayati; nāmetvā; nāmayitvā” occur. For therein, forms such as “namati, namitvā” are found.
The words *pada* should be understood in the sense of bowing and in the sense of paying homage; however, expressions such as “having bowed” (*namo natvā*) refer specifically to paying homage.
Here, this is merely an illustrative formulation of usage:
“A tree, bearing fruit, bends down under the weight of its burden of fruit and then breaks.”
An old man, due to the decrepitude of old age, bows down and then proceeds;
one who has faith bows down to the Buddha and then proceeds;
"Having bowed to the Teacher, the Buddha, he departed"—thus it is said.
In this context, the word *nama* is also found among the indeclinables (*nipāta*). For that reason, the forms for the nominative and accusative cases are seen as identical:
"O King of Gods, let there be homage to you (*namo tyatthu*); having paid homage to the Great Sage (*namo katvā mahesino*).
This [word] may also be joined with prefixes (*upasagga*), such as in "he bows down (*paṇamati*)," "bowing down (*paṇāmo*)," "he rises up (*uṇṇamati*)," "rising up (*uṇṇati*)," and so forth.

*Kham* means to endure; *khamati*, *khanti*, *khama*, and *khamana*—these are used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*). However, in the sense of the agent (*kattar*), there are such usages as “the endurer,” “one who has endured,” and “he is patient toward both cold and heat.
*Sam* means non-appearance; *samati*, [and] fire is extinguished (*vūpasamati*).
*Yam* means to restrain; *yamati*, *yama*, and King Yama.
Sama is sound. It means "to be even.
Sama-thama-velambe: it means "to be even," "to be firm," and "to be slow.
Vāyama is effort and exertion; it means "to strive" (vāyamati). Vāyāma is effort.
*Gam-* in the sense of going: *gacchati*, *gamako*, *gato*, *gati*, *gamanaṃ*. In the causative: *gameti*, *gamayati*, *gacchāpeti*, and so forth.
*Ram-* in the sense of sporting: *ramati*, *viramati*, *paṭiviramati*, *uparamati*. [Nouns derived from it:
*ārati*, *virati*, *paṭivirati*, *uparati*, *veramaṇi*, *viramaṇaṃ*, *rati*, *ramaṇaṃ*, *rato*, *ārato*, *virato*, *paṭivirato*, *uparato*, *uparamo*, *ārāmo*.
Vam: in the sense of vomiting. *Vamati*, *vamathu*, *vammiko*.
"Fie on that poison vomited by me for the sake of life!
I shall vomit it back up again; death is better for me than life."
In this context, "ant-hill" (*vammika*) means that which vomits (*vamati*), it is the vomit (*vantaka*), the abode of vomit (*vantassaya*), and that which is connected to the moisture of vomit;
thus it is called an ant-hill. For it is called an ant-hill because it vomits various kinds of creatures such as snakes, mongooses, rats, and lizards.
It is called an ant-hill because it is vomited by termites (*upacikā*). Having been vomited by the termites, even to the extent of being knee-high with the dust and powder raised up by their snouts—

It is called an anthill (*vammika*) because it has risen to the height of a man. Because it is bound together by the moisture of the saliva vomited by termites, it does not crumble even when it rains for seven days and seven nights;
nor does it disintegrate in the heat of summer, for if one takes a handful of soil from it and squeezes it with the fist, only moisture comes out.
Thus, it is an anthill because of its connection to the moisture of what has been vomited.
In this context, however, words such as “Bhagavā” and “Himavā” are not to be derived solely by means of the *vanta* suffix;
rather, they are also to be derived by means of the verbal root *vam*. Therefore, the author of the *Visuddhimagga* said:

“But because he has vomited out (*vanta*) the ‘going’ (*gamana*), which is to say craving, within the three realms of existence (*bhava*), therefore, although one might say ‘one who has vomited out going in the existences’ (*bhavesu vantagamo’)...”
By taking the syllable *bha* from the word *bhava*, the syllable *ga* from the word *gamana*, and the syllable *va* from the word *vanta*—

lengthening them— the term *bhagavā* is thus explained; this demonstrates the derivation of the word according to the method of etymological analysis (*nirukti*), as when it is said that what should be called "a garland for the privy" (*mekhanassa khassa mālā*) is instead called *mekhalā* in common usage.

Here, it might be argued: "This illustration is inconsistent; for while in the phrase *‘mekhanassa khassa mālā’* the letters *me*, *kha*, and *lā* are seen to be taken in their proper order, in the phrase *‘bhavesu vantagamano’* the letters *bha*, *va*, and *ga* are not seen to be taken in their proper order.
This is true; however, here [the rule applies] as in cases such as *‘aggāhito, vijjācaraṇasampanno’*.
Although it could have been said as "those possessing the going (gamanavanto) into existences" by placing the word *guṇa* later in the compound,
this was not done; rather, because the grammatical treatises generally prefer that words ending in *guṇa* be placed first,

and in order to satisfy the minds of those learned in grammar and certain wise men, the term "Bhagavā" is used here by disregarding the strict sequence of syllables and instead demonstrating the meaning alone.
Just as in expressions such as “one who has established the sacrificial fire” (*āhitaggi*) or “one perfected in true knowledge and conduct” (*sampannavijjācaraṇo*),

the phrase “one who has vomited out existence” (*vantagamano bhavesu*) is stated according to the principle of prior placement (*pubbanipāta*). For in such instances— as in the cases of *āhitaggi* or *aggāhito*,
or *chinnahattho* or *hatthacchinno*— there is no inconsistency in the meaning regardless of how the words are positioned, because those terms are mutually synonymous.
In passages such as "born of the Vedas" (*vedajāto*), however, it should be understood that [the term *bhagavā*] does indeed exist.

Thus, in the *Visuddhimagga*, the derivation of the word "Bhagavā" is shown by means of the verbal root *vam*; and in its commentary (*ṭīkā*) it is also shown: "He vomits (*vamati*) upon the *bhaga* (fortune), thus he is Bhagavā;
he vomits upon the *bhāga* (portions), thus he is Bhagavā. But the etymological analysis (*nibbacana*) should be understood in this way: [he who has] that which is reckoned as *bhaga*...
"The Blessed One vomited forth glory, sovereignty, and fame, and cast them away without regard, like a globule of spittle"—so it is said.

Alternatively, "bhaga" refers to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*); those things which move and proceed together with them are "bhagas," namely the receptacle worlds such as Sineru, Yugandhara, Uttarakuru, and Himavanta, because they possess a state of established beauty based on specific supports.
The Blessed One vomited even these, because he has transcended the abodes of beings that dwell within them.
"By abandoning desire and lust for that [world], he abandoned it," said the Blessed One.
"Because the Sugata, the Blessed One, abandoned the glory of a wheel-turning monarch, as well as fame, sovereignty, happiness, and the worldly mind, therefore [he is so called]."

"Likewise, having completely cut off all proliferation, all bondage, all ties, and all fetters regarding the various categories of phenomena such as the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, and thereby attaining the deathless element, the Blessed One has vomited it up, cast it out without regard, and will not swallow it back.
Alternatively: "All wholesome and unwholesome states, blameworthy and blameless..."

"The Blessed One vomited up, disgorged, renounced without regard for, and abandoned the inferior and superior phenomena— those dark and bright counterparts— by means of the knowledge of the Noble Path. The various categories of phenomena,
such as the aggregates, bases, and elements, were [thus relinquished] by the Great Sage."
"Since both black and white have been vomited out, the Blessed One is considered even beyond that.
Furthermore, in the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*, the derivation of the word "Himava" is shown by means of the verbal root *vam* (to vomit). For instance, in the commentary on the *Sambhava-jātaka*, it says:
"Himava means 'possessing snow' (*himayutta*) during the time of snowfall; [it is so called] in the winter season..."
"It vomits snow, thus it is Himavā"—so it is said. Thus, in the Jātakaṭṭhakathā, the derivation of the word "Himavā" is shown even by means of the verbal root *vam* (to vomit);
this method may be applied to similar instances as well. However, it should not be applied to cases such as "guṇavā" and "gaṇavā.
If one were to apply it there, the words "guṇavā" and "gaṇavā" would have meanings such as "devoid of qualities" (*nigguṇo*) or "one whose qualities have declined" (*parihīnaguṇo*).
Therefore, this method should not be applied in all cases. Here it might be asked:
"If the derivation of words such as 'Bhagavā' occurs by means of the *vam* root, how are forms such as 'Bhagavanto' and 'Bhagavantaṃ' established?
Just as the word 'Bhagavā' is established through the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*), so too are those [other forms] established by that very same method. It is inconceivable.
For the method of etymology (*niruttinaya*) is merely a means of connecting the meaning with the reasoning;
when the meaning and the reasoning are present, even those forms which would otherwise be impossible to produce are established by this very method.
Furthermore, whatever definition of etymology ought to be cited here, we shall set it forth together with examples in the subsequent section on the production of grammatical forms.
Here, O Sāramati, in this system of the King of Munis,
the virtuous person who prizes supreme acuity will find this "Wealthy One’s Ethics," which upholds vast benefit.
Constantly devoted to that which purifies the intellect.

Thus ends the *Saddanīti* treatise, composed for the benefit of the wise in understanding the modes of expression within the Three Piṭakas together with their commentaries, consisting of nine divisions.
The fifteenth chapter: The Classification of Roots, titled "The Section on the Group Beginning with *sar-*.
16. The Chapter on the Group Beginning with *bhū-*.
From here onwards, I shall explain the mixed roots ending in *ya*,
following the tradition of those skilled in the classification of roots and so forth.
[Roots] Ending in *ya*.

Regarding the sense of "attaining a destination": *yāti*, *yanti*; *yātu*, *yantu*; *yeyya*, *yeyyuṃ*, *anupariyeyyuṃ*. The series of forms (*padamālā*) should be applied according to their occurrence:
*yanto puriso* (a man who goes), *yantī itthī* (a woman who goes), *yantaṃ kulaṃ* (a family that goes). Also, *yānaṃ*, *upayānaṃ*, *uyyānaṃ*, and so forth.
However, for this root belonging to the *divādigaṇa*, the forms are *yāyati*, *yāyantī*, and so on.
In this context, regarding the words beginning with *yāna*: that by which one goes is a *yāna*, such as a chariot or a cart.
That by which they approach—that is, go into the presence of a lord or a beloved—is an *upayāna*, meaning a gift or offering.

For in the verse, "They gave me offerings (*upayānāni*) when you had departed, O prince," it is the presents that are called "offerings. [This is said] because of its being endowed with beautiful flowers, fruits, and so forth.
It is called an *uyyāna* (pleasure grove) because they go and move about there while looking upward.
The root *byā* means "to open" (*ummīsane*). Its forms are: *byāti*, *byanti*; *byāsi*, *byātha*; *byāmi*, *byāma*. The paradigm of the word should be applied according to its occurrence.
In this regard, the following canonical passage occurs: “As long as it opens and closes, even there the taste is intense. Therein:
*Yāva* means "as far as" or "until"; this is an archaic term (*purāṇabhāsā*), for it was the common usage among people at the time when the Bodhisatta was the wandering ascetic Cūḷabodhi.
[The root] *yā* is used in the sense of mixing (*missane*) and going (*gatiyaṃ*). *Yā* means "to go. *Āyu* (life) and *yoni* (womb/source).
In this context, *ā* is a prefix (*upasagga*). It is called *āyu* because beings (*sattā*) "age" (*āyavanti*)—that is, they become mixed (*missībhavanti*)—by means of it.
Alternatively, it is called *āyu* because when it exists, immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhammā*) "age" (*āyavanti*), meaning they come into being (*āgacchanti*) and proceed (*pavattanti*).
Thus, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*: "It is *āyu* in the sense of aging (*āyavana*). For when it exists, immaterial phenomena age; they come into being and proceed."
"Therefore it is called 'āyū' (life-span). "Āyu," "jīvitaṃ" (living), and "pāṇo" (breathing being)—these are synonyms used according to worldly convention.
However, according to the Abhidhamma, "ṭhiti" (stability), "yapanā" (sustenance), "yāpanā" (maintenance), and "jīvitindriyaṃ" (the life-faculty)—these too are synonyms along with those very terms.

"Yoni" (womb/source) is that by which there is a mixing together of egg-born beings and so forth, such as the egg-born themselves; that is the womb. This, however, is the etymological derivation here.
“Yoni is that wherein beings, by virtue of having a commonality of birth, become mixed with one another.
Herein, the derivation of the meaning of the word *yoni* is set forth. *Yoni* is a name for a division of aggregates (*khandha*), for a cause, and for the urinary passage.
For in the passage, “There are four *nāga*-births; there are four *supaṇṇa*-births,” it is a division of aggregates that is the *yoni*.
The name [“yonija”] is used here. In the phrase, “This is the source for the attainment of the fruit of the earth,” it refers to the cause.
In the phrase, “And I do not call one a brahmin by birth from a womb or origin in a mother,” it refers to the urinary passage. Regarding this, it is said:
“In the divisions of the aggregates, in the urinary passage, and in the sense of a cause.”
The word *yonis* occurs in these three senses:
(1) in the sense of "restraint" (*saṃvaraṇa*), as in *byāyati*;
(2) in the sense of "occurrence" (*pavatti*), as in *byeti*; and (3) in the sense of "companionship" (*sahabya*), as in *sahabyo*.

Here, *sahabyo* means one who goes together (*saha byeti*) or proceeds together (*saha pavattati*), thus a companion (*sahāyo*), or one who has entered into a single existence (*ekabhavūpago*). For instance, in such passages as “reborn into the company (*sahabyataṃ*) of the Tāvatiṃsa devas,” one who has entered a single existence is called a “companion.
The root *haya* means “to go. It goes; hence, a horse (*hayo*). A horse is indeed called a *hayo* because it goes swiftly (*hayati*).
Its names are as follows: Asso, turaṅgo, turago, vājī, vāho, hayo.
Their varieties are the Sindhu horses, as well as the Goja and the Assatara. One who knows cause and non-cause is a noble thoroughbred, the best of steeds;
a mere horse, however, is called a wild colt (khaḷuṅka), and a mare is called a vaḷavā.
A young colt is called a *khaḷuṅka*; it also means "unbroken.
The root *hari* is used in the sense of going and illness.

It is conjugated as follows: *hariyati*. The roots *ayi*, *vayi*, *payi*, *mayi*, *tayi*, *cayi*, *rayi* are used in the sense of going. They are conjugated as *ayati*, *vayati*, *payati*, *mayati*, *tayati*, *cayati*, *rayati*.

It flows (*cayati*). It glitters (*rayati*). Iron (*ayo*), occasion (*samayo*), age (*vayo*), milk (*payo*), and radiance (*rayo*). The nominal forms of the roots *maya*, *taya*, *caya*, and *dhātu* should be examined therein. Among them, *ayo* is black iron;
it is called *ayo* because it goes into use in various crafts of the smiths (*ayati nānākammārakiccesu upayogaṃ gacchati*).
*Vayo* is a division of the life-span, such as the first stage of youth; it is called *vayo* because it goes toward decline (*vayati parihāniṃ gacchati*). *Payo* refers to both milk and water.
“Nāma” means name. It is called *paya* because it flows (*payati*) and thus becomes something to be drunk by people. “Rayo” means speed, which is also called “velocity” (*java*);

therefore, the act of flowing (*rayana*) or speeding is “rayo. Here, the analysis of the meaning of the word *samaya* is stated according to its etymological derivation: The word *samaya* [is used] in the sense of: 1. Collection (*samavāya*), 2.
Moment (*khaṇa*), 3. Time (*kāla*), 4. Convention (*sammuti*), 5. Cause (*hetu*), and 6. View (*diṭṭhi*).
It is seen in the senses of acquisition, abandonment, and penetration.
For instance, in such passages as, "Perhaps tomorrow we might go, taking into account the time and the occasion," the meaning is "conjunction.
However, in such passages as, "Monks, there is indeed only one moment and one occasion for living the holy life," [the meaning is "opportunity"].
*Samaya* means: 1. Time, as in "the time of heat," "the time of feverish distress," and so forth; 2. A multitude, as in "the great assembly in the forest" (*mahāsamayo pavanasmim*); 3.
A cause or reason, as in "Bhaddāli, you have not even understood this *samaya*";
4. An occasion or context, as in "At that time, the wanderer Uggāhamāna Samaṇamuṇḍikāputta was in Mallikā’s park at Tindukācīra, a place for debating doctrines, in the single-hall [shrine]."
In such passages as "he dwells," it refers to *diṭṭhi* (view).
[As it is said: "The goal that exists in this very life, and the goal pertaining to the future—through the realization of these goals, the steadfast one is called wise."
In such passages as "Through the full realization of conceit, he made an end of suffering," it means acquisition (*paṭilābha*).

In such passages as "The meaning of suffering is oppression, the meaning of the conditioned, the meaning of burning, and the meaning of realization (*abhisamaya*)," it means penetration (*paṭivedha*).
And here, since the prefixes are merely indicators, the word *samaya* itself expresses each respective meaning; thus, even in this enumeration of the meanings of the word *samaya*:
The term *abhisamaya* has been stated as being accompanied by a prefix (*sa-upasagga*).

In this context: it is a *samaya* (conjunction) because it comes together (*sameti*) or meets (*samaveti*) in proximity (*sannijjha*) through the state of being a cooperative cause (*sahakārī-kāraṇatā*); thus it is a conjunction (*samavāya*).

It is a *samaya* (moment) because the path and the holy life (*maggabrahmacariya*) come together (*sameti*) or meet (*samāgacchati*) therein, or because the person who is the support for that [path] is present; thus it is a moment (*khaṇa*). Or, they come together (*samenti*) in this, or by means of this...
"Samaya" means time (*kāla*). It is so called because phenomena (*dhammā*) come together (*saṅgacchanti*) with their co-nascent phenomena such as arising and the rest; thus it is "time.

Although time is non-existent in reality (*attha*) because it is merely the occurrence of phenomena, it is nevertheless spoken of by means of a form established through mere conceptualization (*parikappanāmatta*), appearing as if it were the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the occurrence of phenomena.
Alternatively, "samaya" means the coming together, the simultaneous proceeding, or the persistence of parts (*avayava*); hence it is "samaya."
A collection (*samūha*), as in the term "aggregation" (*samudāya*). For a collection is simply the state of existing together with its constituent parts.
A condition (*samaya*), as in the term "origination" (*samudaya*): from this [condition], when other conditions assemble, the fruit comes (*eti*)—that is, it arises and proceeds.

Or, it is called *samaya* because it "comes together" (*sameti*) through the state of being a fetter (*saṃyojana*), or because it "binds" (*saṃyutta*) by means of a connection, proceeding within its own domain due to the state of firm grasping.
"Samaya" means that by means of it beings go forth and proceed according to their respective adherence; thus it is "view.
For it is by the fetter of view that beings are most tightly bound. "Samaya" means meeting, gathering, or coming together; thus it is "acquisition.
"Samaya" means the going toward cessation (*samam*), or the right going away, the non-arising [of defilements]; thus it is "abandoning. [It is] facing toward [the truth] by means of knowledge.
It is called *samaya* because it is to be approached (*etabbo*) and attained (*adhigantabbo*) correctly (*sammā*). It is the non-erroneous intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena.

It is called *samaya* because one approaches, goes toward, and awakens to it by way of direct confrontation (*abhimukha-bhāvena*). It is the realization of the intrinsic nature as it truly is (*yathābhūta-sabhāvāvabodha*).
In this manner, the application of the term *samaya* should be understood according to each specific meaning.
But is it not the case that sounds adhere to mere meanings, such that many meanings are not expressed by a single sound?

This is true, provided one considers the specific difference between sounds. For when the distinction between sounds is taken into account, the expression of multiple meanings by a single sound is impossible.
Indeed, the word *samaya* which denotes the meaning of "time" does not itself express meanings such as "a collection" and so forth. In this regard—
However, by taking up the commonality of the word *samaya* as being expressible in various senses for those respective meanings, the manifoldness of the word *samaya* has been stated.
Thus, in every instance where a meaning is set forth, the underlying intention (*adhippāya*) should be understood.
From this, one should proclaim the accomplishment of that which has gone and that which has not yet gone.
The wise one should state that the word *samaya*,
which denotes "assemblage" and so forth, is derived from roots having the same meaning, such as *i* (to go) and *yā* (to go),
both preceded by the prefix *sam-*. Thus, words may come to have identical forms.

And in the sense of guiding and protecting. The letter *ca* (and) is used to include the sense of "going. It guides; thus, it is a *naya*. A *naya* is a guiding or a going; thus, a *naya* is the course of the scripture (*pāḷi*). Alternatively, it is a *naya* because by means of it they guide or protect the meaning; such as the *tathatā-naya* (the method of suchness), and so forth.
The root *daya* is used in the senses of giving, going, harming, giving, and protecting.

It gives; thus, it is *dayā*. The word *dayā* refers both to loving-kindness (*mettā*) and to compassion (*karuṇā*). For in the phrase "one who has become compassionate" (*dayāpanna*), loving-kindness is called "compassion," referring to the state of a mind imbued with love.
For the meaning is "has fallen into. In the phrase "one who has fallen into lack of pity" (*adayāpanno*), however, "pity" (*dayā*) refers to compassion (*karuṇā*).
Thus, the meaning is "one who has fallen into mercilessness. In this way, the application of the word *dayā* to both loving-kindness (*mettā*) and compassion should be understood.
For it is said in the *Abhidhammatīkā*: "Wherever the word *dayā* occurs, it should be applied there according to the intended sense (*adhippāya*)."
"For the word *dayā* (compassion), having internally included the sense of protection, occurs as both loving-kindness (*mettā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*).
Furthermore, the meaning of the words here should be understood as follows: it is called *dayā* because by means of it one gives (*dayati*) fearlessness to beings.
It "goes" (*dayati*)—that is, it proceeds equally toward both evil and virtuous persons without making distinctions, pervading them like a cool breeze.
*Dayā* (compassion) is like water that carries away dust and dirt; it is *mettā* (loving-kindness).

Or, it is called *dayā* because it "protects" (*dayati*) or "shields" (*hiṃsati*) the compassionate one from [the world] until the accomplishment of the other's welfare reaches its intended goal. Furthermore, it is *dayā* because a virtuous person "protects" (*dayati*) or "cherishes" (*anuggaṇhāti*) even those who are evil by means of this [attitude].
It is *dayā* because it "protects" (*dayati*) [the practitioner] such that, having abandoned even their own happiness, they take upon themselves weariness [for the sake of others].

It is called *dayā* because the virtuous person (*sajjana*) approaches by means of it. By means of this, the Great Bodhisattvas, at the time of making their aspiration for Buddhahood, desire to rescue sentient beings from the ocean of *saṃsāra*;

they cast aside even the fruit of *arahantship* already in their hands, and endure the great suffering of *saṃsāra*—which provides no consolation and is exceedingly terrifying—and in their final existence, simultaneously with the attainment of the Deathless Element (*amatadhātu*).
Compassion (*dayā*, *karuṇā*) is also that which is adorned with manifold qualities and omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). For all the Buddha-qualities have compassion as their root.

Another method: it is called compassion because by means of it one protects (*dayanti*) beings, or because one oneself feels sympathy (*anudayati*), or because it is merely the state of feeling sympathy;
thus, compassion is both loving-kindness (*mettā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*). Here we shall explain a certain application: "Just as, householder..."
“Just as a vulture, a heron, or a hawk might fly away taking a piece of meat, so did Maddī show compassion toward her sons, and toward her mother-in-law and father-in-law.

O bull among charioteers, she ought to have been shown compassion. In this context, *dayeyya* means “she would fly away”; it should be understood here in the sense of the verb root for going (*gati*).
*Dayesi* means “she would have cultivated a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward them. *Dayitabbo* means “she ought to have been loved. Both of these terms [refer to the same idea].
It should be understood that the commentary (*vivaraṇa*) has been composed according to the intended meaning (*adhippāyattha*), having included [the roots] for the purpose of protection.
*Ūyī* is in the sense of weaving threads (*tantasantāna*). It weaves (*ūyati*). [Past participle: *ūto*, *ūtavā*.

*Pūyī* is in the sense of spreading out and of foul odor (*duggandha*). It putrefies (*pūyati*). [Past participle: *pūto*, *pūtavā*. "A man who carries a rotten fish on the tip of a blade of *kusa* grass..."
*Kanu* is used in the sense of sound: *kanuyati*, *kanuto*, *kanutavā*.
*Khamā* is used in the sense of shaking off: *khamāyati*, *khamāto*, *khamātavā*.
*Phā* and *pā* are used in the sense of growth: *phāyati*, *phīto*, *phatavā*.
In this context, one should understand that there is the *tatavantupaccaya* suffix, the elision of the letter *ya*, and the substitution of the vowel *i* for the final vowel of the verbal root.
This same method should be applied, as far as applicable, to forms such as *pūto pūtavā*. *Pāyati*. *Pāyo*. *Apāyo*.

Here, *apāyo* means "that in which there is no flow (*pāyo*) or increase (*vuddhi*). Alternatively, it is also called *apāyo* because it has departed (*apeto*) from what is beneficial (*ayato*) or from happiness (*sukhato*).

This is to be etymologically analyzed. "Apāya" refers to the four states of misery: hell (niraya), the animal realm (tiracchānayoni), the sphere of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya), and the host of asuras (asurakāya).
The root *tā* is used in the senses of continuity and protection; it means "to protect. One should look at the root *tā* in the sense of "protection" within the *divādigaṇa*;
its forms are "tāyati" and "tāṇaṃ. The verbal form for both is the same. It differs only by the addition of the suffixes *aka* and *ya*.
There is a difference; however, the nominal forms are distinct, such as “tāyanaṃ” and “tāṇaṃ.

The root *cāyu* is used in the senses of worship (*pūjā*) and observation (*nisāmana*). Worship means honoring. Observation is said to mean both looking and hearing. For in such instances as “Come, Maddi, observe!
and “Observe, O virtuous ones!,” the words for looking and hearing are expressed by the term *nisāmana*.
Furthermore, it should be understood that "investigation by means of knowledge" (*ñāṇena upaparikkhaṇa*) is indeed "reflection" (*nisāmana*). [The root] *cāyati* means "to honor," "to revere.

[The term] *apace* refers to those who have gone forth as homeless ones, to those living the holy life (*brahmacāriye*). "Those who honor the elder" (*ye vuddhamapacāyanti*) demonstrates the act of honoring (*apaciti*). "Constantly honoring the elders" (*niccaṃ vuddhāpacāyino*).
These are forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *ya*.
Roots ending in *r*:
*rā* in the sense of taking; *rāti*.
*ri* in the sense of continuity; *reti*. *reṇu*; *reṇū* means dust.
*Ru* is used in the sense of going and in the sense of angering.

*Ravati*, *viravati*. *Ru* means sound. *Roti*, *ravati*. *Ravo*, *uparavo*. *Ruta-manuññaṃ ruciyā ca piṭṭhi*: *ruta* is crying out; *rutaṃ* is sound, noise. *Re* is sound. *Rāyati*. *Rā*. *Ratti*. And here the word *rāti* [is used].

*Rattī* is the time designated as night, the period when the sounds of beings have subsided. It is called *ratti* because therein (*ettha*) one rests (*rāyati*), that is, one is cut off [from activity] (*ucchijjati*).
*Brū* is used for distinct speech. *Api hantvā hato brūti*.
[Conjugations: *bravīti*, *brunti*; *brūsi*, *brūtha*; *brūmi*, *brūma*; *brūte*, *bruvante*; *brūse*, *bruvhe*;
*bruve*, *brumhe*. [Imperative: *brūtu*, *bruvitu*, *bruvantu*; *brūhi*, *brūtha*; *brūmi*, *brūma*; *brūtaṃ*, *bruvantaṃ*.

And here, in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, because the text reads “let the venerable Gotama speak again,” it is stated as “bruvitu. Thus, in all instances, the method should be understood after careful examination.
[The forms are: *bruveyya*, *bruve*, *bruveyyuṃ*; *brueyyāsi*, *bruveyyātha*; *brueyyāmi*, *bruveyyāma*; *brueyya*, *bruveram*; *brueyyo*, *brueyyāvho*; *brueyyam*, *brueyyāmhe*.

*Pabrūti*, *anubrūti*; *pabrūtu*, *anubrūtu*; *pabruveyya*, *anubruveyya*. In this way, throughout all instances, the paradigm should be applied accordingly with the prefixes *pa-* and *anu-*, as far as possible.
[Present tense: *āha*, *āhu*; *brave*, *bravittha*, *bravire*; *bravittho*, *bravivho*; *braviṃ*, *bravimhe*.

These are stated according to the *parokkhā* (perfect) tense. [Aorist tense: *abravā*, *abravū*; *abravo*, *abravattha*; *abravaṃ*, *abravamhā*; *abravattha*, *abravatthuṃ*; *abravase*, *abravhaṃ*; *abraviṃ*, *abravimhase*. These are stated according to the *hiyyattanī* (imperfect) tense.

He spoke, I spoke. He spoke, they two spoke. I spoke, we two spoke. You spoke, you two spoke. You spoke, you all spoke. I spoke, we two spoke. These are stated according to the *ajjatanī* (present perfect) tense. He will speak, they will speak. He spoke, they spoke. All the rest is to be inferred.
The passive voice (*kammapada*) is not commonly established; however, if it were to exist, it would be like the forms "brūyati" or the forms "luyati, lūyati."

*Jīra*: in the sense of maturing. Maturing (*brūhanaṃ*) means increasing (*vaḍḍhanaṃ*). It matures (*jīrati*). That which has matured is *jīraṃ*. That which is maturing is *jīramānaṃ*. The act of maturing is *jīraṇaṃ*.

"This person of little learning matures like an ox. *Pūra*: in the sense of filling. It fills (*pūrati*). "Like the great ocean, it fills. "May all intentions be fulfilled (*pūrentu*). To fill (*pūrituṃ*), having filled (*pūritvā*), full (*pūraṃ*), filled (*pūritaṃ*).
