Full (*puṇṇaṃ*), completely full (*paripuṇṇaṃ*). Fully complete (*sampuṇṇaṃ*), the act of filling (*pūraṇaṃ*). Pūraṇa Kassapa. In the causative sense: "the perfections" (*pāramiyo*).
It fills, it causes to fill, it causes to be filled, it causes to be caused to be filled. Forms such as *pūretvā*, *pūrayitvā*, *pūrāpetvā*, *pūrāpayitvā*, and *paripūretvā* occur.
The root *ghor* means "obstructing movement.
Obstructing movement is the warding off of movement. It obstructs (*ghorati*).
*Dhīra* refers to skill in movement (*gati-cāturiya*). Skill in movement is the state of being adept in movement.

*Dhīra*: [it is used] in the sense of "to move. One moves, moves about, moves forth; thus, *ussāraṇā*, *sara*, *saṃsāra*, and so on. In this context, *sara* means a lake. *Saṃsāra* means the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), which is also called "existence" (*bhava*).
*Cara* is in the sense of "walking. One walks, wanders, follows after, or roams about.

*Car-* [is used] in the senses of going and eating. One goes (*carati*), wanders about (*vicarati*), follows along (*anucarati*), roams about (*sañcarati*), or moves hither and thither (*paṭicarati*). [Nouns derived from it include: *cariyā* (conduct), *caritā* (one who has conducted himself), *cāra* (movement), *vicāra* (wandering), *anuvicāra* (following after), *upavicāra* (close wandering), *caraṇaṃ* (the act of going), *cāraka* (a wanderer), *ocāraka* (a spy), and *brahmacariyaṃ* (the holy life), and so forth.

In this context, "he goes" (*caratīti*) means he moves or he eats. For the teachers explain that the word *carati* has the meanings of both "going" and "eating. Thus, they say that one who "goes" (*gacchanto*) and one who "eats" (*khādanto*) are both said to "move" (*carati*).
"He moves hither and thither" (*paṭicarati*) means he conceals. *Cāraka* refers to those beings who have been introduced into that [place].
One who moves about happily while eating is a *cāraka*, meaning a wanderer. An *ocāraka* is one who moves below.

"Brahmacariya" (the holy life) is said to refer to giving, service, the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), the teaching of the Dhamma, abstention from sexual intercourse, contentment with one's own wife, the Uposatha, the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), the entire Dispensation (*sāsana*), and even one’s underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*).
What was your vow, and what indeed was your holy life?
Of what well-practiced deed is this the fruition:
this supernatural power, radiance, strength, energy, and rebirth?
And this, O Naga, is your great celestial mansion.
Both I and my wife were patrons of giving, endowed with faith, in the world of humans.
My home was then like a well,
and the ascetics and brahmins were satisfied.
That indeed was my vow, and that was my holy life.
"This is the fruition of that well-performed deed:
supernatural power, radiance, strength, energy, and rebirth—
this, O wise one, is my great celestial mansion."
For in this Puṇṇaka Jātaka, giving is described as "the holy life" (brahmacariya):
"With what hand does one give desires? With what hand is there the flow of honey?
By what holy life of yours is merit accomplished in the hand?"
“By that hand, the giver of desires; by that hand, the flow of honey;
by that holy life of mine, merit succeeds in the hand.
In this *Aṅkurapeta-vatthu*, service is called “the holy life” (*brahmacariya*). “This, monks, is that... [text continues].
In this Tittira Jātaka, the training rule is referred to as "the holy life" (*brahmacariya*), as in the statement: "There was a holy life called Tittiriya.

In this Mahāgovinda Sutta, however, the divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) are referred to as "the holy life," as in: "But that holy life, Pañcasikha, leads neither to disenchantment nor to dispassion... [etc. ...only as far as rebirth in the Brahma-world."
In the passage, “In a single holy life, a thousand [who have] abandoned death,” the teaching of the Dhamma is called “the holy life.
In the Sallekha Sutta, however, “abstinence from sexual intercourse” is called “the holy life,” as in: “Others will be non-celibate; we here shall be celibate.”
We do not transgress against our wives,
nor do our wives transgress against us;
apart from her, we lead the holy life.
"Therefore, indeed, we young ones do not die"— thus,
in the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka, contentment with one's own wife is called "the holy life" (*brahmacariya*).
By means of an inferior holy life, one is reborn among the Khattiyas.
“By the middling [observance], one is reborn among the devas; by the highest, one is purified.
Thus, in the Nimijātaka, the Uposatha performed by way of non-transgression is called “the holy life” (*brahmacariya*).
“But this, Pañcasikha, is the holy life for the sake of absolute disenchantment, for the sake of dispassion... this very Noble Eightfold Path...”
In the Mahāgovinda Sutta itself, the Noble Path is called "the holy life" (*brahmacariya*).

In the Pāsādika Sutta, however, the entire teaching—comprising the three trainings—is called "the holy life," as it says: "And this holy life is successful, prosperous, widespread, popular, and well-proclaimed among humans."
“Even for those who are not hasty, the hope for fruit succeeds;
I have matured my holy life—know this thus, O village headman.
Here, the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*) is called “the holy life” (*brahmacariya*). Thus it is said.
Generosity, service, training in the divine abodes,
preaching the Dhamma, abstaining from sexual intercourse, and the Uposatha day;
contentment with one's own wife, and the Noble Path— this is the Teaching.
These [terms]—*ajjhāsaya*, *sadda*, *brahmacariya*, *sara*, and *saraṇa*—are explained as follows: The prefix *hu-* signifies crookedness (*koṭilla*).
It is derived from the root *hurati*.
The root *sar-* signifies sound (*sadda*) and burning (*opatāpa*). It is derived from *sarati*. *Sara* means sound; *saraṇa* means refuge.
And here, "sara" refers both to sound and to heat. It is called "saraṇa" because it causes one to remember (*sarati*), or because it burns (*upatāpeti*) and harms;

for those who have gone for refuge, by that very act of going for refuge, fear, anguish, suffering, miserable rebirth, and affliction are [removed]—thus it is "saraṇa. This refers to the Triple Gem, beginning with the Buddha.
Alternatively, people who possess faith and clarity remember and think, "This is our refuge (*saraṇa*)," and they contemplate it therein.
And they utter speech and even go for refuge.
This is the analysis of *sara*. There are also such usages as *sarati* and *susarati*.
For there is both an increase in the number of syllables and a change in form, as in: "two, duve; *taṇhā*, *tasiṇā*; *pamhaṃ*, *pakhuma*"; and likewise *anussarati*, *paṭissarati*.

*Sati* (mindfulness) is so called because beings remember by means of it, or because it itself remembers, or because it is merely the act of remembering (*saraṇa*). It is *anussati* (recollection) and *paṭissati* (re-recollection).
One who remembers is *sato*; one who remembers again and again is *paṭissato*.

The root *dhar* signifies "restraining" (*saṃvaraṇe*). Restraining is protection (*rakkhaṇā*). One restrains (*dharati*), hence *dvāraṃ* (door/gate). This is also derived from the prefix *dvi-* and the root *ar*.
This form is established as follows. Here are the etymological explanations: it is called a *dvāra* because by means of it one restrains (*saṃvaranti*), guards, or closes off;
or else, it is called a *dvāra* because two door-panels (*kavāṭa*) move (*aranti*), go, or function there.

A house-door, the doors of the body and so forth, and even a means (*upāya*) is called a "door. In the Canon, however, the forms "dvāraṃ" and "dvārā" appear according to the feminine and neuter genders respectively.
The word *dvāra* has been mentioned. For it is stated that it possesses both genders, as in “the door is well-guarded” (*dvārampi surakkhitaṃ hoti*) and “this is a door” (*dvārāpesā*).
[Roots: *gara* and *ghara* mean to sprinkle. One sprinkles (*garati*), one sprinkles (*gharati*).
*Gharaṃ* (a house). [Root] *dhūra* means to bend. Bending (*hucchana*) is crookedness. One bends (*dhūrati*).
*Tara* means a boat, a raft, or a crossing. *Tarati*, *taraṇaṃ*, *titthaṃ*, *tiṇṇo*, *uttiṇṇo*, *otiṇṇo*, and so forth.
In this context, *taraṇaṃ* refers to a boat; it floats upon the surface of the water, and by the sense that "by means of this one crosses or traverses a river.
A boat, a raft, a float, a ship—these are synonyms for *taraṇaṃ*; likewise, *uttaraṇaṃ* is the same.
These are names for water-vehicles, namely boats.
*Tara* means to hasten; *sambhama* means agitation or lack of composure. [From the root] *tṛ*: *tarati*, *tarito*, *turaṅgo*.

Here, the canonical passage, “Having hurried across the field of the moon (*māsakhettaṃ tarito*), he departed,” serves as an illustration. In that context, *tarito* means having hastened or being agitated. *Avāsariṃ* means I approached or I entered.
“Old age as a disease. Here, by virtue of the usage, it is specifically old age as a disease that is intended by the word “disease.

Indeed, the word “disease” is stated [after] the word “old age” in order to restrict the application of the term “old age” to old age as a disease. Therefore, no other disease is referred to here by the word “disease.

[Examples: *jarati* (he grows old); *jaro* (old age); *sajjaro* (with old age); *pajjararogo* (the disease of advanced old age); “men afflicted by old age. However, where this [word] denotes the decline of the life-span (*vayohāni*), [it is used differently].
In that context, regarding the verbal root *jīr*, its forms are *jīrati* and *jarā*.

The root *dar* means "fear. It takes the form *darati*. An example is: "caves as dwellings, caves as abodes" (*bīlāsayā darīsayā*). In this instance, *darī* refers to a cave in the sense of something to be feared.

The root *dar* also occurs in the senses of "respect" (*ādara*) and "disrespect" (*anādara*). It takes the forms *darati*, *ādarati*, and *anādarati*. Its derivatives are *ādaro* (respect) and *anādaro* (disrespect).

And here, "dara" means "it terrifies," "it causes fear," and "it causes disrespect. For just as the word *āraka* denotes both "far" and "near," so too this verbal root *dar* should be understood as denoting both respect and disrespect.
Furthermore, the word *dara* applies to bodily agitation (*kāyadaratha*), mental agitation (*cittadaratha*), and the agitation of the defilements (*kilesadaratha*). For this—
“While I was burning, like a fire sprinkled with ghee, you have sprinkled me with water as it were and extinguished all my distress.
Herein, this refers to bodily agitation and mental agitation. “Free from distress, free from sorrow, free from the dart, having realized through direct knowledge...”

In the phrase "the Buddha spoke," however, *daratha* refers to the distress of the defilements (*kilesa*). "Free from distress" (*vītaddara*) means one whose distress of defilements has departed because all defilements have been utterly eradicated by the supreme path (*aggamagga*). "Nara" [is derived as follows]:
it moves (*narati*), thus a man (*naro*) or a woman (*nārī*).
Here, "man" (*nara*) means a person. For he is called a "man" because he leads (*narati*) or guides.

Just as a being who was originally of a lower nature is later called a "person" (*purisa*) in the sense of being superior (*seṭṭhaṭṭhena*) because he dwells (*seti*) or exists in a high station (*puri*), so too is he called a "man" in the sense of leading.
For even a person who has become a son or a brother stands in the position of a leader for his mother, sisters, and elder brothers.

And so too the other [term] for the others. She is called *nārī* because of her connection with a man (*nara*), or because she goes toward a man; thus she is a *nārī*. Furthermore, there is another etymology here for the word *nara*:
he is a *nara* because he is led (*nariyati*) by his own karma, that is, he is guided; [it refers to] a sentient being or a human. For it is said: "The world is led by karma.
In that context, regarding the word *nara* when used to denote a male: "Men and then women."
This is an illustration. Furthermore, in the seventh instance of the word *nara*, there is the illustration: “This Buddha is such a supreme among men;
gods and humans are filled with joy. Therefore, the meaning should be explained in each respective context as appropriate:
“*Nara* means a man, *nara* means a being, and *nara* means a human.”
*Hara* means taking away. *Haraṇaṃ* is causing to proceed. *Harati*. He dwells at Sāvatthī. He dwelt. They dwelt. He will dwell.

He will dwell diligently. He transacts business. He transacts business together. Or, he takes everything away. The transaction of silver, or the taking away of silver. A miracle. The taking away of rapture and gladness.
A dwelling. Transaction. Bringing forward. He directs the mind.

*Sāsane viharaṃ*: dwelling in the Dispensation; *viharanto*: dwelling; *viharamāno*: while dwelling. *Vihātabbaṃ*: that which is to be dwelt in; *viharituṃ*: in order to dwell. *Viharitvā*: having dwelt.

Other [forms] should also be applied accordingly. In this context, *pāṭihāriya* means: when the mind is concentrated, free from defilements, and has accomplished its task, that which is to be brought forth (*pacchā haritabba*) or manifested (*pavattetabba*) afterwards is a *pāṭihāriya*. For the word *paṭi* here conveys the meaning of "afterwards" (*pacchā*).
It is as in such passages as: “While I had entered therein, another brahmin arrived.

*Vihāra* means a dwelling place (*āvāsa*) for bhikkhus, so called because they dwell there by means of standing, sitting, and so forth; or it is the act of dwelling (*viharaṇa*), the activity of dwelling.
*Vohāra* means conventional usage (*byavahāra*), designation (*paṇṇatti*), speech (*vacana*), and volition (*cetanā*). In that regard:
“Whoever among humans lives off trade—know this, Vāseṭṭha, he is a merchant, not a brahmin.
This is what is called conventional usage (*vyavahāra-vohāra*). “Calculation, designation, description, usage”—this is what is called conventional description (*paṇṇatti-vohāra*).
...is called "name. To speak and to grasp [things] in such and such ways is what is called "verbal convention" (*vacanavohāra*).
"The eight noble conventions and the eight ignoble conventions"—this is what is called "volitional convention" (*cetanāvohāra*). Thus:
In verbal usage and in speech, And in designations and volitions;
The word *vohāra* is seen in these four senses: 1. **Hara** (taking away):
in the sense of removal. Removal means taking out. He removes a fault; he takes it out. *Nīhāra*, he avoids; *parihāra*. Dust-remover (*rajoharaṇa*).
The Dhamma that removes all faults. And [it applies] to the adversaries of the Blessed One and his Teaching.

It is called a *pāṭihāriya* because it carries away (*harati*) those who hold other views. Here, through the variation in measures and forms, there are three word-forms: *pāṭiheraṃ*, *pāṭihīraṃ*, and *pāṭihāriyaṃ*.
[The root] *hṛ* means "to take. It takes what is not given; it will take; it shall take—thus it is said. "Cast away the donkey-skin and the empty [vessel], and the donkey-load..."
"Hāhitī"—this is the illustration here. [The forms are: āharati, avaharati, saṃharati, apaharati, upaharati, paharati, sampaharati, samāharati.

Examples include: the Manohara palace; the seizing of another's property; food (āhāra), carrying away (avahāra), gathering (saṃhāra), offering (upahāra), conflict (sampahāra), and collection (samāhāra).
[Passive forms: hariyyati, āhariyyati, [plural] āhariyyanti. [Past participle: āhaṭaṃ.
*Harituṃ*, *āharituṃ*, *āharitvā*, *āharitvāna*. Other [forms] should also be applied accordingly. *Dhara* means "to hold.
Holding (*dharaṇaṃ*) is the state of existing. He holds; he maintains the Teacher’s instruction (*satthusāsanaṃ*).
*Dhara* also means "not to perish. Nirvana is eternally held (ever-abiding).

*Khara*: to destroy (*khaye*). *Kharati*. The act of destroying (*kharaṇaṃ*). They do not destroy (*na kharanti*) nor do they decay (*na khiyyanti*), thus they are called *akkharāni* (syllables). They do not destroy (*na kharanti*) nor do they perish (*na nassanti*), thus they are called *nakkhattāni* (constellations);

so say the ancients. *Jāgara*: to wake (*jāgaraniddakkhaye*). *Jāgarati*. Wakefulness (*jāgaro*), the act of waking (*jāgaraṇaṃ*), waking (*jāgaraṃ*). Long is the night for one who is awake. While staying awake (*jāgaramāno*). And this root, having entered the *tanādigaṇa*, produces such forms as *jāgaroti* and *paṭijāgaroti*.

*Īra*: in the sense of speaking, going, and shaking. *Īrati*. That which is shaken (*īritaṃ*). *Eritaṃ*. The wind (*samīraṇo*). The Dhamma is shaken by the Victor (*jinerito dhammo*). Even the winds shake when they are stirred up (*eritassa*).

In this context, *samīraṇa* means wind (*vāta*). For it moves (*samīrati*) or blows, and it causes tree branches, leaves, and so forth to tremble violently; thus it is called "the mover" (*samīraṇa*). *Hare* is used in the sense of shame.

This root ends in the vowel *e* without elision (*alutta*), like the root *gile* in the sense of the destruction of bile. [It forms] *harāyati*. [The noun] *harāyanaṃ*. [Phrases such as] "I am distressed, I am ashamed. Here, *harāyati* means to feel shame;
the meaning is that one exercises a sense of moral dread (*hiri*).

The root *para* is used in the senses of protecting (*pālana*) and filling (*pūraṇa*). Its forms are *parati* and *paramo*, just as the forms *narati* and *naro* arise from the root *nara* (to protect).
In this context, *parati* means he protects or he fills. This word is stated here according to the simple agent (*suddhakattar*).
For according to the causal agent (*hetukattar*), forms such as *pāreti* and *pārayati* occur. *Paramo* means a protector or a filler. And here—
The word *pāramī* establishes this meaning. For it is thus: *paramo* means one who goes beyond (*parati*) and one who causes [others] to reach the further shore (*pāreti*);
the Great Bodhisatta is the protector and fulfiller of qualities such as giving. *Pāramī* is that which belongs to the Supreme One (*parama*), or the state or action of the Supreme One;
it refers to the practice of giving and so forth. However, the teachers say: "He fulfills, thus he is supreme (*paramo*); he is the fulfiller of qualities such as giving."
And it is said, “pālaka,” which is to be examined.
*Vara* means to choose; [from] *varati*. *Vāraṇo*, *varuṇo*.
*Gira* means to swallow down; swallowing down is trickling forth. [From] *girati*, *giri*.
In this context, "mountain" (*girī*) refers to hills, which are described by many names such as "rock" (*sela*) and so forth.

It is called a "mountain" (*pabbata*) because it possesses ridges (*paba*), which are known as joints (*sandhi*). It is called a "mountain" (*girī*) because it swallows (*giraṇa*) water and the medicinal substances and other materials that constitute its essence, such as those found in the Himalayas and similar places.
These, moreover, are its names:
mountain (pabbata), immovable (acala), rock (sela), elephant (naga), peak (giri), earth-bearer (mahīdhara), and heap of stones (addi, siluccaya); these are the designations for a mountain.
*Sura* [is used] in the senses of sovereignty (*issariya*) and splendor (*ditti*). It means "he delights" (*surati*). A *sura* is an *asura*.
In this context, one who "flows" (*sarati*), "delights" (*surati*), "rules" (*īsati*), attains divine sovereignty, and shines—such a one is a *sura*.

Or, one who possesses beautiful speech (*rā*) is a *sura*, that is, a god (*deva*). We shall explain the designations for gods in the *div-ādi* group [of roots]. An *asura* is not like a god (*deva*).
He does not rejoice, he does not rule, and he does not shine; thus he is an *asura*. Or, he is an *asura* because he is the adversary of the *suras*, just as enemies are the adversaries of friends.
He is a *dānava*, who is also called a "former god" (*pubbadeva*). For it is said in the *Kumbha-jātaka*:
"Having drunk which, the former gods became intoxicated..."
"Having passed away from the Heaven of the Thirty-Three,
where one dwells in eternal bliss— O Great King, knowing this present intoxicant to be so utterly useless, how could one drink it?"
In the commentary on the Sagāthāvagga, however, it is stated: "They said, 'We did not drink *sura*, we did not drink *sura*'; from that time forth they became known as *asuras*.
These are its synonyms:
*asura*, *pubbadeva*, *dānava*, and *devatāri*.
The wise should explain these names as belonging to the Asuras.
However, regarding the name "Pāka," which belongs to one particular Asura,
some say it is merely a designation (paṇṇatti), while others, the venerable ones, have declared otherwise.
*Kur* is used in the senses of sound and reproach. *Kurati*. *Kurara*, *kurarī*. *Kumma*, *kummī*.
*Khur* is used in the senses of cutting and scratching. *Khurati*. *Khura*.
*Mur* is used in the sense of enveloping. *Murati*. *Mura*, *mora*.
*Ghura*: intoxicated by sounds; it roars; a roar (*ghora*). *Pura*: going at the head.
"Going at the head" means leading the way, or going first of all. It precedes (*purati*). A city (*pura*), a capital (*purī*). It opens wide (*avāpurati*). "Open wide this door of the Deathless.
Taking up the opening, he goes. In that context, *pura* refers to a royal capital; for these are synonyms: "city, *pura*, *purī*, royal capital."
In such passages as “That man Āḷārika [is] in the city (*pura*) with the young maiden,” however, “city” (*pura*) refers to a house.
It is called a “city” because it is to be gone to by going forward and forward (*purato purato gamanena gantabba*); thus it denotes both a royal capital and a house. Regarding “a bolt” (*avāpuraṇa*):
it is a “bolt” because one opens or uncovers the door by means of it; that which is also called a “key” (*kuñcikā*) or a “latch” (*tāḷa*). In such phrases as “he opens” (*avāpurati*), etc.:
Both *ava* and *ā* should be understood as prefixes (*upasagga*).
The root *phara* means "to pervade" (*pharaṇa*). Pervasion (*pharaṇa*) means spreading or going. It pervades equally with cold. It pervades for the purpose of nutriment. [The noun form is] *pharaṇa*.
The root *gara* means "to rise up" (*uggama*). It rises; [the noun form is] *garu*.
"Venerable ones" (*garū*) refers to persons such as parents who are endowed with reverence. For they rise up high; being elevated, they become manifest, and thus they are called "venerable.
Furthermore, they are called "venerable" in the sense of being heavy, like a stone parasol.
The word *garu* [is used] in the case of parents in such passages as: "Please sit on this seat, for you are one of my venerables."
It is seen [in this way]. Regarding the phrase “one who is revered by the world of humans and gods,” it refers here to the Omniscient One, the teacher of the entire world.
Furthermore, the word *garu* (revered) is seen in other senses as well. Having brought all these together, the following is said here:
“Toward parents and teachers, toward those difficult to support and those lacking ability;”
The word *garu* occurs in reference to those who are great and eminent,
to those who perform services such as sweeping, and likewise to specific distinctions of excellence.
However, some teachers, taking the term as "garu" and "garū" in two ways, maintain that the word *garu* is established in the sense of expressing heaviness.
Regarding the status of being a teacher (*ācariya-vācakatta*), however, some say that the word *guru* is used; this should not be accepted.

For within the scope of the Pāli language, the word *garu* alone should be desired to denote all the aforementioned meanings, since we see the form *gārava*—a derivative (*taddhita*) word with the suffix *-a*—where the vowel *a* has been changed to *ā*.
But in the scope of the Sanskrit language, it is indeed the word *guru* [that is used].
It should be desired [as such], because otherwise we see words ending in a *taddhita* suffix where the vowel *u* has undergone *vuddhi*.
[The root] *mar* [means] "to kill. [Examples: *marati*, *mattuṃ*, *maritvā*. In the case of the causal agent (*hetukattari*): "A man kills a man" (*puriso purisaṃ māreti*, *mārayati*).
"A man causes a man to be killed by another man" (*puriso purisena purisaṃ mārāpeti*, *mārāpayati*). "In order to kill," "having killed," and so forth.
Forms. *Macco*, *maru*, *maraṇaṃ*, *maccu*, *maṭṭhu*, *māro*. In this context, *mattuṃ* means "to die.
For instance, in the *Alīnasattu Jātaka*, the canonical text is seen as: "He who would wish to die for the sake of his father's release.
*Macco* is a being who has received the name "macco" because of the nature of having to die (*maritabbasabhāvatāya*). *Maru* refers to one who, though long-lived...
One who has the nature of dying is a *maru*, a deity. "Dying" means passing away (*cuti*).
Death, the ender, mortality, the hunter, time, the destroyer, the casting off, and passing away—these indeed are the names for death.
"Māra" is so called because he destroys the wholesome qualities of beings;
he is Kāmadeva. These are his names:
Māra, Namuci, Kaṇha, Vasavatti, and Pajāpati.

Pamattabandhu (the Kinsman of the Negligent), Maddana (the Deluder), Pāpimā (the Evil One), Dabbaka (the Arrogant), Kandappa (the Lustful), Ratipati (Lord of Pleasure), Kāma (Desire), and Kusumāyudha (He Whose Weapon is the Flower).

Others mention various other names as well, but since they do not conform to the Teaching (*sāsana*), they have not been shown here. In the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, only four names are recorded: Māra, Namuci, Kaṇha, and Pamattabandhu.

And here, "Māra" refers to the five Māras: the Māra of defilements (kilesa-māra), the Māra of the aggregates (khandha-māra), the Māra of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra-māra), the Māra of death (maccu-māra), and the Māra who is a son of the gods (devaputta-māra).
*Dhara* means in the sense of supporting; it supports (*dharati*). *Bhara* means in the sense of nourishing; it nourishes (*bharati*). [Thus] one is supported (*bharito*) or a supporter (*bhattā*).
*Thara* in the sense of spreading out. It spreads, it is spread out. Spreading out.
*Dara* in the sense of splitting. It splits the earth; a pickaxe.
*Dara* in the sense of burning. The body burns; distress, anguish (*daratha*).
*Tira* means in a downward direction; it means to cross over. *Tiracchāno* or *tiracchā* [means that]. *Ara* means in a direction; it means to go. *Atthaṃ*, *attho*, *utu*.
Here, *atthaṃ* refers to Nibbāna. That which performs (*arati*) or carries out (*vatteti*) the various functions of beings is *utu*.
Forms of verbal roots ending in *rak*.
Verbal root ending in *lak*:
*lā* (to take). *Lāti*. *Lānaṃ*, *garuḷo*, *sīhaḷo*, *rāhulo*, *kusalaṃ*, *bālo*, *mahallako*, *mahallikā*.
In this context, *garuḷo* means one who brings (*lāti*), takes (*ādadāti*), or seizes (*gaṇhāti*) what is heavy (*garuṃ*);

thus he is called *garuḷo*, who is also referred to as *supaṇṇo*, *dijādhipo*, *nāgāri*, and *karoṭī*. *Sīhaḷo* means one who brings, takes, or seizes a lion (*sīhaṃ*); thus he is *sīhaḷo*, the ancestor.
Those born in his lineage are all now known as *sīhaḷā*.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Rāhula": he is called Rāhula because he "takes" (lāti) like Rāhu; who is he? It is the Venerable Rāhulabhadda, the Son of the Buddha, who desires training.

For on the day of his birth, King Suddhodana sent a message to the Bodhisatta, who was sporting in the park, saying, "Announce my joy to my son. When the Bodhisatta heard this, he said, "A Rāhu is born—a bond."
"He was born," he said. For the birth of a son is like the seizing by Rāhu;
because it causes the defilement of craving and provides no release from being bound as if by a heavy chain or fetter, he said, "Rāhu is born, a bond is born.
The king, having asked, "What did my son say? and having heard those words, [said], "From this time forth..."
He said, "Let my grandson be named Rāhula," and from that time forth the prince became known by the name Rāhula.
For in the *Mahāpadānasutta-ṭīkā*, regarding the phrase "Rāhu was born," it is stated that "Rāhu means the planet Rāhu";
however, that was said according to the intended meaning (*adhippāyattha*) in order to clarify the sense of the word "Rāhula. Indeed, [the name] is not merely...
The word “Rāhu” expresses the meaning “the planet Rāhu,” yet it does so by receiving the connection with the word “born.
For instance, the statement made by the Bodhisatta, “Rāhu was born,” has the meaning “the planet Rāhu was born”;
therefore, the Great King Suddhodana thought, “My grandson shall be called Rāhula because he takes after Rāhu.”
It should be understood that after reflecting, [the Buddha] said, "Let him be named Rāhula.
However, some read, "Rāhula was born; a bond was born," and this is written in certain manuscripts;
yet that is not good, because it is inconsistent with the meaning and contradicts the commentary (*ṭīkā*). For [the name] "Rāhula" does not refer to the boy...

The name was indeed given first, but it was only subsequently given because it had been bestowed by his grandfather; therefore, it was not appropriate for the Bodhisatta at that time to say, "Rāhula has been born.
For just as the designation "Great King" does not apply to a person who has not yet been anointed king, so too [the name Rāhula was not applicable].
And in the *Ṭīkā* it is said: "Rāhu means the planet Rāhu. Now, they might think: "Rāhula..."

Since the phrase "birth is bondage" (*jāto bandhanaṃ jātaṃ*) exists [in the text], it is also untenable to claim that in the commentary the word *gaha*—which has the same meaning as the suffix *lā* in the sense of a state of being (*bhāva-vasena*)—is used in the sense of "taking" (*ādāna*), as in "the seizing of Rāhu" (*rāhuggaha*).
This is because the reading should have been stated as "the birth of those named Rāhula is bondage" (*rāhulānaṃ jātaṃ bandhanaṃ jātaṃ*). For this word "Rāhula" is [analogous to] the word "Sīhaḷa."
It denotes a substance and never a state; therefore, one should not adopt the reading "Rāhula was born,
a bond was born," which has been wrongly inserted by some, but rather the reading "Rāhu was born,
a bond was born" should be accepted and understood as the essential meaning, since it is seen in many thoroughly purified ancient manuscripts.
And because it has been recited by teachers and their disciples with profound and subtle knowledge.
Here, however, this is the explanation of the meaning according to the intended purpose:

having heard the news of his son's birth, the Bodhisatta, overcome with spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), says, "Now my Rāhu has been born," speaking thus in the sense that [the world] cannot be liberated from him.
The meaning is: "Rāhu has arisen for the purpose of seizing. By the phrase "the bond has arisen," he says, "A bond for me has arisen.
For it is said thus in the *Ṭīkā*: "Rāhu means the planet Rāhu. In that context, "planet Rāhu" (*rāhuggaho*) means: he seizes, thus he is a "seizer" (*gaho*);
Rāhu himself is the seizer, thus "the planet Rāhu" (*rāhuggaho*). The meaning is: "Rāhu, my captor, has arisen. Alternatively, "seizing" (*gahaṇa*) is the "seizure" (*gaho*).
*Rāhuggaha* means the seizing by Rāhu; the meaning is: "The seizing of Rāhu has happened to me. For the son is like Rāhu, and the father is like the moon, because he was seized by the son-Rāhu.
However, some, seeing this passage—"let him be named Rāhula"—and hearing it said, "Rāhu is born," [object that] by this...
Thinking that it accords [with the facts] only when it is stated, "Rāhula was born," they read and write the text in this way;
therefore, that poorly placed reading, recited without investigation, should not be accepted.
Rather, the venerable ones should accept the aforementioned ancient reading, favored by the ancient teachers, because it accords with the meaning, according to the commentary.
And "non-contradiction with the truth.
In this context, "wholesome" (*kusala*) means that knowledge (*ñāṇa*) is called *kusa* because it removes (*sānana*) and diminishes (*tanukaraṇa*) base and evil states;

that which is to be obtained (*lātabba*) or set in motion (*pavattetabba*) by means of that *kusa* is "wholesome" (*kusala*). A "fool" (*bāla*) is one who [is characterized by] what is reckoned as pertaining to the present life and the future life...
A fool (*bāla*) is so called because he brings or takes upon himself two kinds of misfortune, like Devadatta, Kokālika, and others. These, moreover, are his names:
the fool, the ignorant, the other, the one lacking knowledge, the one without vision, the unwise, the unskilled, the dull-witted, the one of poor intellect, and the dullard.
One who is mute and dull-witted, foolish, lacking insight, ignorant, blind and childish, witless, and unlearned. Regarding "mahallaka":
he takes or grasps at greatness, thus he is *mahallaka*; an old man. These are his names:
*Jiṇṇo*, *mahallako*, *vuddho*, *buddho*, *vuḍḍho*, *kattaro*,
and *thero*— these words are designations for one who is aged. For instance:
“In old age, not seeing [clearly], he has come to beg for an eye”—
in such passages as these, the word *thera* should be understood in the sense of "an elderly person.
Furthermore, these names are to be applied to a woman according to the feminine gender:
*Jiṇṇā*, *mahallikā*, *vuddhī*, *buddhī*, *vuḍḍhī*, and *kattarā*, as well as *therī*—these words are names for an old woman.
[The roots] *dala* and *phala* mean "to burst open" (*visaraṇa*). [Examples: *dalati*, *phalati*; *dalito rukkho* (the tree has burst open); *phalito bhūmibhāgo* (the ground has burst open).
*Ala* means ornament (*bhūsana*). It adorns (*alati*). Thus: *alaṅkāra*, *alaṅkata*, *alaṅkataṃ*. For in this poetic composition of the poets, as in the verse:
“Even when joined with faces possessing ornaments (*sālaṅkānana*), [it is] excluding faces possessing ornaments (*sālaṅkānanavajjitā*)”—here the word *alaṅka* denotes a specific kind of ornament.
However, some here read the verbal root as *ala* in the sense of ornamenting, covering, and warding off, and they accept the form *alatī*. We [follow the former].
However, we do not accept that the word *alaṃ* expresses the sense of "preventing study" (*pariyatti-nivāraṇa*), because such usage is not observed.
On the contrary, the particle *alaṃ* is seen expressing the sense of "preventing study," as in: "All this is enough; I have had enough of that kingship," and so forth.
[The root] *mīl* is in the sense of closing. One closes (*mīlati*), one closes the eyes (*nimīlati*), one opens the eyes (*ummīlati*). Closing (*nimīlanaṃ*).
*Bila* means a pillar. *Bilati* means it stands firm.
*Nīla* means blue in color. *Nīlavatthaṃ* means blue cloth.
*Sīla* refers to concentration (*samādhi*). *Sīlati* means it cools. *Sīlaṃ* means cooling; *sīlanaṃ* means the act of cooling.
Here, "virtue" (*sīla*) means virtue in the sense of "conducting" (*sīlana*). For this has been said in the *Visuddhimagga*: "In what sense is it 'virtue' (*sīla*)?
It is virtue in the sense of conducting. What is this so-called 'conducting'? It means either the composure of bodily action and so forth by way of good conduct, that is, non-distraction;
or else, it is the state of being a support through the stabilization of wholesome states."

This is the meaning. For it is precisely these two meanings here that those learned in the characteristics of words (saddalakkhaṇavidū) acknowledge. Others, however, explain the meaning here by such methods as:
"the sense of head (siraṭṭho) is the sense of virtue (sīlaṭṭho); the sense of coolness (sītalaṭṭho) is the sense of virtue.

In this context, the statement "those learned in the characteristics of words acknowledge two meanings" refers to [the roots] "sīla in the sense of concentration (samādhimhi)" and "sīla in the sense of supporting (upadhāraṇe)."
This was stated with reference to the meaning of the root *sīl* belonging to the *cur-ādi* class.
For when this root has entered the *cur-ādi* group, the forms *sīleti* and *sīlayati* occur in the sense of "upholding" (*upadhāraṇe*), and their meaning is "he upholds.

However, here, because it belongs to the *bhū-ādi* class, the form *sīlati* occurs in the sense of "composing" or "concentrating" (*samādhāne*), and its meaning is "he composes himself" (*samādhiyati*). Furthermore, in this context for the sake of the listeners...

Etymological explanations are stated for the purpose of easy comprehension. It is called *sīla* because it cools (*sīlati*), because it concentrates (*samādhiyati*), and because, through the excellence of bodily action and so forth, it does not become distracted.
Alternatively, it is called *sīla* because by means of it they concentrate the mind (*samādahanti*).

These etymologies are according to the *bhū-vādi* class of roots. However, according to the *cur-ādi* class of roots, one "cools" (*sīleti*) by supporting wholesome states through its nature as a foundation.
It is called *sīla* because it supports firmly (*bhuso dhāreti*). Or, according to the etymologies: they support (*sīlenti*) wholesome states by means of it, or they support them firmly;
thus they are "good" (*sādhu*), which is why it is called *sīla*.
[The root] *kila* means to bind. It binds (*kilati*). [The noun] *kila*.

*Kūla* means "obstructing. It is derived from *kulati*. The word *kūla* refers to a bank or a tree growing on the edge of water. One binds the bank (*kūlaṃ bandhati*). "We dwell on the river bank" (*nadīkūle vasāmahe*). It is called a *kūla* because it obstructs (*kūlati*), preventing the water from flowing out.
*Sūla* means "pain. It is derived from *sūlati*. The word *sūla* refers to earache; one does not produce earache (*kaṇṇasūlaṃ na janeti*). *Tūla* means "lightness.
Lightness is so called because it must be measured even by as much as a small amount of chaff (*karīsa*). It is derived from *tūlati*. "The wind carries away the cotton (*tūla*) as if it were straw."
*Pula* means to crush (*saṅghāte*). It crushes; thus, *pañcapuli*.

*Mūla* means to establish (*patiṭṭhāyaṃ*), it establishes; thus, *mūlaṃ*. The word *mūla* is seen in the sense of a root in such passages as, "One should pull up the roots, even down to the size of a grass stalk.
In such passages as, "Greed is a root of unwholesomeness," it refers to an uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇahetu*). [It is used] from midday onwards...

In such passages as “at the time the shadow falls,” “in a windless place the leaves fall,” and “to the extent that it is at the foot of a tree,” [the word *mūla*] means “nearby. Regarding this, it is said:
The word *mūla* appears in the sense of a root, and likewise in other ways;
it occurs in the sense of a unique cause and also in the sense of proximity.

*Phala* [is used] in the sense of production (*nibbatti*). "The tree bears fruit" (*rukkho phalati*). "Eating the fruits of the tree" (*rukkhaphalāni bhuñjantā*). "Great fruit, great benefit" (*mahapphalaṃ mahānisaṃsaṃ*). "The fruit of stream-entry" (*sotāpattiphalaṃ*). In that context, *phalanti* means "producing greatly.
*Phala* [is used] in the sense of splitting (*bheda*). "It splits" (*phalati*). "May your head split into seven pieces" (*muddhā te phalatu sattadhā*).

"His feet split" (*pādā phaliṃsu*). In that context, *phalatū* means "to burst open. *Phala* [is used] in the sense of an unskilled sound (*abyattasadda*). "The thunderbolt splits" (*asanī phalati*). "Monks, these two do not tremble when the thunderbolt splits" (*dveme bhikkhave asaniyā phalantiyā na santasanti*). *Phalantiyā* means "making a sound."
In *culla-hāvakaraṇe*. *Hāvakaraṇa* means the making of coquettish gestures. *Cullati*.
[The root] *phull* is used in the senses of blooming and breaking open. *Phullati*. *Phullaṃ*. "The *kiṃsuka* tree is in full bloom. "A grove of lotuses is in full bloom.
Dīpaṅkara, the Great Sage, was eighty cubits in height.
He shines like a lamp-tree, like a king of sāl trees in full bloom.
Regarding the repair of what is broken and faded:
*seṭhilla* refers to a state of looseness; it means to slacken.

*Velu*, *celu*, *kelu*, *khelu*, *pelu*, *belu*, *selu*, *sala*, *tila*—these are [roots] in the sense of motion (*gati*). *Velati*. *Celati*. *Kelati*. *Khelati*. *Pelati*. *Belati*. *Selati*. *Salati*. *Tilati*. *Celaṃ*, *belako*. Here, *cela* means cloth (*vattha*).
*Pelako* means a hare (*saso*). *Khala* in the sense of moving (*calane*). *Khalati*. *Khalaḥ*. *Khala* means a wicked person, one who is not good, an ignoble person, a sinful person.
*Khala* in the sense of gathering (*sañcinane*). *Khalati*. *Khalaṃ*. *Khalaṃ* refers to a portion of ground that serves as a place for storing grain.
For indeed, it is called *khala* because they stumble (*khalanti*) there, they gather, they make a heap of grains. The usage is seen in:
“He goes constantly to the threshing floor (*khala*), the house (*sāla*), the cattle-pen (*pasu*), and the field (*khetta*).
The root *gila* means swallowing. He swallows. A man does not perceive what he has swallowed and smeared with poison (*gilamakkha*).

*Gala*: swallowing; *galati*; *galo*; *galanti*, *adanti*, *ajjhoharanti*—by means of this they swallow, thus it is called *galo*. *Gala* refers to the neck. *Sala*, *salla*, [occur] in the sense of swift motion (*āsugati*).

Swift motion is rapid movement. *Salati*; *sallati*; *sallaṃ*. And here, "arrow" (*sallaṃ*), "shaft" (*usu*), "missile" (*saro*), "dart" (*sallo*), "barbed arrow" (*kaṇḍo*), and "sting" (*tejano*) are synonyms.
*Khola* [occurs] in the sense of obstructing motion. *Kholati*.

*Gil* (in the sense of destroying bile): *gilāyati*. One who is ill (*gilāna*), illness (*gelañña*). "Ill" means one who is unwell. For it is said in the Vinaya: "I am not unwell. And in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) it is said: "'I am not unwell' means 'I am not ill.
*Mil* (in the sense of withering of the limbs): *milāyati*. Withered (*milāyana*), withering away (*milāyanta*), fading away (*milāyamāna*). *Kel* (in the sense of cherishing):
Cherishing (*mamāyana*) is the grasping of "this is mine" by way of craving and views. *Kelāyati*. Who cherishes you?

*Sal-* and *saṃvar-* mean to move; *val-* and *vall-* mean to move. The letter *ca* is used here in the sense of inclusion (*saṃvaraṇāpekkhāyaṃ*). It moves (*salati*): *kusalaṃ*. It turns (*valati*), it rolls (*vallati*): *vallūra*.
In this context, *kusalaṃ* means that which moves, causes to move, shakes, or destroys base and evil states (*kucchite pāpadhamme*); thus it is *kusalaṃ*.
Or, it is *kusalaṃ* because by means of it the virtuous (*sādhavo*) move toward, restrain, or close the base doors to the states of misery (*apāyadvāraṃ*). *Vall-* [is explained as follows]:...
It is *vallūra* because crows, dogs, and other creatures restrain themselves (*saṃvaranti*) and protect themselves from eating it.
[Root] *mala* and *malla* mean "to hold. *Malati*. *Malam*. *Mallati*. *Mallo*.
[Roots] *bhala* and *bhalli* mean "to revile," "to injure," and "to give. *Bhalati*. *Bhallati*.
*Kala* means to count. *Kalati*. *Kalā*, *kāla*.

Here, *kalā* refers to a division such as a sixteenth part and so forth. *Kāla* means that which is to be reckoned or counted as "this much has passed," etc.; thus it is *kāla*, referring to a time such as forenoon and so on.
*Kalla* means soundless. Soundless means noiseless. *Kallati*.
*Jala* means to shine. It burns; it is *jalaṃ*, burning, blazing, or flaming. "Who comes shining with glory?
"Devadatta stands there like fire with his fame," so I have heard. The lamp of the True Dhamma has been kindled.

*Hula* means to move. It moves; it is *hulo*. *Halo* is a plough; for that indeed *holeti* (plows), moving the clods of earth while breaking the ground, thus it is called "halo" by changing the vowel *u* to *a*.
*Cal* means to shake. It shakes; it has shaken; unshaken. A great earthquake. Shaking, trembling.
*Jal* means grain. It ripens; grain.
*Ṭal* and *ṭul* mean to hang down. It hangs down; it weighs.
"Thala" means dry land. "Thalati," "thalo," and "thaloti" refer to a place devoid of water. Because they share similar characteristics with that, the term is applied to them as well.

Just as in the world a place that cannot be submerged by a flood of water is called "dry land," so too, because they cannot be overwhelmed by the flood of defilements (*kilesa*), both renunciation (*pabbajjā*) and Nibbāna are called "dry land.
As it is said: "He has crossed over, he has reached the further shore, and he stands on dry land."
For it is said, "a ploughman" (*brāhmaṇo*).
*Phāla* means in the sense of scratching. It scratches the earth, it cleaves it; thus it is called a plough (*phāla*).
*Nala* means in the sense of binding. It binds.
*Bala-pāṇane*. Here, *pāṇana* means living and breathing. It is called *balati* (it breathes). *Bala*, *bāla*.
In this context, it is called *bala* because they fashion their life by means of it; thus, it is *bala* such as physical strength, the strength of wealth, and so forth.
Alternatively, it is called *bala* because they live by means of right livelihood through it; thus, it is *bala* such as faith and so forth. [As stated] in the *Āgama-aṭṭhakathā*:

However, when it is stated that "it does not waver in the face of lack of faith, thus it is the power of faith," and so forth, this should be understood as being said for the purpose of showing the unwavering nature of faith and the other factors, which are to be called "powers" (bala) in the sense of their firmness.

Alternatively, because of the preeminence of the meaning of the verbal roots [involved], the sense of "overcoming" should also be taken for the powers of faith and the rest, by way of their overcoming lack of faith and the like; thus [the text says]: "The weak..."
It is as in the phrase, "they do not grow strong. A fool (*bāla*) is so called because he merely "blows" (*balati*), that is, he breathes in and breathes out;

it is said that he lives by the mere act of inhaling and exhaling, and not by the superior life of wisdom (*paññājīvita*). For thus it is stated in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*): "They blow, thus they are fools;
they live by the mere act of inhaling and exhaling, and not by the life of wisdom—this is the meaning. Only those who live by wisdom...
Indeed, life is called the best. Therefore the Blessed One said: "They say that the life lived with wisdom is the best.
*Pula* means greatness. It is derived from *pulati*. Thus, *vipula* (vast).
*Kula* means reckoning and kinship. It is derived from *kolati*. Thus, *kula* and *kola*.

*Salagamane*: it flows (*salati*). It is said [to mean] playfulness (*pīti*) among the playful activities. The state of being playful is "in playfulness" (*pītiyaṃ*), just as in the case of "skill" (*dakkhiyaṃ*). Play is simply "play" (*kīḷā*); it plays (*kilati*). *Ila* means shaking; it shakes (*ilatīti ilā*). *Ela*, *elā*.

Here, *elaṃ* is said to mean fault (*dosa*). In what sense? In the sense of shaking. And here, "fault" should be understood as a lack of virtue (*aguṇa*), not as aversion (*paṭigha*). The example for this is: "With flawless limbs, with a white canopy."

Furthermore, *ela* means water. For instance, when explaining the meaning of the passage, “Just as the *elambuja*, the thorny, water-born [lotus],” the Venerable Sāriputta said, “*Ela* is called water. Also, *ela* refers to saliva, as in the expression “*elamūga*” (dumb from spittle).
Moreover, *ela* refers to phlegm, as in the verse: “Having heard the speech that is not *nelapata*... [and] “The paths are full of wild beasts... [etc.].
It is just as in the phrase "he departed. Here, *nelapatiṃ* means speech that is free from the falling of drops of saliva; this is the meaning.
However, another basis for the application (*pavatti-nimitta*) must be sought for the word *ela*, which denotes saliva and spittle.
For words have many bases for their application. Or rather, what need is there for another basis for application? It is simply the "trembling" (*kampana*) mentioned in the sense of *ila* = trembling.
The *pavattinimitta* (the basis for the application) of the word *elā*, which denotes "saliva," is as follows:
therefore, the meaning should be understood as *elā* = "that wherein people *ilaṃti*—that is, they tremble due to a state of loathing (*jigucchitabbabhāvena*) and their hearts are moved.
For words that share the same *pavattinimitta* can, by way of worldly convention (*lokasaṅketa*), denote various different referents. How so? [For example: *hinoti gacchati* ("he goes").
The reason is as follows: it is called a *sappa* (snake) because it "creeps" (*sappati*) and goes; it is called a *go* (cow) because it "goes" (*gacchati*).

Likewise, even words that express identical referents may have dissimilar modes of activity. For example: he "shines" (*rañcati*) thus he is a *rājā* (king); he "protects the earth" (*bhūmiṃ pāleti*) thus he is a *bhūmipāla* (protector of the earth);
he "rules over men" (*nare indati*) thus he is a *narinda* (lord of men). This same method should be understood everywhere.
*Il* in the sense of going: *ilati*.
*Hil* in the sense of making a sound: *helati*.
*Sil* in the sense of gathering: *silati*.
*Tila* means to press or squeeze; *tilati*. *Tila*, *tela*, *tilo*.
*Cila* means to wear; *cilati*.
*Vala* means to sport or dally; *valati*.
Pila in the sense of grasping; pilati.
Mila in the sense of affection; milati.
Phula in the sense of moving and pervading; phulati.
Forms of verbal roots ending in *l*.
The verbal root *vā* ending in *v*:
in the senses of "going" and "smelling. He smells (*vāti*). Wind (*vāto*).

*Vī* [is used] in the senses of procreation (*pajanana*), movement (*gati*), desire (*kānti*), eating (*asana*), chewing (*khādana*), and going (*gati*). *Pajana* means moving; *kānti* means delight. *Asana* is the consumption of food; *khādana* is the eating of cakes and the like; *gati* is going. *Ve*:
*ve* [is used] in the sense of weaving (*tantasantāna*). He weaves: a weaver.
*Ve* [is used] in the sense of drying (*sosana*). He dries.
*Dhivu* and *khivu* are used in the sense of pointing out (*nidassana*).

*Dhevati*. *Khevati*. *Thivu* is used in the sense of shining (*ditti*). *Thevati*. "The honey-bees (*madhumadhuka*) drip (*thevanti*). *Jīva* is used in the sense of maintaining life (*pāṇadhāraṇa*).
*Jīvati*. [From this come] *jīvitaṃ*, *jīvo*, and *jīvikā*. "O King, we have no livelihood (*jīvikā*), and that [which we have] is of such-and-such a kind. He maintains his life (*jīvitaṃ kappeti*).
*Piva*, *miva*, *tiva*, *niva*, *thūliya*. He drinks (*pivati*). A drinker (*pivara*). He measures (*mivati*). He pierces (*tivati*). He protects (*nivati*).
And here, "a drinker" (*pivara*) refers to a tortoise, or anyone with a stout body. For thus it was said by the ancient teachers: "A drinker (*pivara*) [means] a tortoise or one who is stout.
*Ava* in the sense of protecting (*pālanā*). He protects (*avati*). "The Buddha is my protector" (*buddho mama avataṃ*).
*Bhava* means in a state of existence (*gati*). *Savati* means to flow.
*Kava* means color. *Kavati* means to speak.
*Khivu* means pride. *Khivati* means to be proud.

*Devu* means one who has the leaping gait (*plutagati*). Leaping gait is the act of moving by leaping. *Devati*.
*Dhātu* refers to the purity of the state of existence (*gatisuddhi*). It runs, it runs about; it runs toward, it runs around. *Dhāvako*.
*Civu* refers to grasping and restraint. It moves.
Cevi: in the case of words ending in *ce*. *Cetati*.
These are forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *v*. [Now for] verbal roots ending in the letter *s*.
Sā is in the sense of cooking.
Sāti is in the sense of service. He serves (sevati). Service, a servant, one who is served, auspicious, and prosperity.
A person who serves the base falls away.
One who associates with equals never falls away;
by approaching the best, one quickly rises.
Therefore, one should associate with those who are superior to oneself.
*Si* means "to go" or "to understand. *Seti*, *atiseti*. *Atisitum*, *atisitvā*, *setu*.
*Sī* means "he lies down. *Sayo* means "sleeping. *Seti*, *sayati*. *Senaṃ*, *sayanaṃ*.
*Su* means "to flow. *Savati*, *pasavati*. *Pasuto*, *suto*.
In this context, *suta* means a messenger; for example, there are such usages as “Indeed, wealth finds me when I have heard [of it]” (*sutvā*) and “Mātali, the son of the gods” (*devasuto*).
The root *su* means to hear. Hearing is flowing. It flows: thus, *āsava*.
The root *sū* means to procreate. Procreation is generation. It flows forth; it generates: thus, *sutta*.

In this context, however, "sutta" means that which flows forth (*savati*) or generates meaning; thus it refers to the word of the Buddha contained in the Three Pitakas, or otherwise to other types of "threads" such as the *Hatthisutta* and so forth.
[The verbal roots are: *sū* in the sense of breathing and releasing the womb—*sutī*, *pasūtī*, *pasūto*;
and *su* in the sense of flowing—*sutī*.
*Se* means "to be exhausted. *Sīyati*: the substitution of *ī* for *e*.
*Se* means "to cook. *Seti*: [the root] *si*.
*Se* means "going. *Seti*: [the root] *si*. *Setu*: a bridge.
*Hiṃsa* is in the sense of harming. It harms. [One who] harms, harming, harm.
*Issa* is in the sense of envy. It envies. The gods do not envy the prowess of a man. Envy, envying.

*Namas* is in the sense of salutation and bowing. Salutation and bowing means the act of bending known as salutation; this root takes an object only, and unlike the root *nam*, it is not both transitive and intransitive. It pays homage.
Ghusa means sound. One *ghusati* or *ghosati*. It refers to an echo, a noise, or the sound of speech.
Cusa means to eat. One *cūsati*.
Pusa means growth. One *pusati*. A person (*poso*). My nourishment (*posanaṃ*) is through pressure. Nourishment (*posanaṃ*) means increasing.
*Theyya*: theft, stealing, thievery; it deceives (*musati*). Difficult to look at is the eye-deceiver (*cakkhumusano*).
*Musala*: a pestle. *Pusa*: to cause to grow, to produce;
it grows (*pusati*). *Vāsi*: an axe. *Bhūsa*: ornamentation; it adorns (*vāsati*), it beautifies (*bhūsati*, *vibhūsati*). *Bhūsanaṃ*, *vibhūsanaṃ*: an ornament, decoration.
*Usa* means to suffer.
*Usati*. *Isa* means to seek. *Esati*. *Isi*.

In this context, however, those who seek qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) are called *isayo* (seers); these are the noble ones beginning with the Buddhas, as well as men who have gone forth into the ascetic life of renunciation. “*Isi*, *tāpasa*, *jaṭila*, *jaṭī*, *jaṭādharo*” — these are synonyms for an ascetic (*tāpasa*).
*Kasa* means scratching (*vilekhana*). One scratches (*kasati*) or is scratched (*kassati*). [Examples: a ploughman (*kassaka*), space (*ākāsa*).

Here, "ploughman" refers to one who performs the act of ploughing. "Space" refers to the sky (*nabha*). For it is not ploughed, thus it is called "space" (*ākāsa*). The meaning is that it cannot be ploughed or scratched.
These are its designations: Ākāsa, ambara, abbha, antalikha, magha, nabha.
Vehāsa, gagana, deva, kha, ādiccapatha,
tārāpatha, nakkhattapatha, ravipatha, vehāyasa, vāyupatha, apatha, and anilañjasa.

*Kasa*, *sisa*, *jasa*, *jhasa*, *vasa*, *masa*, *disa*, *jusa*, and *yusa* are [roots] with the sense of harming (*hiṃsattha*). *Kasati* (he hurts), *sisati* (he pierces), *jasati* (he injures), *jhasati* (he strikes), *vasati* (he strikes), *masati* (he strikes). *Masaka* means a mosquito. *Omasati* (he reviles); *omasavāda* is [the act of] reviling.

*Disati* (he points out), *jusati* (he approves), *yūsati* (he strikes). In this context, *omasa* means to pierce. *Omasavāda* is speech that pierces others as if with a needle. *Masaka* is a mosquito.

*Bhassa* means speaking. *Bhassanti* refers to talking, as in such passages as: “The dwelling, the range, the speech, and the speaker of speech. It is spoken (*bhassati*). It is spoken (*bhaṭṭhaṃ*). *Bhaṭṭhaṃ* means that which is spoken; the meaning is “utterance. In this context, however:
“O Great Sage, these well-spoken verses of yours are full of meaning;
I am satisfied by their excellent delivery, and may you be my refuge.”

The Pāḷi provides the illustration. Therein, *nijjhāto* means "inspired" (*nijjhāpito*), having entered into the conceptualization (*paññatti*) by means of the wisdom of the essence of the Dhamma (*dhammaṭṭha-paññā*). *Subhaṭṭhena* means "by way of what is well-spoken. Regarding the roots *jisu*, *nisu*, *visu*, and *misu*:
they signify "to sprinkle" (*vassa secane*). Thus: *jesati*, *nesati*, *vesati*, *mesati*. *Devo vassati* ("the god rains"). Regarding *marisu*: it signifies "to endure" (*sahane*) as well.
The letter *ca* (and) refers back to the sense of sprinkling. Thus: *marisati*.

*Posa* (to nourish). *Posati*. *Poso*. One is nourished by means of karma, consciousness, temperature, and nutriment; thus, one is a *posa*. Furthermore, because it is seen that "another deity also nourishes," we shall explain this root in the *curādigaṇa* as well.
*Pisa*, *siliṣa*, *pusa*, *palusa*, *usa*: to burn. *Pesati*. *Silesati*. *Sileso*. *Posati*. *Palosati*.
*Osati*. *Usu*. *Ghasu*: to strike together. *Saṃhariso* means a collision. *Ghassati*.
*Hasu* means to embrace; *āliṅgo* is an embrace, a hug. It is *hasati*.
*Hasa* means to laugh. One laughs. They laugh, noble steeds laugh, one laughs aloud, one laughs loudly. In the causative, it is “*hāseti*” and so forth;
being made to laugh, laughter, loud laughter, laughing, laughing aloud, the act of having laughed. By the elision of the letter *ha*, it refers to a gentle smile.
“*Sita*” is said in such passages as “he displayed his smile” (*sitaṃ pātvākāsī*).
In this context, *uhasati* means he derides (*avahasati*). *Udasiyamāno* means being derided (*avahasiyamāno*). Here is the relevant scriptural passage:
“In this case, a woman approaches a bhikkhu who has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, and derides him.”
And thus [it is said]: “He was being laughed at by women,” and so forth. *Hāsa* means either laughing or mental joy, as in such passages as “joy arose in me.

The roots are *tusa*, *hasa*, *hisa*, and *rasa*, meaning sound. From these we have: *tusati*, *hasati*, *hisati*, *rasati*, and *rasitaṃ*. Here is the relevant passage from the Canon: “Let all the kettledrums resound; let all the lutes resound (*rasantu*).”
*Rasa* means enjoyment (*assādana*). It relishes (*rasati*), thus it is *rasa*.
*Rasa* means enjoyment and moisture (*assāda-sineha*). It relishes (*rasati*), thus it is *rasa*. *Rasa* means loss (*hāni*).
It causes to waste away (*rasati*), thus it is *rasa*; the act of wasting away is *rasa*.
On this point, the canonical text says:
“Neither when standing nor sitting, nor when lying down nor walking;
as long as one is conscious and blinking—even there, the craving is exceedingly sharp.”
In this context, *rasatibbaya* means that with each passing age one "moans" (*rasati*), that is, one declines and does not increase.

[The root] *lasa* is used in the senses of clinging and playing; thus, *lasati*. *Lāsa*. And those two are "extracted" (*nippalitā*). *Lasi* refers to the brain matter (*matthaluṅga*). *Nippalitā* means "extracted" (*nikkhantā*). [The root] *nisa* is used in the sense of concentration (*samādhimhi*).
Concentration (*samādhi*) is the state of being concentrated, which is one-pointedness of mind (*cittekaggatā*). [Thus, it] "leads toward" (*nesati*).
*Mis* and *mas* mean "to be angry. *Misati*, *masati*, *meso*, *masako*.
*Pis* and *pes* mean "in going. *Pisati*, *pesati*. *Sas* means "in harming.
*Sasati*. *Satthaṃ*; *satthaṃ* is said to be a sword (*asi*).
*Saṃsa* means to praise. The particle *ca* is used here in reference to *hiṃsā* (to injure).

[Examples: *saṃsati*, *pasaṃsati*. *Pasaṃsā*, *pasaṃsanā*. The Blessed One is praised (*pasattho*). [Derivatives: *pasaṃsamāno*, *pasaṃsito*, *pasaṃsako*, *pasaṃsitabbo*, *pasaṃsanīyo*, *pāsaṃso*, *pasaṃsitvā*, and so forth.
*Disa* means to see. Its various forms include: *dissati*, *padissati*, etc., which are intransitive (*akammaka*); and *passati*, *dakkhati*, etc., which are transitive (*sakammaka*).
May he see, may he look, may he perceive. He would see, he would look, he would perceive. He saw, he looked, he perceived.
He was seen, he was looked at, he was perceived. He saw, he looked, he perceived. He did not see, he did not look. He saw a mountain within the ocean.
He saw, they saw, they all saw. He saw, he looked, he perceived.
*Dassissati*, *passissati*, *dakkhissati*. *Adassissā*, *apassissā*, *dakkhissā*. These should be expanded out according to the fifth [tense], the present, and so forth.
In the causative, the forms are *dasseti* and *dassayati*. In the passive, they are *passiyati* and so on.
*Disā*, *passo*, *passaṃ*, *passitā*, *dassetā*, *dassanaṃ*, *vipassanā*, and *ñāṇadassanaṃ*—these are the nominal forms.
In this context, however, the form "dakkhitāye" is used both in the sense of the object (*tadattha*) and the infinitive (*tum-attha*).
For the canonical text reads: "We have come to this assembly of Dhamma, in order to see the unconquered Saṅgha.

In this passage of the canon, "dakkhitāye" is a form of the dative case used either in the sense of the object or as an infinitive. Thus, for "dakkhitāye," one may substitute "dassanatthāya" (for the purpose of seeing) or "passituṃ" (to see).

Or the meaning should be applied accordingly. Furthermore, among the terms beginning with "direction" (*disā*), that which is divided into the eastern and so forth is also called a "direction. As it has been said:
"The four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, above and below—these are the ten directions."
"In which direction does the Naga King stand,
whom Yamadaṭṭha saw in his dream as having six tusks? This also applies to mothers,
fathers, and others, as it has been said:
“Parents are the eastern direction; teachers are the southern direction;
children and wife are the western direction; friends and colleagues are the northern direction;
slaves and laborers are below; and ascetics and brahmins are above.”
"One should revere these directions; such is sufficient for a householder in his family"—this refers also to those who provide the requisites.
As it is said: "Householders who give food, drink, and clothing, and even those who invite one to eat—they too call them 'directions'.
It also refers to Nibbāna. As it is said:
“Such is the supreme state, O Setaketu,
reaching which beings become free from suffering and happy.
Having thus understood the nature of the meaning expressed by the word *disā*, its etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) should now be seen as follows.

*Disā* (directions) are so called because they are seen (*dissati*) and manifested in various ways—as "this is the east," "this is the west," and so forth—by means of the turning of the moon and other such phenomena;
thus, they refer to the eastern direction and the rest. Likewise, they are *disā* because they are to be regarded (*passitabbā*) as "these are our venerable ones," referring to parents and others.
They are also *disā* because these givers are seen and recognized as such by one's own meritorious deeds; thus, they refer to those who provide the requisites.
It is called *disā* (the direction) because it exists at all times due to its eternal nature, being devoid of arising and passing away; thus it is Nibbāna.
One who sees is a *passo* (seer), meaning one who sees what is a cause and what is not a cause. One who sees in this way is a *passaṃ* (one who sees). Here is the canonical text:
"The seer sees the seer, and he also sees the non-seer."
"Not seeing, one does not see even that which is being seen.

"Sees" (*passati*) means the seer (*passitā*). "Shows" (*dasseti*) means the one who shows (*dassitā*). "Seeing" (*dassana*) is the act of seeing. Furthermore, "seeing" is eye-consciousness (*cakkhu-viññāṇa*);
for it is called "seeing" because it sees visible forms as its object. Likewise, [it is said]: "states to be abandoned by seeing."
By way of expression, "seeing" refers to the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*). Why is the path of stream-entry called "seeing"? Because it is the first seeing of Nibbāna. [Objection:
Does not the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*) see even earlier? [Reply: It is not that it does not see;

however, having seen, it does not perform the task that ought to be done because of the non-abandonment of the fetters (*saṃyojana*). Therefore, it cannot be said that "it sees. Just as in any case regarding a king...
The village dweller is the illustration; even after seeing [the gift] and giving a present, because he has not seen the completion of the task, he says, "Even now I have not seen the king.
*Vipassanā* is the knowledge that penetrates the aggregates by way of impermanence and so forth. *Ñāṇadassana* refers also to the divine eye.
Insight, the path, the fruit, the knowledge of review, and even omniscient knowledge are called "knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassana*).
For in the passage, "Being diligent, he attains knowledge and vision," it is the divine eye that is called "knowledge and vision.
In the passage, "He directs and inclines his mind toward knowledge and vision," it is insight-knowledge. In the passage, "They are incapable of knowledge and vision... [it refers to the path].

In the phrase "for unsurpassed full enlightenment," it is the path; in the phrase "this other superhuman state, this distinction of noble knowledge and vision, this attainment of a comfortable dwelling has been reached," it is the knowledge of the fruit; and in the phrase "knowledge and vision arose in me:
my deliverance of mind is unshakable, this is the last birth, now there is no further becoming," it is the knowledge of review.
“Furthermore, knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘Āḷāra Kālāma died seven days ago’”—herein, it is omniscient knowledge.
Regarding this, it is said: “Divine eye, the path, and the fruit, Insight, the knowledge of reviewing, And the knowledge of omniscience— [These are the knowledges].”

“By the term *ñāṇadassana*, these meanings are expressed. [The root] *daṃsa* means “to see. One sees (*daṃsati*), one perceives clearly (*vidaṃsati*). [One who has seen is] *danta*. *Saṃsa* means to speak; *saṃsati*. "He who speaks of me as a Great Nāga.
*Kilisa* means to afflict; *kilisati*. *Kilesa*.
Here, in the sense of afflicting, even lust and the other [defilements] are called "defilements" (*kilesa*), as is suffering. Among these, by way of suffering—
“Having obtained this condition, they formerly wandered joyfully in the delightful Giribbaja, having purified their own defilements”—
thus the grammatical application (payoga) is to be understood. However, for a verb belonging to the *div-ādi* class, the form is “kilissati.”
*Vas* means to moisten; it is that which dwells (*vasati*). It is *vasā*.
And here, *vasā* refers to melted fat. In terms of color, it is the color of coconut oil; it is also appropriate to say it is the color of oil poured over rice-scum (*ācāma*).
The root *īs* is used in the senses of slightness, injury, and going; it is that which moves (*īsati*), and thus it is *īsa*.

This is speech (*vācā*) characterized by proficiency in speaking. One speaks (*bhāsati*). [The nouns derived from this root are: *bhāsā* (speech), *bhāsitaṃ* (that which is spoken), and *bhātā* (a speaker). One reviles (*paribhāsati*). [The nouns derived from this root are: *paribhāsā* (reviling) and *paribhāsaka* (one who reviles).
In that context, it is called *bhāsā* because they express meaning (*atthaṃ bhāsanti etāya*) by means of it; thus, it refers to the Māgadhī language and so forth. *Bhāsitaṃ* is speech (*vacanaṃ*).
For the word *bhāsita*, in the sense of "speech," should always be understood as being of the neuter gender. As in: "Having heard the hunter's speech" (*sutvā luddassa bhāsitaṃ*).

The word *bhāsita* (spoken), however, should be understood as having all three genders, according to its grammatical function (*vāccaliṅga*). For example: "the Dhamma was spoken" (*bhāsito dhammo*), "the Four Truths were spoken" (*bhāsitaṃ catusaccaṃ*), and "speech was spoken" (*bhāsitā vācā*).
Previously, one who speaks is a *bhātā*; this means an elder brother (*jeṭṭhabhātā*). For it is precisely because he was born first that he is entitled to be called so.
Although the word *bhātā* [is used], as in "a hundred brothers" (*bhātikasataṃ*), "seven brothers" (*sattabhātaro*), or "by whom [was] the brother" (*bhātaraṃ kena*)...
In such passages as "Do not [act] out of hatred, O protector of the gift," it applies to both elder and younger brothers;

nevertheless, it is most commonly established in the sense of an elder brother, for when "brother" is mentioned, it is understood to mean the elder brother. Therefore, in certain places, it is stated specifically as "younger brother."
But surely, sir, it has been stated in some places with the qualification "elder brother"? True;
however, because the word *bhātā* (brother) can also be applied to a younger brother, it was stated as "elder brother" for the sake of making the meaning clear.

For just as the word *miga* (deer), when used in reference to antelopes (*hariṇa*), is sometimes applied to all four-footed animals as well, and thus one specifies it as a "deer-antelope" (*hariṇamiga*).
They utter such speech; it should be understood in this way.

And just as, although the word "deer" (miga) is used in a general sense for cows, elephants, lions, hyenas, pigs, leopards, and so forth, in passages where "deer-skin" or "deer-meat" occurs, there is an understanding of the specific meaning—such as "of the *harina* deer"—even without the qualifying term "of the *harina*," as in "the skin of the *harina*-deer" or "the meat of the *harina*-deer."
In this context, neither the hide nor the flesh of cows, elephants, and so forth is intended.
Likewise, regarding the statement "they eat the flesh of wild animals" (*migamaṃsaṃ khādanti*), the meaning "they eat the flesh of cows, elephants, and so forth" is not possible.
In exactly the same way, even without the qualifying word "eldest" (*jeṭṭhaka*), when the word "brother" (*bhātā*) is uttered, the meaning "eldest brother" is understood.
But surely, sir, in the expression "deer-hide, deer-flesh," the specific meaning is understood through the words "hide" and "flesh" alone?
It is not so; for the words "hide" and "flesh" function here as general terms, just like the word "deer.
If it is asked, "In that case, by what means is the specific meaning understood? it is by way of worldly convention (*loka-saṅketa*). For thus, in the word "deer" and in words such as "hide"—
And although [the terms] are used in their general sense, because they are delimited by worldly convention (*lokasaṅketa*), the hides of cows, elephants, and so forth are not known by the world;
rather, it is only the hides of deer and such that are known. For it should be understood that it has been said: "The conventional expression is true; worldly consensus is the cause."
*Anvicchāyaṃ*: repeated desire is *anvicchā*. [The root] *gilesati*. In the sense of exertion (*payatane*):
*yesati*. In the sense of going (*gatiyaṃ*): *jesu*, *nesu*, *esu*, *hesu*.

[The roots] *jesati*, *nessati*, *esati*, *hesati*. However, due to the combination of consonants at the end of the verbal root (*dhātvantassa*), forms such as *jessati* and *nessati* should also be understood. [Present participle: *jessamāno*. [Nouns: *jessaṃ*, *jessanto*. And here—
"Just as the female elephant follows the forest-dwelling tusker,
as he roams through mountain fastnesses, on level ground and uneven terrain"—
this is the canonical illustration.
*Desu hesu* refers to the sounds of the incompetent (*abyatta-sadda*).

*Desati*; *hesati*. *Kāsa* is in the sense of a defective sound (*sadda-kuccha*). *Kāsati*, *ukkāsati*. *Kāsa*. "Coughing, wheezing, spitting, and weakness—thus one whose wisdom is exhausted comes [to such a state].

*Kāsu* and *bhāsu* are in the sense of radiance (*ditti*). Radiance means visibility or brilliance. *Kāsati*, *pakāsati*. "The heat shines forth. "Those who are virtuous shine even from afar. *Bhāsati*, *pabhāsati*: "This celestial palace shines. *Pakāso*. *Kāsu* is effulgence (*obhāsa*).

In this context, *pakāsa* means that which is made manifest (*pakāseti*); the meaning is that it becomes evident (*pākaṭo*). It is called *kāsu* because it is hollowed out (*kāsati*) or made manifest (*pakāsati*) by way of its emptiness or its state as a heap. The word *kāsu* refers both to a pit and to a heap. As it is said:
“O charioteer, why are you digging a pit in such haste?
Being asked by me, friend, tell me: what will you do with the pit?”
For here, *āvāṭa* means a pit or trench (*kāsu*). In the passage, “Other men, their limbs scorched, scatter coals while weeping,” it means a heap (*rāsi*).
In the causative sense: one who makes manifest is a *pakāsaka*; one who illuminates is an *obhāsaka*. In the passive sense:

that which is made manifest is *pakāsita*; likewise, *bhāsita*. In the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*): scattering (*kāsanā*), proclaiming (*saṅkāsanā*), making manifest (*pakāsanā*). In the infinitive and similar forms: “to make manifest” (*pakāsituṃ*).
[The forms] *pakāsetuṃ*, *obhāsituṃ*, *obhāsetuṃ*; [and the absolutive forms] *pakāsitvā*, *pakāsetvā*, *obhāsitvā*, *obhāsetvā*—these are the verbal roots.

In the context of secondary derivation (*taddhita*), one who has this *bhāsa* (splendor) is *bhāsuro*, or *pabhassaro* (radiant), referring to anyone whatsoever. Alternatively, *bhāsuro* refers to a maned lion.
In this sense, the word *bhāsu* denotes the act of shining, just as the word *rāja* in the phrase “*rāja dittiyan*” (the king of splendors) denotes the act of shining.

It may be so; therefore, the etymology should be understood as follows: because he possesses radiance (*bhāsa*) characterized by the perfection of shining with the glory of form (*rūpa-siri*), he is "radiant" (*bhāsura*).
[The roots] *nā* and *rā* mean "to sound. One sounds (*nāsati*); one resounds (*rāsati*). Thus, there are *nāsā* and *nāsikā*.
In this context, even the trunk of an elephant is called *nāsā*, as in such passages as: "If Pabhāvatī, whose thighs are like an elephant’s trunk, should look at me," and so forth.
...like [the word] *vīṇā*. The nose of humans and others is also called *nāsā*, as in such passages as, “He who cut off your hands and feet, and your ears and nose.
It is called *nāsā* because by means of it they produce an indistinct sound (*abyatta-sadda*). *Nāsikā* is simply *nāsā*.
Where we do not provide an etymological derivation (*nibbacana*), it is because it is easily understood or because it is not well-established.
It should be understood that even what is not explicitly stated must be applied by those skilled in the methods of composition after careful investigation. Regarding this, it is said:
The nose, the trunk, and the hand—these are considered synonymous with the word *hatthi* (elephant).
“*Nāsā* and *nāsikā* are considered synonymous in two senses;
[the same applies] to *narā* and so forth.
*Nasa* [is used] in the sense of crookedness. It means “it bends.”
*Bhisi* means fear. *Bhiṃsati*. *Bhiṃsanaka*. That which was terrifying at that time. *Bhesmākāyo*. *Āsisi* is desire.

The prefix *ā-* occurs in the sense of desire. *Āsisati*. A person indeed desires. *Āsisanā*. *Āsisattaṃ*. Desiring, desiring, wishing. The canonical text (*pāḷi*) "desiring a happy destination" (*suggatimāsamānā*) is an illustration here.
*Gasu* in the sense of eating. *Gasati*.
*Ghus* is used in the sense of making noise. This root ends in *ī*; therefore, there is no insertion of the nasal (*niggahīta*) after it.
It forms *ghusati*. *Paṃsu* and *bhaṃsu* are used in the sense of falling away.
They form *paṃsati* and *bhaṃsati*. *Dhaṃsu* is used in the sense of going. It forms *dhaṃsati*. Dust rises upward; thus, *rajo nudhaṃsati uddhaṃ*.

*Pas* in the sense of extension: *pasati*, *pasu*. *Kus* in the sense of calling and weeping: *kosati*, *pakkosati*. *Pakkosaka*, *pakkosita*, *pakkosanaṃ*. *Kass* in the sense of going: *kassati*, *parikassati*, *paṭikassati*.
"One should root it out" (*mūlāya paṭikasseyya*). "Should root out" means one should pull it out; the meaning is that one should establish it in the very state of a root-offense (*mūlāpatti*).
In *asa*, *di*, *tyā*, and *ādāna*. The letter *ca* is for the purpose of including the following roots. *Asati*: in the sense of non-existence. *Disa*:
in the senses of pointing out and restraining. *Dissati*: "the man is seen. *Dāsu*:
in the sense of giving. *Dāsati*.
*Rosa* means to fear; *rosati*; *rosako*.
*Bhesu* means to tremble; *bhesati*.
*Pasa* means binding and contact; *pasati*. *Pāsa*, *nāgapāsa*, *hatthapāsa*.
*Las* means to shine, to desire, or to sport. *Lāsa*, *vilāsa*, and *vilasana* mean sporting or play.
*Cas* means to eat; it takes the form *casati*.
*Kas* means to harm; it takes the form *kasati*.
*Tis* means to satisfy. *Titti* is satisfaction, satiation, fullness, and contentment. *Tisati* means to satisfy. *Titti* means satiety. The root *vas* means dwelling. From it come:

*vasati*, *vasiyati*, *vacchati*. [Derivatives include: *vatthu*, *vatthaṃ*, *parivāso*, *nivāso*, *āvāso*, *upavāso*, *uposatho*, *vippavāso*, *cirappavāsī*, *cirappavuttho*, *vasitvā*, *vattuṃ*, *vasituṃ*, and so forth.
In this context, *upavāsa* is dwelling devoid of food; thus, *upavāsa*. *Uposatha*: it is called *uposatha* because they dwell (*upavasanti*) therein; hence, *uposatha*.
The meaning is: they dwell having approached, being endowed with either virtue (*sīla*) or fasting (*anāsana*). Here, however, is the extraction of the meanings:
in such passages as, "Come, friend Kappina, let us go to the Uposatha," the Uposatha refers to the recitation of the *Pātimokkha*.
In such passages as, "Thus, Visākhā, the Uposatha endowed with eight factors is observed," it refers to virtue (*sīla*). [And] in the passage, "Truly, for one who is pure... [it refers to purity].

In such passages as “Phaggu, the Uposatha of the bright fortnight, always,” it refers to the observance (upavāsa). In such passages as “Uposatha is the name of a dragon king,” it refers to a designation (paññatti).
In such passages as “Monks, on that day of the Uposatha, from a residence where monks are present...,” it refers to the day on which one should observe the fast.
[The root] *vas* means to desire; thus, *vacchati*. [Hence] *jinavacchayo*.
*Sasa* means a cemetery. *Sasati* means to lie down. *Saso* means a hare.
*Sasa* means breathing; he breathes. He breathes in mindfully and breathes out mindfully. *Saso* and *sasanaṃ*. Inhalation and exhalation—while breathing in and breathing out.
*Asa* means "to be"; it exists. *Asa*.
In this context, *atthi* is a verb (*ākhyāta-pada*). *Na atthi khīrā brāhmaṇī* (there is no milk in the Brahmin woman) is an example.

However, in cases such as *atthitā*, *atthibhāvo*, or “*yaṃ kiñci ratanaṃ atthī*” (whatever jewel there is), it is a particle (*nipāta-pada*). Therefore, the word *atthi* should be understood as twofold, by way of being both a verb and a particle.
*Asa* is a noun (*nāmika-pada*) without a case ending (*avibhattika*). And here, the canonical text (*pāḷi*) “*asasmīti hotī*” serves as the illustration.
