*Sajja*: attachment (*saṅga*). Attachment is clinging. It clings (*sajjati*).

*Sajjanaṃ*, *sajjito*, *satto*. *Yuja* means in concentration (*samādhi*). Concentration is the state of being concentrated (*samādhāna*); the meaning is non-distraction through the correct application of bodily action and so forth. It is joined (*yujjati*). *Yoga*, *yogī*.
Here, "yoga" means energy (*vīriya*). For it is said:
"A wise person should indeed exert effort and not become despondent;
I see myself as I am, having become exactly as I desired."
Because it is necessarily to be performed according to the word, and because it is appropriate, it is called "yoga" (joining).

[The root] *rañj* means "to color" or "to be attached. One is colored; one becomes detached. [Derivatives include: being colored (*rajjamāna*), coloring (*rajjaṃ*), coloring (*rajjanta*), passion (*rāga*), detachment (*virāga*), the act of coloring (*rajjanaṃ*), the act of detaching (*virajjanaṃ*), and that which is to be colored (*rajanīyaṃ*).
Through the influence of prefixes, a different meaning arises: "He departs from his kingdom" (*saṃhā raṭṭhā nirajjati*).
The meaning is that he departs from his own kingdom.
In this context, *virāga* means "that in which defiled states (*saṃkilesadhamma*) become dispassionate"; it refers to Nibbāna and the Path. The root *vij* is used in the senses of fear and trembling.

One is agitated (*vijjati*, *saṃvijjati*). Thus there is agitation (*saṃvega*) and that which is provocative of agitation (*saṃvejanīya*). One is terrified (*ubbijjati*). Thus there is terror (*ubbega*) and one whose heart is terrified (*ubbiggahadayo*).
*Luja* means destruction. That which is destroyed is the world (*loka*). [Derivatives include] *lopa*, *lutta*, *lujjana*, and *lutta*.
*Ṭhā* (in the sense of stopping movement): *ṭhāyati*. [Derivatives include] *ṭhāyī*, *ṭhiti*, *ṭhāna*, *ṭhito*, *tatraṭṭho*, *tiṭṭhaṃ*, *kappaṭṭhāyī*, and *āsabhaṭṭhānaṭṭhāyī*.
"I lie down happily, I stand happily; I pass my life happily."
“Within the reach of Māra’s hand—oh, how compassionate is the Teacher!”—this is the canonical illustration (*pāḷi-nidassana*).
And [the phrase] “the quail standing in its feeding ground. Therein, *ṭhāyāmi* means “I stand”;
it belongs to the root *ṭhā*. [From the root *ḍī*: *ḍiyati*, *ḍemāno*, or *ḍino*. The canonical illustration is: “O bird flying high, soaring on your wings, you have indeed spared my left thigh.”
The etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) to be understood here is: "it protects, thus it is a protection" (*ḍiyati iti ḍemāno*).

The root *tā* means to protect; it protects. It is a protection from suffering (*aghassa tātā*). "That poor man is surely a protector (*tāto*); he has long been obstructed in his hermitage. Protection (*tāṇaṃ*), safeguard (*parittaṃ*), and lineage (*gottaṃ*). You, O lay follower (*upāsaka*), are one who has performed what is wholesome and has provided a refuge for those in fear.

In that context, "safeguard" (*paritta*) means that which protects and guards beings on all sides from fear, calamity, and misfortune due to its great majesty; "lineage" (*gotta*) means that which protects the clan.
*Bhatta* means the bending of limbs. The bending of limbs is the tossing of limbs. *Naccati* (he dances); *naccaṃ* (dancing). *Nigaṇṭho Nāṭaputto* (the Jaina leader Nātaputta).
*Dā* in the sense of cleansing; *dāyati* (he cleanses); *dānaṃ* (giving). For the purpose of causing application: having given application; having given a gift. *Dā* in the sense of sleeping;
*dāyati* (he sleeps); *niddāyati* (he sleeps); *niddāyanaṃ*, *niddāyamāno*, *niddāyanto* (sleeping, while sleeping, as one who sleeps).
In the sense of giving: a person gives a gift. In the sense of taking, preceded by *ā-*: he takes what is not given; he undertakes the precepts (*sīla*).
In the sense of the object: a gift is given by a person; what is not given is taken. In the sense of causing to do: he causes to take, he causes to undertake;
he causes to take, he causes to undertake—those who, being virtuous, cause others to take up the Dhamma itself.
*Dā* means to break or cut (*avakhaṇḍane*). It is used as *diyati* and *diyanti*. *Paritta*:

here, it is called *paritta* because it is broken on all sides (*samantato khaṇḍitattā*). Indeed, even a small lump of cow dung is called *paritta*. Therefore, *paritta* is a name for what is small, and for a phenomenon of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) because of its lack of power.

*Dā* means purification (*suddhiyaṃ*). It is used as *dāyati*. It is also *vodāyati*. *Vodāna* (purification). This root is intransitive (*akammaka*). For thus it is said in the commentary to the *Nettipakaraṇa*: "It is called *vodāna* because by means of it one is purified (*vodāyati*) and cleansed (*sujjhati*); [it refers to] serenity and insight."
*Dī* means to perish. It is given (*dīyate*). *Dīna* and *ādīnava*.

In this context, *dīna* refers to one who is suffering due to the complete exhaustion of kinsmen, wealth, and so forth. *Ādīnava*: it is called *ādīnava* because through it one attains (*vāti*) or encounters (*adhigacchati*) *ādīna*, which is suffering; thus it is a fault (*dosa*). *Du* means to torment.
It is tormented (*duyate*). *Duna* and *dūta*.
*Bhidi* means breaking. That which has the nature of breaking breaks. "It breaks" means it is broken (*bhinna*).

The act of breaking is *bheda*. *Chidi* means cutting. A thread is cut. "It is cut" means it is severed (*chinna*). Thus, there is a fissure (*chidda*). The act of cutting is *cheda*. *Khidi* means dejection.

Dejectedness is *dīniya*, just as *dakkhiya* [is derived from *dakṣiṇa*]. It is dejected (*khijjati*), it is exhausted (*khinna*), one whose mind is unexhausted (*akhinnamati*), exhaustion (*kheda*), and the Protector who has gone to exhaustion for the sake of the world’s welfare (*khedaṅgato lokahitāya nātho*).

"Here, one who has reached exhaustion" means one who has encountered fatigue, which is to say physical suffering; the meaning is that he experiences suffering. The root *pad* is used in the sense of "going.
One goes; one sets out upon a path; one enters upon the practice. One is set out upon the road of a journey;
one enters into the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*). One incurs an offense (*āpatti*). It is also used intransitively, as in "their unrighteousness" (*tesaṃ adhammo*).
*Āpajjati*, *pajjo*, *byagghapajjo*, *sampadāyo*. Here, *pajjo* means "path.

One born on the path of the tiger (*byaggha*) is *byagghapajjo*; such is the name of that clansman. That by which the Dhamma is accomplished (*sampadīyati*) and made known (*ñāpiyati*) is *sampadāyo*; thus it is "proclaimed" (*akkhātā*). The root *vid* is used in the sense of existence.
Existence (*sattā*) is the mode of being present. It exists (*vijjati*), it is found (*saṃvijjati*). As in *jātavedo*, *vijjā*, *avijjā*, and *vidito*.
In this context, *jātavedo* means fire. For it, being born (*jāto*), makes itself known (*vedayati*) through the rising of a mass of smoke; therefore, it is called *jātavedo*.
*Vijjā* (clear vision) is knowledge (*ñāṇa*), so called because it makes the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of phenomena known.

*Avijjā* (ignorance) refers to the meaning of a "heap" in the case of the aggregates (*khandha*), the meaning of a "base" in the case of the sense-bases (*āyatana*), the meaning of "emptiness" in the case of the elements (*dhātu*), and the meaning of "suchness" in the case of the truths (*sacca*).
Ignorance (*avijjā*) is so called because it makes the dominant function (*adhipati-ṭṭha*) of the faculties unknown.
Ignorance is delusion (*moha*), because it makes the fourfold meaning—stated by way of oppression and so forth regarding suffering and the rest—unknown.
It causes intoxication (*mada*) and madness (*ummāda*). Madness means being bewildered, loss of mindfulness, or distraction of the mind. One becomes intoxicated (*majjati*).
He is negligent. Intoxicated—drunk with liquor. I was intoxicated, O Great King, and I ate the flesh of my own sons. An intoxicated elephant is negligent and deranged.
Heedfulness is the state of the deathless; negligence is the state of death. Those who are heedful do not die;
those who are negligent are as if already dead.
*Mida* means to love. *Mejjati*. [From this root arise: *mettā*, *metti*, *mittaṃ*, *mitto*. *Antaradhā* [is used] in the sense of non-appearance.

The root *dhā*, preceded by the prefix *antara-*, functions in the sense of the non-appearance of an existing object. [Examples: *antaradhāyati*, *antaradhānaṃ*, *antaradhāyanto*. "That deity disappeared" (*sā devatā antarahitā*).

*Antarāpidhāyati*. *Budha* means to understand. Understanding is knowing. [From this root arise: *bujjhati*, *buddho*, *buddhi*, *buddhaṃ*, *bodho*, *bodhi*. One who has awakened to the truths (*bujjhitā saccāni*). "The Fully Awakened One" (*sakalaṃ buddho*), "one who has awakened" (*buddhavā*), *vibodheti*, *bodhetā*, *buddho*, *vibuddho*, and so forth.
In this context, "Buddha" means one who has awakened to the truths, thus he is a Buddha; or one who awakens the world, thus he is a Buddha.

Alternatively, he is called a Buddha because through wisdom cultivated by the perfections (pāramitā), he has awakened to the entirety of all that is to be known. Some, however, wishing to establish the word "Buddha" through its verbal root as well, provide this etymology:
"The Blessed One is indeed a Perfectly Self-Awakened One (Sammāsambuddha) on account of the distinguished qualities he has attained..."

“He is called ‘Buddha’ because he has awakened to that which is to be awakened to by those whose taints are destroyed. The detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Niddesa*.

Regarding the term *buddhi*: it is called *buddhi* because one awakens (*bujjhati*). Thus, *buddha*, *bodha*, and *bodhi* are likewise [derived]. Alternatively, *buddhi* is the act of awakening (*bujjhana*).
Thus, *bodha* and *bodhi* are also [the act of awakening]; all these are synonyms for wisdom (*paññā*).
Now we shall state the derivation of the meaning of the word *bodhi*.
For *bodhi* refers to a tree, a path, omniscient knowledge, Nibbāna, and likewise to a person so designated.

Thus, in such passages as "He was fully enlightened for the first time at the foot of the Bodhi tree" and "Between the Bodhi [tree] and Gayā," the tree is called *bodhi*. In the four... [text continues]

In the passage where it says, "knowledge of the paths," it refers to the path (*magga*). In the passage where it says, "the wise one of great wisdom attains enlightenment" (*bodhi*), it refers to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
In the passage where it says, "having reached enlightenment, the deathless, the unconditioned" (*nibbāna*), it refers to Nibbāna.
Furthermore, in the passages, "Venerable Sir, Prince Bodhi pays homage at the feet of the Blessed One with his head" and "the noble disciple is called 'Bodhi'," it refers to the noble disciple.
And in the place where he has come, such is the person thus designated.
Herein this is said:
In the tree, on the path, and in Nibbāna; in knowledge, and in omniscience.
Likewise, the word *bodhi* occurs in its conventional designation (*paṇṇatti*).
One who awakens is an *awakened one* (*bujjhatīti bujjhitā*); one who causes others to awaken is an *awakener* (*bodhetīti bodhetā*).

And here, certain grammatical usages and forms such as those ending in the suffix *-tuṃ* are mentioned: "He awakens [others] to the secret meaning that was not yet understood. (*Guyhamatthamasambuddhaṃ, sambodhayati*)
The forms *yo naro*, *paraṃ sambuddhum arahati*, *bujjhituṃ*, *buddhuṃ*, *bujjhitvā*, *bujjhitvāna*, *bujjhituna*, *buddhiya*, *buddhiyāna*, *buddhā*, and *buddhāna* occur.

In this context, *asambuddhaṃ* means "unknown by others"; there is also a reading *asambodhaṃ*, which has the meaning "unfit for enlightening others. *Sambuddhuṃ* means "to fully awaken. *Buddhā* means "having awakened," and the same applies here to *buddhāna*.

However, some say: "In the *Nāmarūpapariccheda*, because we see the word containing the consonant cluster *dh-v* in the phrases ‘having awakened by the path of enlightenment (*bodhimaggena budhvā*)’ and ‘what the Sugata said after awakening at the seat of enlightenment (*budhvā bodhitale yamāha sugato*)’, and because it possesses the suffix *tvā*, the formation of the word ‘*budhvā*’ must be accepted by way of the consonant cluster *dh-v*.
To this they reply: Such a form of word does not exist in the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*).

It should not be accepted because it is not seen [in the tradition], because it does not conform to the Buddha’s word, and because in a pure ancient manuscript the phrase "the Buddhas by way of the path to enlightenment" (*bodhimaggena buddhā*)—devoid of the *va*-conjunction—and the phrase "the Buddhas at the seat of enlightenment" (*buddhā bodhitale*) are seen.
For such a reading does not conform to the Buddha’s word; indeed, even in a hundred years [of searching] within the Buddha’s word, [such a reading is not found].
Even searching for a thousand years, they would not find such a word containing the conjunction of the letters *va* and *dha*.
Thus, the unsuitability of the form of the word "budhvā" for the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*) should be understood.

For that [word] is desired by scholars who are deceived by their familiarity with Sanskrit texts, but not by those who are experts in the principles of the True Dhamma. Here, these illustrative words should be understood:
"Who, having pierced me, now hides? Having obtained what he desires, a mortal—having attained distinction both before and after—shall go out of sight of the King of Death.
I have seen Umādaṇḍī, adorned with necklaces and earrings;
day and night I do not sleep, like one who has lost a thousand coins."
In this context, *viddhā* means having pierced; *laddhā* means having obtained; *laddhāna* means having obtained (the absolutive form); *diṭṭhā* means having seen.
Thus, although the words “*viddhā*, *laddhā*, *laddhāna*, *diṭṭhā*” are connected with the suffix *-tvā*, they are not bound by the letter *v* due to their phonetic combination (*saññoga*).
Therefore, these two [words] as well—“*buddhā*, *buddhāna*”—are like “*laddhā*, *laddhāna*.”
Forms such as these should be understood only as those in which the *va* and *ka* suffixes have been elided.
Those who desire and recite a form such as "budhvā" seem, I think, to be deceived by the *tvā* suffix; they fall into that deception.
Therefore, rather than accepting such a form, the venerable ones should grasp as essential only that grammatical analysis of words as stated in the *Saddanīti*.
*Budha* means "to awaken. This root is both transitive and intransitive. For when the word *bodhana* (awakening) is uttered, it includes the senses of knowing, blossoming, and the end of sleep;
therefore, it is said: "*Budha* in the sense of knowledge, *budha* in the sense of blossoming, and *budha* in the sense of the end of sleep.
Examples: "The Blessed One awakens," "He awakens to the Dhamma," "He awakens fully," and "The lotus awakens. [The] man...
*buddho*, *pabuddho*, *bodhati*, *pabodhati*, and so forth. Regarding *sandhā*: in the sense of "joining" (*sandhimhi*).

The root *dhā*, preceded by the prefix *sam-*, functions in the sense of joining. "Neither his face was distorted, nor did he join [his lips], nor did he weep. "He does not join" (*na sandhiyati*): this is a form belonging to the *div*-class that is not shared with other grammatical treatises.

Regarding *dhanu* in the sense of "begging": "For your mother indeed begs (*irandhati*); the heart of Vidhura shall be made to beg (*dhaniyyati*). This too is a form belonging to the *div*-class that is not shared [with other treatises].
*Dhī* is used in the sense of disregard.

*Dhīyate*. *Dhīno*. *Yudh* is used in the sense of combat. *Yujjhati*. *Yodho*, *yuddhaṃ*; when the letter *y* becomes *v*, the form is *āvudha*. In this context, *caraṇāyudho* refers to a cock. *Kudh* is used in the sense of anger.
*Kujjhati*. *Kodho*, *kujjhanā*, *kujjhitattaṃ*. "An angry person does not know the meaning; an angry person does not see the Dhamma."

*Sudha* means purity (*soceyya*). Purity is the state of being clean; it is that which is purified. [The nouns] *suddhi*, *visuddhi*, *sujjhanaṃ*, and the adjectives *suddho*, *visuddho*, *parisuddho* [are derived from this]. In the causative, there are forms such as *sodheti* (to purify) and *sodhako* (one who purifies).
*Sidhu* means to satisfy or please (*saṃrādhane*).
It is *sijjhati*. The noun is *siddhi*. *Radha* means to harm (*hiṃsāyaṃ*). [It appears in the forms] *rajjhati*, *virajjhati*, *aparajjhati*. The noun is *aparādho* (offense).

*Rādha* and *sādha* mean success (*saṃsiddhi*). One accomplishes (*rādhayati*), one achieves (*sādhayati*). Accomplishment is *ārādhana*, achievement is *sādhana*. One who achieves the welfare of oneself and others is *sādhu*, a "good person" (*sappurisa*). That which is to be achieved absolutely is *sādhu*; it refers to what is obtained that is beautiful, such as generosity, virtue, and so forth.

*Vidha* means piercing (*vijjhana*). One pierces (*vijjhati*), one penetrates (*paṭivijjhati*). *Khaṇa*: pierced, a piercer, one who pierces; pierced, penetrated; the act of piercing, penetration, thorough penetration; having pierced, those pierced, those being pierced. "Who has pierced me and hides? (*Ko maṃ viddhā nilīyati*)?

*Idha* means in this [world]. *Ijjhati*, *samijjhati*. *Iddhi*, *ijjhanaṃ*, *samijjhanaṃ*, *iddho*. Therein, *iddhi* is success (*ijjhanaṃ*); it is called *iddhi* because beings succeed (*ijjhanti*) by means of it, becoming successful (*iddhā*), prosperous (*vuddhā*), and reaching excellence (*ukkaṃsagatā*).
*Gidhu* means longing (*abhikaṅkhāyaṃ*). *Gijjhati*, *gijjho*, *gaddho*. One who was formerly a vulture (*gaddhabādhipubbo*). "One greedy for sensual pleasures (*kāmagiddho*) does not know.

*Gedho*. *Rudhi* means obstruction (*āvaraṇe*). *Rujjhati*, *virujjhati*, *paṭivirujjhati*. One who obstructs (*virodhako*), one who is obstructed (*viruddho*). Obstruction (*rodho*), opposition (*virodho*), counter-opposition (*paṭivirodho*), and continuous opposition (*anuvirodho*).
*Anuvidhā* means imitation (*anukaraṇa*). The root *dhā*, preceded by the prefixes *anu* and *vi*, occurs in the sense of imitating. A man imitates the action of another man;
in this regard, there is this canonical passage: “Defeated by Giridatta, the horse Paṇḍava of Sāma, Having abandoned its former nature, imitates that very [other horse].”

This too is an uncommon form beginning with *div*. *Anurudha kāme*: "Kāma" means desire (*icchā*). The verbal root *rudh*, preceded by the prefix *anu*, functions here in the sense of desire. Thus, *anuruddho* and *anurodho* [are derived]. What is the contradiction in *anusmāti*?

In that context, *anuruddho* means he is attached to (*anurujjhati*) and desires (*kāmeti*) various excellent things; thus he is called *anuruddho*. *Anurodho* means conformity (*anukūlatā*). This passage from the Canon reads: "He is attached to acquired gain and is repelled by lack of gain."
*Byadh* means to strike. *Byajjhati*. *Byādho*: one who hunts. *Byādho* means a hunter; he strikes (*byajjhati*), hits (*tāḷeti*), and harms various wild animals, thus he is a hunter (*byādho*).
*Gudh* means to envelop. *Gujjhati*. *Godhā* (a monitor lizard). *Man* means to know.

*Maññati*, *avamaññati*, *atimaññati*. One conceives (*maññati*) by way of superiority and so forth; thus it is *māna* (conceit). “Conceiving (*maññanā*), the state of conceiving (*maññitattaṃ*), conceit (*māno*), the ‘I-maker’ (*ahaṅkāro*), loftiness (*unnati*), a banner (*ketu*), grasping (*paggaho*), and self-satisfaction (*avalepo*)” are synonyms.
The root *jana* means "to produce. This is a transitive (sakammaka) root. Its form is *jaññati*, which has the meaning "he produces" (*karoti*).

In the causative (*kārita*): *phussatī janesi mamaṃ* ("Phussatī caused me to be born"). *Janayati*, *sukhaṃ janeti*, *janayati*—thus one who produces is a "producer" (*janaka*), such as a father, or anyone who brings something into being.
One who produces various defilements (*puthu-kilese*) is a "worldling" (*puthujjana*). In this context, the forms are *janeti* and *janayati*.
Upon reaching the *curādigaṇa* (the group beginning with *cura*), forms with a pure agent (*suddhakattā*) arise. For their meaning is "he makes" (*karoti*).
That same meaning may also be expressed by way of a causal agent (*hetukattā*) as "he causes to be produced" (*nibbatteti*).

The root *janī* means "manifestation. This root ends in the vowel *ī* and is intransitive (*akammaka*); however, when preceded by the prefix *vi-*, it becomes transitive (*sakammaka*). [Example: "A son is born" (*putto jāyati*).
Born. A *puthujjana* (worldling) is so called because various defilements (*kilesa*) are born therein. Birth (*jāti*) means arising;

"origination" (*sañjāti*), "coming-to-be" (*nibbatti*), "full manifestation" (*abhinibbatti*), and "the appearance of the aggregates" (*khandhānaṃ pātubhāvo*) are its synonyms. A woman gives birth to a son; a woman has given birth to a son.
That man is displeasing even to his own mother who gave birth to him. A woman about to give birth. In the causative sense: "he causes to be born," "he causes to give birth."
“Wisdom that brings about welfare” refers to forms (*rūpa*).
The root *han* means to injure. Here, by the word “injury,” one should understand “striking. Sound is struck against the ear; it rebounds.
The conventional expression of the Buddha, the Blessed One, rebounds against the worldly ear. These are agentive words (*kattupada*) belonging to the *bhūvādi* class.
However, having reached [the point of] "Gold is indeed struck by iron; they do not strike iron with gold," in the Pāḷi the word "is struck" (*haññati*) is the object-case form;
the meaning is that the gold is struck by the iron [hammer] of the smiths. The word "they strike" (*hananti*) is the agent-case form;
for the meaning is that the smiths strike the iron with the gold [anvil]. Here, "striking" (*hanana*) should be understood as "beating."

*Rūpa* means that which is subject to transformation (*ruppana*). Transformation is agitation, impact, and oppression. It is transformed; thus it is *rūpa*, the state of being transformed. Furthermore, regarding this root *rūp* situated in the *curādigaṇa* (the class beginning with *cur*), which carries the sense of "making into form," there are the forms *rūpeti* and *rūpayati*;

thus they become "forms" (*rūpāni*). In that context, in what sense is it "form" (*rūpa*)? It is form in the sense of being transformed. For this was said by the Blessed One: "And what, monks, is form?
It is called 'form,' monks, because it is transformed. By what is it transformed? By cold as well..."
“It is deformed; it is deformed by heat, it is deformed by hunger, it is deformed by thirst, and it is deformed by contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things.
It is deformed, monks, therefore it is called ‘form’ (rūpa).
In this context, “it is deformed” means it is disturbed, struck, oppressed, and broken; “it is broken” means it undergoes change.
It undergoes change (*vikārāpatti*), and this transformation occurs precisely as the manifestation of dissimilar forms upon the encounter with cold and other conditions.

Here, by the word "kuppati" (is disturbed), he shows the formation of the term *ruppa* in the sense of the agent; by the words "ghaṭṭiyati" (is struck) and "pīḷiyati" (is oppressed), he shows it in the sense of the object.
For the very action of being disturbed and so forth is the action of being affected (*ruppanakriyā*). Yet that meaning, whether as agent or as object, when analyzed, [is as follows:]...
The phrase "it is called [rūpa]" is stated in order to show this meaning: "the meaning is that it breaks up.
Alternatively, the derivation of the word *rūpa* is stated in the sense of the agent as object (*kammakattuttha*), according to the principle that "that which is affected (*ruppati*) is *rūpa*.

For "affection" (*vikāra*) is what is called "being affected" (*ruppana*); therefore, by means of the word "breaks up" (*bhijjati*) used in the sense of the agent as object, he demonstrates the meaning.
In this context, when the word "ruppati" (is affected) is used in the sense of an object (*kamma*), then the words "by cold," etc., are instrumental cases used in the sense of an agent (*kartr*).

However, when the word "ruppati" is used in the sense of an agent or in the sense of an agent who is also the object (*kammakartr*), then the instrumental case should be understood as being used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
The term *rūpa* applies to such meanings as the aggregates (*khandha*), existence (*bhava*), signs (*nimitta*), conditions (*paccaya*), the body (*sarīra*), and color-shape (*vaṇṇasaṇṭhāna*), etc.
For this [term "form"] refers to the aggregate of form in the passage: “Whatever form, whether past, future, or present”; it refers to the form-existence (*rūpabhava*) in the passage:
“He develops the path for the arising of form”; it refers to the kasiṇa-sign in the passage: “Perceiving the internal as formless, he sees forms externally”;
and it refers to the physical body in the passage: “O monks, evil unwholesome states arise together with form, not without form.”
In this context, it refers to the condition. In the passage, “Space enclosed is designated simply as ‘form’,” it refers to the body.
In the passage, “Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises,” it refers to color. In the passage, “One who is measured by form and delighted by form,” it refers to shape.
Thus, in this way—
The word *rūpa* occurs in reference to the aggregates (*khandha*), states of existence (*bhava*), signs (*nimitta*), the body (*sarīra*), conditions (*paccaya*), and color, shape, and so forth.
*Kup* means to be agitated. It is agitated; it is agitated even by the movement of the wind. Agitation, intense agitation. One should guard against verbal agitation.
*Tapa* means to heat. It is heated; it is warmed. *Santāpa* is heat.
*Tapa* also means to satisfy. It is satisfied; the act of satisfying.
*Dapa* means to laugh. It laughs.
*Dīpa* means light; it shines, thus it is called a *dīpa*.
*Lupa* means non-appearance; the state of being hidden is *luppana*, *lopa*, or *luti*.
*Khipa* means throwing; it throws, thus it is called *khippa*.
*Lubha* means greed. One is greedy. He stands clutching his own knee.
[Derivatives: *lubbhanaṃ*, *lobho*, *lubbhitvā*, *lubbhitvāna*, *lubbhiya*, *lubbhiyāna*, *olubbhitvā*, *olubbhitvāna*, *olubbhiya*, *olubbhiyāna*, *lubbhituṃ*, *olubbhituṃ*.
In this context, *lobha* (greed) is so called because beings are made greedy by it, or it itself becomes greedy, or it is merely the state of being greedy;

thus it is greed. Furthermore, it should be understood that there are many synonyms for greed, such as: greed, the act of being greedy, the state of being greedy, lust, craving, thirst, infatuation, impulse, the forest, and the thicket.

*Khubbha* means to shake or agitate. It is used as *khubbhati*, *saṃkhubbhati*; for example, "the city was shaken" (*khubbhittha-nagaraṃ*) or "agitation" (*saṅkhobho*). In the causative sense: *khobheti*, *khobhayati*. *Samu* means to become calm or to be pacified.
The mind becomes calm (*sammati*), pacified (*upasammati*), or thoroughly pacified (*vūpasammati*); it is called *samaṇo*, *santi*, or *santo*.

Here, a *samaṇo* is so called because he becomes calm, that is, one whose mind has become tranquil (*sammati santacitto bhavati*). Furthermore, in the sense of the causative, he calms the defilements (*kilese sameti*).

The etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) of "samaṇa" should be understood as "one who pacifies" (*upasameti*). For indeed, there are two forms of activity: "that which pacifies" (*sameti*) refers to the Noble One;
"it brings about peace for beings here" (*samayati*) refers to the world.

[The root] *sam* [is used] in the senses of exhaustion (*kheda*) and cessation (*nirodha*). Exhaustion means weariness. Cessation means going to non-existence. The body of one traveling on a long journey becomes stilled; the fire is stilled. Thus, he is "peaceful" (*santo*).
The word *santa* occurs in the sense of being exhausted in such passages as, “A wearying journey of a yojana.

It occurs in the sense of having ceased in such passages as, “This applied thought and this sustained thought have become stilled (*santa*) and calmed. It occurs in the sense of being the object of noble knowledge in such passages as, “This Dhamma I have attained is deep, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful (*santa*), sublime. [And it occurs in the sense of being tranquil in] “Of one who is ever tranquil...”

In such passages as “of one who possesses peace,” it refers to the subsiding of the defilements. In such passages as “The peaceful indeed proclaim [it] to the virtuous,” it refers to those who are good.
In such passages as “These five, monks, are great thieves existing in the world,” it refers to existence. Regarding this, it is said:
“In the state of being weary, in the state of being ceased, and in the state of being the object of the mind of the peaceful.”
The word *santa* (peaceful/calm) occurs in these six instances: in the pacification of defilements (*kilesa*), in the existence of the virtuous (*sādhu*), and in these [other] six places.

Regarding *dama* (taming): it is the act of taming (*damana*). One is tamed (*dammati*). Thus there are the forms *danto*, *damo*, and *damanaṃ*. In the causative sense, there are the forms *cittaṃ dameti* and *damayati* (“one tames the mind”).

In this context, "taming" (*dama*) is a name for the restraint of the sense faculties and so forth. For in the passage, "Tamed by truth, endowed with taming, having reached the end of knowledge, one who has lived the holy life," it is the restraint of the sense faculties that is called "taming.

In the passage, "If there were anything here superior to truth, taming, generosity, and patience," it is wisdom that is called "taming. [And in the passage], "By giving, by taming, by self-restraint..."
In the phrase "by the utterance of truth," the Uposatha observance is called "taming" (*dama*). In the phrase "by taming and pacification," patience (*khanti*) is called "taming. Thus it is said:
"Restraint of the faculties, wisdom, Patience, and also the Uposatha;..."
"These eight meanings are declared by the word *pariyāya* in the Dispensation.

[The following are examples: *yā* (goes), *pāpuṇesu* (in the attainment of destinations); *yāyati*, *yāyanti* (he goes, they go). *Pariyāyo* (a method or turn). *Yāyamāno mahārājā addā sīdantare nage* (the Great King, while traveling, saw a mountain between the Sīda mountains). *Yāyanto* (while going). *Yāyantamanuyāyati* (he follows one who is going). *Yātānuyāyī* (one who follows those who have gone). *Yāyituṃ*, *yāyitvā*, and so forth. Here, the extraction of the meanings of the word *pariyāya* is stated;
the word *pariyāya* [is used] in the senses of repetition (*vāra*), teaching (*desanā*), and cause (*kāraṇa*). From all sides...

It is used in the sense of a place to be gone to and in the sense of something similar. For instance, it is used in the sense of a turn when one says, “Ānanda, whose turn is it today to exhort the bhikkhunīs?
It is used in the sense of a teaching when one says, “Bear in mind this Discourse on the Honeyball.
It is used in the sense of a reason when one says, “By this very method, Prince, let it be so for you. And it is used in the sense of a path when one says, “the path of method,” and so forth.

In the phrase "a place to be gone to on all sides" (*samantato gantabbaṭṭhāne*), it is used in the sense of a similar thing. In such instances as "the sound of anger is a synonym for agitation" (*kopasaddo khobhapariyāyo*), it functions in a similar way. Thus:
The term *pariyāya* may refer to a turn, a teaching, a cause, And to a place to be gone to on all sides, as well as to a similar thing.
*Ṛi* (ri) is used in the sense of dwelling (*vasane*). *Riyati*.
*Vilī* is used in the sense of melting (*vilīnabhāve*). *Sappi vilīyati* (butter melts). In the causative, *vilāpayati*.
*Vā* is used in the senses of motion (*gati*) and smelling (*gandhana*). *Vāyati*. *Vāyo*, *vāto* (wind).
*Sivu* [is used] in the sense of sewing. It sews; it stitches together. [The forms are: *sibbaṃ*, *sibbanto*. In the causative: *sibbeti*, *sibbayati*, *sibbāpeti*, *sibbāpayati*.
*Sivu* [also occurs] in the senses of going and drying up. [It means] it sews.
*Dhivu* and *khivu* [are used] in the sense of pointing out. [They mean] it points out; it indicates. *Dhibbati*. *Khibbati*.
It is in the sense of making thin (*tanukaraṇa*).

It is "it is" (*siyati*), "they are" (*siyanti*). It is in the sense of the work of ending (*antakamma*). For it is said: "The final path is called 'the ender of conceit' because it ends conceit without remainder, it ends it, it utterly cuts it off.
It is in the sense of tasting (*assādana*). It tastes the flavor (*rasa*). [The forms] "tasted" (*sāyita*) and "tasting" (*sāyana*).
*Si* [is used] in the sense of giving birth (*pāṇippasave*). It is *sūyati*, *pasūyati*. A cow that has given birth is *pasūtā*.
*Kusu* [is used] in the senses of taking away (*haraṇa*) and burning (*ditti*). It is *kusayati*.
*Silisa* [is used] in the sense of embracing (*āliṅgane*). It is *silissati*. An embrace is *sileso*.
*Kilisa* means to torment. It stains, it defiles. *Kileso*, *saṃkileso*. When the vowel *i* is elided, we have forms such as *klissati* and *kleso*.
Furthermore, the word *kilisa* also denotes soiledness, as in "he wears a stained garment.
In passages such as "By a stained mind, young men are stained," the verbal roots possess multiple meanings.
*Masa* means to be displeased; it is *khamāyañca*. It is *massati*.
*Līsa* means to be displeased; it is *lissati*. *Leso*. Teachers also read [the root] as *lisa* in the sense of licking (*lesana*).
*Tasa* means thirst; it is *tassati*, *paritassati*. [The derivatives are] *paritassanā*, *tasiṇā*, and *tasito*.
*Dus* means to hate. It hates (*dussati*). Hate (*doso*), hating (*dosanaṃ*), one who has hated (*dosito*).

*Dus* is used in the sense of displeasure. It hates (*dussati*), it becomes corrupt (*padussati*). Hate (*doso*), corruption (*padoso*), one who is corrupted (*duṭṭho*), one who is thoroughly corrupted (*paduṭṭho*), a corrupter (*dūsako*), one who has been corrupted (*dūsito*), the act of corrupting (*dūsanā*).
*Asu* means to throw away. Throwing away (*khepo*), the act of throwing (*khipanaṃ*). He throws away (*assati*). He rejects (*nirassati*) and grasps (*ādāti*) the Dhamma. A bowman (*issāso*).

And here, "he casts out" (*nirassati*) means he abandons the Teacher as well as the proclamation of the Dhamma and so forth. "An archer" (*issāsa*) is one who "casts" (*assati*) or shoots an arrow (*issu*); thus, an archer is a bowman. [The root] *yasu* is in the sense of exertion.
One exerts oneself (*yassati*). It is an act of banishment (*niyassakamma*).
And here, that disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*) by which one is "banished"—that is, separated from the community with the words, "You must live dependent [on others]"—is called *niyasa*.

*Bālaṃ* (foolishness), that is what is called *niyasakamma* (one’s own action). However, in the phrase “Perform for me, O *yakkha*, your own action (*niyasakamma*)”, here *niyasakamma* refers to an act of subjugation.
*Bhassa*: in the sense of speaking. He speaks; speech; one who makes speech. *Vasa*:
in the sense of sound. A bird cries out. “The lowest of the deer species, dear father, the jackal cries out. A frog croaks.

In the sense of disappearance: it perishes. It is subject to destruction; it perishes; it is destroyed. "Perish, you outcaste! Go away and be destroyed! Destroyed, ruined. In the causative: he causes to perish, he causes to destroy.
In the sense of drying up: a leaf withers. In the causative: the wind dries up the leaf, causes it to dry. In the passive: the leaf is dried by the wind.
The verbal form in the sense of the abstract state (bhāve) is not commonly established. Drying, a withered stick. Withering, withering away; a dried-up lake.

*Tus* is used in the sense of satisfaction. One is satisfied (*tussati*), one is fully satisfied (*santussati*). [The derivatives are: *santuṭṭhi*, *santos*, *tosanaṃ*, *tuṭṭhabbaṃ*, *tussitabbaṃ*, and *tusitā*. In the causative, there are forms such as "he satisfies" (*toseti*).
*Hā* is used in the sense of decline. It declines (*hāyati*), it declines completely (*parihāyati*). "The mares decline there" (*hāyanti tattha vaḷavā*).

In the sense of a state (*bhāve*), there are forms such as "fear, or trepidation, or horripilation—this will be abandoned" (*bhayaṃ vā chambhitattaṃ vā lomahaṃso vā, so pahīyissati*) and "lust is abandoned" (*rāgo pahīyati*). In the passive (*kamma*), the verbal form is not commonly established.

“‘Lust is abandoned’ (rāgo pahīyati): this, however, is the form of the root *hā*, belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa* and meaning ‘to abandon,’ as seen in the agentive construction ‘he abandons lust’ (rāgaṃ pajahati).
[The root] *naha* means ‘to bind. One binds (*nayhati*). One binds closely (*upanayhati*). One binds together (*sannayhati*). Armor (*sannāha*). Armored (*sannaddho*).”
Muha: in the sense of being deluded—*muyhati*, *sammuyhati*, *pamuyhati*; delusion (*moha*), extreme delusion (*pamoha*); one who is deluded;

a person in a state of extreme bewilderment (*momūha*); a mind in a state of extreme bewilderment. In the causative form: *moheti*; one who causes delusion (*pamohaka*). And here, *momūha* means "extremely bewildered" due to a lack of clarity;
the meaning is "one who is greatly deluded. Sa-ha: in the sense of enduring or bearing—*sayhati*, *suyhati*.
In "nhā soceyye": *nhāyati* means "he bathes"; in the sense of the plurality of short vowels, it is *nahāyati*. *Nahāyitvā* means "having bathed.
*Nhānaṃ* means "bathing. In *sīsaṃ nhāto*, the meaning should be understood as "having washed his head and bathed," because this is the interpretation accepted by the ancients (*porāṇehi*).

*Siṇiha* is used in the sense of affection (*pīti*). One feels affection (*siṇiyhati*). It means one who is affectionate, one who has been made affectionate, or one who is tender. "Affection for his son was born. By the elision of the vowel *i*, it becomes *sneha*. For indeed, the Pāli text is seen as: "I desire that which is free from *sneha* (*nisneham abhikaṅkhāmi*).

*Viriḷa* is used in the sense of modesty (*lajjā*) and also in the sense of urging (*codanā*). It means one who is urged (*viriḷito*). The meaning established by usage is based on modesty, not on urging. For thus the venerable commentators explain the meaning: "'Viriḷito' means 'lajjito' (modest)," and they say, "one who has reached the state of the mode of being modest. Thus far have the roots beginning with *div* been seen by me according to my ability.
"Having observed other [roots] as well in the sutta-s, you should grasp them according to their meaning and application.
This is the *div-ādi* group.
[Now for] the *sv-ādi* group.
In the sense of hearing: *suṇoti*, *suṇāti*; *suṇiṃsu*; *paṭissuṇi*, *paṭissuṇiṃsu*; *assosi*, *assosuṃ*;
*paccassosi*, *paccassosuṃ*, and so forth; as well as *suṇissati*, *sossati*, and so forth. In the sense of repeated hearing (*abbhāsa*): *sussūsati*, *sussūsā*, and so forth.
In the sense of non-repeated hearing (*anabbhāsa*): *sāvako*, *soto*, *suṇaṃ*, *suṇanto*, *suṇamāno*, *suyyamāno*.
*Savanaṃ*, *sutaṃ*. Or, that which was heard is *sutaṃ*. [Derivatives: *sutavā*, *sotaṃ*, *soṇo*, *suṇituṃ*, *sotuṃ*. [Absolutives:
*suṇitvā*, *suṇiya*, *suṇiyāna*, *sutvā*, *sutvāna*. In the causative: *sāveti*, *sāvayati*. In the passive: the sound is heard (*suyyati*), and it is also *sūyati*.
A verbal form in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*) is not well-established.
In this context, a "disciple" (*sāvaka*) is a resident pupil (*antevāsika*). He is of two kinds: one who has attained the fruit and one who has not yet attained the fruit.

Therein, one who has attained the fruit is called a "disciple" because he was born into the noble birth at the conclusion of hearing [the Dhamma]; the other is called a "disciple" because he listens to the instruction of his teachers.
"Disciple," "resident pupil," and "student" (*sissa*) are synonyms.
Here we shall state the extraction of the meaning of the word *suta* together with the extraction of the meaning of the word *sota*.

The word *suta*, both with and without prefixes, and without accompanying nouns, is seen in the following senses: in "gone," "famous," "drunk," "appointed," "honored," "sound," and "known through the ear-door."
For instance: in such passages as “pasuto senāya,” the meaning is “going”; in “sutadhammassa passato,” the meaning is “of one who has heard the Dhamma”;
in “avassutā avassutassa purisapuggalassa,” the meaning is “of one who is moistened (with passion)”;
in “ye jhānappasutā dhīrā,” the meaning is “devoted to”; and in “tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakan,” [the meaning is likewise].
The meaning is "accumulated. In such passages as "the seen, the heard, the sensed, and the cognized," the meaning is "sound.

In such passages as "he is one of great learning, a bearer of what is heard, an accumulator of what is heard," the meaning is "one who bears in mind the phenomena cognized by following the door of the ear.
The word *sota* (ear/flow) also has many distinct meanings; for instance:

The word *sota* is seen in the sense of "fleshly ear" (*maṃsa-sota*) in such contexts as "knowledge of the consciousness of the fleshly ear" (*maṃsa-viññāṇa-ñāṇa*), in [the list of] craving and so forth, in the stream [of the Dhamma], in the Noble Path, and also in the continuity of consciousness (*citta-santati*).

In such expressions as "the ear-base" (*sota-āyatana*), "the ear-element" (*sota-dhātu*), and "the ear-faculty" (*sota-indriya*), the word *sota* is seen in the sense of the "fleshly ear. By the ear...

In such passages as “having heard a sound,” it refers to ear-consciousness (*sotaviññāṇa*). In such passages as “with the divine ear-element (*dibbāya sotadhātuyā*),” it refers to the stream of knowledge (*ñāṇasota*).

Regarding the statement, “Those streams that exist in the world,” these are the streams that have been proclaimed, fully proclaimed, declared, taught, established, set forth, opened up, analyzed, made plain, and revealed by me. That is to say: the stream of craving (*taṇhāsota*).
It refers to the five phenomena in such passages as, "the stream of views, the stream of defilements, the stream of misconduct, and the stream of ignorance";
to the flow of water in such passages as, "The Blessed One saw a great log being carried away by the current of the river Ganges";
and to the Noble Path in such passages as, "Friends, 'stream' is a designation for this Noble Eightfold Path."

In such passages as, “One understands a person’s stream of consciousness as uninterrupted on both sides, established in this world and established in the other world,” it refers to the mental continuity (*cittasantati*).
*Soṇa* means a dog; for it is called *soṇa* because it hears (*suṇāti*) its master’s words.
These are its names:
sunakha, sārameyya, suṇo, sūno, kukkura,
soṇo, svāna, suvāna, sāḷura, and migadaṃsana.
She hears these sounds: "pumāna" and "puruṣa" are used for males;
"sunakhī," "kukkurī," and "śunī" are used for females.
Furthermore, "sunakhā" and "sārameyyā" and so forth are plural forms.
This principle applies among males and females, and even elsewhere:
the term "dog" (kukkura) is applied there to a young one because of its barking,
and it is also used by conventional usage for an old dog.
For thus did the commentators of the *Aṭṭhakathā* explain the meaning of this passage in the *Kukkurajātaka*:
"Those dogs who were raised in the royal household, well-bred and endowed with beauty and strength. Regarding the phrase "those dogs," they mean "those hounds.
For just as even fresh urine is called "putrid urine" (*pūtimutta*), and even a jackal born that very day is called "an old jackal" (*jarasiṅgālo*), so too even something delicate...

Just as a *gaḷācīlatā* creeper is called a "rotten creeper" (*apūtilatā*), and even a body the color of gold is called a "rotten body" (*pūtikāyo*), so too even a hundred-year-old dog is called a "dog" (*kukkuro*).
Therefore, although they have attained bodies as adults, they are still called "dogs. What is this "kiṃ"?
It means he buys, she buys, they buy. (*Kiṇoti*, *kiṇāti*, *kiṇanti*).

*Saka* [is used] in the sense of capability (*sāmatthiya*). Capability is the state of being capable (*sāmatthiya*), just as *dakkhiya* [is the state of being clever]. [Examples of usage: *sakkuṇāti*, *sakkuṇanti*; *asakkhi*; *sakkhissati*; *sakko*; *sakkī*. Here, *sakko* refers to the King of the Gods (*devarāja*).
For he is called *Sakka* because he is able (*sakkuṇāti*) to accomplish the welfare of others and his own welfare.
Furthermore, it may refer to anyone born into the Sakya clan. Thus it is said: "Then Mahānāma the Sakyan," and so forth. And [regarding the phrase] "the Blessed One..."
"Piṅgiya, O Sakyan, please lift me up! he cried. Based on this statement—"O, these princes are indeed Sakyans;
O, these princes are most excellent Sakyans"—all those born into the Sakya clan are called "Sakyas," "Sākiyas," and "Sakkas.
Here, even though the root contains multiple vowels, it should be understood that only the *uṇ* suffix occurs, and not the *ṇu* or *ṇā* suffixes.
*Khī* means "exhausted. *Khīṇo*, *khīṇā*, *khīṇā jāti*, *khīṇo*: [these are examples]. Through non-application, there is the destruction of abundance.
*Ge* is for the sound. *Giṇoti*, *giṇāti*.

*Ci* is for the sense of "piling up. The substitution of *ṇa* for *na*: he piles up a rampart (*pākāraṃ cinoti*). "Piled up" (*citaṃ*) refers to the wholesome. "Ceto" refers to the person (*puggalo*).
*Ru* means to afflict. It takes the forms *ruṇoti* and *ruṇāti*.
*Rādha* and *sādha* mean accomplishment. They take the forms *rādhuṇāti* and *sādhuṇāti*. The nouns are *rādhanaṃ*, *ārādhanaṃ*, and *sādhanaṃ*.
*Pī* means delight. It takes the forms *pīṇoti* and *pīṇāti*. The nouns are *pīti* and *piyo*.

Regarding *pāpuṇe* and *sambhu*: [the roots] *pāpuṇoti*, *pāpuṇāti*, and *patto*. "The Teacher has attained omniscience (*sabbaññuta*). "He has fully attained (*sampatto*) the means of self-restraint (*yama-sādhana*). Regarding *sambhuṇāti*: he does not fail to accomplish any purpose. [Examples: *sambhuṇanto*, *abhisambhuṇamāno*.
In this context, the prefix *pa-* in the word *patto* is a preverb (*upasagga*), just like the prefix *pa-* in the word *pappoti*.

For instance, in the case of "attained" (*patto*), when the sense is "he attains" (*pāpuṇi*), there is a doubling of the suffix *-ta* after the root *ap-* (from *āp-*) when the prefix *pa-* is elided.
In this context, *na abhisambhuṇāti* means "he does not reach," which is to say "he does not accomplish.
*Khipa* is the root for throwing. *Khipuṇāti*. *Khippaṃ*. *Khippanti* refers to a fish-trap.
*Āpa* is the root for pervading. *Āpuṇāti*. *Āpo*.
It is not to be placed within me. He measures; thus, he is a friend (*mitta*). And here, among all secret things, one who is measured—that is, deposited—is a friend.

However, the statement, "A friend indeed [is won] by seven steps," is spoken according to conventional usage (*vohāra*), not according to the ultimate sense (*attha*). For if it were taken literally, anyone who is untrustworthy would be called a friend.
Even one who is opposed to oneself might be called a friend; however, it should not be viewed in that way. Rather, it should be understood thus:

"One becomes what is called a friend by merely walking together for the distance of seven steps, or by the mere act of exchanging greetings and conversation with one who walks alongside, through the utterance of pleasant words. For what reason? Because of firm trust."
"One should not become a non-friend" is said thus by way of praising the qualities of a friend.

*Vu* is in the sense of binding (*saṃvaraṇa*). One binds (*vuṇoti*), one binds (*vuṇāti*), one binds together (*saṃvuṇoti*), one binds together (*saṃvuṇāti*). "The wise person is restrained by virtue. *Su* is in the sense of pressing out (*abhisava*).
Pressing out (*abhisava*) means squeezing, churning, distilling, or clarifying. One presses out (*suṇoti*), one presses out (*suṇāti*).
*Si* is used in the sense of binding (*bandhane*).
*Sinoti*. *Si* is used in the sense of sharpening (*nisāne*). *Siṇoti*, *siṇāti*. A sharpened weapon.
Surely this hunchback woman does not deserve to have her tongue cut out.
By the teacher Sunīta, speaking such ill-spoken words:
"In this matter they say, 'they say.
*Vusa* means one who is impudent (*pāgabbiye*). Impudence (*pāgabbiya*) is the state of being shameless through the body, speech, and mind. *Vusuṇāti* [means he speaks]."
*Asu* means "to pass away. *Assu* means "he hears.
The root *hi* is used in the senses of going, understanding, and affliction; it means "he goes.
Here, however, the combination of words with identical meanings is stated even when they do not share the same grammatical form.
*Tika*, *tiga*, *sagha*, *dikkha*, *kivi*, *ciri*, *jiri*, *dāsa*, and *du*—these are for the purpose of expressing injury (*hiṃsā*).
[The forms] *tikuṇāti*, *tiguṇāti*, *saghuṇāti*, *dikkhuṇāti*, *kivuṇāti*, *ciruṇāti*, *jiruṇāti*, *dāsuṇāti*, and *duṇoti*, *duṇāti* are indeed verbal forms that signify injury.
These many roots beginning with *su* have been seen by me according to my ability.
Having observed other [roots] as well in the sutras, you should include them in the *gaṇa* according to their semantic suitability.
This is the *svādi-gaṇa*. [The following] belongs to the *kiyādi-gaṇa*.
Regarding "in the exchange of goods" (*dabbavinimaye*): the exchange of goods is the bartering of merchandise by way of buying and selling.

[The forms are: *kiṇāti*, *kiṇanti*; *vikkiṇāti*, *vikkiṇanti*. [Infinitives: *ketuṃ*, *kiṇituṃ*; *vikketuṃ*, *vikkiṇituṃ*. [Absolutives: *kiṇitvā*, *vikkiṇitvā*. [Nouns: *kītaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ* (purchased goods);
*kayo*, *vikkayo* (buying, selling). [Optatives: *vikkiṇeyya*, *haneyya* (one might sell or one might strike).
In the sense of *gati* (going). It means "to go" (*khiṇāti*). An arrow that has gone too far is *atikhiṇa*. *Khaṃ*, *khāni*.
There is the substitution of *ṇa* for the letter *na*. In this context, *khiṇāti* means "it goes. *Atikhinoti* means "it has gone beyond. Here is the canonical passage (*pāḷi*):

"They lie like arrows shot from a bow, sighing over things of the past. In this passage, *cāpātikhiṇā* means "gone beyond the bow," having departed from the bow. [As stated] in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).

However, regarding the analysis of the word-meaning provided as “*cāpātikhiṇā* means *cāpato atikhiṇā*, i.e., released from the bow,” that too should be understood as having been composed by way of the intended meaning (*adhippāyattha*), referring precisely to what has already been explained.
In this context, *khanti* is heaven (*sagga*). For it is called “*kha*” because it is to be reached by those who have performed meritorious deeds. *Khāni* refers to heavens.

*Ci*, *caye*. One accumulates merit (*puññaṃ cināti*). One builds a wall (*pākāraṃ cināti*). One investigates and examines the perfections (*pāramiyo vicināti, vicinati ca*). One gathers flowers (*pupphaṃ ocināti, ocinati vā*).

One plucks (*pacināti*). Having plucked (*pacinitvā*). Merit that has been accumulated (*citaṃ kusalaṃ*). Accumulation (*cayo*) means a collection (*sañcayo*). A wall that has been built up (*cito pākāro*).

That which accumulates is a "mind" (*ceto*), as in a bricklayer (*iṭṭhakavaḍḍhakī*). A being who is a collection of merit (*puññasañcayo*). "Collection" (*sañcayo*) means a heap (*rāsi*), a multitude (*samūho*), a mass (*piṇḍo*), a group (*gaṇo*), or a community (*saṅgho*).
*Kadamba*, *vagga*, *kara*, *ghaṭā*—these and others are synonyms. The root *ji* means "to conquer.
One conquers (*jināti*), overcomes (*vijināti*), or is conquered (*jiniyati*). A conqueror (*jetā*), a Victor (*jino*). Māra is conquered. Māra has been conquered. [The forms:

one who has conquered (*jitavā*), one who has become a conqueror (*jitāvī*), that which is to be conquered (*jitabbo*), that which is to be won (*jeyyo*), the act of conquering (*jayanaṃ*), what is conquered (*jitaṃ*), what is overcome (*vijitaṃ*), victory (*jayo*), the act of defeating (*parājayanaṃ*), defeat (*parājayo*). Of whom it is said: "That which was conquered..."
He is not defeated. No one in the world can overcome him. For this is the victory of the glorious Buddha and the defeat of Māra, the Evil One.
In this context, "the Victor" (*jetā*) means one who conquers; he is any person. "The Conqueror" (*jina*) refers to the Omniscient King of Dhamma.

What did he conquer? Evil, unwholesome states and enemies such as Māra. Thus, because he conquered evil, unwholesome states and enemies such as Māra, he is a "Conqueror" (Jina). And this has also been said:
"Those like me are indeed Conquerors who have attained the destruction of the taints."
"I have conquered evil states; therefore, Upaka, I am a Conqueror (Jina).
And: "The Tathāgata, bhikkhus, is the Overcomer, the Unconquered.
For the word *jina* alone applies to the Omniscient One (*sabbaññu*), whereas when accompanied by a prefix, it applies to those such as the Paccekabuddhas.

And it proceeds according to what is appropriate. “The Solitary Victor (paccekajina), the Victor of the Stream (odhijina), the Victor Beyond the Stream (anodhijina), the Victor over Ripening (vipākajina), and the Victor over Non-Ripening (avipākajina)”—these are the illustrative phrases here.

[The root] *ji* means to conquer. He conquers; he does not fail to conquer, nor does he cause others to conquer. The Victor [conquered] the chariot, the gold, and the jeweled earrings; likewise the Victor [conquered] his sons and his wives. The Victor [conquered] wealth and slaves.

*Ñā* means "to understand. One knows (*jānāti*), one is known (*ñāyati*), or one leads (*nāyati*). "Those without signs do not lead" (*animittā na nāyare*). "He would know if he were to neglect [them]" (*jaññā so yadi hāpaye*).
"May they not know me" (*mā maṃ jaññūti*)—thus he desires. In the sense of being known as "these are ours," one is a *ñāti* (relative) or a *ñātaka* (kinsman).

Relatives and dear friends (*ñātimitta-suhajjā*). "A kinsman is seated with us" (*ñātako no nisinno*). That which is to be known is the *ñeyya*; it refers to the phenomena (*dhammā*) characterized by conditioned formations, change, and Nibbāna.
In such instances, the word *ñeyya* is invariably neuter; when it follows the gender of its referent (*vāccaliṅgatta*), it takes all genders, as in:

*ñeyyo phasso* (contact is to be known), *ñeyyā vedanā* (feeling is to be known), *ñeyyaṃ cittaṃ* (mind is to be known), *ñeyyo puriso* (a man is to be known), *ñeyyā itthī* (a woman is to be known), and *ñeyyaṃ dhanaṃ* (wealth is to be known).

[Now for the root] *thu*, meaning praise (*abhitthava*). [Derivatives: *thunāti* (he praises), *abhitthunāti* (he praises); *thuti*, *abhitthuti* (praise); *thavanā*, *abhitthavanā* (the act of praising); *thuto*, *abhitthuto* (praised).
Regarding yawning: "He yawns.
"Arise, O Revatī of evil character!
You whose door is open and who are of a nature that does not give!"
"Let us go to that place where the miserable ones,
the denizens of hell, overwhelmed by suffering,
lament their past deeds"— this is the application [of the term].
From *du* [comes] *hiṃsāyaṃ*. It torments (*dunāti*). A betrayer of friends (*mittaddu*). A tree (*dumo*).
Here, regarding "a betrayer of friends" (*mittaddu*): he torments (*dunāti*), harms (*hiṃsati*), or acts treacherously (*dubbhati*) toward a friend;

thus, he is a betrayer of friends (*mittaddu*). In this regard, the canonical text (*pāḷi*) provides the illustration: "The Vedas do not provide protection for that man who betrays his friends and destroys living beings. Regarding "tree" (*dumo*): it is that which is difficult to move (*duniyati*).

A *duma* (tree) is so called because it is harmed or cut down for the sake of building materials and the like, or because it is oppressed by those seeking leaves and flowers through the taking of those leaves and flowers.
The root *dhū* means to shake. It shakes; thus: *dhūmo*, *dhonā*, *dhono*, *dhuto*. "Shaking my bark-garments, I then went into the sky.
In that context, *dhūmo* means that which shakes or trembles, hence *dhūmo*. The word *dhūma* [also] refers to anger, craving, and thought, as well as among the five [aggregates].
The term *dhūma* (smoke) is used in these senses: in the context of teaching the Dhamma regarding the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), it refers to their inherent nature;
in the passage “Anger is the smoke, falsehood is the ash,” it refers to anger; in the passage “He was always smoking with desire,” it refers to craving (*taṇhā*);
and in the passage “Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu was sitting smoking not far from the Blessed One,” it refers to discursive thought (*vitakka*).
“Sensual pleasures are mud and sensual pleasures are a mire;
this fear has been proclaimed by me as manifold.
Dust and smoke have also been explained by me.”

“Having abandoned [them], go forth, Brahmadatta!”—here it refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*). “He becomes a maker of smoke”—here it refers to the teaching of the Dhamma. “The banner is the sign of the chariot, smoke is the sign of the fire”—here it refers to natural smoke. Thus, in this way:
In anger, craving, and thoughts, and in the five strands of sensual pleasure;
And during the teaching, smoke arises from natural incense.
"Dhonā" means wisdom (*paññā*). For this is said in the *Niddesa*: "Dhonā is called wisdom; that which is wisdom, understanding, right view—by what reason is wisdom called 'dhonā'?
Because by means of that wisdom, bodily misconduct is shaken off and washed away."
“Misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind have been shaken off, washed away, cleansed, and thoroughly purified.
For that reason, wisdom is called ‘the shaker’ (dhona). Alternatively, right view has shaken off, washed away, cleansed, and thoroughly purified wrong view;
for that reason, wisdom is called ‘the shaker. [Regarding] the one who is a shaker...
"Indeed, there is nothing anywhere in the world for one who has formed views regarding various states of existence"—this is the scriptural passage illustrating this point.
Here, "one who is cleansed" (*dhona*) means one who possesses cleansing; thus, *dhonassa* is the grammatical analysis.
Because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *dhū* applies both to the sense of shaking (*kampana*) and to the sense of washing (*dhovana*).

In the case of *muna* (to know), it means "he knows. Thus, there are the forms *monaṃ* and *muni*. In this context, when the verbal root (*dhātu*) functions as a noun (*nāma*), the final vowel is invariably elided.
However, in the verses of the Elder Sobhita, in the future tense, another form is seen due to the lengthening of the vowel *u*:
"I shall know by means of knowledge" (*ahaṃ monena monissam*). Therein, *monissanti* means "I shall know. In the case of nouns, the elision of the final vowel does not occur.

Regarding this, although in the passage “One does not become a sage by silence” (*na monena muni hoti*) the term “silence” (*mone*) refers to the state of being quiet, nevertheless, because the word “knowledge” (*ñāṇe*) is used here, that [silence] is not intended;
rather, knowledge itself is intended. Therefore, the knowledge of the path, which consists of the practice of sagacity (*moneyya*), must also be understood.
A sage (*muni*) is one who knows (*munāti*), understands, and discerns what is beneficial and what is harmful.

Alternatively, he is a *muni* because he measures both these meanings—“these are internal aggregates, these are external,” and so forth—just as one who weighs things on a scale in the world of the aggregates and so on. Therefore the Blessed One said:
“One does not become a sage (*muni*) by mere silence; one who is dull-witted and ignorant is no sage.”
But the wise one who, having taken up the best as if choosing from a scale,
avoids all evils— he is a sage by that very fact.
He who understands both worlds is called a sage for that reason.
Furthermore, there is here an exposition of the meaning: "Muni" refers to *mona*, which is knowledge; or else it refers to any one of the forms of composure such as bodily composure (*kāyamoneyya*).
Because he is endowed with that, a person is called a "muni. Moreover, this [muni] is of many kinds:

the householder-muni, the homeless-muni, the muni-in-training (*sekkha*), the muni-beyond-training (*asekkha*), the solitary-muni (*pacceka-muni*), and the muni-of-munis. Among these, the "householder-muni" refers even to a layperson.
One who has attained the fruit and understood the teaching; one who has gone forth as a sage of homelessness (*anagāriya-muni*) is likewise such a person.

A trainee sage (*sekha-muni*) refers to the seven types of trainees. A non-trainee sage (*asekha-muni*) is one whose taints are destroyed. A solitary sage (*pacceka-muni*) is a paccekabuddha. A sage among sages (*muni-muni*) is a perfectly enlightened Buddha (*sammāsambuddha*).
For thus did the Venerable Sāriputta say: "The Tathāgata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One is called a sage."
*Pū* means purification (*pavane*). Purification is cleansing (*sodhanaṃ*). It purifies; [thus it is] merit (*puñña*), a son (*putto*), or a toothpick (*dantapoṇaṃ*).

And here, "merit" (*puñña*) is so called because it purifies—that is, cleanses—the one who performs it. Alternatively, it is merit because it purifies—that is, cleanses—the continuum (*santāna*) in which it has arisen.
What is that? It is good conduct, wholesome action (*kusalakamma*). Because it possesses an object of its own activity...
The explanation of the meaning is obtained by way of the functional activity (*kāritava*) of the term. "Son" (*putta*): he purifies (*punāti*) and cleanses his own family, thus he is a son.

And this being so, one should not say that the son of those of low birth, such as Caṇḍālas and others, would not be called a "son," because the explanation of the meaning of words proceeds in various ways;
therefore, [he is a son] because he fills the heart of his own father.

The etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) should also be understood through such terms as "putta" (son). Indeed, words attain their established forms even by way of various roots (*dhātu*). A son (*putta*) is fourfold:
one born of oneself (*atrāja*), one born of the field (*khetraja*), a pupil (*antevāsika*), and one given (*dinnaka*). Among these, one born dependent upon oneself is called *atrāja*.
One produced on a bed, a couch, the breast, and so forth, is called *khetraja*. [One who is] in close proximity...
A pupil who learns a craft is called an *antevāsika*. One given for the purpose of being supported is called a *dinnaka*.
Regarding "tooth-stick" (*dantapoṇa*): it is called a tooth-stick because by means of it one cleanses or purifies the teeth (*dante punanti visodhenti*).
[The root] *pī* occurs in the senses of satisfying and delighting. That which satisfies is *pīti*. And here, *pīti* means satisfying; it is satisfying and delightful.
And thus it is said. This is the etymological derivation by way of the abstract state (*bhāva*): "it gladdens" (*piṇayati*) is *pīti*;

the meaning is "it satisfies. Furthermore, this [joy] is fivefold: minor joy (*khuddakā-pīti*), momentary joy (*khaṇikā-pīti*), ascending joy (*okkantikā-pīti*), uplifting joy (*ubbegā-pīti*), and pervading joy (*pharaṇā-pīti*).
It is as follows: therein, minor rapture (*khuddakā-pīti*) is only able to cause the hair on the body to stand on end;

momentary rapture (*khaṇikā-pīti*) occurs like the flashing of lightning at every moment; showering rapture (*okkantikā-pīti*) descends upon the body again and again and breaks up, like a wave upon the shore of the ocean;
and transporting rapture (*ubbegā-pīti*) is powerful, raising the body upward and having the capacity to leap into the air.

When the pervading rapture (*pharaṇā-pīti*) has arisen, the entire body becomes suffused—like a bladder filled [with air] after being blown, and like the interior of a mountain when it is inundated by a great flood of water. Thus there are five kinds of rapture.
Because its characteristic is gladdening (*sampiyāyana*), it is called "rapture" (*pīti*) in the sense of the simple agent (*suddha-kattar*), as it is said: "it gladdens. Herein...
“*Piyāyati*, *pitā*, *piyo*, *pemo*,” and so forth, are all forms of the verbal root *pī*. Regarding these, they say: “One who loves a son is a father (*pitā*).
That which is to be loved is “dear” (*piyo*). The act of loving is “affection” (*pemo*).

The root *mā* signifies measure. One measures; thus there is *mānaṃ* (measure), *parimāṇaṃ* (extent), *mattaṃ* (measure), *mattā* (measure), *mano* (mind), *vimānaṃ* (palace), *minitabbaṃ* (to be measured), *metabbaṃ* (to be measured), and *chāyā metabbā* (the shadow must be measured). In such instances as these, the suffix *-anīya* is not applied.
Here, "mind" (*mano*) is so called because it measures and delimits the object, as if measuring with a single *nāḷi* measure and a single balance scale.
Specifically, that which is measured and delimited is a "mansion" (*vimāna*), a celestial abode produced by the power of the merit of the gods.
This mansion is praised in such passages as: "This mansion is resplendent; it shines in the sky."
*Mī* means to injure; it injures (*mināti*). *Mīna*, *kumīna*.
Here, *mīna* means a fish. For a fish has many names, such as: "mīna, maccha, ambuja, vārija, vāricara.
But its specific names are: "amara, khalisa, candakula, kandaphali, indaphali, indavala."
“*Kulisa*, *vāmi*, *kuṅkutalo*, *kaṇḍiko*, *sakulo*, *maṅguro*, *siṅgī*, *satavaṅko*, *rohito*, *pāṭhīno*, *kāṇo*, *savaṅko*, *pāvuso*”—such are the names;
and there are also such as "*timi*, *timiṅgalo*," and so forth. As for *kumīna*:
it is called *kumīna* because by means of it they "fish" (*minanti*) or harm fish in a contemptible manner (*kucchitena ākārena*); it is a net for catching fish.
However, in the Pāḷi it is expressed by the word *kumīna*.
For instance: “Just as for a fish dwelling in the water at the mouth of a trap, So he reviles and strikes me, who cannot see my dear sons.”
The Pāli text is seen:
*mū* means "to bind. One who measures (*munāti*) is a sage (*muni*).
Here, a sage (*muni*) is so called because he measures his own mind; that is, he restrains it and does not allow it to fall under the influence of passion, hatred, and the like.
In the *gatidesanā* [section]: *ri*. *Rikāti*. *Reṇu*. There is the substitution of *ṇ* for the letter *n*.
*Lī* in the sense of clinging: *lināti*, *nilināti*. *Līnaṃ*, *sallīnaṃ*, *paṭisallānaṃ*.
*Vī* in the sense of weaving: *vatthaṃ vināti*. By this rule: "Weave the robe (*cīvaraṃ vināhi*). In the object case (*kamma*): "This, friend..."
“Robe-cloth is being woven for me; it has been woven; it has been well woven; there is little yet to be woven.
When it is caused to be made, there are such expressions as “he causes it to be woven,” “we shall have robe-cloth woven by weavers,” and “they had robe-cloth woven.
The root *vī* means to injure. *Vināti*. *Veṇu*. *Veṇū* means bamboo.
*Lū* means cutting. *Lunāti*. *Loṇaṃ*, *kusalaṃ*, *bālo*, *lūto*. And here, *loṇaṃ* (salt):
it cuts away the state of being sapless, destroys it, and makes it possess flavor; thus it is *loṇaṃ*, which is *lavaṇaṃ* (saline).
It cuts away unwholesome states from the region of the hand like a blade of grass; thus it is *kusalaṃ*, characterized by blamelessness and the highest fruit.
The Dhamma cuts away two kinds of welfare—pertaining to this present life and pertaining to future lives—from the fool who is ignorant. "Lūta" refers to a spider;
for they call its thread "lūta-sutta. It is called "lūta" because it cuts away the life of the moth, fly, and other insects that seek to drink its sap.
*Si* means to bind. *Sināti*. *Sīmā*, *sīsaṃ*.
Here, *sīmā* is so called because it is bound (*sinīyate*) by a unanimous Saṅgha through a formal act (*kammavācā*). It is twofold:
the established boundary (*baddhasīmā*) and the unestablished boundary (*abaddhasīmā*). Among these, the unestablished boundary should be understood as "boundary" by way of its function as a limit.
It is called the *sīsa* (head) because one binds or ties the hair there by way of forming a topknot (*moḷikaraṇa*). Other [derivations] should also be applied accordingly.
It is *sā* in the sense of cooking;
it cooks. *Si* is in the sense of harming; it harms. *Su* is in the sense of hearing; it hears. *Para-su*: that by which others are heard—that is, harmed—is a *parasū* (axe).
*Asa* means eating. One eats the fruit of what has been spoken;
thus it is *asana*. Here, *asana* means nutriment (*āhāra*). For that which is eaten and consumed is called "eating" (*asana*). "Eat, chew, and drink"—this is the illustration here.
*Kilisa* means to afflict. It afflicts; thus it is *kilesa*.
And here, "defilement" (kilesa) refers both to lust and the like, as well as to suffering.
Regarding "uddhasa uñche": *uñcha* means seeking; thus, it is "seeking upward.
Regarding "isa abhikkhaṇe": *isnāti* [means to seek].
*Visa* means separation. It causes one to separate; thus, *visa*.
*Pusa* [is used] in the senses of affection, flowing, and filling. It nourishes; thus, *pusa*.
*Posa* means nourishment. It nourishes; thus, *posa*.
"Take it away! He steals! A thief!"—however many such views have been seen, I have [disclosed] the elements according to my ability;
having examined others as well in the Suttas, you should accept them according to what is consistent with the meaning.
These [examples] are shown from the world for the benefit of the Dispensation; among them,
they are presented according to the world.
Those [words] have been stated accordingly.
This is the *kiyādi* group.
It belongs to the *gahādi* group.
Now the group beginning with *gaha* is stated. Here, some think as follows:
"A group (*gaṇa*) of words such as *gaha* is not found individually;
rather, there is a single verbal root *gaha*, which may constitute the group of words beginning with *gaha*."
"Since questions would arise concerning the elements (dhātu) in the teaching of the Conqueror,
and since those [elements] do not exist elsewhere except for the element of grasping (gaha-dhātu), some,
through such reflection, [conclude that] the element of grasping belongs to the Kriyādins and others."
They have thus included [the term] within the group [of words];

they did not mention "house" (*gaha*) and so forth [as separate]. A wise and discerning person should not accept their inclusion, because Kaccāyana has stated that the group beginning with "house" is distinct.
"Is it not indeed shown by the venerable Kaccāyana, while explaining the grammatical characteristics, in the Teaching [with the words]: ‘The group beginning with *gaha*’?
If a group called ‘the group of *gaha* and so forth’ cannot exist as a separate entity,"
In the *Gahādidīpaka* Sutta, having excluded this [term] from the external list, one should either state:
"From *gaha* onwards, it is called *appaṇhā*," or rather, one should establish a single grammatical characteristic by stating: "From *kiyā* onwards, it is not *appaṇhā*."
Since it has not been stated in that way, nor does it possess the same characteristic as what has been done,
therefore this is understood to be a distinct group.
It is like the rules "vowels [are elided] before vowels" and so forth, which are indeed grammatical characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*).
This characteristic is profound and difficult to be understood by one who relies on mere reasoning.
Even with reference to the root *us*, the inclusion of the prefix was made there;
for thus, forms such as "he makes warm" (*uṇhāpeti*) are seen at the beginning.
Now, having made it clear, I shall explain the group of roots beginning with *gaha*, together with their suffixes (*yoga*), which is the fruit of the word "etc. (*ādi*); listen to me.

*Gaha* means "clinging" (*upādāna*). This clinging refers to grasping, not to the clinging that is a defilement (*kilesupādāna*). In this context, the prefix *upa-* does not convey any specific meaning.
It speaks. Alternatively, the prefix *upa* has the sense of proximity, as in "approaching with body or mind, taking hold, grasping" (*upādāna*).
For in some instances, when the word *upa* is joined with the word *ādāna*, it denotes firm grasping, as in "clinging to sensual pleasures" (*kāmupādāna*) and so forth.
But here, whether it be firm grasping or loose grasping, any kind of grasping whatsoever is simply *upādāna*.
Therefore, the meaning of the verbal root *gaha* should be understood as "to grasp. It means "it is grasped" or "one grasps. [Derivatives include:
*pariggaṇhāti*, *paṭiggaṇhāti*, *adhigaṇhāti*, *paggaṇhāti*, *niggaṇhāti*. One who exerts effort (*padhānagaṇhanaka*). Infinitives: *gaṇhituṃ*, *uggaṇhituṃ*. Absolutive:
*gaṇhitvā*, *uggaṇhitvā*. There are also other forms. "I shall seize Jāli. Infinitive: *gahetuṃ*. Absolutive: *gahetvā*.

One who grasps, one who gathers, one who has plunged in. Regarding causing [to grasp]: "he causes to take," "he causes to take," "they cause them to learn a certain foundation of mindfulness," "having caused him to take it together with a thousand ministers.
One who is to be made to take formal dependence (*upajjhāya*); "having caused him to take formal dependence.
He causes to take, he causes to cause to take, he will cause to cause to take. They cause the true state to be taken. One who takes; having caused to take.
And so forth. Regarding the object (*kamma*): it is *gahati*, *saṅgahati*, or *gaṇhiyati*. For indeed, the Niddesa commentary is seen to read: “*gaṇhiyanti uggaṇhiyanti*.
Such forms as “*gehaṃ*, *gāho*, *pariggaho*, *saṅgāhako*, *saṅgahetā*” should be applied accordingly.
In that context, for words ending in long vowels, there are [forms such as] “*gheppati*, *gheppanti*; *gheppasi*,” and “*gaṇhati*, *gaṇhanti*.”
In this manner, beginning with "Gaṇhasi" (you take), the entire series of forms (*padamālā*) should be applied across all case endings (*vibhatti*) in every way.

For words ending in the vowels *ā* and *ī*, such as "gaṇhāti" (he takes) and "gaṇhāpeti" (he causes to take), the series of forms should be applied according to possibility, excluding those instances where they are prohibited.
However, these following well-known forms are the [preterite] endings for today (*ajjatanī*): "aggahī mattikāpattaṃ" (he took the clay bowl); "aggahuṃ" (we took); "aggahiṃsu" (they took).
"Aggaheṣun"ti. In "bhavissanti" and so forth, [the forms] will be "gahessati" and "gahessanti.
The remainder should be completed. [The aorist forms are] "aggahissā" and "aggahissaṃsu.
The remainder should be completed. *Usa* means burning. Burning is heat (*uṇha*). That which burns, scorches, is "heat. The word *uṇha* occurs in such expressions as "He eats hot food," and so forth.

In such cases as “it looks for grass,” it refers to the substance; however, in “it wards off cold and heat,” and so forth, it refers to the quality (*guṇa*), because the state of being hot is what is intended. For both the state of being hot and the state of being cold are qualities.
[The term *taṇhā*] occurs in the sense of thirsting. What is the meaning of *taṇhā*? It is in the sense that one thirsts, one is agitated (*paritassati*).

Regarding "in times of drinking and service": this refers to the bright season. Whether it be dark or bright, whenever the wind blows—therein, "bright" (*juṇha*) means that which gladdens the world and arouses joy and happiness;

thus it is "bright. The root *juti* means "splendor. A "bright night" (*juṇhā ratti*) is so called because, although it is itself devoid of light, it shines, gleams, and becomes radiant through the splendor of the moon and the stars; thus it is "bright."
*Sā* [means] in the sense of making thin. *Saṇhavācā*: it is made thin, it is made not harsh by way of its roughness; thus it is "smooth" (*saṇha*).

*So* [means] in the sense of bringing to an end. *Saṇhaṃ ñāṇaṃ*: it is brought to an end by itself through its subtle nature; it brings even an extremely subtle matter to its conclusion and to fulfillment; thus it is "subtle" (*saṇha*). *Tija* [means] in the sense of sharpening.
Sharpening is sharpness. A battle-axe is "sharp. It sharpens; thus it is "sharp" (*tiṇha*).
This is service (*sevā*). A craft (*sippa*) is that which should be practiced by those desiring their own welfare;
it refers to any field of craft (*sippāyatana*) that ought to be learned for the sake of livelihood. Furthermore, "craft" refers to the eighteen great crafts:

grammar (*suti*), heroic intelligence (*sūramati*), etymology (*byākaraṇa*), prosody (*chandoviciti*), philology (*nirutti*), the science of astrology (*jotisattha*), phonetics (*sikkhā*), the knowledge of liberation (*mokkhañāṇa*), ritual procedure (*kriyāvidhi*), archery (*dhanubbeda*), elephant training (*hatthisikkhā*), and the science of erotics (*kāmatanta*).
The ancient marks, history, ethics, reasoning, and medicine. *Ku* means in the sense of contempt.
Contempt is censure. Dark qualities. A dark person.
In this context, they are called "dark" (*kaṇhā*) because, by causing a state of lack of luster, they are to be despised and censured by the wise.
Unwholesome states (*akusaladhammā*). Because they are black in color, they are to be loathed and censured when compared with the golden color and so forth;
thus they are "black" (*kaṇha*), meaning black-colored. And this has also been said:
"Truly black is this man; he eats black food."
“Even in the land of Kaṇha, he is not dear to my mind”; and:
“One is not a brahmin by outward appearance; for a brahmin is one who possesses inner essence.”
"In whomsoever there are evil deeds,
he indeed is Kaṇha Sujampati.
Thus it is said.
With reference to the group of roots beginning with *gaha*, such as *tasi* and others,
the inclusion of "beginning with" (*ādi*) was made in the questions regarding *gaha* and the rest as appropriate.
Indeed, from the root *gaha*, the suffix *ppa* is seen to occur when it functions as a verb.
In the verbal class (*ākhyātatte*) and in the nominal class (*nāmatte*), the word *ṇha* is likewise [used] after the suffix *usa*.
From words other than those beginning with *usa*, two are considered to belong to the nominal class alone.
Thus should the determination of the *gaha*-group and so forth be understood in detail.
In this context, although the verbal form *taṇhāyati* is indeed found in the Dispensation (*sāsana*),
nevertheless, because it is established by means of the suffix *-āya*— which is prescribed after a noun, as in examples such as *pabbatāyati* and *mettāyati*—
it cannot be said that the suffix *-ṇha* is primarily present even when it functions as a verb. For this term *taṇhāyati* possesses the suffix *-ṇha*.
