It is derived from the word *taṇhā* (craving) formed with the suffix *tasa*, and from that, it is derived by means of the suffix *āya* for another [word]. Likewise,
although in the commentary on the training rule concerning trading in silver, at this passage— "having heated an axe-head, one heats water or milk"—
the verb "heats" (*uṇhāpeti*) appears as a verbal form expressing the causal agent, nevertheless...

Since the word "uṇhāpeti" is derived from the aforementioned word "uṇhā" by means of the suffix *ṇāpe*—which carries the designation *kārita* (causative)—and is thus produced as a verbal form (*kriyāpada*), it cannot be said that the suffix *ṇhā* is primarily applicable here.
This term "uṇhāpeti" is produced by means of the suffix *ṇāpe* from the word "uṇhā" in the manner already described; this being observed...
The word *uṇhāpayati* is indeed already seen.
Furthermore, because the causative form *uṇhāpeti* is seen in the Vinaya-ṭṭhakathā,
the agentive form *uṇhati* is also seen by logical inference, since both agentive and causative forms are found within a single verbal root.

How so? Because one grasps (*gaṇhati*), causes to grasp (*gaṇhāpeti*), goes (*gacchati*), or causes to go (*gacchāpeti*), therefore, considering that the form *uṇhati* is found for the root *usa* (to burn), the etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) should be made thus: "it is called *uṇha* because it burns (*uṇhati*).
Thus, the suffix *ppa* is obtained in one way from both *gaha* and others; however, the suffix *ṇha* is obtained in two ways—from *gaha* and from *usa*, while from others [it is obtained] in one way.

It should be understood that "it is obtained in one way. Although this rule has been stated here, nevertheless, within the word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana) consisting of the three baskets (Tipiṭaka) together with the commentaries (Sāṭṭhakatha), other two nominal and two verbal forms for each individual root should also be sought out.
Furthermore, according to the method consistent with the word of the Buddha, in the *gaha*-group and others, by means of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), roots such as *tasa* and so forth [are included].
"We have grasped it; there is no method other than this one that is more excellent; this alone is more excellent.
Therefore, for the sake of the stability of the Teaching, this method should be thoroughly retained and recited by the Venerable Ones.
Thus far have the bases (gaha) and so forth been seen; the primary elements (dhātu) have been explained by me according to my ability."
Having observed other [roots] as well in the sutta-s, you should accept them according to their semantic fitness.
This is the *gahādi* group. [The following] belongs to the *tanādi* group.
*Tanu* means extension. It extends (*tanoti*). *Āyatana* (base) is derived from *tanu*. In the sense of action, there are forms such as *taniyyati*, *taniyyanti*, and *vitaniyyati*.
Here is the canonical passage: "Just as a bull's hide is stretched out over the earth. However, the venerable teachers state that there are forms such as *patāyate* and *pataññati*.
The forms ending in the suffix *-tu* include *tanituṃ* and *tanitvāna*. These are examples of forms ending in the infinitive suffix and others.
In this context, *āyatana* means that which stretches out (*tanoti*) and expands (*vitthāreti*) the phenomena that constitute a basis (*āya*). *Tanū* refers to the body (*sarīra*).
For the body is called "body" (*tanū*) because, starting from the embryonic stage (*kalala*), it is stretched out, expanded, and brought to greatness by karma and other factors as they arise.
Words such as "tanu," "vapu," "sarīra," "puṃ," "kāya," and "deha" are synonyms for the body. *Sarīraṃ*.
The pentad of aggregates. For that which the common world calls "the body" is, in the ultimate sense, merely the pentad of aggregates;

therein neither a self nor anything belonging to a self is found. However, in such passages as "the consciousness of the once-returning path, which effects the attenuation of sensual lust and ill will," the word *tanu* signifies "little.
Yet, we do not see a verbal form for this word when it signifies "little."
Therefore, it must be a particle (*nipāta*). We do not see even a single instance where the word *tanu* is stated to be a particle;
rather, it must certainly be understood as an un-derived primary form (*anipphanna-pāṭipadika*).
*Tanoti*, *tanonti*. *Tanosi*, *tanotha*. *Tanomi*, *tanoma*. *Tanute*, *tanunte*. *Tanuse*, *tanuse*, *tanuvhe*. *Tane*, *tanumhe*. The remainder should be expanded according to the possibilities.
*Tanotu*, *tanontu*. *Taneyya*, *tane*, *taneyyuṃ*. *Vitana*, *vitanu*. *Atanā*, *atanu*. "O mother, let the hair fall away.
*Atani*, *ataniṃsu*. *Tanissati*, *tanissanti*. *Atanissā*, *atanissaṃsu*. In the passive voice (*kamma*), it should be expanded as follows: "*taniyyati*, *taniyyanti*, *taniyyasi*," and so forth.

Regarding the word *satti*: *satti* means the state of being capable (*samatthabhāva*). One who is able is *sakko*. He was able to make himself understood; he will be able; he can. "You too, mother, will be able to go forth," and "one is able to make a remedy for old age"—such are the canonical passages.

In this context, it is the King of Devas who is able. For he is called "Sakka" because he is able to accomplish the welfare of himself and others by being capable of contemplating even a thousand matters in a single moment.
However, in other instances, outside the scope of verbal roots, it is by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix.

“He gave a gift respectfully” (*sakkaccaṃ dānaṃ adāsī*): even by taking the meaning in this way, the word *sakka* is to be established according to the method of etymological analysis (*niruttinaya*).
For it was said by the Blessed One: “Mahāli, Sakka, the lord of the gods, when he was formerly a human being, gave a gift respectfully;
therefore he is called ‘Sakka’. [Examples: *sakkonto*, *sakkontī*, *sakkontaṃ kulaṃ*.
*Khuṇu* and *khiṇu* mean to injure. *Khuṇoti*; *khiṇoti*. *Iṇu* means to go. *Iṇoti*.
*Iṇaṃ* is that which is owed; thus, one who owes a debt is an *iṇāyika*.

*Tiṇu* means to eat. *Tiṇoti*. *Tiṇaṃ*. Here, *tiṇa* refers to fodder (*yavasa*). For it is called *tiṇa* because it is eaten (*tiṇiyate*) by cattle and other animals that consume grass; it is consumed (*khādiyate*), hence it is *tiṇa*.
Ghiṇu means to shine. Ghiṇoti.
The root *han* is used in the sense of removing. Removing means making one unable to speak or making one mute. Hanoti. Hanute.
The root *pan* is used in the sense of giving. Panoti. Panute.
The root *man* means "to know" (*bodhane*). [From it derive: *manoti*, *manute*, *mano*, *manaṃ*, *mānasaṃ*, *manusso*, *mānavo*, *māṇavo*.
Herein, it is called *mano* because it knows (*manoti*) or cognizes (*manute*), that is, it awakens (*bujjhati*); thus also *manaṃ*.
However, regarding these two words for *manas*, their masculine and neuter gender should be understood from such passages as: "In which the mind (*mano*) dwells; his mind (*manaṃ*) is at peace. etc.
*Mānasa* means lust, mind, or even Arahantship. In the passage, “The snare that moves through the sky, which wanders as *mānasa*,” it refers to lust.
In the passage, “Mind (*citta*), intellect (*mano*), *mānasa*,” it refers to the mind.
In the passage, “A trainee who has not attained his heart’s desire (*appattamānaso*) might pass away, though he be learned,” it refers to Arahantship. This is what is meant here.
Lust, the mind, and Arahantship are designated as “mental” (mānasa) within the Teacher’s dispensation, the evil dispensations, and all other dispensations.
In that context, lust is “mental” because it is associated with the mental faculty (manas). By taking “mind” itself to be “mental,” consciousness (citta) is also called “mental.”

Because it completely eradicates conceit (*māna*) without remainder, the highest path is "conceit" (*mānasam*); however, because it brings about that [path], the state of being "conceit" should be understood as applying to *arahantship*.
*Manu* means a sentient being (*satta*). For in the passage, “By which clarity of the eye one sees forms, O *manu*,” the word “*manu*” refers to a sentient being.
Alternatively, *manu* refers to the mother and father of humans during the time of the first eon.
There stood a man named Manu, who is called the "Mahāsammata King" in the Teaching. He is called "Manu" because he thought of and knew how to bring about the welfare of the entire world.

A human being (*manussa*) is so called because he thinks of and knows his own welfare according to his strength, or because of the abundance of *manas* (mind), or else because he is a descendant of the aforementioned Manu.
Thus, by changing the letter *na* to *ṇa*, the form "māṇavo" is established from "mānavo. However, some have said:
"The word *mānava*, when accompanied by the term 'tooth-born' (*dantajanaka*), is a term common to all beings;

but the word *māṇava*, when accompanied by the term 'head-born' (*muddhaja*), is a term for those who are contemptible and deluded. This should be examined, and if it is logical, it should be accepted.

However, one should not say here that this statement contradicts the enumeration of the meanings of the word *māṇava*, because we see that when enumerating the meanings of the word *antara*, the words *antarakā* and *antarikā* are also brought forward.
In this regard, the investigation is as follows: for in the *Cūḷakammavibhaṅgasutta*, it says, "Subha Māṇava, the son of Todeyya."
Regarding this passage, the commentators (*aṭṭhakathācariyā*) state: "It is said that he was handsome (*subha*), beautiful to behold, and pleasing;

because of the excellence of his limbs, they gave him the name 'Subha. Furthermore, they addressed him as 'Māṇava' during his youth, and even in his old age, he continued to be addressed by that same term.
Thus [they explain] the word *māṇava* used for one who has produced a son.
The meaning has been elucidated; in the *Taṭṭīkā* as well, the teachers have explained the meaning of the word *māṇava*—which denotes one who produces a head—as follows:
"In the world, the term *māṇava* refers to that offspring which is either contemptible (*kucchita*) or a head (*muddha*);
and since beings for the most part desire their heads while they are young, it is said that 'they used [the term] in the time of youth. Now, regarding the word *māṇava*:
The extraction of the meaning is as follows: the term *māṇava* refers to a being, a thief, or a youth.
For in such passages as, “Those youths (*māṇavā*) who, when exhorted by the messengers of the gods, are heedless,” a living being is called a *māṇava*.

In such passages as, “They go together with the *māṇavas*, both those who have performed their duties and those who have not,” it refers to a thief. In such passages as, “The youth Ambaṭṭha (*ambaṭṭho māṇavo*),” a young person is called a *māṇava*.
*Appa* means to reach (*pāpuṇe*). *Appo* is [the nominative]. *Āpo*:
here, *āpo* is derived from *appoti*, meaning it flows (*vissarati*) to various places; thus it is *āpo*. *Mā* is used in the sense of measure (*parimāṇe*).
*Minoti* (he measures). [Derivatives include] *upamā*, *upamānaṃ*, and *vimānaṃ*. Other [derivatives] should also be applied accordingly.
And here, that which does not measure [anything] absolutely and does not cut it off exists in proximity to *māna* (measure);
thus the simile is like "a bull-like ox" (*gavajo*). "Upamāna" is simply the simile itself; for it is said: "The peerless, the immeasurable, the protector of the protectorless.
Here, "peerless" (*vītopamāna*) means "beyond comparison" (*nirupama*). Alternatively, "upamāna" refers to the mode of being comparable.

“‘The Blessed One is like a lion’—here, the lion is the simile (*upamā*), the Blessed One is the object of the simile (*upameyya*) because he is to be compared by way of his brilliance, prowess, and so forth;

and brilliance, prowess, and so forth are the aspects to be compared. However, although there is no aspect of the Blessed One’s brilliance and so forth that can be compared to the lion’s brilliance and so forth due to the Blessed One’s preeminence, nevertheless, by way of a comparison with something inferior, it is said: ‘The Blessed One is like a lion.’”

It should be understood as "said. Regarding *vimāna*: even though it is temperature-originated (*utusamuṭṭhāna*), because it is specifically originated by temperature conditioned by karma (*kammapaccayautusamuṭṭhāna*), it is measured and delimited particularly by karma; thus it is a *vimāna*.

[The root] *kara* is used in the sense of doing. "He does" (*karoti*), "it is done" (*kayirati*), "he makes" (*kubbati*), "he performs" (*krubbati*), "he performs thoroughly" (*pakaroti*), "he assists" (*upakaroti*), "he harms" (*apakaroti*).
In such cases as "paṭikaroti," "nirākaroti," "paṭisaṅkharoti," and "abhisaṅkharoti," [the suffixes] occur in the sense of the agent (*kattari*).
In the case of the object (*kamme*), according to the method of the Pāli tradition, there is a doubling of the letter *y* in place of the augment *i*.
When there is a transposition of *r* and *y* in that very same place, there is no doubling. Likewise, in place of the augment *ī*, [we have] "kariyyati," "kayirati," and "karīyati."
“Is being made,” “is being performed,” “is being executed,” “is being conditioned,” “is being conditioned thoroughly”—these and others are [forms] in the passive (kamma).
And here, the word *kayirati* is seen in two places: in the agent (kattar) and in the object (kamma).
According to the agent, it should be construed as: “A person performs the work”; but according to the object, this scriptural passage is: “A hut is being made for me.”
“[It is] that whose basis has not been taught. In this context, the agent-word (kattupada) stated by way of the agent is established by means of the *yi* suffix.

However, the object-word (kammapada) stated by way of the object should be understood as resulting from the transposition of the *ra* and *ya* sounds of the augment *i*, which occurs at the beginning and end [of the root].

However, if it is a component of the first person plural (*mhasevacana*), then the word *akaramhase* is the third person plural ending of the aorist in the attanopada voice. Thus, it should be understood that there are five types of the letter *s*.
*Akari*, *kari*, *akāsi*, *akaruṃ*, *akariṃsu*, *akaṃsu*, *akaṃsuṃ*. *Akarō*, *akarittha*, *akāsittha*.

And here, one should connect *akaroti* with *tvaṃ akaroti*. For the word *akarō* should be regarded as having the sense of the second-person singular (*majjhimapurisa-ekavacana*), just like the word *ado* in the passage “*varaṃ ce me ado sakkā*,” even though it does not actually appear in the Pāḷi text.

Because it must be understood according to the method of grammatical derivation (*nayavasena*). However, the teachers maintain that where the word "akāro" is used, the middle-person form "akāsī" is intended;
for such a word is mostly found in the first-person form. Indeed, many scriptural passages (*pāḷi*) in the first person are seen, such as "adāsi me" (he gave to me) and "akāsi me" (he did for me).
"Do not commit evil with the mouth... [mākāsi mukhasā pāpaṃ, mā kho...]

In such passages as "sūkaramukho ahū," however, because of the connection with the particle *mā*, the construction of the sentence should be understood as: "Do not commit evil; do not become one with the face of a pig.
Akarim, kariṃ, akāsiṃ, akarimha, karimha, akāsimha. Akarā, akarū. Akaruse, akarivhaṃ. Akaraṃ, akarimhe. These are the forms stated according to the *ajjatanī* (present) tense.
*Karissati*, *karissanti*; *karissasi*, *karissatha*; *karissāmi*, *karissāma*;
*karissate*, *karissante*; *karissase*, *karissavhe*; *karissaṃ*, *kassaṃ*—thus it is also [used]. For the Pāḷi is seen thus: “*kassaṃ purisakāriyan*” (I shall do manly deeds).
[Also] *karissamhe*. Likewise: *kāhati*, *kāhanti*; *kāhasi*, *kāhatha*; *kāhāmi*, *kāhāma*; *kāhiti*, *kāhinti*.
One should apply [the forms] such as *kāhisi* and so forth according to their respective occurrences.
The forms stated by way of the future (*bhavissanti*) are: *akarissa*, *akarissa*, *akarissaṃsu*; the remainder should all be applied accordingly.

The forms stated by way of the past conditional (*kālātipatti*) are: *kayirati*, *kayiranti*; *kayirasi*, *kayirātha*; *kayirāmi*, *kayirāma*; *kayirate*. The remainder should be applied accordingly. These are the forms stated by way of the present (*vattamāna*).
Let one do, let them do. The remainder should be applied accordingly. These are the forms stated by way of the fifth (person).

*Kayirā*, *kuyirā*. *Kayiruṃ*. Here is the canonical text (*pāḷi*): “*Kumbhimhipa’ñjaliṃ kuyirā, cātañcāpi padakkhiṇan*” (“One should make an añjali toward the water-pot, and also circumambulate it”).
Therein, the analysis is: *kumbhimhipi añjaliṃ*. *Kayirāsi*, *kayirātha*. *Kayirāmi*, *kayirāma*. *Kayiretha*.
*kayireraṃ*. *Kayiretho*, *kayirāvho*. *Kayiraṃ*, *kayirāmhe*. These forms are stated according to the seventh case (the optative).
Therein, *kayirā* should be construed with the first person, as seen in the phrase “*puññañce puriso kayirā*” (“If a man should do merit”).

Also in the phrase “*adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā*” (“A charioteer might do what is unrighteous”), it should be construed with the first person as “*sārathi bhavaṃ adhammaṃ kareyyā*” (“May you, O charioteer, do what is unrighteous”).

It should be construed not according to the middle person (*majjhimapurisa*). Alternatively, it should be understood that although "kayirāsi" ought to be said, the form "kayirā" is stated as a middle-person expression by means of eliding the *sikāra* (the *s* sound).
Here, however, one might object: just as in the Pāḷi passage "puttaṃ labhetha varadaṃ," regarding this word "labhetha,"...

In passages such as “One should associate only with the virtuous; one should cultivate intimacy with the virtuous,” the commentators did not take the meaning according to the first person—as in “one should associate” (samāsetha)—but rather applied a change of person and took the meaning according to the third person as “one might obtain” (labheyya).
Likewise, in the phrase “A driver might do what is unrighteous” (adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā), [the word] “kayirā” [is explained similarly].
Having applied a masculine reversal (*purisavipallāsa*) to the word *pada*, the meaning should be stated in the second person as "you should do" (*kareyyāsi*);
for the commentators of the Aṭṭhakathā have also stated that its meaning is "you should do. True;

nevertheless, because the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā possess supreme skill regarding conventional meanings, the word *bhavam* occurs in the sense where "you" (*tvam*) should be said, as in "O Sir" (*bhavam*).

Considering that the suffix *tvaṃ* occurs when there is a meaning to be expressed [in the optative], the sense “you should do” was stated according to the intended meaning (*adhippāyattha*), and not by way of a grammatical substitution of gender (*purisavipallāsa*).

For instance, in the commentary on the phrase “May you obtain a son, O Giver of Boons,” having cited the form “labhetha,” the explanation is made as “labheyya” by way of a substitution of gender. [Likewise regarding] “unrighteousness” (*adhammaṃ*)...
Regarding the phrase "sārathi kayirā," the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) on this passage cites "kayirā" and provides the explanation "kareyyāsi" (you should do).
Therefore, in the expression "adhammaṃ sārathi kayirā," one should not consider it a grammatical substitution for the masculine gender (*purisavipallāsa*).
Alternatively, just as in the case of "puttaṃ labhetha varadaṃ" and in expressions such as "kāye rajo na limpetha," the second-person singular form is used [in place of the third person].
It has been grasped; thus, instead of taking the expression as "aggahetvā," one should make the word-division "labhe athā.

For if this is the case, there is no need for a grammatical substitution (vipallāsa) of the masculine gender. In that context, "labhe" is the third person singular (uttamapurisa) of the seventh case, like the phrase "vajjhañcāpi pamocaye.
The word "atha" is a particle used to mark a change of subject or for the purpose of completing the meter. And here, by way of marking a change of subject—

The meaning is: "May I obtain another excellent son. However, since the arising of two meanings is seen here, and because the Blessed One’s intention regarding these two is difficult to discern, both meanings must indeed be accepted.
In this context, although there may be a reversal of gender, a reversal of case, a reversal of number, or a reversal of tense—[these are to be understood as occurring].
The sixfold perversion—namely, perversion of persons and perversion of syllables—should be presented by bringing it forth;
nevertheless, it has not been shown here because it will become clear later. In that context, the word *kayirātha* is divided twofold:

by way of the seventh case (locative) and the *parassapada* (active) voice, and by way of the *attanopada* (middle) voice; likewise, it is divided by way of the third person plural and the first person singular.

For instance, in the passage, “Just as one should perform meritorious deeds, giving again and again,” the word “kayirātha” is stated in the seventh case, in the *parassapada* (active) voice, and in the plural number of the second person. For the meaning is:
“one should indeed perform meritorious deeds according to what is appropriate. However, in the passage, “The wise person should perform meritorious deeds,” [the word] “kayirātha”...
This is stated according to the seventh case (*attano-pada*) and the first person singular ending;

for the meaning is "he would do. Here, forms accompanied by the *yira* suffix (the optative) and so forth, based on the remote past tense (*parokkhā*) and others, are generally not shown because they are little known in the Teaching (*sāsana*).
It is called a "cause" (*kāraṇa*) because it produces its own fruit. One who "does" is an "agent" (*kattā*); thus, one is an "agent" (*kāraka*) or that which is done by an agent. For in this context:
The word *kāraka* is masculine where it denotes agentive factors such as the agent (*kattukāraka*) or the object (*kammakāraka*), but it is generally neuter.
However, where it denotes specific artisans such as a silver-worker (*rajatakāraka*), a smith (*kammakāra*), or an iron-worker (*lohakāra*), it is exclusively masculine.
One who causes to do is a *kārāpaka*. [Synonyms include: *karaṃ*, *kubbaṃ*, *krubbaṃ*, *karonto*, *kubbanto*, *kubbāno*, *kurumāno*.

Being made (*pakruṃbbamāno*). A maker (*kārikā*), one who causes to be made (*kārāpikā*). One who does (*karontī*), one who performs (*kubbantī*). A family that acts as a maker (*kārakaṃ kulaṃ*). One who causes to be made (*kārāpakaṃ*), one who is doing (*karontaṃ*), one who is performing (*kubbantaṃ*), one who is making (*kurumānaṃ*).
Volitional formation (*saṅkhāro*), requisites (*parikkhāro*), prepared (*parikkhato*), honored (*purakkhato*), the act of making (*karaṇaṃ*), action (*kriyā*).
Furthermore, grammarians accept the word "action" (*kriyā*) as a term [for volition]. Here, although the word "action" (*kriyā*) is indeed [used], it is "fruitless" (*aphalā*).
In such passages as “hoti akubbato,” words containing the conjuncts *ka* and *ra* are seen;
nevertheless, although the word *klesa* does not appear in the Pāli text itself, it must nonetheless be accepted because it was adopted by the venerable masters of the Aṭṭhakathās and others.
For indeed, such linguistic formulations as “the teacher who explains the distinctions between action, non-action, and transgression” are found.

*Kātuṃ*, *kattuṃ*. *Kātave*, *kāretuṃ*. *Katvā*, *katvāna*, *kātuna*, *karitvā*, *karitvāna*, *kacca*, *adhikacca*, *kariya*, *kariyāna*, *purakkhitvā*, *kāretvā*. Other forms ending in *-tuṃ* and so forth should also be applied accordingly. In this context, *kacca* means "having done. *Adhikacca* means "having done excessively.
However, based on the principles of the science of grammar (*saddasattha*), etymologists (*akkharacintaka*) prefer the form *adhikicca*;
we, however, do not consider such a form to be in accordance with the Canon (*pāḷi*).
We do not accept that this is so. For instance, in the *Therīgāthā*, in the statement regarding Gotamī’s final nibbāna, the Pāli text reads:
“*Padakkhiṇaṃ kacca nipacca pāde*. Here, the meaning is “having performed a circumambulation (*padakkhiṇaṃ katvā*”).
By the appearance of the word *kacca*, the word *adhikacca* is also clearly seen; this same principle should be understood accordingly in other instances as well.

Now we shall explain a slight application of the preeminence of meaning for the root *karoti* (to do): *taṇhaṅkaro* (the maker of craving). This is the reason. "When one is provoked by harsh words, he does not act with hostility toward those who are good"—this is the context.
In this regard, *taṇhaṅkaro* means that he makes (*karoti*) or destroys (*hiṃsati*) the craving and greed of those to be trained; thus he is *taṇhaṅkaro*.
Alternatively, it means that through the perfection of his physical body and his Dhamma-body, he creates (*karoti*) or generates (*janeti*) craving and affection for himself in the entire world.
*Tanhaṅkaro*: "Causing harm" (*kāraṇā*) means injuring. *Pakrubbamāno*: injuring. *Sante na kurute piyaṃ*:

the meaning is that he does not treat as dear, desirable, beloved, or agreeable those who are virtuous (*sappurisa*), even though they are dear to himself. Alternatively, the meaning is that while being fond of, pleased with, satisfied with, and delighted by what is dear, he does not practice or serve those who are virtuous.
This is just as in the expression, "He serves the king," which carries this same sense.

Those learned in the science of grammar explain that [the word *parikkhāra*] means "to make dear to the king"; however, this technical rule (*nīti*) is difficult to grasp and should be carefully attended to.

Herein, the derivation of the meaning of the word *parikkhāra* is being set forth: in such passages as, "It is well-fortified by the seven fortifications of a city," it refers to a "retinue" or "surrounding.
In such passages as, "The chariot with its white equipment (*setaparikkhāra*), with meditation as its axle and energy as its wheels," [it refers to the parts of a chariot].
“Requisite” (*parikkhāra*) is used in such passages as, “And these requisites for the life of one gone forth that must be procured,” where it means equipment.
Regarding this, it is said by those wise ones who know the Teaching:
In the Teaching, the word *parikkhāra* is spoken of as: An entourage, an ornament, and an equipment.
Regarding "at the end of sleep through wakefulness": "wakefulness" (*jāgara*) means wakefulness (*jāgaraṃ*). For one who is awake, the night is long.

Having seen these [elements] beginning with earth for so long, and having observed others as well while asleep, take them up according to their meaning and application, in accordance with my own strength.
This is the *tanādigaṇa*.
The six classes beginning with *rudh* possess the essence of various meanings;
they bring wisdom to those who understand them and are a delight to the wise.
Like a pure place frequented by golden swans,
it is well-served by those of noble aspiration.
Thus, regarding the various modes of expression within the Three Piṭakas together with their commentaries— the ninefold division— this is for the wise.
In the treatise *Saddanīti*, composed for the sake of proficiency,
the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Hexad Beginning with *Rudh*," is concluded.
18. Exposition of the Curādigaṇa Henceforth I shall explain the name of the eighth class,
the Curādigaṇa, which brings about manifold meanings and benefits.
Theft (*theyya*). Theft, stealing, or robbery—this is what is meant. In this sense of theft, the verbal root *cur* is employed.
[Derivatives include: *coreti*, *corayati*, *coro*, *corī*, *corikā*, *coretu*, *corayituṃ*, *coretvā*, *corayitvā*.
The characteristic of the *cur-ādi* group is that the suffixes *-ṇa*, *-ṇaya*, and *-tā* are used in the sense of the agent. In the causative: *corāpeti*, *corāpayati*, *corāpetuṃ*, *corāpayituṃ*.

Having stolen (*corāpetvā*), having caused to steal (*corāpayitvā*). Wealth is stolen by thieves (*corehi coriyati*); wealth that has been stolen (*coritaṃ dhanaṃ*). This same method applies everywhere.

The verbal root ending in *k* (*kakārantadhātu*) is used in the sense of seeing (*dassane*). [One] looks (*loketi*), looks about (*lokayati*), looks down (*oloketi*), looks around (*olokayati*), looks up (*ulloketi*), looks up at (*ullokayati*), looks away (*apaloketi*).

He looks at, he looks toward, he looks upon, he looks around, he looks about. World, light, looking, gazing, looking up, looking toward, looking around, looking away, looking down. To look at, to cause to look; having looked at, having caused to look.
In the causative, however: "he causes to look," "he causes to look upon," "to cause to look," "to cause to look upon," "having caused to look."
“Having observed,” and so forth—these [phrases] are to be applied accordingly.

This method applies everywhere. In this context, “world” (*loka*) refers to three worlds: the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*), the world of beings (*sattaloka*), and the world of space (*okāsaloka*). Therein, in passages such as “One world:
all beings subsist on nutriment,” the world of formations is to be understood. Or, in the case of “The world is eternal” or “The world is not eternal”...
In the passage where it says "the world," it refers to the world of sentient beings.
"As far as the moon and sun revolve,
illuminating the quarters with their radiance..."
"In as many as a thousandfold world-systems,
here your power prevails"— in such passages,
it refers to the world as space.
Alternatively, "the world" (*loka*) is threefold: the world of defilements (*kilesaloka*), the world of existence (*bhavaloka*), and the world of faculties (*indriyaloka*).

Among these, beings of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) constitute the world of defilements due to their abundance of defilements such as lust. Beings of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) constitute the world of existence due to the development of meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).

Beings of the immaterial sphere (*arūpāvacara*) constitute the world of faculties due to their preponderance of imperturbable concentration (*āneñjasamādhi*) and the clarity of their faculties. Alternatively, "defilement" (*kilesa*) means that which defiles; it is the suffering of result (*vipākadukkha*).
This is the meaning. Therefore, because of the abundance of suffering, beings in the states of deprivation are the world of defilements (*kilesaloka*).

Other beings, because they possess the existence of success (*sampattibhava*), are the world of existence (*bhavaloka*). Among them, those beings who are endowed with faculties that ripen for liberation should be understood as the world of faculties (*indriyaloka*).
However, in the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*—

“The world is manifold: the world of formations (*saṅkhāraloka*), the world of beings (*sattaloka*), the world of space (*okāsaloka*), the world of aggregates (*khandhaloka*), the world of bases (*āyatanaloka*), and the world of elements (*dhātuloka*).

Herein, when it is said, ‘One world: all beings subsist by nutriment… [and so on] … eighteen worlds: the eighteen elements,’ it is the world of formations that is spoken of. The worlds of aggregates and the rest are included within that very same category. ‘This world, the other world…’”
"In such passages as 'the Brahma-world together with its devas,' the world of beings (sattaloka) is spoken of.

In the passage: 'As far as the moon and sun revolve, shining and illuminating the quarters, so far extends the thousandfold world-system; herein there are three hundred and sixty-four worlds,' the world of space (okāsaloka) is spoken of.

As for the meaning: the world of beings is the collection and the continuum of the aggregates bound to the faculties (indriya), because of their being attached to and fettered by form and the other sense objects.
It is called "the world" (*loka*) because beings (*satta*) and wholesome and unwholesome deeds along with their results are found therein.

The collection and the continuity of material phenomena not bound by faculties constitute the "world as space" (*okāsa-loka*), because moving and stationary beings are found therein, and it serves as the space for them;

furthermore, because it is the support for those beings, it is also called the "receptacle world" (*bhājana-loka*). Both of these types [of worlds] are conceptual designations based on derived matter (*upādā-paññatti*), since they are designated in dependence upon such phenomena as material form.

Furthermore, since the ultimate nature of conditioned phenomena—both material and mental—is designated by depending upon their respective substrata (*upādāna*), it should be understood figuratively that both types of phenomena exist in dependence on conditions (*paccayāyattavutti*) by way of those substrata.
In this context, the aggregates within both [classes of phenomena] constitute the "world of formations" (*saṅkhāraloka*);

they are called "formations" because they are conditioned by causes, and they are called "the world" because they disintegrate and fall apart. This is due to their existence in dependence on conditions.

Although the states of the paths and fruits (maggaphaladhammā) are subject to disintegration and dissolution, they do not incur the status of being "the world" (loka), because by "world" only the phenomena belonging to the three planes (tebhūmakadhammā) are intended. For that reason, they are called "supramundane" (lokuttara).
"Light" (āloka) means a ray; it is called light because by means of it people see intensely, or because it is the eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa). "Beholding" (olokana) means...
*Heṭṭhā-pekkhanaṃ* (looking downward). *Vilokanaṃ* (looking around) is looking upward. *Ālokanaṃ* (looking ahead) is looking forward.
*Vilokanaṃ* (looking about) is looking toward both sides, or looking in various ways. *Apalokanaṃ* (informing) is making known, as in expressions such as "having informed the Saṅgha.
*Avalokanaṃ* (looking back) is turning the front part of the body, as in expressions such as "having looked back with the gaze of an elephant."

Regarding "looking" (*pekkhana*): in the passage, "He acts with clear comprehension when looking forward and looking around," the meaning should be understood here also in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*); that is, looking forward is "the act of looking forward" (*ālokita*), and looking around is "the act of looking around" (*vilokita*).
Regarding *thaka* in the sense of warding off: a man wards off, or causes to be warded off, a door.
*Takka* means *vitakka*. It is called *takka*, it is called *vitakka*, it is the act of *vitakkana*.
*Takka*, *vitakka*, and *vitakkita*—therein, *takka* is the act of *takkana*; what is meant is "investigation" (*ūhana*); thus it is *vitakka*.
Alternatively, it is *vitakka* because one investigates by means of it, or it itself investigates, or it is merely the act of investigating. *Takka, vitakka, appanā.*
“Application, the directing of the mind”—these are synonyms stated in the Abhidhamma.
One who thinks is a “thinker,” which refers to a person. The Pāli passage reads: “Without thinking, they go forth unto death.
The root *aki* signifies a characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*). A characteristic is a sign; what is meant is the cause of perceiving. Herein, this should be observed.
Those roots in this curādigaṇa that are indicated as having multiple vowels, ending in a non-conjunct consonant, and having the letter *i* as an affix (*anubandha*),—
when they possess these three aforementioned characteristics, they attain the status of both verbs (*ākhyātatva*) and nouns (*nāmikatva*),
and exclusively take forms produced by the insertion of the nasal (*niggahīta-āgama*); nowhere do they take forms in which the nasal insertion has been lost.
[The roots] *bhavanti*. *Aṅketi*, *aṅkayati*. *Aṅkanaṃ*, *aṅko*. In compounds, however, forms such as *sasaṅko* and *cakkaṅkitacaraṇo* occur.
*Sakka* and *vakka* [mean] speaking: *sakketi*, *sakkayati*; *vakketi*, *vakkayati*.
*Nakka* and *vakka* [mean] driving away: *nakketi*, *nakkayati*; *vakketi*, *vakkayati*.

*Cakka* and *cukka* mean to cause pain. One *cakketi*, *cakkayati*; one *cukketi*, *cukkayati*. A *cakka*. In what sense is it called a *cakka*? It is a *cakka* in the sense that it "causes pain" (*cakketi*), meaning it afflicts or harms.
The word *cakka* appears in the following senses: prosperity, a characteristic mark, a part of a chariot, a mode of deportment, giving, a jewel, the Wheel of Dhamma, a hoof, and so forth.
“In these passages—‘Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels, possessed of which gods and humans... and so forth—it is seen in the sense of excellence (*sampatti*).
In ‘Wheels have appeared on the soles of the feet,’ it is in the sense of a mark (*lakkhaṇa*). In ‘Like the wheel of one who drives [a chariot],’ it is in the sense of a chariot part (*rathaṅga*).
In ‘The four-wheeled, nine-gated [body],’ it is in the sense of a mode of deportment (*iriyāpatha*). ‘Give! Enjoy!’...”

In the passage, "And do not be negligent; set the wheel in motion for living beings," it refers to giving. In the passage, "The divine wheel-treasure appeared," it refers to the treasure-wheel (*ratnacakra*).
In the passage, "The wheel set in motion by me," it refers to the Dharma-wheel (*dharmacakra*).

In the passage, "The wheel revolves upon the head of the man overcome by desire," it refers to the razor-wheel (*khuracakra*). And in the passage, "Even with a wheel whose edge is as sharp as a razor," it refers to...
In the wheel of weapons (*paharaṇacakkam*). Regarding "the thunderbolt-wheel" (*asanivicakkam*), here it means the circle of the thunderbolt (*asanimaṇḍalam*).
The root *taki* means to bind; it binds, thus it is *taṅka*.
The root *akka* means to praise; praise is *thuti*. It praises, thus it is *akka*. *Akka* is the sun (*sūriya*); for he, by virtue of his great radiance...
It is called *akko* because it is praised (*akkiyati*) and extolled (*abhitthaviyati*) by people who have faith in it.
For indeed, its praise is seen in such passages as: “There is no radiance equal to the sun; this One-Eyed King rises,” and so forth.
The root *hikk-* means to injure (*hiṃsā*). Thus: *hikketi*, *hikkayati*.
*Nikka* in the sense of measure. *Nikketi*, *nikkayati*.
*Bukka* in the sense of barking. Here, "barking" should be understood as the barking of a dog, not speech in the sense of verbal expression. *Bukketi*, *bukkayati*.
And here, the worldly usage “*bukkayati sā core*” (she barks at the thieves) is to be understood. [These belong to] the *bhūvādi* group.
However, the form *bukkati sā* occurs. But another reads *bukka* as "in reviling"; even when reading it thus, what is intended is still the barking of a dog.
*Daka* and *laka* mean "to taste. Thus: *daketi*, *dakayati*; *laketi*, *lakayati*.
*Takka* is in the worldly language (*lokabhāsā*). *Takketi* means "he reasons" (*takkyati*). *Loketi* means "he observes" (*lokyati*).
*Cik* and *sik* are [roots] for touching (*āmasana*). *Ciketi* means "he touches" (*cikayati*). *Siketi* means "he touches" (*sikayati*).
These are the forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *k*.

The verbal root ending in *kh* (*khakārantadhātu*) [is used] in the senses of seeing and marking. Seeing is looking. Marking is branding. Regarding "mark" (*lakkha*): one marks, one sees. One observes closely, one examines closely. One pierces the mark with an arrow; one makes a mark.
The sands of the Ganges might be exhausted, the water in the great ocean might be exhausted; [but the Buddha’s qualities cannot be measured].
The clay on the earth would be exhausted, but my intellect would not reach even a hundred thousand *lakh*.

[This refers to] the characteristic of an eon (*kappa-lakkhaṇa*), the characteristic of a cow (*go-lakkhaṇa*), the characteristic of a woman (*itthi-lakkhaṇa*), and the characteristic of phenomena (*dhammānaṃ lakkhaṇa*). There is primary observation (*sallakkhaṇā*), secondary observation (*upalakkhaṇā*), and close observation (*paccupalakkhaṇā*). In the root *lakkha* with the suffix *yu*, the letter *n* is dental after the preceding forms beginning with *sam-*.

In the sense of eating, there is the root *bhakkha*. One eats (*bhakkheti*, *bhakkhayati*). "Food (*bhakkha*) has been obtained by us. "Beasts of prey eat (*bhakkhayanti*). However, in the *bhūvādi* class, the form is "he eats" (*bhakkhati*).
*Nakkha* means to smear (*sambandhe*). One smears (*nakkheti*), one smears away (*nakkhayati*). *Makkha* means to smear (*makkhane*).
One smears (*makkheti*), one smears away (*makkhayati*). *Makkha*, *makkhī*. In this context, *makkha* refers to that which smears and grinds away virtues performed by others;
it is the destruction of virtues. Furthermore, in the phrase "unable to endure *makkha*," it refers to [the inability to endure] [praise] from others directed toward oneself.
Contemptuous speech is called *makkha*. Regarding the term *yakkha*:
it is that which worships (*yakkhati*) or causes one to worship. A *yakkha* is a being of great power (*mahānubhāva*).
For instance, in the passage, "I ask you, O Great Yakkha, Lord of all beings," Sakka, the King of the Devas, is referred to as a "yakkha."
[The word] is spoken. Alternatively, a *yakkha* is a being reborn in the *yakkha*-womb; or rather, all beings whatsoever are called "yakkhas.
For in the phrase "proclaiming the supreme purification of the *yakkha*," the word *yakkha* refers to sentient beings (*satta*).
Thus, a *yakkha*, a sentient being, a deity, a *sakka*, and even one whose taints are destroyed—all these are indeed called a "yakkha" because of their great majesty.
A *yakkha* is so called because it is worshipped with various offerings and various sacrifices by people who have gone for refuge.
The word *yakkha* applies to these five meanings: sentient beings, gods, Sakka, those whose taints are destroyed, and *rakkhasas*.
*Lakkha* [is used] in the sense of observing. *Lakkheti*, *lakkhayati*. One pierces the target (*lakkha*) with an arrow.
*Mokkha* [is used] in the sense of sitting. *Mokkheti*, *mokkhayati*.
*Rukkha* [is used] in the sense of harshness. Harshness is the state of being harsh. *Rukkheti*, *rukkhayati*. In a compound, [it becomes] "rukkhakeso" (one with tree-like hair).
"Excessively harsh speech" refers to forms [of nouns]. Here, the canonical passage "This ascetic is wicked and excessively harsh in speech" serves as an illustration.
In that context, "atirukkhavāco" means "one whose speech is exceedingly harsh.
These are forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *kha*.

The verbal root *gakāra* (the root *ga*) belongs to the class [beginning with] *liṅga*, in the sense of "making an object of thought" (*cittīkaraṇe*). "Making an object of thought" means making something manifold in nature. Regarding *liṅga*: it is that which is marked (*liṅgayati*), thus it is a mark (*liṅga*).
Here, a "mark" (*liṅga*) refers to shape (*saṇṭhāna*), distinguished as long, short, thin, thick, circular, and so forth; it is exceedingly useful for the purpose of grasping [an object].

It is appropriate [to explain it thus]. For that is diverse in many ways. It is called *liṅga* because it is marked (*liṅgiyati*), variegated (*vicittaṃ kariyati*), or because it is the body (*sarīra*) by means of ignorance, craving, and karma, or by means of the season, or by means of powders and so forth.
This should be understood by way of the shapes occurring in internal continuums, in grasses, trees, and so on, as well as in bracelets, baskets, and the like.
The word *liṅga* [also applies] to sound, to the cause for the occurrence of sound, and to the female sex organ.
The term *liṅga* is seen in these senses: as a sign (*saññāṇa*), as a characteristic mark (*ākāra*), and as a male characteristic (*purisabyañjana*).

Indeed, in the passage “the word ‘tree’ is the *liṅga*,” it is used in the sense of sound (*sadda*). In the phrase “of a meaning possessing a hundred *liṅgas*,” it refers to the cause for the occurrence of sound (*saddappavattinimitta*).
In the passage “at that time, a certain bhikkhu’s female characteristic (*itthiliṅga*) became manifest,” it refers to the male characteristic (*itthibyañjana*).
In the phrase “the male gender, the sign, the gesture, and the deportment,” it refers to the male sex organ (*purisabyañjana*).

In the phrase “by that sign we know for certain that he will surely become a Buddha,” it refers to a mark of recognition (*saññāṇa*). In the phrase “by those signs, those marks, and those modes, the state of being a guest is to be known as ‘these are guests,’” it is seen as a mode (*ākāra*).
The word *liṅga* occurs in the sense of sound, its cause, a trap, a characteristic mark, and a formal appearance. The root *mag* means to search.
From it come the forms *mageti*, *magayati*, *migo*, *mago*, *maggo*, and *magayamāno*.
And here, the Pāḷi passage “just as a cat seeking a mouse” is the illustration. Both “migā” and “magā” refer to four-footed animals.
Here, a *miga* is so called because he “seeks” (*magayati*)—that is, he searches for and pursues his range of food here and there;
thus it is a *miga*. Specifically, the deer (*hariṇa*) is what is called a *miga*; but in a general sense, all other four-footed animals are included as well.
“They are called ‘deer’ (miga). For instance, in the Susīma Jātaka, in this passage from the Pāḷi:
‘These black deer with white teeth, more than a thousand of them, covered with nets of gold,’ even elephants are spoken of by the word ‘deer’ as ‘black deer.

Alternatively, they are called ‘deer’ because they are sought after (magiyati)—that is, they are pursued and hunted—by hunters who require their meat and other parts for the sake of sustaining their lives.”
*Mago* refers to four-footed animals born in the forest, such as hares, deer, antelopes, and *eṇeyya* deer; thus it means "wild beast.
However, in the phrase "the wild beast finds no goal" (*atthaṃ na labhate mago*), it means "like a wild beast," that is, a fool.
[The root] *magga* is in the sense of seeking. One seeks (*maggeti*, *maggayati*). [The nouns are] *maggo* (a path) and *magganā* (seeking).
And here, "path" (*magga*) is a designation for the way of practice (*paṭipadā*), the natural path (*pakatimagga*), and the means (*upāya*).
However, in such passages as “The recitation-path of the Mahāvihāravāsins,” even a continuous discourse is called a “path.
Among these, the way of practice is exclusively for the purpose of leading beings—afflicted by the sufferings of birth, aging, sickness, and so forth—to Nibbāna, the destruction of suffering.
That which is to be sought and searched for is the *magga*. Furthermore, a conventional path (*pakatimagga*) is called *magga* because it must be sought by those who have lost their way.

And among those who have lost their way on a conventional path, there are many who have actually lost their way on the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), which is designated as the "way of practice" (*paṭipadā*).
For a conventional path is lost only occasionally to travelers, and guides who can say, "This is the path," are not difficult to find. But as for the Noble Path—
At all times, for the entire world, he is forgotten; leaders are extremely difficult to find. Therefore, he alone must be sought by those deluded by ignorance;
thus, he is the "path" (*magga*). Furthermore, the teachers explain the meaning by way of two other elements:
"It is the path because it goes while slaying the defilements. It is called the path because it is sought and investigated by those desiring to accomplish various tasks or benefits.
“Way” (*magga*) means “means” (*upāya*). For the word “way” is used even in the sense of a means, as in the passage: “He set forth the discourse on the Abhidhamma way for the gods.

Thus it is said in the *Abhidhammaṭīkā*: “‘Way’ means ‘means,’ because it is the means for the realization of the aggregates, bases, and so forth, as well as for the penetration of the truths, [it is called] the ‘discourse on the Abhidhamma way.’”

Or rather, a continuous composition (*pabandha*) is called a "path" (*magga*). For it is like a path because of its length; thus, a continuous discourse on the Abhidhamma is called an "Abhidhamma-discourse-path.
Now we shall state the names for the paths of natural progression (*pakatipaṭipadā*). Among them, for the path of nature:
"Path, road, way, track, highway, route, journey, and course;"
“Addhāna, addhā, padavī, vattaṇī, and santati”—these are its names.
Furthermore, for the path of practice (paṭipadā-magga):
“Magga, pantha, patha, pajja, añjasam, vaṭumā, and ayana.”
"A boat, a bridge, a raft, a mat, and a causeway"—these are its many names.
Now, some say that "boat" and so forth are names for the natural path;
that should not be accepted, because there is no instance in any part of the Canon where the natural path is expressed by such terms as "boat."

Furthermore, in the treatises on terminology (*abhidhānasattha*), because designations such as "boat" (*nāvā*) and so forth have not yet been introduced [in this context], the following is the etymological explanation (*vacanattha*) here:
it is called a "boat" (*nāvā*) because one goes by means of it; it is called "crossing" (*uttaraṃ*) because people cross by means of it.
Indeed, these are synonyms for "boat": *taraṃ*, *taraṇaṃ*, *poto*, and *plavo*. These too are merely its synonyms. *Uttaraṃ*.

It is called a *viyāti* because it goes across (*viyāti*). It is called a *setu* because it is a bridge (*setu*). It is called a *kullo* because it is a raft (*kullo*). It is called a *bhisi* because it is a mat (*bhisi*).

It is called a *saṅkamo* because it is like a causeway, or because they cross over by means of it; all these are names for the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) alone, not for an ordinary path. For thus it is said:
"Having boarded the boat of Dhamma, I shall ferry across the world with its devas," and "The firm bridge of Dhamma..."

Having done this, that Bull among Men has attained Nibbāna; and as it is said elsewhere, “Monks, ‘raft’ is a designation for the Noble Path,” the Blessed One has described the Noble Path by many names such as “boat” and so forth in various places.
Furthermore, the teachers of the commentaries, in the *Sutta Nipāta Aṭṭhakathā*, [cite]: “The well-constructed cushion was bound, O Blessed One.”
In this passage, the commentary on the meaning is as follows: “*Bhisī*—that which is bound by spreading it out and making it wide is called a ‘raft’ (*kulla*) in the world;
however, in the discipline of the Noble One, it is the ‘Noble Path.
[Synonyms for path are: *maggo*, *pajjo*, *patho*, *pantho*, *añjasam*, *vaṭumā*, *ayanaṃ*;”
"A boat, a bridge, a raft, a float, a ford;
a journey, and likewise a source—these are explained in their respective places.

Because this commentary on the meaning was composed by the teachers, one should not accept the statement that "boat" and so forth are names for the natural path; rather, only the previously stated statement should be accepted.

However, someone here might say: "Regarding the phrase 'having made firm the bridge of Dhamma' (*dhammasetaṃ daḷhaṃ katvā*), since it is stated that 'the bridge of Dhamma' means 'the bridge of the Path,' the word *dhamma* refers to the Path, but the word *setu* does not. That is not so; for just as the word *dhamma*, the word *setu* also refers to the Path.
Thus, by way of meaning, it is a "bridge" (*setu*) because it is like a bridge; it is a "Dhamma-bridge" (*dhammasetu*) because it is the Dhamma itself that is the bridge. This is the method.
It is otherwise as well. One might further say:

"In the *Brahmajāla-sutta-aṭṭhakathā*, at the point where it says, 'Having entered the seat of enlightenment from the south-east and circumambulated the king of trees, the Assattha, he stood on the north-eastern side,' does not the word 'south-east' (dakkhiṇuttara) here refer to the southern path? No; for in many passages of the Canon...

Since the word *uttara* (northern) is not used as a designation for the path in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) or in the treatises on terminology (*abhidhānasattha*), the meaning there should be understood in this way:
"The northern portion that is to be traversed from the southern direction is called 'south-north' (*dakkhiṇuttara*);
it is with such a south-north [direction] that he entered the seat of enlightenment. Thus, [it is said] "with the south-north."
It is said, "having entered the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Alternatively, "south-east" means south-west-north;
here, by the inclusion of the beginning and the end, the inclusion of the middle should also be understood.
For this very inclusion is what is stated in the *Jātaka-nidāna*: "The Bodhisatta, having taken grass and ascended the seat of enlightenment, [stood] in the southern direction..."

He stood facing north; at that moment, the southern world-system seemed to sink down as if reaching the Avīci hell below, while the northern world-system seemed to rise up as if reaching the peak of existence above.
Thinking, "This is not the place where the Bodhisatta will attain perfect enlightenment," he turned clockwise toward the western direction.
“Having gone, he stood facing the east,” and so forth; it is consistent with that. Furthermore, one might say:
“If the word *uttara* denotes a direction, then since this is the case, instead of using the *ena*-suffix in ‘dakkhiṇuttarena,’ one ought to use the *āya*-suffix as in ‘dakkhiṇuttarāya.
That is not so; for even a word denoting a direction can take the *ena*-suffix, as in: “To the north of the river Sītā, [the land] is deep and difficult to cross.”
This is because it is spoken by way of this conjunction. Furthermore, the expression "to the south and north" was stated with reference to a portion of a direction;
for it should be understood here that a portion of a direction is indeed a direction.
These are the forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *g*.

The verbal root *ghakārantadhātu* [ending in *gha*] is *lighi*, meaning "to leap. Examples are *laṅgheti* and *laṅghayati*. Although these are not well-established in the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*), they are included here by way of showing their usage in the worldly language.
For in the Teaching, there exists a root belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa* and *curādigaṇa* classes, which expresses the sense of moving and indicates the meaning of leaping.
The form *dhātu* is extremely well-established [in the sense of "element"].
[The root] *laṅgh* means "to leap. [From it come] *laṅgheti* and *laṅghayati*.
"O Teacher Atikaramakara, even this does not please me."
Regarding the phrase "In the fourth [case], having leaped over; in the fifth case also,
he is obstructed," in this *Sattilaṅghanajātaka*, when the forms "laṅghayitvā" and "laṅghayitvāna" are seen from the root *laṅgh*— which belongs to the *cur-ādi* group, expresses the sense of going,
and indicates the meaning of leaping— one should understand that there are also the forms "laṅgheti" and "laṅghayati."
The forms [of the verb] are indeed already seen. However, such forms have not been seen by the author of the *Bhāsatthavācaka*;

nevertheless, because they were accepted by the ancient teachers (*pubbācariya*) who possessed long-range vision, it should be understood that the root *laṅgh* exists as a verbal form expressing the sense of "speaking" (*bhāsa*).
In this same way, even among all the groups beginning with *bhū*, there are forms that are not well-established in the tradition (*sāsana*).
One should understand the inclusion of those things that are conducive to the Teaching (sāsana) and the rejection of those things that are not conducive and are unestablished.
*Agha* means to do evil. It is derived from *aghayati*. Thus: *agha*, *agho*, *anagho*.
In this context, *agha* means suffering (*dukkha*). “I shall resort to the edge of the forest, which is crowded with wild beasts and frequented by rhinoceroses and leopards.”
This is the illustration. *Agha* means defilement (*kilesa*). One who is free from that *agha* is an *anagha* (one without evil).

In this context, *agha* is so called because by means of it beings "go toward" (*aghayanti*) evil—that is, they commit sin. What is that? Suffering (*dukkha*); thus it is *agha*. But do not noble persons refrain from committing sin even for the sake of their own happiness, both when there is a cause for suffering and when there is a cause for defilement? For instance:
The wise do not perform evil deeds for the sake of their own happiness;
even when touched by suffering and faltering, they remain steadfast.
It is said: "They do not abandon passion and hatred for the Dhamma.

This being so, why is the verbal root *agha* used in the sense of "committing evil," and why are such statements as "it is called *agha* because by means of it beings commit (*aghayanti*) evil" and so forth spoken?
True; however, for the most part, beings [act] on account of suffering and the like.
They commit evil deeds; among these, only the true persons (*sappurisa*) do not do so, while others do.
Thus, for the performance of evil, suffering and defilement are the causes. For it is said:
"Some, even though happy, do not commit evil..."
Furthermore, some, fearing association with disrepute,
though being wealthy and contemplating vast wealth,
ask: "For what reason do you not cause me suffering?"
It has been said. For this verse illustrates the point that beings commit evil even when motivated by suffering:
"An angry man kills his father; an angry man kills his mother. This [other] verse, however, illustrates the point that beings commit evil even when motivated by defilement (kilesa).
Therefore, we have stated the words beginning with "agha pāpakaraṇe" (aghā for the committing of evil).
Forms of verbal roots ending in *gha*.
Verbal roots ending in *ca*:
*Loca* (to see). *Loceti*, *locayati*. *Locanaṃ*. It sees—that is, it observes—visible objects as its objective field; thus it is *locanaṃ*, the eye.
*Kiñci maddane*. *Kiñci* means it crushes (*kiñcayati*). *Kiñcana*, *akiñcana*.

In this context, *kiñcana* means an impediment (*palibodha*). It crushes beings, thus it is *kiñcana*. The word *kiñcana* is used in the sense of crushing. For when people are threshing rice, they say to the ox, "Crush them, Kapila!
Crush them, Kapila! *Paci* means expansion (*vitthāra*). *Pañca*, *pañcayati*. *Papañca*, *papañcayati*. *Papañcā*.

Here, "papañca" refers to craving, conceit, and views. For these cause the saṃsāra of beings who depend upon them to *papañcati*—that is, they make it extensive—and thus they are called "papañca. Alternatively, they are called "papañca" because they *papañcenti*:
wherever they themselves arise, they extend that continuum and cause it to endure for a long time. However, worldly people [say], "We [have no quarrel] with you..."
By saying such things as, “For those who speak, there is *papañca*,” they claim that the long duration of time is *papañca*.
However, both [meanings] are found in the Teaching (*sāsana*).
[The root] *sic* means to wet; it is *siccayati*.

*Vaṅc* is used in the sense of deceiving. Deceiving (*palambhana*) means deluding (*upalāpana*). One deceives (*vañceti*), one causes to deceive (*vañcayati*). A deceiver (*vañcaka*), deception (*vañcana*). However, in the *bhūvādigaṇa*, the root *vañc* occurs in the sense of going. For the Pāli text says: “There are feet that do not deceive” (*santi pādā avañcanā*).
*Cacc* is used in the sense of study (*ajjhāyana*). One studies (*cacceti*), one causes to study (*caccayati*).

*Cu* is used in the sense of causing to fall away (*cavana*). One causes to fall away (*cāveti*), one causes to cause to fall away (*cāvayati*). Another says: “*Cu* is used in the sense of enduring (*sahana*). One causes to endure (*cāveti*), one causes to cause to endure (*cāvayati*); the meaning is “one endures.”
*Añc* means to move. *Añceti*, *añcayati*.
*Loc* is in the sense of speech. *Loceti*, *locayati*. *Locanaṃ*: it is called *locana* because it is as if it points out (*ācikkhantaṃ*) what is even and uneven; thus *locana* is the eye.
*Rac* is in the sense of arranging. *Raceti*, *racayati*. *Racanā*, *viracitaṃ*, *kesaracanā*, *gāthāracanā*.
*Sūca* means backbiting. *Pesuñña* is the state of being a backbiter (*pesuṇa*). One backbites (*sūceti*, *sūcayati*). A backbiter (*sūcaka*). *Pacca* means to restrain.
One restrains (*pacceti*, *paccayati*).

*Rica* means to separate or to succeed. One separates (*receti*, *recayati*). One might purge a merchant’s son (*seṭṭhiputtaṃ vireceyya*). One purges (*vireceti*, *virecayati*). A purger (*virecaka*), a purgative (*virecanaṃ*).
The root *vac* means "to speak. It forms *vaceti* and *vacayati*. This root also occurs in the *bhūvādi* class; in that case, its forms are *vatti*, *vacati*, *avoca*, *avocu*, and so forth.
In the causative (*kārita*), however, the forms are *antevāsikaṃ dhammaṃ vāceti* and *vācayati*. [The infinitive and gerund forms are] *vattuṃ*, *vattave*, and *vatvā*;
[the past participle and passive forms are] *vuttaṃ* and *vuccati*.
*Acca* means to worship; it is *acceti* or *accayati*. One who is honored by Brahmās, asuras, and suras.
*Sūca* means to indicate (*gandhana*). It is *suceti* or *sūcayati*. A pointer (*sūcaka*) and a thread (*sutta*).

And here, it is called a *sutta* because it indicates (*sūcati*) meanings such as one's own welfare, the welfare of others, and so forth; that is, the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Baskets (*Tepiṭaka*).
*Kaca* means "splendor. *Kacca* means "he shines" (*kaccayati*).
A *kacca* is one who shines, gleams, or radiates due to the perfection of his form; he was a primordial person of such a name.
The men born in his lineage are called "Kaccānas," "Kaccāyanas," or "Kātiyānas," while the women [of that lineage] are called...
However, they are also called *kaccānī*, *kaccāyanī*, and *kātiyānī*.
These are forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *c*. [Next is] the verbal root ending in the letter *ch*.
*Milecha* means "one with unintelligible speech. *Mileccheti*, *milecchayati*. *Milakkhu*.
Here, *milakkhu* means one who *mileccheti*, that is, one who speaks unintelligible speech; thus, he is a *milakkhu*. *Kuccha* means "rejection.
Rejection (*avakkhepa*) is throwing down (*adhokhipana*). One rejects (*kuccheti*), one rejects (*kucchayati*).
In the Vedic language (bhāsāyaṃ): *viccheti*, *vicchayati*.
These are forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *c*. [Next,] verbal roots ending in the letter *j*.

*Vajja* [is used] in the sense of avoiding. It means to avoid (*vajjeti*), to cause to avoid (*vajjayati*). One who avoids (*parivajjanaka*). "Being avoided by those possessed of virtue, how will you act, O monk?
*Tujja* [is used] in the senses of protecting with strength, striking, and giving strength.

It means to strike (*tujjeti*), to cause to strike (*tujjayati*). *Tuji*, *piji* [are used] in the senses of harming, giving strength, and dwelling. Dwelling (*niketana*) means residence. It means to strike (*tuñjeti*), to cause to strike (*tuñjayati*). It means to harm (*piñjeti*), to cause to harm (*piñjayati*).
*Khaji* means to live with difficulty. It is conjugated as *khañjeti*, *khañjayati*.

A person who is lame is called *khañjo*. The root *khaji* is used in the sense of protecting; its forms are exactly like those [of the previous root]. In the *bhūvādi* class, from the root *khaji* meaning "to go" or "to be deficient," the form *khañjatī* arises.

*Pūja* means worship. It is conjugated as *pūjeti*, *pūjayati*. Worship (*pūjā*) is better than this very act of honoring (*pūjanā*). [The derivatives are: *pūjako* (one who worships), *pūjito* (worshipped), *pūjanīyo* (worthy of worship), *pūjaneyyo* (fit for worship), *pūjetabbo* (to be worshipped), and *pujjo* (venerable).
In the sense of "elephant" and "crushing": *gaja* means "he causes to go"; thus, *gaja*.
In the sense of "sharpening": *tija*; it sharpens (*tejeti*, *tejayati*).
In the sense of "path" and "volitional formations": *vaja*; it goes (*vajeti*, *vajayati*).
*Tajja*: in the sense of threatening. *Tajjeti*, *tajjayati*; *santajjeti*, *santajjayati*. *Santajjito* (threatened). *Ajja*: in the sense of sending away.
*Ajjeti*, *ajjayati*. *Sajja*: in the sense of preparing.
*Sajjeti*, *sajjayati* (prepares a gift). Having become ready for departure (*gamanasajjo hutvā*).
*Bhaja* means "to trust. *Bhajeti* (causative) means "to cause to trust. In the *bhūvādi* class, however, the form is *bhajati*, meaning "devotion" (*bhatti*) or "complete devotion" (*sambhatti*).

*Tuji*, *piji*, *luji*, and *bhaji* belong to the sense of speaking. *Tujeti*, *tujayati*. *Piñjeti*, *piñjayati*. *Luñjeti*, *luñjayati*. *Bhañjeti*, *bhañjayati*; the meaning is "he speaks. *Ruja* belongs to the sense of harming.
*Rojeti*, *rojayati*. *Rogo* (disease).

*Bhāja* means separate actions; the meaning is "separate action," "separation," or "individual activity. [From this root one forms: *bhājeti*, *bhājayati*; *vibhājeti*, *vibhājayati*; and *vibhatti*. *Sabhāja* is used in the senses of cooling and serving.
[From this root one forms: *sabhājeti*, *sabhājayati*. *Laja* is used in the sense of manifesting.
[From this root one forms: *lajeti*, *lajayati*; and *lājā*.
*Yuj* means to restrain; with the prefix *sam*, it means to bind. One *yojeti*, *yojayati*; one *saṃyojeti*, *saṃyojayati*. *Saṃyojanaṃ* (fetter).
*Majj* means to cleanse or to adorn. One *majjeti*, *majjayati*; one *sammajjeti*, *sammajjayati*. *Sammajjā* (sweeping). *Bhāj* means to divide or to give. One *bhājeti*, *bhājayati*.
"How does Vessantara divide the elephant among his sons? (*kathaṃ vessantaro putto, gajaṃ bhājeti sañcaya*).
Forms of verbal roots ending in *ja*.

Roots ending in *jha* are rarely encountered. In the *Saddasattha*, however, they read “*ñā* in the sense of enjoining,” but that form does not conform to the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*); therefore, it has not been shown by us.
Verbal roots ending in *ṭa*.

*Ghaṭṭ* [is used] in the sense of striking. Striking (*ghaṭṭana*) is the act of exerting effort. One strikes (*ghaṭṭeti*), one causes to strike (*ghaṭṭayati*). Here, however, the illustration is: “You struck, you struck; for what reason did you strike? I know that. *Ghaṭ* [is used] in the sense of collection.

As with the preceding verbal forms, in the nominal state the forms are *ghaṭo* (a pot) and *ghaṭā* (a collection). Here, *ghaṭo* refers to a water-pot. *Ghaṭā* refers to a multitude, as in expressions such as *macchaghaṭā* (a shoal of fish), and so forth.
*Ghaṭṭ* [is used] in the sense of moving. One moves (*ghaṭṭeti*), one causes to move (*ghaṭṭayati*).
*Naṭ* means "to bend. *Avasandana* is the bending or flexing of the limbs. *Naṭeti* means "he bends" (*naṭayati*).
*Cuṭ*, *chuṭ*, and *kuṭṭ* mean "to cut. *Cuṭeti* means "he cuts" (*cuṭayati*). *Chuṭeti* means "he cuts" (*chuṭayati*). *Kuṭṭeti* means "he cuts" (*kuṭṭayati*).
*Puṭṭ* and *caṭṭ* mean "to become small. *Puṭṭeti* means "he makes small" (*puṭṭayati*). *Cuṭṭeti* means "he makes small" (*cuṭṭayati*); the meaning is that it becomes small (*appaṃ bhavati*).
*Muṭa* means to crush; it forms *moṭeti* and *moṭayati*.
*Aṭṭa* and *suṭṭa* mean disregard; they form *aṭṭeti*, *aṭṭayati*, *suṭṭeti*, and *suṭṭayati*.
*Khaṭṭa* means to restrain; it forms *khaṭṭeti* and *khaṭṭayati*.
*Saṭṭa*, *tuvaṭṭa*, and *chaṭṭa* [are used] in the senses of harming, giving strength, and a dwelling, respectively.

*Saṭṭa*: it means "he harms" (*saṭṭayati*). *Tuvaṭṭa*: it means "lying down" (*nipajjāyaṃ*). It means "he lies down" (*tuvaṭṭeti*) or "he causes to lie down" (*tuvaṭṭayati*). For example: "The group-of-six monks lie down on the same bed. *Chaṭṭa*: it means "covering" (*chaṭṭane*).

It means "he covers" (*chaṭṭeti*) or "he causes to cover" (*chaṭṭayati*). Here is the canonical text (*pāḷi*) regarding this: "If he covers it himself, that is good. If he does not cover it himself, a monk endowed with five qualities should be appointed as the 'money-coverer' (*rūpiyachaṭṭaka*)."
*Puṭ* means to injure; *poṭeti*, *poṭayati*. *Kīṭ* means to bind;
binding is the act of tying. *Kīṭeti*, *kīṭayati*.
A *kīṭa* (insect). *Cuṭi* means to cut; *cuṇṭeti*, *cuṇṭayati*.
*Luṭi* means to steal. *Luṇṭeti*, *luṇṭayati*.
*Kūṭa* means to deceive. *Kūṭeti*, *kūṭayati*. *Kūṭaṃ rajataṃ* (false silver). *Kūṭā gāvī* (a cow with a hornless head).
*Kuṭatāpaso* (a deceitful ascetic). *Cuṭa*, *puṭa*, *phuṭa* mean to break apart. *Cuṭeti*, *cuṭayati*. *Poṭeti*, *poṭayati*. *Phoṭeti*, *phoṭayati*. They snapped their fingers.
*Ghaṭa* [is used] in the senses of joining and killing. *Ghaṭeti*, *ghaṭayati*.
*Paṭa*, *puṭa*, *luṭa*, *ghaṭa*, *ghaṭi* are in the sense of speech. *Pāṭeti*, *pāṭayati*. *Poṭeti*, *poṭayati*. *Loṭeti*, *loṭayati*. *Ghāṭeti*, *ghāṭayati*.
*Ghaṇṭeti*, *ghaṇṭayati*. *Paṭa*, *vaṭa* are in the sense of binding. *Paṭeti*, *paṭayati*. *Vaṭeti*, *vaṭayati*.
*Kheṭ* means to eat. One *kheṭeti*, *kheṭayati*.
*Khoṭ* means to throw. One *khoṭeti*, *khoṭayati*.
*Kuṭ* means to burn. One *kuṭeti*, *kuṭayati*.
*Yuṭ* in the sense of connection: *yoṭeti*, *yoṭayati*.
*Vaṭ* in the sense of dividing: *vaṭeti*, *vaṭayati*.
These are the forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *ṭ*.
Roots ending in the letter *ṭh*:
*saṭh* is used in the sense of deceptive mental formations (*saṅkhāra-gati*). *Saṭheti*, *saṭhayati*.
*Suṭh* is used in the sense of laziness (*ālasiya*). *Soṭheti*, *soṭhayati*.
*Suṭhi* is for drying. *Suṇṭheti*, *suṇṭhayati*.
*Saṭha* is for praising. *Saṭheti*, *saṭhayati*.
*Saṭha* is for speaking improperly. *Saṭheti*, *saṭhayati*; *saṭho*.
Here, "deceitful" (*saṭha*) means one who is crafty. He deceives, thus he is "deceitful"; the meaning is that he does not speak rightly.
*Saṭha* and *ketava* [are synonyms]. The form is exactly the same.
"The fault of others is easy to see, but one's own is hard to see... and so forth.
"But he conceals his own [fault], like a dishonest gambler concealing his loss.
Here, the fowler is called "the gambler" (*kitavā*). The meaning is: this is his gambling (*ketavaṃ*); this verbal root (*dhātu*) functions in that sense of gambling.
The root *kaṭh* means to grieve; it forms *kaṇṭheti* and *kaṇṭhayati*.
Roots ending in the letter *ṭha*.
Root ending in the letter *ḍa*:
*paṇḍ* (to mock). *Paṇḍeti*, *paṇḍayati*; *uppaṇḍeti*, *uppaṇḍayati*. They mocked that nun among the people.
*Laḍi* means to throw up. *Laṇḍeti*, *laṇḍayati*.
*Khaḍi* and *kaḍi* mean to cut. *Khaṇḍeti*, *khaṇḍayati*; *kaṇḍeti*, *kaṇḍayati*. *Khaṇḍo*, *kaṇḍo*.
*Piḍi* means to press together. *Piṇḍeti*, *piṇḍayati*. *Piṇḍo*.

And here, "piṇḍa" refers both to a collection, meaning a group—as in the expression "clothing, food, pleasure, and play"—and also to that which is reckoned as nutriment; in both cases it is simply "piṇḍa.
The root *kuḍ* means "to pierce. From it come *kuṇḍeti* and *kuṇḍayati*, and the word *kuṇḍala*.
The root *maḍ* means "adornment" and "laughing. From it come *maṇḍeti*, *maṇḍayati*, *maṇḍo*, *maṇḍanaṃ*, and *maṇḍito*.
*Bhaḍi* means "goodness" (*kalyāṇe*). Goodness is the state of being good (*kalyāṇatā*). It is derived from *bhaṇḍeti*, *bhaṇḍayati*. Thus, *bhaṇḍo*.

And here, *bhaṇḍo* means wealth or an ornament, as in such expressions as "he takes the goods" (*bhaṇḍaṃ gaṇhāti*) or "having adorned himself with the goods" (*samalaṅkaritvā bhaṇḍena*), and so forth.
*Daṇḍi* means "to inflict punishment" (*daṇḍavinipāte*). It is derived from *daṇḍeti*, *daṇḍayati*. Thus, *daṇḍo*.

*Chaḍḍa* means to discard. *Chaḍḍeti*, *chaḍḍayati*. One who discards (*chaḍḍanaka*). It is discarded (*chaḍḍiyati*), discarded (*chaḍḍita*). To discard (*chaḍḍituṃ*), to cause to discard (*chaḍḍayituṃ*), having discarded (*chaḍḍetvā*), having caused to discard (*chaḍḍayitvā*).
These are the forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *ḍa*. [Roots] ending in the letter *ḍha*.
*Vaḍḍha* is used in the sense of pouring in. He pours milk-rice (*pāyāsa*) into a bronze bowl; he increases it (*vaḍḍheti*, *vaḍḍhayati*). Having increased the food, he gave it.
These are the forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *ḍha*. [Now] the verbal roots ending in the letter *ṇa*:

*Vaṇṇa* [is used] in the senses of color, praise, elaboration, quality, and speech. *Vaṇṇa* means praise. *Kriyā* means making. *Vitthāra* means extensiveness. *Guṇa* refers to qualities such as virtue (*sīla*). *Vacana* means speech. One praises (*vaṇṇeti*, *vaṇṇayati*). [Examples are: *vaṇṇa*, *vaṇṇaṃ*, *suvaṇṇaṃ*, *saṃvaṇṇanā*.
The word *vaṇṇa* is seen in the sense of skin, praise, clan, group, cause, shape, measure, the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), and so forth.

Among these, in passages such as "The Blessed One has a golden complexion" (*suvaṇṇavaṇṇosi bhagavā*), it refers to the skin. "But when were you conceived, householder, for that ascetic... [and so on].
In such passages as “the praises of Gotama,” it refers to praise. In such passages as “These four, O Gotama, are the castes,” it refers to a class of people.
In such passages as “Now by what quality is one called a thief of fragrance? it refers to a cause. In such passages as “having manifested the form of a great king of elephants,” it refers to shape.
In such passages as “there are three qualities of a bowl,” it refers to measure. “Quality... [and so forth].
In such passages as "smell, taste, nutritive essence," it refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*).

Regarding that, others say that in the phrase "the skin" (*chaviyaṃ*), it is the color-element (*vaṇṇadhātu*) residing in the skin itself that is included by the mention of "color" (*vaṇṇa*) in the expression "golden-colored.
"Color" (*vaṇṇa*) means praise; it is the proclamation of one's reputation, that is, eulogy. It is called "color" because it is distinguished from other things without confusion.

It is called *vaṇṇa* because it is defined; thus, it refers to a class of colors. It is called *vaṇṇa* because by means of it the fruit is colored—that is, manifested according to its true nature—thus, it refers to a cause.
It is called *vaṇṇa* because they shape it according to length, shortness, and so forth; thus, it refers to shape.

It is called *vaṇṇa* because it is colored—that is, measured—by way of size such as half-a-measure or a full measure; thus, it refers to measurement. It is called *vaṇṇa* because it expresses the state of having reached the heart when undergoing a transformation.

"It reveals" (*pakāseti*) is "color" (*vaṇṇo*); this refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*). Thus, one should understand the application of the word "color" to its various meanings according to each respective cause for its occurrence.

Furthermore, we shall state another enumeration of the meanings of the word "color": the word "color" applies to shape, genus, the sense-sphere of visible form, cause, measure, quality, praise, gold, sand, syllables, and so forth.
It is seen [in various senses]. For this term is seen in the sense of *saṇṭhāna* (shape/form) in such passages as, “having manifested the form of a great king of serpents”;
in the sense of *jāti* (birth/caste) in such passages as, “the brahmin caste alone is the best caste; other castes are inferior”;
and in the sense of the *rūpāyatana* (visible object sphere) in such passages as, “endowed with the highest excellence of complexion.”
In such passages as, “I do not take away, I do not break, I merely smell the water-born flower from afar;
now by what reason is one called a ‘thief of fragrance’?

it refers to the cause (*kāraṇa*). In such passages as, “There are three qualities of a bowl,” it refers to measure (*pamāṇa*). [And in the passage: “But when were they gathered together, householder?”...
In such passages as "the praises of the ascetic Gotama," it refers to *guṇa* (qualities). In "he speaks praise of one worthy of praise," it refers to *pasaṃsā* (praise).
In "we sought gold in the Kāliṅga forest with gold-colored ointment," it refers to *jātarūpa* (gold). In "not weary, digging on the gold-path (*vaṇṇapatha*)," it refers to *puḷina* (sand).
In "the addition of a syllable (*vaṇṇāgama*), the substitution of a syllable (*vaṇṇavipariyāya*)," and so forth, it is seen in the sense of *akkhara* (syllable). Thus, in every respect—
The word *vaṇṇa* occurs in the sense of skin, praise, a clan-group, and a reason;
in the sense of shape, measure, the sense-sphere of visible form, and types [of beings];
and in the sense of qualities, syllables, and sand.
The word *suvaṇṇa* occurs in reference to the excellence of complexion, to the golden eagle (*garuḷa*), and to gold (*jātarūpa*).

Indeed, it occurs in reference to the excellence of complexion in such passages as “whether beautiful or ugly, whether well-gone or ill-gone,” and “the state of being golden and the state of having a sweet voice.

It occurs in reference to the golden eagle in such passages as “the golden [eagles] surround the crow. And it occurs in reference to gold in such passages as “golden-hued, with skin resembling refined gold.”
Furthermore, *puṇ* means to gather together; it forms *puṇeti* and *puṇayati*. *Cuṇ* means to contract;
it forms *cuṇeti* and *cuṇayati*. *Cuṇṇ* means to crush;
it forms *cuṇṇeti* and *cuṇṇayati*. *Cuṇṇaṃ* means to reduce to powder; it means to make something finely pulverized.
*Saṇa* means to give. *Saṇeti*, *saṇayati*.
*Kuṇa* means contraction. *Kuṇeti*, *kuṇayati*. *Kuṇo*: a withered hand; one who has a withered hand.
*Tūṇa* means to fill. *Tūṇeti*, *tūṇayati*. *Tūṇī*: a quiver.
In this context, *tūṇī* means a quiver. For it is called *tūṇī* because arrows (*sara*) are stored (*tūṇenti*) or filled therein.
[The root] *bhūṇ* is used in the sense of speaking: *bhūṇeti*, *bhūṇayati*.
[The root] *kaṇ* is used in the sense of closing the eyes: *kāṇeti*, *kāṇayati*; [the derivative] *kāṇo*.
In this context, "one-eyed" (*kāṇa*) refers to one who is deprived of one or both eyes. However, the masters of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*) state: "One-eyed means one-eyed in one eye;
blind means one-eyed in both eyes. This is appropriate when the terms "one-eyed" and "blind" are used as synonyms.
Otherwise, in the *Kāṇakacchapa-sutta* (The Simile of the One-Eyed Turtle), the turtle mentioned would have to be one-eyed in only one eye.
Furthermore, such a person should not be called "blind. Therefore, since these two form a pair, it should be understood that each one denotes two aspects as they occur.
For instance, in the *Kosalasaṃyutta-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "One-eyed means either having one eye impaired or both eyes impaired.
Alternatively, regarding the phrase "he should exhort and instruct," [the same principle applies] to the exhortation and the instruction.
The state of being specific and the state of being non-specific are to be understood as such.
[The root] *gaṇ* means "to count. [From it come the forms] *gaṇeti* and *gaṇayati*. [The derivatives are] *gaṇanā* (counting) and *gaṇo* (a group).
Here, *gaṇanā* means number; *gaṇo* means a collection of monks, or the collection of any persons whatsoever. There are many names for a collection, namely:
Saṅgha, gaṇa, and samūha;
khandha, sannicaya, and caya;
