samuccaya and nicaya.
A group, a multitude, and a heap;
a body, a class, and a collection;
a cluster, a scattering, and a mass.
A collection (*samudāya*), a mass (*sandeha*),
a combination (*saṅghāta*), a conjunction (*samaya*), and a making (*kara*).
A flood (*ogha*), a heap (*puñja*), and a cluster (*kalāpa*).
"Piṇḍa," "jāla," "maṇḍala," "saṇḍa," and "pavāha"—
these are designations for the sense of a collection."

Although these terms—*saṅgha*, *gaṇa*, *samūha*, and so forth—are words denoting a collection, nevertheless, only the words *saṅgha* and *gaṇa* refer to a collection of monks even without a qualifying word; other terms do not.
Furthermore, while other terms may sometimes have the same scope and meaning as *saṅgha* and *gaṇa*, and sometimes have a different scope and meaning, therefore:
It should be applied without confusion according to the specific grammatical rule (*yathāpāvacana*). It is called a *gaṇa* because it is to be counted by means of "one, two," and so forth.
The root *kaṇ* means "to hear. From *kaṇ*, one forms *kaṇṇayati*. Thus, *kaṇṇo*. That by which they hear sound is *kaṇṇo*; that which is called "hearing" (*savana*) or "ear" (*sota*) in the world.
The roots *kuṇ* and *guṇ* mean "to address" or "to call out. From *kuṇ*, one forms *kuṇeti* and *kuṇayati*. From *guṇ*, one forms *guṇeti* and *guṇayati*. Thus, *guṇo*. [Also] *goṇo*.
Here, "virtue" (*guṇa*) refers to such qualities as moral conduct (*sīla*). In what sense are they called "virtues"?
They are called "virtues" because a person who is established in them is drawn toward (*āmantāpiyati*), or invited (*āmantāpiyati*), by people who desire to see, hear, and honor them.

Although there is no actual drawing toward or inviting of the phenomena of moral conduct and so forth themselves, nevertheless, it is precisely those [phenomena] that constitute the cause for being drawn toward and invited.
"They perform [the name]" is what was said. For it is thus:
"Just as even a small seed planted in a fertile field..."
In the verse, "When it rains properly,
the fruit satisfies the farmer," there is a "satisfying" of the fruit—
even though it is insentient— by way of a cause, because it is the cause for the arising of satisfaction in the farmer.
It has been stated [elsewhere]; likewise here too, it is stated thus because it serves as the cause for addressing.
Others, however, explain the meaning as: "They resound (*guñjante*) and do not perish (*abyayante*), thus they are *guṇā*. Yet we do not see a verbal root (*dhātu*) word corresponding to that;
we see only "guṇa in the sense of addressing" (*āmantane*). This should be accepted after due consideration.
*Vaṇa* means to wound or to crush. One wounds (*vaṇeti*), one causes to wound (*vaṇayati*). A *vaṇa*. Here, *vaṇa* means a sore.
For it wounds the body, crushes it, and makes it perforated and full of holes; thus it is called a *vaṇa*. *Paṇṇa* means greenery.
One greens (*paṇṇeti*), one causes to green (*paṇṇayati*). A palm leaf (*tālapaṇṇa*). A leaf for soup (*sūpeyyapaṇṇa*).

And here, it should be understood that even when the state of being green has passed away from the object, the term "paṇṇa" (leaf) occurs by way of conventional usage (*rūḷhi*). "Paṇṇa," "patta," "palāsa," and "dala" are synonymous.
[The root] *paṇ* means "to transact. One transacts (*paṇeti*, *paṇayati*). A king also transacts a heavy fine (*daṇḍaṃ garukaṃ paṇeti*).
These are forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *ṇ*.

The verbal root *cinti* ending in the letter *t* means "to think. [Its forms are: *cinteti*, *cintayati*; *cittaṃ*, *cintā*, *cintanā*, *cintanaka*. In the causative (*kārita*), there are the forms "he causes to think" (*cintāpeti*) and "he causes to cause to think" (*cintāpayati*).
In this context, "mind" (*citta*) is so called because it thinks upon an object (*ārammaṇa*); the meaning is that it cognizes. This is stated by way of what is common to all types of consciousness.

It should be understood. Here it might be asked: why, after stating that "it is called *citta* because it thinks upon an object," is it further said that "the meaning is 'it cognizes' (*vijānāti*)"? Are not thinking (*cintanā*) and cognizing (*vijānanā*) of different natures?
For the meaning "it cognizes" cannot possibly apply to the word "it thinks"; for even though one of dull wisdom may think in various ways, there is no attainment of subtle meanings.

Is it so? True. The term "it cognizes" (*vijānāti*) is stated to indicate the grasping of an object that is distinguished from the functions of perception (*saññā*) and wisdom (*paññā*), because the word "consciousness" (*citta*) is common to all states of mind. For whatever class of phenomena is called "mind," that itself is consciousness;
therefore, having taken the sense of "cognizing," [the phrase] refers to the grasping of an object not distinguished from the functions of perception and wisdom.
It is stated as "it cognizes" (*vijānāti*) in order to illuminate this.
Now, we shall also clarify the etymological derivation by way of other grammatical roots (*dhātu*):

among all states of consciousness, that which is a mundane wholesome, unwholesome, or great functional consciousness is called *citta* because it accumulates (*cinoti*) its own continuum by way of the impulsion process (*javana-vīthi*); and [the resultant consciousness] is called *citta* because it is accumulated (*cita*) by kamma and defilements.

"Citta"—this is the derivation by way of the *cittadhātu* (the element of consciousness). Whatever kind of diverse craft (*sippajāta*) exists in the world, because all of that is performed by means of the mind alone, it is called "citta.
It is "citta" because it makes diverse (*vicitta*); it is "citta" because it is made diverse by this—thus it is stated as "citta" due to its quality of making diverse.
This is the derivation by way of the *cittadhātu*. "Citta" because of its state of being conscious (*cittatāya*)—this is [the derivation] by way of the primary suffix (*pāṭipadika*).

This is the etymological derivation. Therefore, the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā said: "Everything is 'consciousness' (citta) because it is conscious in its respective way, and it is 'consciousness' because it performs the function of consciousness;
thus should the meaning be understood here.

For in this context, because consciousness is divided into various types such as with lust, with hatred, and so forth, [it is distinguished] by way of its associated states, its plane, its object, and its predominants—whether inferior, medium, or superior.
The state of being "mind" (cittatā) should be understood by way of its variety.

Although a single moment of consciousness does not possess such variety, nevertheless, because it is included within that which is variegated, even a single constituent part is called "mind" by way of a collective designation (*samudāya-vohāra*), just as when a portion of a mountain, a river, or the ocean is seen, one says "the mountain" and so forth has been seen. Therefore, the teachers of the Commentaries said:

“Granted that in this case there is not just one single such consciousness; nevertheless, because they are included within the category of consciousness, it is appropriate to call any one of them ‘consciousness’ by virtue of their common nature as consciousness.
And here follows the detailed exposition of the meanings described above. How so? Because wherever and in whatever manner—
In whatever way a meaning is obtained, it should be understood accordingly in each instance.

Therefore, that which accumulates by way of being a condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*), and that which is accumulated because it is conditioned by karma—on account of those reasons, it is called "mind" (*citta*).

However, that which does not function in such a way—the two types of limited functional states (*parittakiriya*) and the final impulsion (*antimajavana*)—is [called mind] by virtue of the existing variety of its cognitive processes and so forth.
It should be understood as "citta"; however, the smile-producing consciousness (hasituppāda) belongs to the same category as other types of javanas.
These are the names for citta:
citta, mano, mānasa, viññāṇa, hadaya, and mana.
These names circulate in common usage from ancient times.
The word *citta* is seen in such meanings as "conceptual designation" (*paññatti*), "consciousness" (*viññāṇa*), "variegated painting" (*vicitte cittakamme*), and "wonderful" (*acchariya*).

Indeed, it is seen in the sense of a conceptual designation in such instances as "the householder Citta" and "the month of Citta. It is also seen in such contexts as "mind" (*mano*), "mentality" (*mānasa*), and so forth.

In the context of *viññāṇa* (consciousness). In such passages as “women with variegated garments and ornaments,” it refers to the variegated (*vicitte*). In such passages as “Bhikkhus, have you seen the painting called ‘Character’?
it refers to the craft of painting (*cittakamme*). In such passages as “Come, Maddi, look!

It appears like a painted form,” it refers to the marvelous (*acchariyeti*). [The root] *cita* means volition (*sañcetane*). One intends, one wills. “O Brahmin, one who is impassioned, overcome by passion, even for his own harm...”
One intends; one intends for the harm of another; one intends for the harm of both. One desires and intends—that, O Jutindhara, you must restrain.
Intention (*cetanā*), volition (*sañcetanā*). That which has been intended, having intended, having willed. "Intentionally, he deprives a living being of life.
In this context, "intention" (*cetanā*) means "he intends" (*cetayati*); it is so called because it binds together the associated mental states along with itself toward an object.
Meaning: "Volition" (*sañcetanā*) is a term expanded by means of a prefix. "That which is willed" (*cetayitaṃ*) is the mode of volition.
"Having intended" (*sañcicca*) means having known for oneself; the sense is "having willed" (*cecca*) and "having reflected upon" (*abhivitaritvā*).
These are synonyms for volition: Volition, that which is willed, Volition, and indeed action;
For "kamma" has indeed been declared by the Conqueror as being "volition" (*cetanā*).
Here is the canonical text (*pāḷi*) on this: "O monks, I say that volition is kamma; having willed, one performs kamma by way of body, speech, and mind.
[The root] *mant* is used in the sense of speaking guardedly: *manteti*, *mantayati*, *nimanteti*, *nimantayati*, *āmanteti*, *āmantayati*.
People gather together; they deliberate, they have deliberated in private. They invited the king.
The Lord of Devas addressed Visukamma, who possesses great psychic power. *Mantā*, *manto*. In the causative, there are forms such as *mantāpeti* and *mantāpayati*.
Here, *mantā* means wisdom (*paññā*); some also say it means "the perception of seeking. *Manto* means guarded speech. "Those who eavesdrop..."
"They hear the counsel; therefore, indeed, counsel quickly leads to division. Here, "counsel" (*manto*) refers to guarded speech.
Furthermore, "counsel" refers to the six-limbed counsel (*chaḷaṅgamanto*). And it is said: "Those who recite the counsel, the six-limbed thought of the Brahmā.

In this context, [the six limbs] are by way of training (*sikkhā*), grammar (*nirutti*), ritual rules (*kappa*), etymology (*byākaraṇa*), the science of astrology (*jotisattha*), and prosody (*chandovicitī*).
The *manta* should be understood as "six-limbed. These very six are called the "limbs of the Vedas" (*vedaṅga*). For it is the Veda itself that is also called "the *manta*" and "the *suti*.
Alternatively, *manta* refers to the knowledge of the Vedas and so forth.

[Regarding the word] *yanta*: the root is *yant*, meaning "to contract. Thus, *yanteti* means "it contracts. Just as an oil-press (*telayanta*) moves according to its wheel, so does the earth tremble.
In the sense of going (*gati*). *Satta*: it causes to go (*sattayati*).

In the sense of being quiet (*santa*), when combined with the prefix *ā-*. "The application of *ā-*" (*āmappayoga*) means intense activity. *Santa*: it causes to become quiet (*santayati*). *Kitta* in the sense of connecting (*saṃsandana*). *Kitta*:

it connects (*kitteti*) or it causes to connect (*kittayati*). However, in such passages as, "Those whom I shall praise (*kittayissāmi*) with words in successive order; praise (*kittanā*), thorough praise (*parikittanā*)," etc., it is called "praising" (*katthanā*) that is "praise" (*kittanā*).
*Tanta* is used in the sense of maintaining a family. *Tanteti* means he maintains; the meaning is "one who has a lineage" (*satanto*) or "one who possesses a stream" (*sappadhāno*).
*Yata* is used in the sense of groups and assistance. *Yateti* means he assists. *Ni* is used in the sense of giving back.

The verbal root *yata*, when preceded by the prefix *ni*, functions in the sense of giving back: *niyyāteti*, *niyyātayati*. Furthermore, when the letter *ta* is changed to *da*, it becomes: *niyyādeti*.
He bestows. Having bestowed the chariot, come debt-free, O charioteer—thus [he speaks of] forms (*rūpa*).
The root *vat* is used in the sense of speaking. It becomes *vatteti* or *vattayati*.
The root *pat* is used in the sense of going. It becomes *pateti* or *patayati*.

*Vāta*, *gati*, *sukha*, and *sevane*. Regarding "going, happiness, and service," there are three meanings. Therein, *sukhanaṃ* is *sukhaṃ*. *Vāta*: it causes to blow (*vātayati*). Wind (*vāto*), the *vātapuppha* flower, the breeze behind a robe.
*Keta*: in the sense of addressing. *Keteti*, *ketayati*. *Ketaka*. *Satta*:
in the sense of the action of continuity (*santānakriyā*). The action of continuity means the action of binding, the making of no interruption. *Satta*: it binds (*sattayati*). *Satto*.
“Why do you, O old bull whose life has departed, pull up green grass in haste and bleat, ‘Eat! Eat!’?
However, regarding the reading “gatasattaṃ jaraggavaṃ” in the canonical text (Pāḷi), the meaning is “an aged ox whose vitality has vanished.”
They praised it. By this, it appears that the word *satta* signifies "life," just as the word *paggaha* signifies "alms-bowl" in the passage, "It is not easy to subsist on alms-gathering.
This must be thoroughly investigated. [The root] *sū* is used in the sense of "untying.
Regarding *sutta*: it means "it is unknotted" (*suttayati*).
*Mutta* means in the sense of urinating. *Mutta* means he urinates. *Omutta* means he urinates. *Muttaṃ* (the past participle). Here the canonical text (*pāḷi*) says:
*“mutteti ohadeti cā”* (“he urinates and he voids”). In that context, *mutteti* means he passes urine; *ohadeti* means he discharges feces.
In the causative form, the forms are *“muttāpeti”* and *“muttāpayati”*.
*Kattara* means "worn out. *Kattarati*, *kattarayati*. *Kattaro*. *Kattaradaṇḍo*, *kattarasuppaṃ*. In this context, *kattaro* means "old";
it is synonymous with "aged. In what sense? In the sense that one "wears out" (*kattarayati*) through the looseness of the limbs;
that is, one becomes slack. *Kattaradaṇḍo* refers to [the staff] used by *kattarehi*, that is, by old people.
A *kattaradaṇḍa* is a staff for those who must rely on it exclusively; hence the teachers of the commentaries said:
"A *kattaradaṇḍa* is a staff to be taken up in one's old age. A *kattarasuppa* is a worn-out fan.
It is a compound meaning "that which is both *kattara* and a *suppa*."

*Citta* [is used] in the sense of "making variegated" (*cittakaraṇe*), and sometimes also in the sense of "seeing. "Making variegated" means making something diverse or multicolored. *Citteti* means "he makes variegated. Thus, it is *citta*.
These are forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *t*. [Next is] the verbal root ending in the letter *th*.

*Katha* means speaking. One *katheti* or *kathayati*. One converses about the Dhamma. There are: conversation (*sākacchā*), discourse (*kathā*), detailed discourse (*parikathā*), and commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
In this context, "converses" (*sākacchati*) means he speaks together with [others]. It is called *aṭṭhakathā* because meaning (*attha*) is explained (*kathiyati*) by it;
here, the letter *tth* becomes *ṭṭh*. That by which they praise the meaning, following the phrasing, the sense, and the words—[that is commentary].
This commentary is considered to be connected with the introductory narrative (*nidānavatthusambandha*).
Furthermore, "commentary" (*aṭṭhakathā*) and "explanation of the meaning" (*atthasaṃvaṇṇanā*) are not different. [The root] *pathi* means "going.
They cause to go (*panthenti*), they cause to traverse (*panthayanti*); thus, *pantha*. In the *bhūvādigaṇa*, [the root] "patha gatiyaṃ" is given according to its form ending in the vowel *a*.
Regarding that which is stated as *pathati* and *patho*, the forms occur excluding the insertion of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra);
however, it should be understood here that for that which is stated by way of the vowel *i*, the forms including the insertion of the *niggahīta* occur invariably.
*Puttha* [is used] in the senses of respect and disrespect. *Puttha* means he respects; *putthayati*.
*Muttha* means to strike. *Muttheti* means he strikes; *mutthayati* means he causes to strike.
*Vattha* means to weave. *Vattheti* means he weaves; *vatthayati* means he causes to weave.
*Putha* means speech. *Potheti* means he speaks; *pothayati* means he causes to speak. The meaning is that he speaks.
*Putha* in the sense of striking: *potheti*, *pothayati*. Having struck the boy, he departed.
*Katha* in the sense of speech or composition: *katheti*, *kathayati*. Discourse (*kathā*).
*Satha* in the sense of deceit: *satheti*, *sathayati*.

*Attha* and *pattha* are used in the sense of requesting. *Attheti*, *atthayati*: *attha*. *Pattheti*, *patthayati*: *patthanā*. Those who oppose (*paccatthika*) by opposing (*atthayanti*) or desiring [harm] are called enemies.
*Thoma* is used in the sense of praise. *Thometi*, *thomayati*: *thomanā*.
*Kātha* is used in the sense of harming. *Kātheti*, *kāthayati*.
*Satha* means "in binding. *Satheti*, [causative] *sathayati*.
*Santha*, *gantha*, and *santhambha* [mean "to bind"]. *Santheti*, [causative] *santhayati*. *Gantheti*, [causative] *ganthayati*. *Gantho* [means "a knot" or "binding"].
These are the forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *tha*.
Roots ending in *da*: *hada* in the sense of voiding excrement. Voiding excrement means the discharge or emission of feces. One *hadeti*, one *hadayati*; one *ohadeti*, one *ohadayati*.
*Vida* in the sense of obtaining. In this context, "obtaining" (*lābha*) means experiencing; therefore, the root *vida* functions in the sense of experiencing.
The meaning should be grasped as follows: one feels a pleasant feeling; one feels a painful feeling. It is felt;
it is sensation (*vedanā*), experiencing (*vitti*), that which is felt (*vedayitaṃ*). While feeling a pleasant feeling.
[From the root] *kud* in the sense of speaking falsely: *kundeti*, *kundayati*.
*Mida* means to soften. Here, "softening" (*sineha*) refers to joy (*pīti*). *Medeti*, *medayati*: it softens. *Chada* means to cover.
It covers the house; it covers over. It covers over the fault; it conceals. It is hidden, it is concealed. An umbrella. A covered hut. In that context, "umbrella" (*chatta*) is a sunshade.
It is called an "umbrella" because it covers the heat (*ātapa*); it is "covered" (*channa*) because it is being concealed.
Regarding *sañcodana* (urging) and *āṇatti* (command): one urges, one incites. The urger, the one urged, and the urging. Ānanda was urged by the Buddha.
In this context, "urging" (*codanā*) means shaking (*cālanā*). "Shaking" means the attribution of faults; such is the meaning. Regarding *chadda*, it means vomiting. One vomits, one causes to vomit.
*Mada* is in the sense of intoxication. It intoxicates; it causes to intoxicate.

*Vid* is used in the senses of perceiving (*cehaṇā*), naming (*ākhyāna*), and dwelling (*nivāsa*). *Cehaṇā* means recognition; *ākhyāna* means speaking; *nivāsa* means residing. It perceives; it causes to perceive. It makes known; it causes to make known. "I make known to you, O Great King.
*Sadd* is in the sense of sounding. It sounds; it causes to sound. It resounds; it causes to resound. Sound, sounded. In its long form, the word-form is "saddāyati."
And here, the reading in the Aṭṭhakathā—“He plunges into the water with speed because of the perception ‘It calls me’”—is an illustration;
it should not be said that this form *pabbatāyati* is not produced by way of a verbal root (*dhātu*), for it must be understood as being produced precisely by way of a verbal root.
*Saddo* means that which is sounded (*saddiyati*); *vacanaṃ* means that which is spoken (*yathāvuccati*). Now...

Or, *sadda* is so called because meaning (*attha*) is conveyed (*saddiyati*) by it; thus, it is "sound. However, others say: "It is 'sound' because it is respected (*sappati*). The meaning is that it is uttered (*udīriyati*) or expressed (*abhilapiyati*).

[The root] *sūd* is used in the sense of sprinkling (*āsecane*). One sprinkles (*sūdeti*), one causes to sprinkle (*sūdayati*). A *sūda*. A *sūda* is a cook, who is also called a "flavor-maker" (*rasaka*).
*Kanda* means to cause to tremble (*sātacce*). Trembling (*sātacca*) is the state of constantness, the state of being uninterrupted.
*Kandeti*, *kandayati*. *Muda* means in contact (*saṃsagge*). Contact is the act of making into one. *Modeti*, *modayati*—as in "he causes the enemies to rejoice with ghee.

*Nada* is used in the sense of speaking (*bhāsāyaṃ*). *Nādeti*, *nādayati*. It should not be said that these are forms of the causal agent (*hetukatturūpāni*), because they are seen in the Canon (*pāḷidassanato*): "The lion..."

And with a lion’s roar, he made it resound loudly. One should not entertain doubt even in other instances, because in this curādigaṇa (the class beginning with *cur*), both forms with a pure agent (*suddhakattarūpa*) and those resembling a causal agent (*hetukattarūpa*) are seen together.
*Sada* means to taste. [It appears as] *sādeti*, *sādayati*; *assādeti*, *assādayati*. Here, the prefix *ā-* stands by way of shortening (*rassavasena*).
*Gada* means "the sound of the gods. The "sound of the gods" (*devasadda*) refers to the sound of clouds.

*Gadeti*, *gadayati*. [The root] *pada* is used in the sense of "going. *Padeti*, *padayati*. A "footstep" (*pada*). In this [root] belonging to the *divādigaṇa*, the form is "pajjati," but here it is of such a kind [as above].
*Chidda* means "piercing the ear. *Chiddeti*, *chiddayati*. A "hole" (*chidda*).
[The root] *chid* means "to split. Now, sir, is it not the case that for one who cuts something into four, five, or even many hundreds of pieces, that cutting is not called "splitting into two"?
This being so, why was the specific term "splitting into two" (*dvedhākaraṇe*) used instead of speaking in general terms? It should not be said that it is not "splitting into two."
Cutting into many hundreds of pieces is indeed the same as making two parts.
For when one severed portion is viewed together with another preceding portion, it certainly constitutes being made into two parts. He cuts, he causes to cut:
"He who cut off your hands and feet, and your ears and nose."
"Be angry with him, O Great Hero; let not this kingdom perish!
He who has cut off my hands and feet, and my ears and nose—may that king live long, for those like me do not give way to anger."
*Chad* is used in the sense of concealing. It forms *chādeti* and *chādayati*. *Chattaṃ* (an umbrella). "He conceals the meal of a person.
*Īdī* is used in the sense of kindling. It forms *īdeti* and *īdayati*. Because it is taught with a long vowel (*ī*), forms with the nasalized augment (*niggahīta*) do not occur.
*Adda* is used in the sense of harming. It forms *addeti* and *addayati*.
Regarding the word *vāda*: [it is derived from] *vādeti* and *vādayati*. The term *vādo* [is the noun form].
In this context, the meaning of these two—*vādeti* and *vādayati*—should be understood solely by way of the "pure agent" (*suddhakattā*), and not by way of the "causal agent" (*hetukattā*).
For it is said: "Having made an agreement, he deceives (*visaṃvādeti*); he should exhort and instruct (*ovadeyya anusāseyya*); this very..."

The canonical texts show the phrase "they speak of truth" (*saccaṃ ti ca vādayanti*) as indicating a pure agent (*suddhakattū*), and in the grammatical treatises (*saddasattha*), the word "he causes to speak" (*vādayati*) appears as a term for a pure agent. In this context, "to deceive" (*visaṃvadeti*) means to speak falsely, or else to mislead;
"speech" (*vāda*) refers to utterance. Among the three types of discourse such as these—namely, "discourse" (*vāda*), "prattle" (*jappa*), and "cavil" (*vitaṇḍā*)—[it is the first].

“Speech” (kathā) is what is designated as *vāda*. In the expressions “he causes to speak” (*vādāpeti*) and “he causes to cause to speak” (*vādāpayati*), there are only two instances of the causal agentive suffix (*hetu-kattūpada*).
The root *chad* signifies desire. This verbal root ends in the vowel *ī*; therefore, its forms do not undergo the insertion of the nasal *niggahīta* (anusvāra).
“He covers the food for a man” (*purisassa bhattaṃ chādeti*, *chādayati*); the meaning is that it is pleasing to him. [The phrase] “covering the food for a man” (*purisassa bhattaṃ chādayamānaṃ*).
*Tiṭṭhati* means "standing while covering.
*Vadī* is used in the sense of salutation and praise. This root also ends in the vowel *ī*; therefore, for this root as well, forms with the insertion of *niggahīta* (anusvāra) do not occur.
*Vādeti*, *vādayati*, *vandati*, or *thometi*—this is the meaning. These are forms without prefixes (*anupasagga*).
In the *Saddasattha* as well, the word "vādayati" is stated in the sense of salutation (*vandana*) and praise (*thuti*) without a prefix;
however, in the Dispensation (*sāsana*), forms with prefixes such as "abhivādeti," "abhivādayati," "abhivādanaṃ," and "bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā" are seen.
Among these, "abhivādetvā" means having saluted or having praised; this is our preference. But in the *Aṭṭhakathā* of the Āgama, however—

Regarding the phrase “having saluted” (*abhivādetvā*): the meaning of the word *abhivādana* is stated according to the agentive cause (*hetukattā*) as “having caused [the other] to say, ‘May you be happy and free from illness’”;

for when one pays homage, one effectively causes [the other] to say this very thing. However, we have explained the meaning according to the simple agent (*suddhakattā*), without adopting the method of grammatical science (*saddasatthanaya*) regarding the word *vandana*.
For *abhivādana* is indeed just *vandana* (homage); it is not “causing to speak,” because of the prefix *abhi*.
Because of their relatedness, as in the case of the expression “one whose habit is to pay homage.

For here it is not said, “one whose habit is to cause [others] to pay homage. And if the meaning intended in the grammatical treatise (*saddasattha*) were “causing to speak,” then the statement would have been made without doubt as “*vadī* in the sense of causing to speak and in praise”;
but it was not stated thus, rather it was stated: “*vadī* in the sense of paying homage and in praise. Therefore...
It is understood that "causing to speak" (*vadāpana*) is not intended here.

Furthermore, if it were argued that "for someone, causing to speak in a distinguished manner by means of one's seniority is 'salutation' (*abhivādana*)," even this is untenable, because the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) cannot be stated as something caused to be done (*kārita*).
For instance, [the meanings are given] as "√pac in the sense of cooking," "√chid in the sense of cutting into two," and so forth.

By way of the state of being (bhāva), for the mere purpose of clarifying the meaning, verbal forms such as “he cooks, it is cooked, he causes to cook; he cuts, it is cut, he causes to cut,” which are both transitive and intransitive and possess various modes of action (sakārita), are produced;
yet, for that specific purpose, a separate definition of the verbal root (dhātu) is not provided. Therefore, [it is said]: “*Vadī* is used in the sense of salutation and praise.”

In this context, it cannot even be said that the meaning of a *dhātu* (verbal root) is stated by way of its function (*kārita*), because roots possess the intrinsic nature of action (*kriyā-sabhāva*).

Just as "he reasons" (*takketi*), "he applies thought" (*vitakketi*), "reasoning" (*takko*), and "applied thought" (*vitakko*) have the same meaning, so too "he plays an instrument" (*vādeti*) and "he pays homage" (*abhivādeti*) have the same meaning.
Therefore, in the science of grammar (*saddasattha*) as well, those learned in grammar [state]: "The root *takka* means 'to reason' (*vitakke*)."

In the case of roots such as *vad* in the expressions "in salutations and praises" (*abhivādana-thutīsu*), forms such as "he reasons" (*takkayati*) and "he causes to speak" (*vādayati*) are shown even without prefixes;

moreover, these are exclusively active-voice bases (*suddha-kattupada*), not causative-voice bases (*hetu-kattupada*). Therefore, the meaning "in causing to speak and in praising" (*vadāpana-thutīsu*) is not applicable to the term "in salutations and praises" (*abhivādana-thutīsu*).
Furthermore: “abhivādeti,” “abhivādayati,” “abhivādetvā,” and “abhivādayitvā” have the same meaning;
they differ only by the addition of the *ṇe* and *ṇaya* suffixes.

If the word “abhivādetvā” were to mean “having caused [him] to say, ‘May you be happy and free from illness,’” then the word “sirasā” (with the head) would not need to be stated in the phrase “sirasā abhivādayiṃ.”

It might be argued that [the meaning of] "causing to speak" (vadāpana) is not applicable because of the lack of connection. Since that word has been stated, it is understood that in expressions such as *abhivādetvā*, the sense of "causing to speak" is not intended;
rather, the sense of "worshiping" (*vandana*) and the sense of "praising" (*thomana*) are intended.
This is because, in the *bhū-vādi* class of roots, for this root *vanda*—meaning "to worship, to salute, and to praise"—the form of the word *vandatī* [is used]. "He worships," *abhivandati*.
The meaning must be accepted as "praises" (*thometi*) alone, not in the sense of "causing to speak.

For even by the commentator, while explaining the meaning of the words "I revere the Sugata who is liberated from rebirth," he showed the meaning to be that of "revering" and "praising"—saying "I revere" (*vandeti*) means "I revere" (*vandāmi*) and "I praise" (*thomemi*)—rather than the sense of "causing to speak" based on the word *abhivādana*.
Therefore, here too in the phrase "having paid homage" (*abhivādetvā*), [the same applies].
It should be understood as having the purpose of paying homage and showing respect, not the purpose of causing someone else to speak.
Now, it might be argued: "In the word *vande*, there is no causative suffix (*kāritapaccaya*), whereas in the word *abhivādetvā* there is;
therefore, the meaning of 'causing to speak' is not applicable there, but it is applicable here. That is not so, for even in the simple agentive form *karoti*...

Regarding the term “nipphādeti,” just as in the case of the explanation provided by way of the causal agent (*hetukattā*), one must also state for the word “vande” (I pay homage) an explanation such as “having caused [him] to say, ‘May he be happy and free from illness’.
Furthermore, this word “abhivādetvā” (having saluted) does not end in a causative suffix (*kāritapaccaya*) in the same manner as the word “vande.
Why is that? Because [it is not like] the forms “cinteti, cintayati; manteti, mantayati,” and so forth.
In the case of roots belonging to the *curādi* class that have simple active endings, only forms such as *cintāpeti* and *cintāpayati* are seen as causative active endings;
therefore, if a causative active ending were intended here, one would have to say either *abhivādāpetvā* or *abhivādāpayitvā*.
Since it is not stated thus, it is established that this [ending] does not possess the *kārita* suffix.
To clarify this meaning, we shall cite here a passage from the Vidhura-jātaka together with its commentary:
“How might he pay homage to us, or rather, cause us to be paid homage?
That deed which a man desires to commit against us does not come to pass.”
This, first of all, is the Jātaka-pāḷi. This, however, is the reading of the commentary (Aṭṭhakathā):
“For how indeed would a man who wishes to kill salute him? Or how could he possibly cause himself to be saluted by him? For that deed of his does not hold together.
In this context, in the Pāḷi, *abhivādeyya* is a simple active verb form (*suddhakattupada*) because it expresses the agent; [whereas] *abhivādāpayetha*...

The word *veti* is a term expressing the causal agent (*hetukattupada*), because it denotes that [agent]. Having thus understood the analysis, one should grasp the intended meaning of both the canonical text (*pāḷi*) and the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*):
"How indeed would a man who desires to kill a certain person—that killer—pay homage to that person condemned to death?
Or how could that killer, saying 'Venerate me by means of this one condemned to death,' cause himself to be venerated?"

In this context, however, the phrase "by that one deserving of execution" (*tena vajjhenā*) is construed with the instrumental case, as in expressions such as "kings have criminals devoured even by dogs.

Yet, the meaning should be understood through the accusative case as "that person deserving of execution" (*taṃ vajjhaṃ*), because the causative suffix (*sakārita-paccaya*) belongs to a transitive root (*sakammaka-dhātu*).
If this is so, [one might ask]: "Should not the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā be consulted?"
"Do they not see [the danger], yet they leap across where there is no ford"? Is it their fault? It is not so;

listen to our justification. For in this regard, the masters of the commentaries (aṭṭhakathācariya), having taken the meaning of the verbal root *vad* in the sense of "salutation" and "praise" from the phrase "having saluted" (*abhivādetvā*), [taught] that because [the author] possesses skill regarding conventional usage, he intended for the listeners a subtle and refined meaning.

In order to make [the meaning] clear, the word "abhivādetvā" (having saluted) is explained by taking the sense of the verbal root itself—namely, "speak"—and then applying the concept of the *kārita* suffix to assume the sense of causing to act.
Thus, it is said that the meaning of the word "abhivādana" is expressed according to the agentive cause (*hetukattā*), as in: "having caused [him] to say, 'May you be happy and free from illness';
for when one bows, one effectively causes [the other] to say this in substance. Therefore, there is no fault in their position.
For those venerable ones are worthy of worship; let us simply pay homage to them. This point, too, which is subtle, should be carefully attended to in the mind.
For one who acts in this way, wisdom increases.
Thus ends the forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *da*.
The verbal root *randh* ending in *dhakāra* means "to cook. A cook cooks the meal; he causes it to be cooked (*randheti*, *randhayati*). "Cook the crow for sorrow! The cooker.
Rice is caused to be cooked by the cook. It has been cooked (*randhito*). The act of cooking (*randhanaṃ*). A man causes the cook to cook rice, or [causes] rice to be cooked by the cook.
*Randhāpayati*. *Randhetuṃ*, *randhayituṃ*. *Randhitvā*, *randhayitvā*, *randhiya*, etc.
*Dhū* (to shake). *Dhāveti*, *dhāvayati*. *Gandha* (to indicate and to sprinkle).
Indication (*sūcanaṃ*) means making manifest (*pakāsanaṃ*). Sprinkling (*addanaṃ*) means splashing (*pariplutā*). *Gandheti*, *gandhayati*, *gandho*.
In this context, *gandha* means that which "indicates" (*gandheti*) and "manifests" (*pakāseti*) its own basis; thus it is called *gandha*.
Alternatively, it is called *gandha* because it manifests—just as one might bring forward slander, saying "this is here"—something hidden such as flowers, fruits, and so forth.
Furthermore, the meaning of the word *gandha* may also be explained by way of the two verbal roots *gam* (to go) and *dhar* (to hold): "that which goes and is held is *gandha*."

Thus it is said, and he further states: "It is called *gandha* because it goes (*gacchanto*), or else because it indicates (*sūcanato*). Furthermore, in the phrase "the female hawk with the scent of blue lotuses" (*uppalagandhatheṇī*), the word *gandha* should be understood as signifying cutting (*chedane*).
[The root] *vadha* means restraint (*saṃyame*). One restrains (*vadheti*), one causes to restrain (*vadhayati*).
*Budhi* means to harm. One *bundheti*, or *bundhayati*. One *palibundheti*, or *palibundhayati*. *Palibodho*: the prefix *pari-* has undergone a change and become otherwise [as *pa-*].
In this context, *palibodha* refers to the "hindrance of dwelling" (*āvāsa-palibodha*) and so forth.
Furthermore, *palibodha* refers to the triad of craving (*taṇhā*), conceit (*māna*), and views (*diṭṭhi*).
*Vaddha* is used in the sense of cutting and filling. *Vaddheti*, *vaddhayati*. *Vaddhakī*. *Vaddhakī* means a house-builder.
*Gaddha* is used in the sense of longing. *Gaddheti*, *gaddhayati*. *Gaddho*. *Gaddho* means a vulture. “One who was formerly oppressed by vultures” (*gaddhabādhipubbo*) is the illustration here.
*Sādhu* is used in the sense of praising. *Sādhayati*, *sādhayati*.
*Vaddha* is in the vernacular (*bhāsāyaṃ*). It means *vaddheti* or *vaddhayati*.

*Andha* [is used] in the sense of the removal of vision (*diṭṭhūpasaṃhāre*). "Removal of vision" (*diṭṭhūpasaṃhāro*) means the withdrawal, taking away, or destruction of that which is called "vision" (*diṭṭhi*), namely, the eye-consciousness (*cakkhusaññitāya*).
For the eye is called "vision" (*diṭṭhi*) because one sees by means of it. With reference to this, it is said in the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathāsu*).

It is said: “In the visual orb (*diṭṭhimaṇḍala*), which is the locus for the arising of the bodily configuration of those standing directly in front [of it], and which is situated in the middle of the black circle surrounded by a white circle, together with its equipment. And in the *Ṭīkā* as well:
“In the ‘visual orb’ means in the orb of the vision known as the eye, which is the locus for the arising of the bodily configuration of those standing directly in front.”
It has been stated. In the application of such a view, the root *andha* (blindness) is employed. It means "to blind" (*andheti*) or "it blinds" (*andhayati*).
Their eyes were blinded; thus, he is "blind" (*andha*). He is called "blind" because he blinds (*andheti*), or because his vision is lost due to the impairment of both eyes or one.

Thus, here the root *andha* is used in this sense. However, in the *Kaccāyana*, by the rule stating, "For the roots *khād*, *am*, and *gam*, [the suffixes] *kha*, *ndha*, and *ndha* [are applied]," it is [derived as follows].
The production of form (*rūpa*) is shown by way of making the blind see the element of space (*ākāśadhātu*).
[Regarding the root] *badh* in the sense of binding: it binds a deer; it causes [the deer] to be bound. A deer is bound; "you are bound by the snare of Māra.

In that context, the meaning of "binds" (*bādheti*) should be understood as "ties" (*bandhati*) according to the simple agentive (*suddhakattu*) voice. The same applies here to "causes to be bound" (*bādhayati*).

For instance, in the verse, “You try to bind with a net the wind, you who desire her who does not desire you,” the word *bādhesi* means “you bind” (*bandhasi*) according to the sense of the simple agent (*suddhakattu*).

However, in the *bhūvādigaṇa*, by way of the root *bādh* in the sense of “binding,” the agentive form *bādhati* becomes the agentive term, while *bādheti* and *bādhayati* become the causative agentive terms. [In this context] “bound” (*baddho*) means “is bound” (*bādhiyate*).
He is bound, thus he is "bound" (baddha).
These are forms of the verbal root ending in the letter *dh*. [Now for] the verbal root ending in the letter *n*.

In honoring, in worshiping, in loving, and in investigating—*māneti*, *mānayati*; a mother (*mātā*). To honor, to cause to honor; to measure against, to cause to measure against; to counter-honor, to counter-cause to honor. Honoring, proper honoring, dishonoring, a palace (*vimāna*), the act of measuring against, honored.
Where there is dishonor for the virtuous, or dishonor toward the virtuous, or even the honoring of the base—one should not dwell in such a place.
He investigates; investigation; that which is being investigated as "it will be investigated" is "being investigated.
He is investigating. Therein, "he honors" means he worships. However, in the Aṭṭhakathās, at this point in the phrase "they honor," this meaning is shown:
"They honor means they love with the mind (*manas*). They worship means they worship with the requisite conditions (*paccaya*). This is by way of explaining the meaning of synonyms.

It should be understood as "spoken. For the words *mānana* (honoring) and *pūjana* (worshiping) are indeed synonymous terms due to their being interchangeable expressions. *Vimāneti* means "he despises.

*Vimāna* is so called because it is distinguished by its possession of exceptional splendor; for it is a *vimāna* because it is specifically to be honored (*mānetabba*), that is, a celestial mansion (*byamha*) which serves as the dwelling place of the gods.
*Mana* means a pillar (*thambha*). A pillar is the stiffness of the mind. It honors; it causes one to honor: thus, *māna*.
*Thana* refers to the sound of a thundercloud (*devasadda*). The sound of a thundercloud is the sound of a rain-cloud; it thunders; it causes to thunder.
Just as a rain-cloud, garlanded with lightning and possessing a hundred peaks, thunders.
It fills the high ground and the low, raining down upon the earth, like a rain-cloud that thunders and flashes with lightning.
Regarding "deficiency" (*ūna*) and "decline": it means to be deficient, to cause deficiency; the world is deficient.
The root *dhana* means "to sound. It appears as *dhaneti*, *dhanayati*, and *dhaniyyati*. From it come the words *dhanī* (possessor) and *dhanaṃ* (wealth).

In this context, the word *dhanī* refers to a possessor. As for *dhanaṃ*, it means "one's own property," for that which is thought, "This is mine," and thus considered as something to be cherished (*dhanāyitabba*) or made to resound (*saddāyitabba*), is called *dhana*.
Furthermore, this verbal root also functions in the sense of "desire": "For your mother desires you, O Vidhūra... [etc.]
The Pāḷi passage “hadayaṃ dhaniyyatī” serves as an illustration. In that context, *dhaniyyati* means he yearns for or desires. *Thenena coriyaṃ*:

*thena* is the state of being a thief (*cora*), hence *coriyaṃ*. It is like *sūriyaṃ* and *dakkhiyaṃ*. Regarding *theneti*, it is from the root *thena*; *theno*, *thenetvā*. The verbal root *tan* is used in the senses of extending and heating.
*Tāneti*, *tānayati*. Here, this form includes the vowel increment (*savuddhikā*). In the *tan-ādi* group, in the sense of extension, the non-incremented forms “*tanoti*, *tanute*” are used.
Roots ending in the letter *v*.
The root *pak* (ending in *a*) means "to please" and "to observe": *ñāpeti*, *ñāpayati*, *paññāpeti*, *paññāpayati*, *paññatti*.
And here, in the Niddesa, the word "paññāpeti" (he makes known) is an illustration.

Therein, the meaning is that by means of the constituent parts of the sentence—whose etymologies have been established—it completely satisfies the minds of those to be trained and sharpens their intelligence through a detailed exposition.
The prefix *pa-* is used in the sense of placing down (*nikkhipane*). One "makes known the seat," or "prepares the seat. Thus: "He prepares the seat."

It is also seen in the short vowel form (*paṇṇatti*). It designates the door to the Deathless; this is wisdom (*paññā*). In the causative, as in “a man has a seat designated by another man,” it is a single word.
When those forms *paññāpeti* and *paññāpayati* are forms of the root *ñā* in the sense of “understanding,” they are forms of the causal agent (*hetukattā*).
However, in this context, they are forms of the simple agent (*suddhakattā*) because they express that [agent].
*Lap* means in speech that is distinct. [One] speaks (*lapeti*), causes to speak (*lapayati*). [The nouns are]: *lāpo*, *lapanaṃ*, *ālāpo*, *sallāpo*, *kathāsallāpo*, *lapitaṃ*.
*Byap* means to burn. [One] burns (*jhāpeti*), causes to burn (*jhāpayati*). [The nouns are]: *jhatto*, *jhānaṃ*.
In this context, *jhatto* means one who is afflicted by hunger, burnt by the fire of digestion; as it is said: “May they be burnt, may they be exhausted.”

And the Pāḷi [is as follows]: *Jhāna*. It is called *jhāna* because it burns (*jhāpeti*) the states that are hindrances; this is the causative form. In the causative, however: *jhāpāpeti*, *jhāpāpayati*. *Rūpa* is used in the sense of the action of making manifest (*rūpakriyā*).
The "action of making manifest" means the action of revealing. Thus: *rūpeti*, *rūpayati*; [the noun] *rūpaṃ*. In this context, *rūpaṃ* is so called because it makes manifest (*rūpayati*);

the meaning is that, by undergoing a transformation of color, it reveals the state present in the heart. In the *Divādigaṇa*, however, this root is established in the sense of being broken, etc., as in: "matter (*rūpaṃ*) is that which is broken (*ruppana*)."

*Kappa* [is used] in the sense of "method" (*vidhi*) and "action" (*kriyā*). "He adopts the lion’s posture": *kappeti*, *kappayati*. "The peacock adopted its dwelling": *morovāsam akappayi*. "I revere the Buddha Gotama as he was adopting the lion’s posture. *Kappa* [also occurs] in the sense of "thought" (*vitakka*), "method" (*vidhi*), and "cutting" (*chedana*).
"He adopts," "he causes to adopt": *kappeti*, *kappayati*; "the peacock adopted its dwelling": *morovāsam akappayi*. "It has been adopted": *kappitam assu*.

"He intends," "he causes to intend": *pakappeti*, *pakappayati*. "He resolves," "he causes to resolve": *saṅkappeti*, *saṅkappayati*. [Examples include]: *kappa*, *saṅkappa*, *vikappa*, *kappasamaṇo*, and so forth.

In this context, *kappa* means that which is made allowable by way of delimitation; thus it is *kappa*. *Saṅkappa* means intention (*saṅkappana*). *Vikappa* means various imagining; it is the state of the meaning being manifold. Herein, the extraction of the meanings of the word *kappa* occurs as follows. The word *kappa* has many meanings, such as:
conviction, conventional usage, time, designation, cutting off, alternative, a small part, and all-inclusiveness. For instance, [it is used in the passage]:
"This is to be accepted from Master Gotama, as it is for one who is an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha."
In such contexts as these, the meaning is "firm conviction. In such passages as, "Monks, I allow you to consume fruit according to the five ascetic conventions," it means "convention" (vohāra).
In such passages as, "By which indeed I always abide according to convention," it means "time" (kāla).

In such passages as, "Thus spoke the venerable Kappa," it means "designation" (paññatti). In such passages as, "Adorned, with hair and beard trimmed," it means... [the sense of being "prepared" or "adorned"].

* kappa* means cutting off (*chedana*). In such phrases as “the two-finger-breadth allowance is permitted” (*kappati dvaṅgulakappo*), it means an arrangement (*vikappa*). In such phrases as “there is the possibility of lying down” (*atthi kappo nipajjituṃ*), it means a slight degree (*leso*).
In such phrases as “having illuminated the entire Veḷuvana grove” (*kevalakappaṃ veḷuvanaṃ obhāsetvā*), it means all-aroundness (*samantabhāvo*).

Alternatively, the word *kappa*, both with and without prefixes, signifies thought (*vitakka*), a type (*vidhāna*), a resemblance (*paṭibhāga*), a designation (*paññatti*), time (*kāla*), lifespan (*paramāyu*), conventional usage (*vohāra*), and all-aroundness (*samantabhāva*), as well as conviction (*abhisaddahana*).

The term *kappa* is seen in the contexts of cutting (*chedana*), application (*viniyoga*), discipline (*vinaya*), action (*kriyā*), a different reading (*lesantara*), desire for existence (*taṇhā*), views (*diṭṭhi*), incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*), great eons (*mahākappa*), and so forth.
Thus, it occurs in the sense of "thought" (*vitakka*) in such passages as “the thought of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saṅkappa*), the thought of non-ill-will (*abyāpāda-saṅkappa*)”;

in the sense of "arrangement" (*vidhāna*) in such passages as “one might enter upon an arrangement regarding robes (*cīvare vikappaṃ āpajjeyya*)”, for the meaning here is that one would enter upon an additional arrangement; and in the sense of “resembling the Teacher” (*satthukappena*).
In such passages as "Alas, sir! While consulting with a disciple, we did not realize [this]," it refers to a resemblance;

for in that context, the meaning is "one who resembles the Teacher. In such passages as "Thus said the Venerable Kappa," it refers to a designation. In such passages as "By which indeed I dwell constantly throughout the aeon (kappa)," it refers to time.
[And in: "If he so desired, Ānanda, the Tathāgata could remain for an aeon, or for the remainder of an aeon."
In such passages as "or," it refers to the maximum lifespan; for here, "kappa" is intended in the sense of a life-span.
In such passages as "I allow you, monks, to consume fruit according to the five monastic conventions (samaṇakappa)," it refers to the terminology of the ascetics.

In such passages as "having illuminated the entire Veḷuvana grove," it refers to the state of being all-pervasive. In such passages as "faith is believing, conviction, trust," it refers to the act of believing.

The meaning is "they have faith. In such phrases as "adorned, with hair and beard trimmed," it means cutting. In such phrases as "even so, what is given from here benefits the departed," it means application.
In such phrases as "what is made allowable by one who has made it allowable is joined together," it refers to an act of discipline (*vinaya-kriyā*).
In such phrases as "there is time to lie down; come now, I shall lie down," it means a small portion. "One bound for the states of deprivation..."
In such passages as, "The schismatic of the Saṅgha, destined for hell, remains for an eon; he is tormented in hell for an eon," it refers to an intermediate eon (*antarakappa*). Also:
"They do not construct [concepts], they do not place them before them;
even the teachings are not accepted by them."
In such passages as, "A brahmin is not to be led by virtue;
one who has gone to the further shore does not return, such a one," [the term refers to] craving and views.
For it is said in the Niddesa: "As for 'an eon' (kappa), in brief there are two kinds of eons: the eon of craving (taṇhākappa)..."
“...a conceptualization of views. In such passages as “many eons of world-contraction, many eons of world-evolution,” it refers to *asaṅkhyeyya-kappa* (incalculable eons).
In such passages as “Monks, there are these four incalculables of a *kappa*,” it refers to *mahākappa* (great eons).
Thus it is said: In thought-conception (*vitakka*), in arrangement (*vidhāna*), and likewise in the counterpart (*paṭibhāga*).
In designation, likewise in time, in the supreme life-span, and in cutting off;
in totality, in conventional usage, and also in firm conviction;
in application, in the act of discipline, and also in a minor point.
The word *kappa* occurs in such contexts as *vikappanta-kappesu*, *taṇhā-diṭṭhi-saṅkhaye*, and *kappe*. [The root] *kapi* means "to move.
It signifies "it moves," "it causes to move," or "it goes. These forms are similar to verbal nouns (*rūpa*) that function as agents expressing the sense of motion.
[These] exist. For in the sense of moving, from the verbal root *kampa* in the sense of "shaking" (*kampane*), the form *kampati* is a pure intransitive agentive form.

Forms such as *kampeti* and so forth are transitive causative agentive forms; this is because we see a transitive form of an intransitive root in the passage: "This too is a second arrow; it shakes my heart."
In the sense of patience (*khanti*): *khampeti*, *khampayati*.
In the sense of a heap or elevation (*samussaya*): *samussaya* means height or elevation. *Thūpeti*, *thūpayati*. A stupa (*thūpa*), a small stupa (*thūpikā*).
In the sense of exhaustion (*khaya*): *tapeti*, *tapayati*.
In *upapajjane*: *upeti*, *upayati*.
In *capakakkane*: *capeti*, *capayati*.
In *suppamāne*: *suppeti*, *suppayati*.
*Ḍap* and *ḍip* mean to crush (*saṅghāte*). [One] causes to crush: *ḍāpeti*, *ḍāpayati*. [One] causes to move: *ḍepeti*, *ḍepayati*. *Kap* means to shake (*avakampane*).

[One] causes to shake: *kapeti*, *kapayati*. *Kapaṇo*. *Kapaṇo* means one who is to be pitied (*karuṇāyitabbo*). In other contexts, however, they state the form *kappati*. *Gup*, *kup*, and *dhūp* pertain to speech (*bhāsāyaṃ*).
[One] causes to guard: *gopeti*, *gopayati*. [One] causes to agitate: *kopeti*, *kopayati*. [One] causes to fumigate: *dhūpeti*, *dhūpayati*.
*Kipa* means to weaken. *Kipeti*, *kipayati*.
*Khepa* means to crush; crushing is the act of pulverizing: *khepeti*, *khepayati*.
*Tapa* means to satisfy: *tapeti*, *tapayati*.
*Āp*: in the sense of reaching. *Āpeti*, *āpayati*. *Āpo*. *Tap*: in the sense of burning. *Tapeti*, *tapayati*.
*Tapo*, *tāpo*; *ātāpo*, *santāpo*. In the causative: *tāpeti*, *tāpayati*. Therein, *tapo* is virtue (*sīla*) in the sense of tormenting unwholesome states.
*Opa-thap*: in the sense of placing. *Opeti*, *opayati*. "They do not place them in the storehouse. *Thapeti*, *thapayati*. *Thapito*. Having placed [it], he sets up a cover. *Voṭṭhabbanaṃ*.

And here, the analysis is: “vi ava thapeti, vi ava thapanan. In the former [term], there is the elision of the vowel (*saralopa*), the substitution of *ṭha* for *tha*, and doubling (*dvitta*) due to dissimilarity.

In the latter, however, there is the elision of the vowel, the substitution of *o* for *ava*, the substitution of *ṭha* for *tha*, the substitution of *va* for *ssa*, the doubling of *va*, and the substitution of two *ba*s for the two *va*s. Thus, it becomes *voṭṭhabbanam*.
And this is the name for the determining consciousness (*vyavatthāpaka-citta*). When the letter *n* is elided, another form, "voṭṭhabba," also occurs.
*Māpa* means measuring. One measures a leaf-hut; one causes it to be measured. He who measures out living beings excessively;
the leaf-hut is well-measured. *Yapa* means maintaining. Maintaining is continuity. By that, he maintains himself there; he causes [others] to be maintained. Maintenance.

In this context, *yāpeti* (he causes to live) is a causative form (*kāritapada*) when it functions as the application of the root *yā*. For indeed, the Pāḷi text is seen as "they cause to exert themselves" (*uyyāpenti nāmā*).
These are forms of roots ending in the letter *pa*.
Forms of roots ending in the letter *pha* are rarely encountered (*appasiddhāni*).
The root *bakāra* (with the suffix *-anta*) means "to bind. Binding is a firm connection. It binds (*sambeti*), it causes to bind (*sambayati*). It is a "bond" (*sambala*).
[The root] *sab-* means "in a circle" (*maṇḍale*). A circle (*maṇḍala*) is roundness. Form (*rūpa*) is just like that.
*Kub* means to cover. *Kumbeti*, *kumbayati*.
*Lub* and *dub* mean to injure. Injury (*addana*) is harm. *Lumbeti*, *lumbayati*; *dumbeti*, *dumbayati*.
*Pubb* means a dwelling place (*niketana*). A dwelling place is an abode (*nivāsa*). *Pubbeti*, *pubbayati*.

Do not be conceited (*māna*). Conceit (*māna*) is egoism (*ahaṃkāra*). "Gabba" means he conceals (*gabbayati*). The state of concealing is *gabbanaṃ*; one who has concealed is *gabbito*. In this context, "he conceals" (*gabbati*) means he does not shrink back.
These are forms of verbal roots ending in the letter *b*. [Next is] the verbal root ending in the letter *bh*.

*Bhū* is the attainment [of a state]. *Patti* means causing to attain; it is a root with an object. [Examples: *bhāveti*, *bhāvayati*; *pabhāveti*, *pabhāvayati*. "Become thus" (*itthambhūto*): one who has become vision, one who has become knowledge, one who has become the Dhamma, one who has become Brahmā.
In this context, "he develops" (*bhāveti*) means that a person, following a person who is walking, reaches him.

This same method applies to the remaining verbal forms as well. And here, regarding "he develops" and so forth, if it is from the root *bhū* in the sense of "existence" (*sattāya*), [the meaning is as follows].
There are forms; therein, they are called "forms with a causal agent. Phrases such as "he develops a wholesome state" (*kusalaṃ dhammaṃ bhāveti*) serve here as illustrative examples.
For "develops" (*bhāveti*) means "increases" (*vaḍḍheti*). But here, because it is a form with a pure agent (*suddhakatturūpa*), the meaning is "he attains" (*pāpuṇāti*).

"Thus become" (*itthambhūto*) means having become or reached this particular state. However, in cases such as "become the eye" (*cakkhubhūto*), [the root] *bhū* is used in the sense of existence (*sattāyaṃ*).
Thinking, "May you have faith," we shall explain the meaning based on the commentaries and sub-commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā-ṭīkā*) by way of two pairs of elements,
for the sake of proficiency among those who follow the scriptures (*āgamika*). In this context, "become as the eye" means that just as the eye leads beings toward seeing,
so too [the Buddha] is the leader in the function of seeing by way of being the means for the world to see things as they truly are.
He has become vision (*cakkhubhūta*). Alternatively, he has become like vision, thus he is "become-vision.

Or, because it consists of the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*), he has become—has attained—the eye of wisdom by means of self-existent knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*); thus he is "become-vision. In the sense of making things known, he has become—has attained—knowledge;

or, because he has attained knowledge that is not shared [with others], he is "become-knowledge" (*ñāṇabhūta*), in the sense of having an unerring nature and because of his promulgation of the Dhamma of the scriptures.
He is "Dhamma-become" (dhammabhūta) because he has become Dhamma by having contemplated it with his heart or having uttered it as Dhamma through speech.

Alternatively, he is "Dhamma-become" because he has arisen from the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma), and because he has attained the Dhamma that is not shared by others, having brought the world to its arising.
He is "Brahma-become" (brahmabhūta) in the sense of being supreme. Or else, the Path is called "Brahma," and because he has arisen by means of it, he is Brahma-become.
And because he has brought about that state for the world, and because he has become (bhūta) it through self-born knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*), he is "become Brahmā" (*brahmabhūta*).
Thus the meaning should be understood according to the two roots (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, other illustrative phrases should be understood here: "Dear ones, we are old; [we have seen] the son of the Great King Suddhodana..."
“Whether we should regard him as having become a Buddha or not, you should go forth in his teaching,” and also:
“Then the elder bhikkhus regarded the Venerable Revata as one who had been born together with them.
Furthermore, other phrases such as “having become a human” and “having become a deva” should also be applied here. For instance, in the commentary on the *Saṃsāramocaka-petavatthu*, it says:
The meaning is glossed as: “born among non-humans while being human, or having attained the human state. The root *bhū* means “to tremble” (or “to move”).
This is also transitive. [From it come] *bhāveti* and *bhāvayati*. “Bhikkhus who are mind-developing” (*manobhāvanīyā*).
And here, “he develops” (*bhāveti*) means he feels compassion for someone—whether a son, a brother, or anyone else. “Mind-developing” (*manobhāvanīyā*) means “long-lived.”
“May the venerable ones be free from illness and free from affliction”—those who are to be developed and shown compassion in this way and so forth are called *manobhāvanīya*.
Elsewhere, however, *manobhāvanīya* means "those who increase the mind. For those whom one sees and whose sight causes the mind to expand are called *manobhāvanīya*.
*Labha* [is used] in the sense of speaking. [Examples: *labheti*, *labhayati*.
*Jabhi* [is used] in the sense of causing to perish. [Examples: *jambheti*, *jambhayati*.
*Lābha* [is used] in the sense of sending. [Examples: *lābheti*, *lābhayati*. “If these forms of the root *labha-lābheti* are indeed forms of the causative (*kārita-rūpa*),” [it is said].
*Dabh* means to fear. This root ends in the vowel *ī*; therefore, forms with the nasalized augment (*saniggahītāgama*) do not occur.
*Dabheti*, *dabhayati*. *Dūbha* means to stiffen or paralyze. *Dūbheti*, *dūbhayati*. *Vambha* means to destroy or ruin.
*Vambheti*, *vambhayati*. *Vambhanā* (insulting). "The group-of-six monks insulted a monk."
Forms of verbal roots ending in *bhakāra*.
A verbal root ending in *makāra*:
*ā + cam* in the sense of washing. The root *cam*, preceded by *ā*, is used in the sense of washing. [Examples: *ācameti*, *ācamayati*; *ācamanakumbhī*.
In this context, however, the passage from the *Petavatthu*—“Then that Licchavi, having rinsed his mouth, gave the pairs of cloths to the Elder and stood there”—serves as an illustration.
Therein, “having rinsed his mouth” (*ācamayitvā*) means having washed his hands and feet and then sipped water to cleanse his mouth.
This verbal root, however, stands in the sense of eating (*bhakkhana*), being included in the *bhūvādi* class as “*camati*.”

“Kāma” [occurs] in the sense of desire and longing. One desires (*kāmeti*), one longs for (*kāmayati*). It is desire (*kāmo*), longing (*kanti*), intense longing (*nikanti*), the act of desiring (*kāmanā*), one who is desiring (*kāmayamāno*), one who longs (*kāmento*), and “excellent” (*abhikkantaṃ*). “Of excellent beauty” (*abhikkantavaṇṇā*). And here, “desire” (*kāmo*) means that which desires objects such as forms (*rūpa*);

thus it is called *kāma*. Alternatively, it is called *kāma* because it is desired (*kāmiyati*); this should be understood by way of both defilement-desire (*kilesa-kāma*) and object-desire (*vatthu-kāma*).
For indeed, both the defilement and the object—comprising the three planes of existence known as the round of rebirth (*vaṭṭa*)—are called “desire. Or else, Māra...

The son of a god is called "Kāma. For he is called "Kāma" because, due to his possession of an utterly black nature, he desires to bring even the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha—who have transcended conceptual proliferation (papañca)—under his own sway.
And this has been stated in an ancient poetic composition:
“I pay homage to the one who has been worshipped, who is at peace, and by whom—
having crossed the flood of sensual desire and dwelling in mindfulness— the Buddha, being victorious, has conquered the one who was provoked and defeated.
These, moreover, are his names:
Kāma, Namuci, Kaṇha, Vasavattī, Pajāpati;
Madana, the kinsman of the heedless, Pāpimā, and Damaka;
Kandappa, Ratipati, and Māra, the one whose weapons are flowers.

Others state various other [names], but since those do not conform to the Teaching (*sāsana*), they have not been shown here. In the Commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, only four names are recorded: "Māra," "Namuci," "Kaṇha," and "Pamattabandhu.

Now, regarding the extraction of the meaning (*atthuddhāra*) for the word *abhikkanta*, it is based on the root *kam*—which, in the *bhūvādigaṇa*, is stated under the heading of conventional usage as "to step" (*padavikkhepa*)—and also on the root *kam* as stated here [in the Dhatupāṭha] as "to desire" and "to like" (*icchākantī*).
Let us explain. The term *abhikkanta* is seen in the senses of excellence (*khaya*), beauty (*sundara*), and appreciation (*abhirūpa-abbanumodana*).
In such passages as, "Venerable sir, the night has passed; the first watch has ended; the community of monks has been seated for a long time," it is used in the sense of excellence.
In such passages as, "This person is more excellent and more sublime than these four persons," it is used in the sense of beauty.
In such passages as, “Who is worshipping my feet, shining with success and glory, illuminating all directions with most excellent beauty,” it means “handsome.
In such passages as, “Excellent, venerable sir,” it means “rejoicing. Thus it is.
The word *abhirūpa* is seen in the Dispensation (*sāsana*) in the senses of "beautiful," "excellent," and "praiseworthy.

*Thoma* means praise (*silāghā*). Praise is commendation (*pasaṃsā*). One praises (*thometi*), one causes to praise (*thomayati*). [The derivatives are] *thomita* (praised) and *thomanā* (the act of praising).
*Yama* means in the sense of non-transgression. It restrains; thus, *yama*. Restraint (*yama*).

*Sama* means in the sense of stilling thoughts. It stills; thus, *sama*. Stillness (*samā*). It observes closely; thus, *nisāma*. Close observation (*nisāmana*). It composes; thus, *paṭisāma*. Composing (*paṭisāmana*).

In this context, *samā* refers to a year; it is expressed in the feminine gender as "a *samā*. For in the phrase "one who would sacrifice for a hundred *samā*s," the word *samā* is feminine, though it is here stated as "a *sama*" by way of the accusative case.
These are the names for a year: *saṃvaccharo*, *vaccharo*, *samā*, *hāyano*, *sarado*, *vasso*, and so forth.
*Nisāmeti* means one reflects upon or examines. Here, the canonical text provides an illustration: “Come now, Maddī, examine (*nisāmehi*) what kind of sound there is in the forest.
In that context, *nisāmehi* means “reflect upon” or “examine. *Paṭisāmeti* means...
He deposits his belongings in a guarded place.
*Sama* means looking (*ālocane*). Looking is gazing. He composes, he settles. It is observation.
Here, however, "he observes" means he gazes, he looks upon. For it is said: "Come, Maddi, observe; [be like] the mind regarding form..."
The Pāḷi "dissatī" is seen [in the texts]. For in that context, "nisāmehi" means "look.

However, because of the statement that there is a connection with the excellence of the meanings of verbal roots (dhātu), this word also applies to the sense of hearing due to its connection with a prefix (upasagga).
Indeed, such Pāḷi passages as "Then, O bull among charioteers, look even at the black antelope skin" are found. In that case, "nisāmehi" means "listen."
*Ama* means disease (*roga*). It causes one to be ill; it makes one ill. *Andha*: one with a cleft foot and dark nails.
Here, *andha* refers to one whose eyes are lost. *Andhanakha* refers to one with putrid nails. In both cases, the state of being diseased is indicated.
*Bhāma* means anger. It causes one to be angry; it makes one angry.
*Gom* in the sense of smearing. *Gom* means "he smears" (*gomayati*).

*Sām* in the sense of self-reference and addressing. Self-reference is the application of the *sāman*. Addressing is calling out or summoning. [The forms are] *sāmeti*, *sāmayati*. *Saṅgām* in the sense of battle.
[The forms are] *saṅgāmeti*, *saṅgāmayati*. Two kings fought in battles. Battle. [Roots ending in] *ā* take *gamu*.

In the context of preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*): *āgameti*, *āgamayati*—the form and formless phenomena arise (*samudāgameti*), cause to arise (*samudāgamayati*) depending upon sense-sphere phenomena.
A lay follower (*upāsaka*), not wishing for an obstacle to hearing the Dhamma, says: "Wait, wait! (*āgametha āgametha*).
[The meanings are] arising (*samudāgamana*), coming (*āgamana*). [Participles: *āgamanto*, *āgamayamāno*.
In this context, "approaches" (*āgameti*) means he tolerates slightly; "comes together" (*samudāgameti*) means it proceeds fully.

In the *bhūvādigaṇa* [of verbal roots], the form "causes to go" (*gamayati*) is stated by way of a causal agent; however, here, because they are preceded by prefixes and particles, forms such as "approaches" (*āgameti*) and so forth should be understood as stated by way of a simple agent.
The forms of verbal roots beginning with the letter *m*.
Thus, the forms of verbal roots ending in the *pavagga* (labial) consonants in the *curādigaṇa* are completed.
The verbal root *yu* with the letter *y* as its final sound is used in the sense of loathing: *yāveti*, *yāvayati*. *Yava* (barley).
The root *bya* is used in the sense of destruction: *byayeti*, *byāyayati*. *Abyayībhāva* (an indeclinable compound).
*Byaya* means in the relinquishing of consciousness. It is the same form [as before].
These are the verbal roots ending in *ya*.
Now, the verbal roots ending in *ra*:

*Para* means to go. It is *parati*, *parayati*. Here, the canonical text provides the illustration: “Thus indeed, Ānanda, wholesome virtues gradually lead (*parenti*) to the summit. In that context, “they lead to the summit” means they proceed toward the state of Arahatship.
*Gara* means to rise up. It is *gareti*, *garayati*. *Garū* (venerable).
*Cara* means to move without hesitation. It is *careti*, *carayati*.
*Pūri* means to fill; it is *pūreti* or *pūrayati*.
*Vara* is in the sense of wishing; it is *vareti* or *varayati*. *Varo*, *varaṃ*, and *varanto*—these four I choose as boons (*varānaṃ*). "O Sakka, choose this boon (*varaṃ vare*).
In that context, *varo* means that which is chosen (*variyyate*) or ought to be chosen (*varitabbo*). *Varam* means he chooses (*vareti*); the meaning is one who wishes or desires.
“O Great Sage, Sakyanamuni, free from hindrances and conflicts, liberated, well-seen, liberated—homage to you, the most excellent, the supreme Awakening One.
This is like the word “varaṃ” in the composition of the ancient poet. Thus, he chooses, so he is a chooser (*varanta*). He chooses, so I choose (*varemi*).
“I wish,” I entreat. In the causative, the form is *pavāreti*; the meaning is “he causes to wish. However, this causative does not occur in the sense of prohibition.
*Sara* means “to throw. *Sareti*, *sarayati*. *Saro*. *Saroti* is a sound.
*Sāra* means “weakness. *Sāreti*, *sārayati*. The meaning is “he becomes weak.”
*Kumāra* means play (*kīḷā*). *Kumāra*: he plays (*kumārayati*). *Kumāra*, *kumāraka*; *kumārī*, *kumārikā*. Here, "he plays here and there" is *kumāra*.
That same one, because of being very young, is *kumāraka*. This method applies to the other [feminine] forms as well. *Sūra* and *vīra* mean valor (*vikkanti*).
Valor is the act of advancing (*vikkamana*). *Sūra*: he is brave (*sūrayati*). *Vīra*: he is heroic (*vīrayati*). *Sūra*...
Regarding the word *vīra*: although the etymologies of the words *sūra* and *vīra*— which share the same essential nature (*dhātusabhāva*)—

have not been explicitly shown by those within the Dispensation who are learned in the True Dhamma, they have merely provided explanations of the meaning in various places, such as "a *sūra* is one with distinguished courage" (*visiṭṭha-ura*),
"a *mahāvīra* is one who has great prowess" (*mahā-vikkanta*), and "a *vīra* is one possessed of energy" (*vīriyavā*).
*Pāra-tīra* refers to the successful completion of an action. "Completion of an action" (*kamma-sampatti*) means the finishing or bringing to a conclusion of an action.
One completes (*pāreti*, *pārayati*); one brings to an end (*tīreti*, *tīrayati*). *Pāraṃ*; *tīraṃ*. "I take my stride, yet I cannot reach the further shore; I sweep the ground with speed.
Having brought that task to its conclusion, he departed. Here, terms such as *santīraṇaṃ* (investigation) and *tīraṇa-pariññā* (full understanding through investigation) should also be illustrated.
In this context, *na pāremi* means "I am not able to cut through.
The root *īr* signifies shaking; it takes the forms *īreti* and *īrayati*.
The root *jar* signifies the decline of age; it takes the forms *jareti* and *jarayati*, and the noun *jarā*. However, in the canonical text (*pāḷi*), the reading is *jīrati*.

*Vara* means to ward off. One wards off (*vāreti*, *vārayati*). One wards off thoroughly (*nivāreti*, *nivārayati*); a warder-off (*nivāretā*). One surrounds (*parivāreti*, *parivārayati*); a surrounding (*parivāro*). One invites to partake (*pavāreti*, *pavārayati*); an invitation (*pavāraṇaṃ*). "Invitation" (*pavāraṇa*) refers either to a prohibition or to the giving of what is desired.
*Dhara* means to hold. One holds (*dhāreti*, *dhārayati*). Support (*ādhāro*), supporter (*ādhārako*), the Dhamma, and so forth.
Therein, regarding the "Dhamma" among the many kinds of phenomena, it is the supramundane [Dhamma] that has been produced and realized, which [protects one] from the four states of misery.

It is called *dhamma* because it supports beings so that they do not fall into *saṃsāra*. Alternatively, it is *dhamma* because it is upheld by noble ones such as stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), and not by worldlings (*puthujjana*).
Furthermore, it is *dhamma* because it possesses its own characteristics across the four planes of existence.
Moreover, it is *dhamma* because it is upheld and discerned by the wise through their respective natures—such as hardness and so forth, touching and so forth, and peace and so forth.
Furthermore, the Pāḷi Dhamma of the Tipiṭaka is called "Dhamma" because it upholds (dhāreti) meanings such as one's own welfare and the welfare of others.

Some scholars, however, offer an etymological derivation based on the verbal root *dhū* (to shake), stating that it is "Dhamma" because it shakes, agitates, and destroys evil, unwholesome states (*pāpakā akusalā dhammā*).

This [derivation] is highly appropriate for the Dhamma of the Path (*magga-dhamma*), but it is applicable only in a figurative sense to the Dhammas of the Fruit, Nibbāna, and the Discourses (*pariyatti*).

The word *dhamma* is seen in such senses as the teaching (*pariyatti*), cause (*hetu*), quality (*guṇa*), and the absence of a sentient being or soul (*nissatta-nijjīvatā*). Indeed, it is seen in the sense of the teaching in such passages as, "He masters the *dhamma*:

the Sutta, the Geyya," and so forth. It is seen in the sense of a cause in such passages as, "Knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of *dhamma* (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*)," and so forth.
[And it is said: "For neither *dhamma* nor *adhamma* have equal results..."
In such passages as, "Unrighteousness leads to hell; righteousness brings one to a happy destination," it refers to *guṇa* (quality).

In such passages as, "At that time, there are phenomena (*dhammā*); he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena," it refers to the absence of a sentient being and the absence of a soul (*nissatta-nijjīvatā*).

Alternatively, the word *dhamma* [denotes] intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), wisdom (*paññā*), merit (*puñña*), designation (*paññatti*), transgression (*āpatti*), the teaching (*pariyatti*), the absence of a sentient being and the absence of a soul (*nissatta-nijjīvatā*), modification (*vikāra*), quality (*guṇa*), and condition (*paccaya*).

It is seen in such contexts as "arisen through conditions" (*yapaccayuppanna*). For this [term] is seen in its own nature (*sabhāva*) in passages such as: "Wholesome states, unwholesome states, and indeterminate states.
"He who possesses these four qualities—a man of faith seeking the household life:
truth, the Dhamma, fortitude, and generosity—he indeed does not grieve after passing away."
In such passages as:
“For neither merit nor demerit have equal results;
demerit leads to hell, while merit brings one to a happy destination. In these and similar instances, it refers to wisdom (paññā).

In the phrase "in merits" (*puññe*), it refers to conceptualization (*paññatti*). In phrases such as "states that are designations, states that are linguistic expressions, states that are synonyms," it refers to conceptualization. In phrases such as "offenses entailing defeat (*pārājika*), offenses entailing suspension from the Saṅgha (*saṅghādisesa*)," it refers to transgression (*āpatti*). In phrases such as "here a bhikkhu knows the Dhamma:

the discourses (*sutta*), mixed prose and verse (*geyya*), and expositions (*veyyākaraṇa*)," it refers to the scriptures (*pariyatti*). In the passage "at that time, indeed, there are states (*dhammā*); among states... [it refers to phenomena].

In such passages as “he dwells contemplating phenomena,” it refers to the state of being devoid of a sentient being or a soul (*nissatta-nijjīvatā*). In such passages as “subject to birth, subject to aging, subject to death,” it refers to a transformation (*vikāra*).

In such passages as “of the six qualities of a Buddha,” it refers to a quality (*guṇa*). In such passages as “knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*),” it refers to a condition (*paccaya*).
In such passages as “the fixedness of the element, the stability of phenomena, the regularity of phenomena,” it refers to that which has arisen through conditions (*paccayuppanna*).

Alternatively, the word *dhamma* has been seen used in many senses, such as the scriptures (*pariyatti*), the truths (*sacca*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*paññā*), nature (*pakati*), merit (*puñña*), attainment (*patti*), and the knowable (*ñeyya*).
For instance, it is seen in the sense of the scriptures in passages such as, "Here, a bhikkhu masters the Dhamma.

It is seen in the sense of the truths in passages such as, "One who has seen the Dhamma, one who has attained the Dhamma. And it is seen in the sense of nature in passages such as, "Such was the nature of those Blessed Ones."
In such passages as “Truth, the Dhamma, fortitude, and generosity,” it refers to wisdom (*paññā*). In such passages as “Bhikkhus, among beings subject to birth...,” it refers to nature (*pakati*).
In such passages as “The Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives according to the Dhamma,” it refers to merit (*puñña*).

In such passages as “The four *pārājika* offenses are Dhammas,” it refers to an offense (*āpatti*). In such passages as “Wholesome Dhammas,” it refers to the knowable (*ñeyya*). Such are the spheres in which the word “Dhamma” occurs.

Various [meanings] have been shown by the masters of the *aṭṭhakathās*; however, in various places, meanings such as "logical scope" (*yutti-visaya*) and so forth should also be understood through the word "and so on" (*ādi*).
For instance, the word *dhamma*—“This is not the *dhamma*, O Great King, that you should go alone... —[is used in this sense].
In such passages as, "I too shall go by that same way you are going, O Kṣatriya," it functions as a logical connection (*yutti*).
In such passages as, "Dependent upon the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises," it functions with respect to the object (*visaya*).
In the passage, "The Dhamma of the virtuous does not age," it functions with respect to Nibbāna. Therein, it is the state of being devoid of a sentient being (*nissatta*).
That itself is the state of being soulless (nijjīvatā). And that which is the cause (hetu) is itself the condition (paccaya). Thus:
In the conditions for the scriptures, in the qualities, and in the absence of a sentient being (nissattatā);
In the sense of intrinsic nature, in wisdom, in merit, and in designation;
in offense, in transformation, and in that which arises dependent on conditions;
