*Dāpeti*, *dāpayati*. *Hāpeti*, *hāpayati*. *Nhāpeti*, *nhāpayati*. *Nahāpeti*, *nahāpayati*. These are forms of verbal roots ending in long vowels (*ākāra*).
*Soseti*, *sosayati*. *Sosāpeti*, *sosāpayati*. *Ghosāpeti*, *ghosāpayati*. These are forms of verbal roots ending in short vowels (*akāra*).
The path makes the world known from the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*); it causes it to be known. Here, the meaning of these [forms] is "to cause to go out" (*niggacchāpeti*).

For these are causal agent-forms (*hetukatturūpa*) derived from the verbal root *idh* preceded by the prefix *ni*. Thus, because it functions as a pure agent (*suddhakattubhāva*), the Path itself is known;
it is called "knowledge" (*ñāya*) because it goes forth from saṃsāra.
[The forms] *pāveti*, *pāvayati*, and *vadāpeti* are agent-forms of the verbal root *udh*. For these indeed [are derived] from the verbal root *udh* preceded by the prefix *pa*.

The forms of the causal agent (*hetukattarūpa*) arise by virtue of [the suffix *a*]. For instance, the simple active form (*suddhakattupada*) is seen spoken directly as: "yo ātumānaṃ sayameva pāvā" ("who himself purifies his own self").
[Examples include: *khepeti*, *khepayati*; *kaṅkheti*, *kaṅkhayati*, *kaṅkhāpeti*, *kaṅkhāpayati*; *ācikkhāpeti*, *ācikkhāpayati*. These are the verbal forms ending in the vowel *i*.
*Khiyeti*, *khiyayati*; *milāyeti*, *milāyayati*. These are forms of verbal roots ending in the vowel *e*. *Siyeti*, *siyayati*.
These are forms of verbal roots ending in the vowel *o*. *Pabbatāyāyati*, *puttiyāyati*.
These are forms not based on verbal roots (*adhātunissita*). By this method, the remaining [forms], though not explicitly mentioned, [should be understood].
Forms can indeed be cognized by a wise person who knows the method of the Pāḷi; thus, the detailed exposition is not shown here.

In this way, the application of the *kārita* suffix has been explained in brief. Now, we shall discuss those [forms] where the action is performed by oneself (*sakārita*), having a single object, and so forth.
Verbs are indeed either intransitive, transitive, or even doubly transitive;
when the *kārita* (causative) suffix is applied, they become both transitive and doubly transitive.
He cleans the ground himself, or he causes others to clean the earth.
A person causes an action to be performed; this is to be understood according to its function.
Herein, those with two objects of action arise, and those with three objects of action are illustrated as follows:
"The lord leads the servant to the village, [and] the goat."
“‘A man [goes] with a man to the village,’ or ‘he leads a goat’”— here too,
it is intended that the instrumental case (*karaṇa*) indicates the object of the action (*kammattha*).
Thus, the single object and other cases involving an agent have been explained.
Now we shall explain the group of forms to be inferred: *hoti*, *bhoti*, *sambhoti*—this is a form belonging to the *bhū-ādi* (first) class.
*Sumbhoti*, *parisumbhoti*—this is a form belonging to the *rudh-ādi* (seventh) class. *Nindati*, *vinindati*, *bandhati*—this is a form belonging to the *bhū-ādi* class.
*Chindati*, *bhindati*, *rundhati*—this is a form belonging to the *rudh-ādi* class. *Deti*, *neti*, *vadeti*, *anveti*—this...
*bhūvādi-rūpaṃ* (the form belonging to the *bhū* class): *rundheti*, *paṭirundheti*—this is *rudhādi-rūpaṃ* (the form belonging to the *rudh* class).
*buddheti*, *palibuddheti*—this is *curādi-rūpaṃ* (the form belonging to the *cura* class). *jayati*, *sayati*, *palāyati*, *milāyati*, *gāyati*—this is *bhūvādi-rūpaṃ*.
*hāyati*, *sāyati*, *nhāyati*—this is *divādi-rūpaṃ* (the form belonging to the *div* class). *kathayati*, *cintayati*, *bhājayati*—this is... [the *curādi-rūpaṃ*].
*Curādi-rūpaṃ*: *gabbati*, *pagabbati*—this is *bhūvādi-rūpaṃ*. *Kubbati*, *krubbati*—this is *tanādi-rūpaṃ*. *Hinoti*, *cinoti*—this is *svādi-rūpaṃ*.
*Tanoti*, *sanoti*, *karoti*—this is *tanādi-rūpaṃ*. *Cinteti*, *cintayati*—this is both the form of the agent (*kattu-rūpaṃ*) and the form of the causal agent (*hetu-kattu-rūpaṃ*).
*Kanteti*, *kantayati*—this is only the form of the causal agent (*hetu-kattu-rūpaṃ*).
*Bhakkheti*, *bhakkhayati*, *vādeti*, *vādayati*: these are both the form of the simple agent (*suddhakatturūpa*) and the form of the causal agent (*hetukatturūpa*).
*Miyyati* is both a verb of the agent (*kattupada*) and a verb of the object (*kammapada*). *Bhāveyya* is both the plural and the singular.
*Saṃyamissanti* is both the future tense and the past tense. *Anusāsati* is both a verb (*ākhyāta*) and a noun (*nāmika*). *Gacchaṃ vidhamaṃ*.
They indeed insert both nouns and verbs. Herein, regarding the verb: "they go" is a term for the future; "they dispel" is a term for the past;
"they bury" is a term for the conditional (parikappa). Or rather, it is entirely appropriate to say that this entire phrase is a designation for the future.
Following this method, other words to be inferred should also be applied in their various ways.
These words contain distinctions that are difficult to discern and may cause confusion for those of dull intellect; they are to be understood by attending upon teachers and their predecessors.
Thus, the section on the group of roots beginning with *ūha* has been elucidated.

Now we shall discuss the group beginning with *ekagaṇika*: *dhā* is used in the sense of "holding" (*dhāraṇe*); according to its inclusion in the *bhūvādigaṇa*, this root *ekagaṇika* is transitive (*sakammikā*).
*Dhātu*. The Blessed One bestows (*dadhāti*) and ordains (*vidadhāti*) welfare for the entire world; a man procures (*saṃvidheti*) wealth; he deposits (*nidheti*) a treasure.
These are examples of the agentive case (*suddhakattari*). “*Saṃvidhāpeti*” and “*vidhāpeti*” are examples of the causative agentive case (*hetukattari*).
However, in the objective case (*kamme*) and the impersonal state (*bhāve*), there are forms such as “*anuvidhīyati*. Thus, in the objective case, [there is] “*nidhi*...”
The forms "nāma nidhīyati," "dhīyati," and "dheyya" (as in "dhapiyati") are seen. Therein, regarding the object (*kamma*), it should be applied as follows:
"Action is followed by beings; actions are followed by beings. O action, you are followed by beings;
I am followed by action by beings," and so forth. Regarding the abstract state (*bhāva*), however, [it is used as]: "A being..."
“Suffering conforms [to beings], beings conform to suffering; therefore, you, being a being, conform to suffering”—thus it should be construed.
This method is exceedingly subtle and conforms to the method of the Pāḷi.
In the case of nominal forms, there are such terms as “dhātu” and so forth. Therein, “dhātu” means that which holds (dadhāti) or maintains its own characteristic (salakkhaṇa).

*dhātu*. In the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*), however, it is said: "They are called *dhātus* because they bear their own characteristics (*salakkhaṇa*), because they inflict suffering (*dukkhavidhāna*), and because they contain suffering (*dukkhadhāna*). By "elements" (*dhātū*) is meant the earth-element and so forth.

Therein, "because they bear their own characteristics" means that unlike the "primordial nature" (*pakati*), "self" (*attā*), and so on imagined by the non-Buddhist sectarians (*titthiya*), which do not exist by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), these [elements] are not like that; rather, they possess their own characteristics and intrinsic nature.
They are called *dhātuyo* because they bear (*dhārenti*). "From the burning of suffering" means from the consuming of suffering.

For these elements, being established as causes, burn the manifold sufferings of saṃsāra—such as iron, copper, and so forth—just as the elements of iron, copper, and so on [burn their respective ores].
"From the mere bearing of abundant suffering" means because one lacks mastery over it, or because that suffering is merely borne.
It conforms to these elements which have become its causes; and being so disposed, it is placed and established within them.
Thus they are called "elements" (*dhātu*) because they are the bearers of suffering (*dukkhadhāna*). Furthermore, the meaning of "element" should be understood as "devoid of a soul" (*nijjīvattha*).
For this reason, the Blessed One gave the teaching on the elements in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, a person consists of six elements," for the purpose of uprooting the perception of a soul.

However, regarding that which we have stated there in the section on the meaning of "being" (*bhāva*)— namely, the first-case construction consisting of both singular and plural forms, adorned by the three lineages of teachers, stating "the sentient being (*satta*) conforms to suffering"—
it is as follows: "The horse of Sāma, Paṇḍava, was corrupted by Giridatta."
This should be understood according to its essential meaning by way of these scriptural passages: “Having abandoned his former nature, he conforms to that very [new one]”;
“For your mother Irandhatī will indeed cause the heart of Vidhura to yearn”;
and “Those defiling states will be abandoned. In this context, the horse named Paṇḍava—
The meaning is that it conforms to or imitates the nature of the horse-keeper named Giridatta.
In this context, if an active verb were intended, the Pāli should have been stated as "anuvidadhāti" (it conforms).
If an object were intended, the third-case active noun "paṇḍavena" should have been stated; by not stating it thus—
The term "anuvidhiyyati" is established as a verb expressing a state (bhāvapada).

Because the element (dhātu) is itself form (rūpa), the word "will abandon" (*pahāyissanti*) could be a nominative agentive form; this is seen in the case of an intransitive verb where the nominative agent is used, as in:

"The stallion exerts speed, while the mares lag behind. Therefore, since the author does not say "they will abandon" (*pahāyissanti*) but rather "they will be abandoned" (*pahīyissanti*), it is understood that the suffix *ya* is employed here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).

However, some might say here: “In such instances as ‘That will be abandoned,’ ‘Those defiled states will be abandoned,’ ‘Form will cease to exist,’ and ‘It existed even before the fire was produced,’ the suffix *ya* is prescribed only for the object (*karman*), not for the abstract state (*bhāva*).
For these constructions should be understood according to the agentive-objective relation (*karmakartṛ*): ‘The water drinks itself,’ ‘The mat [is made] by itself.’”

“*Kariyate* is the form [of the verb] in the passive sense (*payoga*); this is not so. For if that were the case, forms such as “*pajahiyissanti*” and others would have to be stated as transitive verbal forms (*sakammaka-dhātu-rūpa*), just like the forms “*pīyate*” and “*kariyate*. However, the fact that the agent remains present in the state of being (*bhāva*) has already been demonstrated in various ways below, and thus it is not mentioned here.
This is the view held by those venerable teachers of the Dispensation (*sāsanika-garū*) who have adopted the opinions found in the grammatical treatises (*saddasattha*).

Since there is a single state (bhāva) for one whose conduct is not insentient, there is only the singular number because of the oneness of that state; and they state that this belongs only to the first person, giving the usage:
“*bhūyate devadattena*” (it is being experienced by Devadatta), and providing the explanation of its meaning as: “Devadatta experiences prosperity.
However, their statement does not accord with the Pāḷi or the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*) and so forth; therefore, the meaning is exactly as previously stated.
It should be maintained by the Venerable Ones.
Regarding *jara* (old age) and *roga* (disease): *jarati*, *jariyyati*. In the sense of the decline of vitality through old age: *jīrati*, *jiyyati*.

These two [roots] belong to the same class by way of being included in the *bhūvādigaṇa*. This is the exposition of their common grammatical forms: "That by which one is satisfied... [and] "that by which..."

"And by which one will grow old," and so forth. Therein, "by which one will grow old" means that by which [element] belonging to the heat-property, when disturbed, this body will grow old—that is, it decays—through the diseases of aging such as those occurring on the first day [of fever], etc.
Alternatively, "by which one grows old" means that by which this body becomes decrepit, reaching a deficiency of the faculties, a loss of strength, gray hair, wrinkles, and so on.
*Mara* [is used] in the sense of "giving up life. This root belongs to the *bhū-vādi* class and is intransitive (*akammaka*). A sentient being dies, perishes.

Although this verbal root appears as if it were transitive (*sakammaka*) because of the statement "mara pāṇacāge" (mara in the sense of giving up life), nevertheless, there are usage examples devoid of an object, such as:
"The son dies," and "Alas, this world has fallen into distress; it is born, it ages, and it dies. Thus, etc.

It should be understood that [the root *mṛ*] is indeed intransitive (*akammaka*) from the perspective of its primary meaning (*dassana*). However, by way of connecting the meaning (*atthayojanā*), it is possible to explain it as transitive (*sakammaka*) by bringing in the sense of "he dies" (*marati*) as "he abandons life" (*pāṇaṃ cajati*).
The terms "he dies" (*marati*) and "he perishes" (*miyati*) are examples of simple agentive forms (*suddhakattupada*).

The terms "a being kills a being" (*satto sattaṃ māreti*), "he causes to kill" (*mārayati*), "he has killed" (*mārāpeti*), and "he causes to have killed" (*mārāpayati*) are examples of causal agentive forms (*hetukattupada*), which are designated as derivative verbal forms (*kāritapada*).

And herein, one who causes a living being (*satta*) that is immortal to meet death is called "the slayer" (*vadhaka*), and is said to "kill," "cause to kill," "cause to cause to kill," and "cause to cause to cause to kill.
"The being is killed by beings" and "is caused to be killed by beings"—these are the words for the action (*kamma-pada*). The word for the state (*bhāva-pada*) is not commonly established.
In this way, elsewhere too, both common establishment and lack of common establishment should be examined.
*Khāda* (to eat) belongs to the *bhūvādigaṇa*; it is a single-rooted (*ekagaṇika*) verbal root that takes an object (*sakammaka*).

*Khādati* and *saṅkhādati* are examples of simple agentive forms (*suddhakattupada*). *Puriso purisena purisaṃ vā pūvaṃ khādeti, khādayati, khādāpeti, khādāpayati*—these are examples of causal agentive forms (*hetukattupada*). And here, [the one] who [causes] one who is not eating or one who is eating...
"One who causes to eat" (*khādāpeti*) is called a "causer of eating" (*khādāpaka*); he eats, he causes [another] to eat, and he causes [another] to cause to eat.
It is eaten, it is thoroughly eaten, it is consumed. These are the passive (kamma) forms. Herein, this passage from the Pāli is:
"In the past, I was eaten by form, just as I am being eaten by form now in the present."
"If I were to delight in future form, I would be devoured by future form, just as I am being devoured now.
The verbal form (*bhāvapada*) is not obtained because this root is transitive. It belongs to the *bhūvādi* class.
This nominal root (*nāmadhātu*) is not well-established, as it belongs to the *ekantarudhādi* class.

In the *divādigaṇa*, *tā* means "to protect. He protects (*tāyati*) the world, he thoroughly protects it (*saṃtāyati*). These are transitive forms with a pure agent (*suddhakattupada*). However, forms with a causal agent (*hetukattupada*), an object (*kammapada*), and an abstract state (*bhāvapada*) are not well-established [for this root].
*Sudh* means "purification. The mind is purified (*sujjhati*), it is thoroughly purified (*visujjhati*). These are intransitive forms with a pure agent (*suddhakattupada*).
*Sodheti*, *sodhayati*, *sodhāpeti*, *sodhāpayati*—these are forms with a causal agent (*hetukatturūpa*). And herein, he who [purifies] what is impure...
One who makes a place clean is a cleaner; he cleanses, and thus he is called "one who cleanses. This same principle applies elsewhere in similar instances.
However, one who does not himself clean an unclean place but employs another, saying, "You clean it," is a causer of cleaning;
he causes to be cleaned, and thus he is called "one who causes to be cleaned. This same principle applies elsewhere in similar instances.
For indeed, this method is not found in such instances as “kāreti,” “kārayati,” “kārāpeti,” and “kārāpayati”;
thus, both the method that is applicable and the method that is not applicable must be examined in all cases. Here are the relevant canonical passages:
“In a border region, having invited the Tathāgata...”
“With joyful minds they clear the path for his coming,” and “Then we cleared the path.
These scriptural passages refer to clearing by one’s own hand.
However, as for the passage, “The Venerable Pilindavaccha had a mountain slope cleared at Rājagaha, desiring to build a cave,” [the question is] “Venerable sir, what...”
The canonical text reads: “The Elder is having it built,” and “Great King, I am having the mountain slope cleared, desiring to have a cave constructed.

These [examples] are stated with reference to having something cleared by others. “Whose path is being cleared?”—this is an object case (kamma-pada); however, the abstract state case (bhāva-pada) is not commonly established.
Following this method, [the formation] should be applied up to the *cur-ādi* class.
In the sense of the doubling of the object (*dvigaṇikatte*), there are *subha* and *sobhe*. Indeed, this person shines (*sobhati*).

In the sense of striking (*pahāre*), one who strikes us like cattle is seen as *sumbhati*; it is also seen as *sumbhoti*. Furthermore, according to the opinion of Kaccāyana, *sumbhoti* is a verbal form;

these are agentive words (*kattupadāni*). He beautifies the city (*nagaraṃ sobheti*, *sobhayati*). A man causes the thief to strike other men (*puriso purise coraṃ sumbheti*, *sumbhayati*, *sumbhāpeti*).

*sumbhāpayati*. These are the words for the agent as cause (*hetukattupadāni*). The words for the object and the state (*kammabhāvapadāni*) should be applied as appropriate according to whether they are applicable or not. These are the forms belonging to the *bhūvādi* and *rudhādi* classes [of roots].

The root *pac* means "to cook. A man cooks rice. A denizen of hell is cooked in hell. Karma is cooked. Rice is cooked. The perfections (*pāramiyo*) ripen; the meaning is that the fruits ripen, i.e., become ripe. But Garu said:
“Having given there a superior connection endowed with knowledge, possessing three roots;
afterwards, among the eight [types of] resultants in the course of existence, two ripen. And:
“The non-determined does not ripen; the determined does not ripen as resultants”—thus is the word *paccati* used in its doubled form.

They maintain that it is transitive (*sakammaka*). But how could this be possible in the word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*) consisting of the Three Baskets (*Tepiṭaka*) together with the commentaries (*Sāṭṭhakatha*)?

For in the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Baskets, only intransitivity (*akammakatta*) is seen, as in: "He cooks in hell for an eon; as long as the evil is not cooked, he was cooked in hell. Here they might say:
"Is it not the case that *paca* in the sense of 'cooking'..."

The root *dhātu* is transitive; therefore, even though the word *paccati* belongs to the *divādi* class, its status as transitive is appropriate. For this very reason, it is stated in such passages as:
"In the eightfold [classification] of the process of cooking (*pāka*), there are two [roots]" and so forth.
Here it is said: Just as for roots occurring in the *rudhādi* class, such as "√*chid* in the sense of cutting in two" and "√*bhid* in the sense of splitting,"...
Although the verbal forms *rukkhaṃ chindati* (he cuts the tree) and *bhittiṃ bhindati* (he breaks the wall) are transitive,
the corresponding nominal forms of those roots belonging to the *divādigaṇa*— namely *udakaṃ chijjati* (the water is cut off) and *ghaṭo bhijjati* (the jar is broken)—
are strictly intransitive, just as the nominal form *bhattaṃ pacati* (he cooks the meal) is of the root *pac* which functions within the *bhūvādigaṇa*.

Even though it possesses an object, for the root *paca* which has entered the *divādigaṇa*, verbal forms such as “he cooks in hell” (*niraye paccati*) and “karmas ripen” (*kammāni vipaccanti*) are indeed intransitive.
Now, they might say: “But surely, sir, just as in the phrase ‘the minds were liberated from the taints’ (*āsavehi cittāni vimucciṃsu*), here [the ablative] ‘from the taints’ (*āsavato*)—”

The forms *cittāni vimucciṃsu* (“the minds were liberated”) and *āsavehi kattubhūtehi cittāni vimucciṃsu* (“the minds were liberated by the defilements acting as agents”) demonstrate that for the root *muc*, belonging to the *divādi* class, the verbal form *vimucciṃsu* can be both intransitive (*akammaka*) and transitive (*sakammaka*).
Likewise, it must also be understood as intransitive in such cases as *niraye paccati* (“he is cooked in hell”) and *kammāni vipaccanti* (“karmas ripen”). [In the phrase] *paccati pākānaṃ*...

"Two [types of consciousness] ripen in the course of existence during the eight [moments], while those with and without volitional effort do not ripen"—thus it must be [understood] as being intransitive, not transitive.

It must be understood as intransitive alone, not as transitive, because the grammatical constructions stated such as "it is cooked (paccati) as cooked things" are not identical to the construction "the minds were liberated from the taints (vimucciṃsu). For in this case:

The word *vimucciṃsu* can function as a verb expressing the agent (*kattuvācaka*) with the suffix *-ya* (the aorist passive) even when it lacks an expressed object (*kammarahita*), and it can also express the object (*kammavācaka*) with the suffix *-ya* when accompanied by an agent (*kattusahita*).
Indeed, because the word *vimucciṃsu* possesses the suffix *-ya* without an expressed object, the instrumental case *āsavehi* functions as the ablative case (*apādānakāraka*).
However, the nominative plural *cittāni* functions as the agentive case (*kattukāraka*).

It occurs thus. Likewise, because the word *vimucciṃsu* expresses the object (*kamma*) accompanied by the agent (*kartr*), the instrumental case *āsavehi* becomes expressive of the agentive factor (*kartṛ-kāraka*).
However, the nominative case *cittāni* is expressive of the objective factor (*karma-kāraka*).
This method does not apply to constructions such as *paccati pākānaṃ*, for in those instances, the nominative case [expresses the agent].
It should be understood that [the suffix] *kattṛ* denotes the agent (*kartṛ*), while the accusative case denotes the object (*karman*).

In the causative (*kārita*), as seen in the examples: "A man causes a man, by means of a man, or for a man, to cook rice" (*puriso purisena purisaṃ vā bhattaṃ pāceti pācayati pācāpeti pācāpayati*), and "The Leader has brought to maturity the infinite requisites for enlightenment" (*anante bodhisambhāre, paripācesi nāyako*), there also occur the forms *paripāceti* and *paripācayati*.
These are the forms for the agentive cause (*hetukattupadāni*). In the sense of the object (*kamma*): "Rice is cooked by Yaññadatta.

The abstract state (*bhāvapada*) is not well-established [here]. These are the forms belonging to the *bhū-ādi* and *div-ādi* classes. In this manner, other forms belonging to the two classes should also be applied.

In the sense of the three classes (*tegaṇikatte*): "He brings forth" (*pasave*). "The cause-and-effect brings forth" (*savati*, *pasavati*). In the sense of hearing (*su savane*): "The faithful one hears the Dhamma" (*saddho dhammaṃ suṇoti*).
He hears. *Su* is used in the sense of harming. A warrior hears his enemy. These are, respectively, agent-nouns derived from the *bhū*-class and the *svādī*-class (the sixth class) of verbal roots.
Likewise, the fruit is produced by the cause; the sound of a loud cry is heard, like the sound of the earth-shaking drum.
By the warrior, the enemy is slain. These are object-nouns. An abstract noun (*bhāvapada*) is not found here.
Because these verbal roots are transitive (*sakammaka*). Following this method, other groups of verbal roots (*dhātu*) should also be examined and applied accordingly.
Herein, this is the exposition of the method:
The roots beginning with *bhū* and *rudh*, as well as those beginning with *svādi* and *divādi*;
Those beginning with *rudh* and *div*, those beginning with *bhū* and *cur*;
those beginning with *gah* and *svādi*, and those beginning with *bhvādi* and *kriyādi*—
let the wise expand [this list] through such various divisions.

Thus, in brief, according to what is appropriate, the terms for the pure agent, the agent with a cause, and the state of the object—namely, those consisting of one, two, or three factors—have been shown as having both uncaused and caused actions, as well as those consisting of one, two, or three actions.
Now the occasion has arrived to speak of the terms for those consisting of one or two caused actions; therefore, we shall explain them. "He [is] at the final action.
The path of Arahantship may exist; the action is brought to completion. These, first of all, are the terms for the pure agent. Herein:
Thinking "let there be conceit," he utterly cuts off conceit. "Kamma is brought to completion" means that kamma is brought to fruition.
For this verb becomes intransitive through the prefix *pari-ava-icc-* (pari-ava-sā), yet its meaning should be understood as transitive, namely "he goes to the end.
He brings to completion by himself what was begun by himself. This is one instance of causing to do (*kārita*).

The phrase "hetukattupadaṃ" (the agentive base with a causal agent). Here, however, because the root *sudh*—which is intransitive (*akammaka*) by virtue of the prefixes *pari-* and *ava*—has acquired the *kārita* suffix, it becomes a single-object (*ekakamma*) verb possessing an agentive function (*sakāritapada*).
One causes others to bring to completion what has been half-finished by oneself.
This is a "causal agentive base" (*dvikārita-hetukattupada*) characterized by two functions. And here, by virtue of the prefixes *pari-* and *ava*...
Because the root *sudhātu*, which is originally intransitive (*akammaka*), possesses two causative suffixes (*kāritapaccaya*), it becomes a transitive (*sakammaka*) verbal form with two objects.
Regarding the term "pariyosāvāpeti": this is formed by adding the two suffixes *ṇāpe* and *ṇāpe* to the root *sudhātu* preceded by the prefixes *pari* and *ava*;
then, changing the vowel *o* of the word *ava* to *u*, adding the augment *ya* after that, and dropping the consonant *ṇa* as an *anubandha* in the first suffix.
It should be understood that the letter *va* arises from the letter *pa*, and in two instances, it is produced by eliding the preceding vowel.
Now, in order to clarify their distinct meanings, we shall explain those canonical passages together in the manner of a direct exposition:
"If one completes by oneself what was begun by oneself, there is an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*). If one has [begun] by oneself..."
Regarding the phrase, "If he causes it to be completed, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*," the word "monks" (*bhikkhū*) must be supplied here as the causal agent.
In the expression "by himself [having left it] unfinished" (*attanā vippakataṃ*), the word "by himself" (*attanā*) is an instrumental case expressing the agent of the action of leaving unfinished.

"Unfinished" (*vippakataṃ*) is an accusative case expressing the object of that action. Furthermore, in the expression "he causes it to be completed by himself" (*attanā pariyosāpeti*), [the same principle applies].
*Attanā* is either an indeclinable word (*abyayapada*) that has the same meaning as the indeclinable word *sayaṃ*, being a nominal form (*vibhatyantapatirūpaka*),
or it is an indeclinable word ending in the third case (*tatiyāvibhatyanta*) similar to the word *sayaṃ*. For instance,

the statement "attanā pariyosāpeti" (he brings to completion by himself) has the meaning "sayaṃ pariyosāpeti" (he brings to completion himself), as seen in such expressions as "attanā ca pāṇātipātī" (and one who takes life by oneself).

...as it were. Regarding the phrase "he causes others to bring it to completion": here, "by others" (*parehi*) should be understood as an instrumental expression denoting the agent (*kammakāraka*), just like the word "by dogs" (*sunakhehi*) in the expression "they cause even dogs to eat [it].
For just as in the sentence "The kings cause the thief to be eaten by dogs," the meaning is expressed through the accusative case (*upayoga*), so too [here] "the monk himself..."
The meaning occurs by way of the instrumental case: “He brings to completion what has been left unfinished by other people.
Thus, in this Blessed One’s teaching, which is variegated with wonderful and marvelous methods, it should be understood as essential that there exists even a single word possessing two functions.
This method is subtle; therefore, the Venerable Ones should apply their minds thoroughly, showing reverence for the Dispensation.

It should be done. For that purpose for which we have composed this treatise, it should be understood that this is not our own opinion, but rather the opinion of the ancient masters themselves, as it was received from them.

Now the occasion has arrived to discuss the roots (*dhātu*) that take two objects (*dvikammika*) but do not require an agent (*akārita*); therefore, let us explain them, and they should be understood according to their verbal roots along with their determinations (*savinicchaya*). For example:
*Duh*, *kṛ*, *vah*, *i*, *pṛcch*, *yāc*, *bhikṣ*, and *nibrū* [are roots that take two objects];
likewise *bhaṇ*, *vad*, *vac*, *bhāṣ*, *sās*, *diś*, *nāth*, and *dhātṛ*.
The wise have stated that those beginning with *rudh*, *ji*, *ci*, and *prabhū* are also roots that take two objects.
The ancient masters have declared that even when separated from their functions and from the conditional suffixes (*paccaya*),
[the case endings] beginning with the ablative (*apādāna*) are,
according to the previous rule, called "causes" (*nimitta*) for the accusative case.
These roots beginning with *duh* (to milk) can also take three objects;
when a causative suffix (*kārita-paccaya*) is applied, so say the teachers.
Here are examples: "The cowherd milks the cows' milk. "The cowherd's son milks the cow for milk."
In this context, *payo* is the accusative case (*upayogavacana*), just as the word "glory" (*yaso*) is in the phrase, "Having obtained glory, one should not become intoxicated.

For the *manogaṇika* (the class of nouns denoting mental objects), such an accusative form occurs, as well as others. [Examples: "The master has the cowherd have the cow milked for milk" (*issaro gopālaṃ gavaṃ payo duhāpeti*);

"By the cowherd, the cows were milked for milk" (*gopālena gāvo khīraṃ duhitā*); and "From the cows, he milks milk" (*gohi payo duhati*). In these cases, because they fall within the scope of the ablative (*apādāna*), [the forms are established].

There is no state of having two objects [in this case]. However, in the passage, “He milks the cow from its horn where he finds no milk,” although the horn is within the scope of the ablative (*apādāna*), it is nevertheless mentioned separately as a part of the cow;
therefore, it should be understood that the state of having two objects—“milking the milk of the cow”—is obtained. This is an application of the root *duh*.
In the usage of *karoti*: "He makes wood into charcoal; he makes gold into a bracelet; if what you say is true, I will make you my slave.
And here, "he makes into charcoal" is stated by way of relinquishing the previous state. For wood is the cause for the state of being charcoal;
once it has been made into charcoal, the wooden nature of the wood, which was the cause, disappears.
"He makes a bracelet" is said with reference to the cause not being relinquished. For gold is the cause for the state of being a bracelet;
even when the bracelet is made, the golden nature of the gold—which serves as the agent—does not disappear, but rather it comes about through the arising of a specific distinction.
"I am making him a donor," however, is said with reference to the granting of a different status, such as "viceroy" or "great king."
It is as in the phrase "I do. In that context, one should also observe the three-object construction (tikammika-payoga), such as: "The Lord causes a man to make a man, or wood to become charcoal;
likewise, he causes gold to be made into a bracelet. Similarly, there is the two-object construction (dvikammika-payoga), such as:
"Brahmadatta exercises sovereignty," and "While Brahmadatta is exercising sovereignty."
Here some might say: "But, sir, is it not the case that here only one single action (*kamma*) is seen? By what means does this application become an application involving two actions?
Although only one is seen, nevertheless, it must be understood that in terms of meaning (*atthato*), two actions are indeed seen.
For instance, in the expression "Brahmadatta rules the kingdom," Brahmadatta [is seen] by the great multitude [to exercise] his own status as king.
The meaning is "he causes to be done. However, when this meaning is accepted, even in such phrases as "O Blessed One, exercise sovereignty; what will you do in the forest? the sense established is:
"Have us cause your own royal status to be performed; have yourself consecrated in the kingdom;
we desire to consecrate you in the kingdom."
Regarding the phrase "while Brahmadatta was exercising kingship," here too the meaning is that Brahmadatta was having his own status as king exercised by the great multitude.
For in the grammatical tradition (*sāsana*), when the object of the causative construction is used, the instrumental case indicates precisely the sense of the accusative;

therefore, we say that in actual meaning, only two types of objects are seen. This point is explained in the *Abhidhammaṭīkā* in the analysis of the etymological meanings of the eye-faculty (*cakkhundriya*) and so forth.
It should be explained as follows. For this is stated in the Abhidhamma-ṭīkā: "It exercises lordship (indatta) over the eye-door;
thus, in the state of being the eye-door, it causes those [mental factors] associated with that door to exercise their own lordship and supreme sovereignty—this is the meaning.
For it makes itself conform to them in the apprehension of visible forms, and they conform to it. However, if the verbal root *kara*...

[Objection: Since [the root *kṛ*] has two objects, this being the case, in expressions such as “Brahmadatta causes the kingdom to be ruled,” because the suffix *-ap-* (indicating the agent) is obtained, must the words beginning with “causes to rule” (*kāreti*) necessarily be three-object [roots]?
[Reply: No, because there is no such restriction, and because such usage does not enter the path of common linguistic practice.
Wood is turned into charcoal by a man; gold is turned into a bracelet by a smith; a female slave is made a wife by her master.

In this way, the application of two objects (dvikamma) should be understood here. For in the expression "he makes a bracelet from gold" (*suvaṇṇena kaṭakaṃ karoti*), it should be seen that the status of having two objects is not obtained because the object of the act (*karaṇa*) functions there in the sense of a qualification (*visesanattha*). This...
This method should be applied elsewhere as well, after investigation, according to what is possible. This is the application for the verb *karoti*:
"The king’s men carry the chariot to the village. The application for *vahati* and others: "This king asks me by name.
"We ask Gotama about the person who is perishing. "The Venerable Upāli [was asked] by the Venerable Mahākassapa."
Questioned about the Vinaya: Devadatta asks the king for a blanket. They asked me for horses. He asks for wealth, dear father.
The brahmin asks for a nāga and a jewel. The nāga, having been asked for a jewel by the brahmin, [is like] the Blessed One, who, having been asked by Brahmā, gives a teaching on the Dhamma.
The ascetic begs for food at a family’s house. He leads the goat to the village. The goat [goes to] the village.
[The Campeyya elephant] was led away. Once released, the Campeyya elephant spoke this to the king.
Here, "the king" is stated as the primary object (*kamma*); "this" is stated by way of its quality. Likewise, "the king" is stated as the unexpressed object (*akathita-kamma*);
"this" is the expressed object (*kathita-kamma*). This same method should be applied elsewhere as well, having examined each case appropriately.
In the same way, in such cases as "Speak, Blessed One," because the object falls within the scope of the recipient (*sampadāna*), the status of having two objects (*dvikammaka*) is not obtained.

Examples include: *Bhikkhu mahārājānaṃ dhammaṃ bhaṇati.* (The monk speaks the Dhamma to the great king. *Yaṃ maṃ bhaṇasi, sārathi.* (That which you say to me, charioteer. *Yaṃ maṃ vadati.* (That which he says to me. *Bhagavantaṃ etadavoca.* (He said this to the Blessed One.
*Pitā puttaṃ bhāsati.* (The father speaks to the son. *Yaṃ maṃ tvaṃ anusāsasi.* (That which you instruct me. *Sakyā kho pana, Ambaṭṭha, rājānaṃ...* (But the Sakyans, Ambaṭṭha, [speak] to the king...)
They burn Okkāka, their grandfather. The Blessed One exhorts the bhikkhus to various beneficial practices.
A cowherd keeps the cattle within the pen. A rogue wins wealth from a group of rogues.
And here, the *Puṇṇaka-jātaka* commentary serves as the illustration for the phrase: "Which unsurpassed, supreme jewel shall we win? Therein, this is the meaning: "O lords of men, which king..."
“...the unsurpassed, supreme jewel of the Conqueror. Just as a mason builds up a wall of bricks, other [examples] should also be applied accordingly.

Here, some might ask: “In such formulations as ‘He circumambulates the Gandhakuṭī,’ ‘I go for refuge to the Buddha,’ and ‘May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka),’ is the state of having two objects (dvikammakabhāva) applicable? Regarding this:

It is said: in the phrase “he circumambulates the fragrant chamber,” [the accusative case] is not applicable because it is understood by way of the relationship between the quality and the possessor of the quality (*guṇa-guṇin*).

In the phrase “I go for refuge to the Buddha,” it is also not applicable because it is stated with the elision of the particle *iti*, as in “I go [to him], [thinking] ‘this is the refuge. For thus, *buddham* is the accusative case, while *saraṇam* is the nominative case.
With the intention expressed by the words, “The Buddha is my refuge and ultimate resort, the protector from suffering and the provider of welfare,” the meaning is:

“I honor, I serve, I awaken. However, regarding the phrase, “May the venerable Gotama accept me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*),” one must state that a double object is obtained here, because the sense arises as:
“From this time forward, may he accept me as a lay follower.”
“Moreover, Ambaṭṭha, they can indeed regard King Okkāka as their grandfather”—this is because of the common application of the verbal root *dhā* (to hold/bear).
However, from the perspective of the intended meaning, it should be understood that the sense “May he hold me [thinking], ‘He is my lay follower (*upāsaka*)’” is possible.
Thus have the forms of verbal roots governing two objects (*dvikammika-dhātu-rūpa*), when not explicitly prescribed, been explained.
Thus, we have explained the relics and their characteristics from the beginning for the sake of the Blessed One’s teaching, according to our ability and strength,
by joining them with various words, various meanings, and various methods appropriate thereto; yet even while explaining them in this way,
it is not possible for us to provide a complete definition of their true nature or a complete definition of their meaning.

To speak [of them] fully: who indeed, other than those great ones whose taints are destroyed, who are endowed with the attainment of the scriptures and realization, and who have attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), would be able to speak of both of these in their entirety?

Even though roots (dhātu) possess an abundance of meanings, they may belong to this or that category; for roots must be understood according to their specific application, as they are indeed many-meaninged.
Various [teachers] wander about, upholding the same meanings in the excellent teachings of the Protector;
therefore, when together in various circumstances, they indeed uphold those same meanings.
Yet, regarding the ultimate meaning of those verbal roots, only the wise ones whose taints are exhausted [possess it].
"Who speaks entirely [correctly], having avoided [errors] through the wisdom of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*)?

Thus ends the *Saddanīti* treatise, composed for the sake of the proficiency of the wise in the modes of expression within the three baskets (*piṭaka*) together with their commentaries (*sāṭṭhakatha*), consisting of nine divisions.
The nineteenth chapter, titled "The Decision on All Groups," is concluded.
Along with the analysis of form, the analysis of the elements is finished.
The *Dhātumāla* (Garland of Elements) is completed.
